Section  80-IC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deductions -  Special provisions in respect of certain undertakings or enterprises in certain special category States (Computation of deduction) - Assessment years 2012-13 and 2013-14 - Assessee-company had claimed deduction under section 80 - IC in respect of profits of its Baddi unit including income arising from sale of scrap - Assessing Officer questioned allowability of deduction on such income and called upon assessee to justify its inclusion in eligible profits for purpose of deduction under section 80 - IC - It was noted that assessee had duly explained that scrap was a by-product arising directly from manufacturing process undertaken at Baddi unit, and thus formed an integral part of its business receipts - Assessee had consistently included such scrap income as part of eligible profits for deduction under section 80 - IC in preceding years - Whether therefore, scrap income was derived from industrial undertaking and eligible for deduction under section 80 - IC - Held, yes [Para 9.4] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee had claimed deduction under section 80-IC in respect of the profits of its Baddi Unit, including income arising from sale of scrap.

■

The Assessing Officer held that the income from scrap was merely incidental or ancillary in nature, not forming a core part of the manufacturing operation. He, thus, disallowed the claim of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), directed deletion of the disallowance, holding that the scrap income was derived from the industrial undertaking and eligible for deduction under section 80-IC.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The issue in dispute pertains to the allowability of deduction under section 80-IC on income arising from sale of scrap generated in the eligible unit at Baddi. The Assessing Officer had disallowed the claim on the ground that such income is not "derived from" the manufacturing activity, holding that the same is incidental and does not have a direct nexus with the core operations of the industrial undertaking. It is noted that the assessee had duly explained that the scrap was a by-product arising directly from the manufacturing process undertaken at the Baddi unit, and thus forms an integral part of its business receipts. The assessee had consistently included such scrap income as part of the eligible profits for deduction under section 80-IC in preceding years. The Commissioner (Appeals) has rightly appreciated the factual and legal matrix of the case and referred to the decisions in the assessee's own case for earlier assessment years. It is seen that the Co-ordinate Bench has already upheld the Commissioner (Appeals) view in assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12, thereby allowing similar deduction. [Para 9.4]

■

In view of the above binding precedent in assessee's own case and applying the principle of consistency, there is no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in directing deletion of the disallowance in respect of scrap income. Accordingly, the grounds raised by the revenue on this issue is dismissed. [Para 9.5]

HEADNOTE: Section 147 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income escaping assessment - Non-disclosure of primary facts - Assessment years 1979-80 to 1984-85 - Petitioner’s claim for deduction under section 80HH was allowed for some years by Assessing Officer, for other years by Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal - Subsequently, Assessing Officer issued notices for reassessment alleging that entire manufacturing activity was not carried on in backward area and petitioner had failed to disclose fully and truly all material facts for making assessment - Petitioner contended that all facts had been disclosed before assessment was made and Assessing Officer was not able to specify exact information which was required and which was not disclosed - Whether, therefore, revenue could claim that there was no true and full disclosure of facts - Held, no

FACT: The petitioner-company, which was carrying on the business of manufacturing and sale of beedies, set up a factory in a backward area. Some of the raw beedies were entrusted to contractors for being manufactured and with that along with raw beedies manufactured by the assessee itself in the industrial undertaking, the further processes of heating, ringing, belleying, wrapping and packing were carried on with the consequence that the finished product was made in the factory which was in the backward area. The petitioner claimed deduction under section 80HH. Deduction was allowed for some years by the ITO, for some years by the Commissioner (Appeals) and for some years by the Tribunal. On the ground that a part of the manufacturing activity was carried on outside the backward area, notices were issued alleging that the petitioner had failed to disclose fully and truly all the material facts for making the assessment. Petitioner questioned the issue of notices contending that they lacked jurisdiction inasmuch as the facts had been disclosed before the assessments were made.

On petition :

HELD: Sub-section (2) of section 80HH lays down certain conditions, one of which is that the industrial undertaking should manufacture or produce articles in any backward area and another condition is that it should employ 10 or more workers in the manufacturing process carried on with the aid of power. It was not the case of the revenue that any of these conditions were not fulfilled. Their only case was that the entire manufacturing activity from beginning to end was not carried on in the backward area and an initial part of it had been entrusted to the contractors who carried on that part of the activity outside the backward area. The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5]

was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25] Thus, there was no nexus between the brass scrap obtained on dismantling of the guns and the main activity of the assessee of steel rerolling. Gun was not an essential raw material of appellants’ industrial unit, in any case, brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling. Thus, separation of brass could not be said to be in the process of manufacture or a product or a by-product of the activity of the assessee’s industrial undertaking. There was no direct nexus between the separation of the brass from the guns and the main activity. Thus, considering the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, it could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking. Thus, deductions on profits and gains under sections 80HH and 80-I were not admissible and had been rightly disallowed by the Tribunal. [Para 28]

Resultantly, the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 29]

HEADNOTE: Section 80-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from Industrial undertakings, etc., after certain dates/infrastructure undertakings (Manufacture) - Assessment year 1997-98 - Assessee, a private limited company, was repairing and manufacturing transformers - It claimed 100 per cent deduction in respect of transformer oil, scrap and labour charges for sale of scrap - Transformer oil had been purchased by assessee from market and centrifuging i.e., processing, had been done by centrifugal machine in order to make it usable in transformer - In substance, no new articles or things had emerged from said processing, but only some special processing or treatment had been given to transformer oil through a particular method and, thus, it was a sort of processing only and could not be termed as manufacture of centrifuged transformer oil - Whether since there was no change in substance and no new article had come out, assessee was not entitled deduction under section 80-IA - Held, yes [Paras 26 and 27] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where transformer oil had been purchased by assessee from market and centrifuging i.e., processing had been done by centrifugal machine in order to make it usable in transformer and no articles or things had emerged from said processing, assessee was not entitled to benefits of 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA

FACT: The assessee, a private limited company, was repairing and manufacturing transformers. It claimed deduction under section 80-IA in respect of transformer oil, scrap and labour charges for sale of scrap.

The Assessing Officer noticed that company had been engaged in repairing of old transformer and it did not manufacture new transformer.

The assessee submitted that company had been manufacturing aluminium HT/LT Leg Coils which were used in old burnt transformers and on the basis of the said manufacturing, the assessee had claimed 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA(2)(iv)(c).

The Assessing Officer had held that assessee had not manufactured or produced transformer oil and scrap, rather had purchased the T/oil from market and only centrifuging i.e., processing had been done, but no new article or thing had been produced/manufactured. Finally, the Assessing Officer had turned down the plea of the assessee of 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled for the benefits under section 80-IA.

On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed deduction under section 80-IA on transformer oil, which was not sold, but was a part of assembly of transformer, and disallowed deduction under section 80-IA on scrap and the labour charges for the sale of scrap.

On further appeal:

HELD: As per the provision of section 80-IA, the same would be applicable to a company, which manufacture or produce any article or things. In the present case, the assessee company perform work in the nature of business for repairing and manufacturing of transformer. It has also been contended by the assessee that the company has been manufacturing aluminium HT/LT Leg Coils, which were used in old burnt transformers and in this regard, it had also submitted in detail before the assessing authority. The company did not manufacture or produce transformer oil and scrap, rather it has purchased the T/Oil from the market and only centrifuging has been done and no new article or things has been produced/manufactured, only processing has been done. In the processing scrap, it had obtained from old/burnt Transformers Coils, which were made of aluminium wires of different amperes. It also appeared from the record that the scrap has not been manufactured/produced. Certain more small parts have been purchased and have been used in manufacture of new HT/LT Leg Coils. It also appears that the assessee has purchased the transformer oil from the market and after centrifuging the transformer oil by centrifugal machine, the centrifuged transformer oil has been made useful in old/burnt transformer. It is a sort of processing only and cannot be termed as manufacture of centrifuged transformer oil. [Para 19]

It is apparent that the assessee did indulge in processing activities, but no manufacture or production of new articles or things is involved in this processing. [Para 20]

An industrial undertaking which is engaged in manufacture and production of an article or thing would be eligible for the deduction under section 32AB; it would be eligible for the deduction under section 80HH if situated in backward area; it would, if established after 31-3-1976, be eligible for the deduction allowed under section 80J. In the instant case, all the ingredients were undisputedly satisfied. [Para 6.4]

PRODUCTION : MEANING OF : In the instant case, the relief was claimed on the ground that the establish-ment of the assessee was engaged in the production of logs. Trees cannot be sold in the open market with all their branches and leaves even if felled, as a whole. The branches are slopped, the trunk is cut into pieces and then converted into logs which primarily involves effort or exercise or enterprising or undertaking of some process. The conversion of trunk into logs is the first step towards extraction of timber for which human efforts are necessary. In order to make it a saleable commercial article, the logs are seasoned. The commercial activity that the assessee undertook was the sale of logs, the main purpose of the assessee’s business. The enterprise undertaken in the industrial undertaking of the assessee was to produce commercially saleable logs out of the felled trees. Thus, the production of logs, though may not involve manufacture, is yet a production within the meaning of sections 32AB, 80HH and 80J respectively. [Para 6.5]

The conversion of logs would not amount to manufacture since no article other than wood is brought out and no change in the characteristics is effected. Conversion of tree into logs would not change the character, which remains wood as before. Admittedly, in the instant case, the assessee did not claim conversion of felled tree to log as manufacture. An establishment, which is engaged in production of something is an industrial undertaking eligible under the provisions of sections 32A, 80HH and 80J. [Para 6.8]

The de-embarking of the trunk of the tree and cutting the same into pieces and seasoning the same in order to convert the tree trunk into logs as commercially saleable commodity requires a human effort to undertake such process and the end-product is something different from the tree though its characteristics remains the same, viz., wood yet definitely it is an article or thing which is commercially saleable and as such the process undertaken for conversion of trees into logs as commercially saleable commodity would amount to production within the meaning of the provisions of the said section . [Para 6.9]

The word ‘production’ has been used in a very wide sense within the scope of section 32A to mean to bring out a commercially new product. [Para 6.13]

CONCLUSION :

Thus, the de-embarking and seasoning the tree trunks and converting the same into logs would amount to production of a new commercial article or thing within the meaning of sections 32AB, 80HH and 80J. The assessee was entitled to the benefit of deductions thereunder for the relevant assessment years. [Para 7]

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Whether ship breaking activity results in production of a distinct and different article and, therefore, assessee doing said activity would be entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in the business of ship breaking, claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim. On the revenue's appeal, the High Court held that when a ship breaking activity is undertaken, the articles, which emerge from the activity of ship breaking, continue to be the part of the ship and such parts do not constitute new goods and, consequently, the assessee was not entitled to claim the benefit under sections 80HH and 80-I as there was neither production nor manufacture of new goods by the process of ship breaking.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: The important test, which distinguishes the word 'production' from 'manufacture', is that the word 'production' is wider than the word 'manufacture'. Further, the Legislature has used the words 'manufacture' or 'production'. Therefore, the word 'production' cannot derive its colour from the word 'manufacture'. Further, even according to the dictionary meaning of word 'production', the word 'produce' is defined as something which is brought forth or yielded either naturally or as a result of effort and work. It is important to note that the word 'new' is not used in the definition of the word 'produce'. [Para 8]

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in allowing the deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to the assessee holding that the ship breaking activity gave rise to the production of a distinct and different article. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of certain incomes of hotels or industries in backward areas - Assessee-company was engaged in business of centrifuging rubber latex and had employed more than ten persons - On 8-7-1983 Government of India issued a Notification No. 189/83 under rule 8 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, granting exemption to preserved latex and latex concentrate considering these to be items manufactured or produced - Whether decision of Government taken under the Central Excise Act had to be applied with equal force under the present Act - Held, yes - Whether assessee would be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

Section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertakings, ships or hotels - Whether on basis of facts under head ‘Deductions - In respect of certain incomes of hotels or industries in backward areas’, assessee would be entitled to deduction under section 80J - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of centrifug- ing rubber latex. It had employed more than then ten persons

in its concern. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under sections 80J and 80HH. The ITO rejected the assessee’s claim on the ground that it was not an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced any article or thing. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the ITO.

On second appeal:

HELD: By virtue of Notification No. 189/83-Central Excises, dated 8-7-1983, the Government of India granted exemption to preserved latex, latex concentrate, etc., because it considered the said goods as goods produced or manufactured in India. If preserved latex was not to be considered as goods produced or manufactured in India there would have been no necessity of exempting the same by issuing the aforesaid notification under rule 8 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. From this it had to be fairly inferred that the Government of India itself considered that preserved latex was an item manufactured or produced. The Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 and the Act in question are both Central enactments. The words used in the relevant sections are ‘produced or manufactured’. So, the decision of the Government taken under the Central Excise Act had to be applied with equal force under the Act also. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to deduction under sections 80J and 80HH.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Whether assessee engaged in business of rearing and development of chicks into broilers, could be said to be ‘manufacturing’ a product - Held, no

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the business of rearing of chicks to broilers, a saleable product, by applying scientific process and technology, established an industrial unit in the backward area and claimed deduction under section 80HH and section 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the claim. On the revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal, however, set aside the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) and affirmed that of the Assessing Officer.

On reference :

HELD: The process involved in the development of chicks into broilers is nothing but basically the chicks remains chicks only. There is no substantial change so as to acquire new commercial identity. Chicks are smaller ones and when they are reared for sometime, they develop suitably for table purposes. Therefore, there is no change of substance. Manufacture implies a change, but every change is not manufacture and yet every change in an article is the result of treatment, labour and manipulation and does not necessarily mean that on account of certain treatment and manipulation, new identity has come to be acquired.

In the instant case, chicks were only reared up for a few days and they were developed, thereafter they became broilers. Therefore, even after rearing, they remained chicks only. Hence, the view taken by the Tribunal that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I as an industrial undertaking was correct.

HEADNOTE: SECTION 80HH OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-DEDUCTIONS-PROFITS 
AND GAINS FROM NEWLY ESTABLISHED INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS IN 
BACKWARD AREAS-WHETHER INTEREST ON FIXED DEPOSITS MADE OUT OF ACCUMULATED PROFITS AND RESERVES IS INCOME DERIVED FROM INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING-HELD, YES-WHETHER DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH IS ALLOWABLE ON SUCH INTEREST INCOME-HELD, YES

FACT: The assessee-company had not paid any dividend since its inception, but had invested its accumulated profits and reserves in fixed deposits, the interest income from which was assessed under the head ‘Income from other sources’. The assessee’s claim that deduction under section 80HH should be allowed on this interest income also, was rejected by the ITO, whose order was upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In second appeal, the assessee contended that the fixed deposits represented accumulated funds not required immediately, but intended to be spent on various projects the company planned to undertake, some of which had in fact been undertaken and as such constituted funds invested in its business undertaking and, therefore, the interest earned thereon should be regarded as income derived from the assessee’s business undertaking. The revenue contended that the nexus of the interest income was the invest- ment in fixed deposits and not the manufacture or production of goods dealt in by the assessee and, therefore, it could not be equated to income derived from profits and gains of industrial undertaking.

HELD: Section 80HH speaks of deduction in respect of any profits and gains derived from newly established industrial undertaking. The term ‘undertaking’ has not been defined in the Act and has to be given the normal meaning. It envisages not only the activity of manufacture or production of goods or arti-cles but the entire set up including all the paraphernalia, the various assets and liabilities, i.e., the entire set up with which the business of manufacture or production of goods is carried on. Therefore, cash resources not imme-diately ploughed back in the day to day operations but nonetheless forming part of the undertaking, are also a constituent part of the undertaking. It is, therefore, obvious that income generated by way of interest on deposits of money held as part of the industrial undertaking is nothing but an ingredient of the profits and gains derived from such undertaking. It makes no diffe-rence whether any such income is assessed under the head ‘Profits and gains of business or profession’ or under the head ‘Income from other sources’. Even if the interest income cannot be strictly referable to the business activity of manufacture of goods dealt in by the assessee and has no direct nexus thereto, it can still be regarded as profit or gain derived from the undertaking as a whole.

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified.

HEADNOTE: Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings [Manufacture] - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with help of machines and then end product was rubber crumb, which was sold to tyre manufacturing company - It claimed deduction under section 80-IB - Whether assessee was engaged in manufacturing of rubber crumb and hence eligible to deduction under section 80-IB - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with help of machines and then end product was rubber crumb, assessee was engaged in manufacturing of rubber crumb and hence eligible to deduction under section 80-IB

FACT: The assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with the help of machines and then the end product was rubber crumb, which was sold to the tyre manufacturing company. It claimed deduction under section 80-IB.

The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) disallowed the claim of deduction.

On second appeal, the Tribunal found that the end product of the assessee was different from its raw material and secondly it was commercially known to be different in the market. It, therefore, held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IB.

On appeal to High Court:

HELD: The manufacturing process of rubber crumb not only involves recycling of the old tyres but also rubber scrap to be converted and transformed into rubber crumb, which incidentally can be reused for manufacture of new tyres. There is nothing to indicate that the old rubber tyres and rubber scrap could be straightway reused for manufacture of new tyres without resorting to processing, as is being done by the assessee. [Para 4]

The Tribunal was justified in concluding that the product (rubber crumb) produced by the assessee was commercially different from its raw material and further it is commercially known to be different in the market. In other words, the assessee was engaged in manufacturing of the said product. Therefore, it was entitled to deduction claimed under section 80-IB. As a result, the appeal filed by the revenue was liable to be dismissed. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1988-89 and 1989-90 - Whether, where assessee was engaged in business of fire works on job work basis and was supplied with raw materials by its customers and had engaged 200 labourers for producing end- product of crackers, it could be said that assessee had satisfied test of manufacturer as well as an industrial undertaking - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of fire works on job work basis. It was supplied with the raw materials by its customers, and had engaged coolies, viz., 200 labourers, to produce crackers. The assessee claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of the assessee on the ground that the assessee was only a labour contractor and not an industrial undertaking eligible for the benefits of sections 80HH and 80-I. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal held that the assessee was an industrial under-taking eligible for the benefits of sections 80HH and 80-I.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the assessee had only been supplied with the raw materials by its customers and of course, the assessee had engaged coolies, viz., 200 labourers, to produce the end-product of crackers. Thus, the assessee satisfied the test of manufacturer by producing the new material, namely, crackers, and also satisfied the test of industrial undertaking, as the assessee had involved in a systematic activity, organized by cooperation between employer and employees, viz., 200 labourers, and for the production and distribution of goods, viz., new product, crackers. [Para 10.3]

In that view of the matter, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal rightly held that the assessee was an industrial undertaking eligible for the benefits of sections 80HH and section 80-I . [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1991-92 - Whether if a new industrial undertaking fulfils conditions laid down in sections 80HH and 80-I, deduc-tions are permissible under both sections - Held, yes - Whether where on 
 same set of facts, revenue authorities in later years allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to a factory treating it as new industrial undertaking, deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I could be denied in relevant assessment year on ground that said factory was not new industrial undertaking - Held, no - Whether for claiming deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I, it is necessary to manufacture a product different from products which assessee was already manufacturing - Held, no

Section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Revision - Of orders prejudicial to interest of revenue - Assessment year 1991-92 - Whether merely because an assessment order results in loss of revenue, Commissioner cannot revise order unless he proves that order resulting in such loss was also erroneous - Held, yes - Whether proceedings under section 263 can only be invoked if basis adopted by Assessing Officer is patently wrong or deduction or relief was allowed in contravention of statutory provisions; in exercise of power under section 263, Commissioner cannot substitute his subjective opinion in place that of Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether where Assessing Officer had accepted profits of undertaking eligible for deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I only after examining relevant information, Explanation and after verifying records, and no infirmity was pointed out by Commissioner in order of Assessing Officer or working of profits and basis adopted, Commissioner was justified in holding that Assessing Officer had allowed excessive relief to assessee and, therefore, directing Assessing Officer to withdraw deduction allowed - Held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on the business of manufacture of tyres and tubes. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I in respect of profit derived from factory No. III. The Assessing Officer allowed the claim after being satisfied that the conditions laid down in sections 80HH and 80-I were fulfilled by the assessee. However, the Commissioner, in exercise of his power under section 263, directed the Assessing Officer to withdraw relief allowed under sections 80HH and 80-I holding that the undertaking situated in the backward area was not entitled to simultaneous reliefs under two sections, i.e., 80HH and 80-I; that although in the impugned assessment, the Assessing Officer had made addition on account of understatement of sale of tyres to close business associate, yet he accepted the working of profits of the new industrial undertaking as made by the assessee which resulted in determination of excessive profit relatable to eligible undertaking; that the assessee was already in the business of manufacture of tyres and tubes for the past several years and, therefore, the third unit could not be said to be newly established industrial undertaking qualifying for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I; and that no deduction was permissible under sections 80HH and 80-I in view of the inadequacy of the profits of the said industrial undertaking.

FACT: The assessee-company, a small-scale industrial undertaking, was carrying on the business of manufacturing ‘Jarda’ from raw tobacco in a backward area. The processing operations employed by the assessee were that raw tobacco (angad) was stripped off the midrib by manual labour. It was then sand-screened to control the moisture content. The raw tobacco was fed into a vibratory feeder and it was conveyed into a pneumatic pick up duct where heavy stems and stones would drop down. In the pick up duct, the tobacco was lifted up by suction and discharged into first tower classifier. In this tower classifier, the heavier tobacco flakes were separated from lighter ones and left behind. The lighter flakes were carried by air into second tower classifier. Here, the tobacco dust and flakes were differentiated. Finally, the lamina was sent to a sleeve chamber where it was cut and graded to suit the requirement of beedi manufacturer. The pure tobacco flakes came out after the dust was sucked out in the dust collecting unit. The end-product was called ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’. The assessee claimed reliefs under sections 32A, 80HH and 80-I for the assessment years 1984-85 and 1985-86. The assessee also claimed that it should be charged at a concessional rate treating it as an industrial company as defined under section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1985. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claims on the ground that the assessee was not manufacturing or producing any article or any thing. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance.

On second appeal:

HELD: The instant case was not a border line case and a firm conclusion was easily approachable. By subjecting tobacco to treatment beedi patti was produced. By ginning cotton, pure cotton is obtained or pressed cotton is produced. Raw wool subjected to processing to eliminate dirt, grease and other vegetable matter results in production of pure wool. Leather is said to be manufactured when raw hide is treated. In all these cases a different product in commercial realm is said to be produced. In the same strain, it was equally possible to say that ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’ was produced or manufactured from raw tobacco as a result of some manual or mechanical treatment, or both. Anybody could go to the market and purchase the article known as raw tobacco and it is equally possible to go and purchase in the market an article called Jarda or Jardi. The physical property in raw tobacco and Jarda or Jardi might be same. While raw tobacco is unfit for beedi manufacture in the same condition, Jarda or Jardi can ready be used in the beedi manufacture. In commercial parlance Jarda or Jardi is distinctively different from raw tobacco. For the aforesaid reasons, in the instant case, the assessee’s business was one of manufacture or production of an article or thing. The assessee’s business undertaking was in a backward area and there was no dispute about it. Then, if the assessee was manufacturing or producing an article, it must be taken that all the conditions in sub-section(2) of section 80HH were fulfilled. The assessee was having a mechanised tobacco processing plant which was even patented. It was registered as a small scale industrial unit by the Government. The most vital was the schedule of assets which formed part of the balance sheet, which showed that the cost of machinery employed was below the limit placed in Explanation to section 32A(2) or Explanation 3 to section 80-I(2), read with section 80HHA(8). The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the reliefs under sections 32A, 80HHA and 80-I. Since the assessee was found manufacturing an article it should be treated as an industrial company as defined in the Finance Act, though even processing, which the assessee was certainly doing, may be sufficient to justify a claim for concessional rate of tax. Thus, the assessee was also entitled to concessional rate of tax for both the years being an industrial company within the meaning of section 2(8)(c).

-IA, revenue receipts can be adjusted against revenue expenditure of the like nature. In the instant case, revenue receipt in the form of interest went to reduce the revenue expenditure of interest, because funds were borrowed for the purpose of business of industrial undertaking and funds were kept in deposit for the purpose of business of the assessee’s industrial undertaking. Thus, interest income or expenditure was inextricably linked and was having direct and proximate connection with the business of industrial undertaking. [Para 16] In view of the above and keeping in view the findings recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals), there was no reason to interfere with his order. [Para 19]

In respect of other miscellaneous income, arising from sale of empty drums/containers and sale of useless materials,all the sale proceeds were only out of the business of industrial undertaking of the assessee. Therefore, even for determining the profits and gains ‘derived from any business of industrial undertaking’, manufacturing or producing any article or thing includes sale proceeds of such article or thing or scrap generated during the course of such manufacturing activity which amounts to increase in the sale consideration. After all what is to be determined is the profits and gains of business of industrial undertaking and there is no warrant to stop for the above purpose at sale of main products only. The controversy was not when manufacturing activity of the assessee was over, but what was the profit and gains of the business of the industrial undertaking and how was it to be determined. For determining the profits of business of industrial undertaking, it was not possible to ignore the said sales which were closely and directly connected with the outcome of the manufacturing process itself. Thus, there was a direct nexus between the sale of those items and carrying on of the business of industrial undertaking. [Para 20]

In the result, all the appeals of the revenue were to be dismissed. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment years 1983-84 to 1987-88 - Whether process of processed (including frozen) fish and fish products should be regarded as an activity of manufacture or production of an article, or thing entitled to benefit of section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacture or production of frozen sea foods from shrimps obtained from the sea. The catch obtained from the sea was cleaned, beheaded, deskinned, sorted, frozen and was converted or produced into frozen sea foods which were exported in packs to foreign countries. The assessee claimed that it was an industrial undertaking engaged in the business of manufacture or production of frozen sea food and, thus, claimed deduction under section 80HH. The ITO allowed the said claim of the assessee. The Commissioner, however, exercising his powers under section 263, disallowed the said deduction.

On appeal :

HELD: In section 80HH the words ‘manufacture’ or ‘produce’ appear. The same words appear in section 33 of the Act which relates to grant of relief of development rebate to the assessee. It is implicit in section 33(1)(b )(B)(i ) that processed (frozen).fish and fish products produced by the assessee constituted new commercial article compared to raw fish as far as provisions in section 33 were concerned. Thus, the legislative intent under the provisions of the Act is that process of the processed (including frozen) fish and fish products should be regarded as an activity of manufacture or production of an article or thing eligible for grant of development rebate. There is no reason why the same intent should not be presumed to be present in enacting section 80HH where same words ‘manufacture’ or ‘production’ of articles have been used. Consequently, as far as the Act was concerned, processing which resulted in processed (including frozen) fish and fish products amounts to an activity of manufacture or production of an article or thing within the ambit of sections 33 and 80HH. Consequently, in the present case, the activity of the assessee would be regarded as an activity of manufacture or production of an article or thing. Accordingly, the order of Commissioner was to be set aside and that of the ITO was to be restored.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1977-78 - Whether assessee buying shrimps, peeling them and freezing them could be said to be engaged in manufacture or production, in absence of material on record to indicate what was done by assessee and how it was done, so as to eligible for allowance under section 80HH - Held, no

FACT: The assessee bought shrimps, peeled them and froze them. It claimed allowance under section 80HH on the ground that it was an industrial undertaking that manufactured/produced articles. There was no other material on the record which indicated what was done by the assessee and how it was done. The claim was rejected by the Assessing Officer but upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal. On reference, the High Court upheld the decision of the Tribunal on ground that buying and processing of shrimps involved production.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: There was, upon the record before the Court, no detailed description of what the assessee did to the shrimps it bought, other than the bald statement that it peeled and froze them. The Court could not accept the statement at the Bar that the process to which the assessee put the shrimps was the process that CIT v. Marwell Sea Foods [1987] 166 ITR 624/ 34 Taxman 52 (Ker.) used in regard to its prawns. That apart the Supreme Court in Sterling Foods v. State of Karnataka [1986] 68 STC 239, held that processed or frozen shrimps and prawns are commercially regarded as the same commodity as raw shrimps and prawns. When raw shrimps and prawns are subjected to the process of cutting of heads and tails, peeling, deveining, cleaning and freezing they do not cease to be shrimps and prawns and become other distinct commodities. There is no essential difference between raw shrimps and prawns and processed or frozen shrimps and prawns. In common parlance they remain known as shrimps and prawns. Therefore, the assessee who bought shrimps, peeled them and froze them was not entitled to the allowance under section 80HH as it did not involve in activity of manufacture or production.

HEADNOTE: SECTION 80J OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-DEDUCTIONS-PROFITS AND GAINS FROM NEWLY’ ESTABLISHED INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS-ASSESSEE-COMPANY, ENGAGED IN MANUFACTURING OF STEEL TUBES, SET UP A NEW PLANT FOR MANUFACTURE OF ANOTHER TYPE OF STEEL TUBE-WHETHER MERELY BECAUSE OLD MACHINERIES WERE UTILISED IN SAME PROCESS FOR MANUFACTURE IN NEW UNIT, IT COULD BE TREATED AS SPLITTING UP OF UNDERTAKING, SO AS TO DISENTITLE ASSESSEE TO DEDUCTION-HELD, NO-WHETHER CAPITAL EMPLOYED WAS TO BE COMPUTED ON VALUE OF ASSETS EMPLOYED IN NEW UNDERTAKING AS ALSO AMOUNT OF BORROWINGS AND DEBTS RELATING THERETO ONLY, AND ENTIRE DEBT OF ASSESSEE SHOULD NOT BE CONSIDERED FOR NEW UNIT-HELD, YES-WHETHER ASSETS AND DEBTS AS ON FIRST DAY OF ACCOUNTING PERIOD HAD TO BE TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT AN. NOT AS THEY STOOD ON LAST DAY OF THAT YEAR-HELD, YES

SECTION 80HH OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-DEDUCTIONS-IN RESPECT OF INCOMES OF INDUSTRIES OR HOTELS IN BACKWARD AREA-WHETHER ON FACTS UNDER HEAD ‘DEDUCTIONS - PROFITS AND GAINS FROM NEWLY- ESTABLISHED INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING’ ASSESSEE WOULD ALSO BE ENTITLE TO RELIEF UNDER SECTION 80HH-HELD, YES

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the manufacture and sale of black steel tubes and galvanised steel tubes. The assessee set up a new project consisting of a moulding plant for the manufacture of steel tubes of four inches diameter. Earlier it was manufacturing such tubes only of two inches diameter. The assessee claimed reliefs under section 80J and section 80HH. The ITO found that not only the mill compound but also the factory building were the same for both the projects. The earlier tin-shed had been extended to accommodate the new project and there was only one composite structure for both the projects. Further, he found that several machinery, plant ‘ land, building, store room, workshop, generating set and factory office were common to both the projects. The ITO rejected the assessee’s claim on the ground that no separate profit and loss account and balance sheet had been prepared in respect of that new project and it was a clear case of mere splitting of the old undertaking. He also observed that the entire borrowings and debts owed by the undertaking as a whole had to be deducted in computing the capital employed in the undertaking which in the present case exceeded the value of the assets of the undertaking. He also observed that the computation submitted by the assessee was also incorrect as it had taken the value of the assets as on the last day of the accounting year instead of their value as on the first day of the amounting year. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the ITO’s order.

On second appeal :

HELD: In view of the decision in Textile Machinery Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 107 ITR 195 ( SC), for purposes of relief under section 80J, one has to come to the conclusion that the assessee’s new project was a new industrial unit, which was separate physically from the old one, the capital of which and the profits thereon being ascertainable. The mere fact that some of the processes for the manufacture of new tubes in the instant case were carried on with the help of the old machines or there was common store room and common factory office were not fatal to the claim of the assessee. Thus, the assessee was entitled to reliefs under sections 80J and 80HH and the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in taking the contrary view.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of newly established industrial undertaking in backward areas - Whether assessee engaged in business of rearing and development of chicks into broilers, could be said to be 'manufacturing' a product - Held, no

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the business of rearing of chicks to broilers, a saleable product, by applying scientific process and technology, established an industrial unit in the backward area and claimed deduction under section 80HH and section 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the claim. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal, however, set aside the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) and affirmed that of the Assessing Officer.

HELD: AS HELD BY HIGH COURT

The process involved in the development of chicks into broilers is nothing but that the chicks basically remains chicks only. There is no substantial change so as to acquire new commercial identity. Chicks are smaller ones and when they are reared for sometime, they develop suitably for table purposes. Therefore, there is no change of substance. Manufacture implies a change, but every change is not manufacture and yet every change in an article is the result of treatment, labour and manipulation which does not necessarily mean that on account of certain treatment and manipulation, new identity has come to be acquired.

In the instant case, chicks were only reared up for a few days and they were developed, thereafter they became broilers. Therefore, even after rearing, they remained chicks only. Hence, the view taken by the Tribunal that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I as an industrial undertaking was correct.

AS HELD BY SUPREME COURT

It was not in dispute that the case was covered against the assessee by the judgment of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Venkateswara Hatcheries (P.) Ltd. [1999] 237 ITR 174/103 Taxman 503. The further point that was made by the assessee was that it not only reared the chicken but also dressed them for sale in the market and, therefore, a process of manufacture was carried out. But, it appeared that there was no material laid before the Tribunal in this behalf. It was, therefore, not possible to conclude in the present matter that the dressing of poultry tantamounted to manufacture.

The appeal was dismissed.

HEADNOTE: III. Section  80-IB , read with sections  80-IC  and  80-IE , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deductions  -  Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings (Sale of scrap/empty containers)  - Assessment years  2013-14 and 2015-16 to 2017-18  - Assessee had multiple eligible units claiming deduction under sections 80IB/80IC/80IE and earned receipts from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing - AO held such receipts were merely incidental, not profits derived from eligible undertakings, and excluded them while computing deductions - CIT(A), noting that scrap and empty containers arose from manufacturing process of eligible units and following Tribunal’s orders in assessee’s own case for earlier years, allowed receipts as part of eligible profits - Whether since revenue had not brought on record any material demonstrating a change either in factual matrix or in legal position prevailing during year under consideration, impugned order of CIT(A) allowing deduction under sections 80IB, 80IC and 80IE in respect of profits arising from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing process was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 9.7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee had multiple eligible units claiming deduction under sections 80IB/80IC/80IE and earned receipts from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing.

■

The AO held such receipts were merely incidental, not profits derived from the eligible undertakings, and excluded them while computing deductions (e.g., disallowance around Rs. 36.24 lakhs in AY 2013-14 and similar disallowances in later years for specified units).

■

The CIT(A), noting that the scrap and empty containers arose from the manufacturing process of the eligible units and following the Tribunal’s orders in the assessee’s own case for earlier years, allowed the receipts as part of eligible profits.

■

On the revenue’s appeals to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

It is found that the CIT(A) has granted relief by faithfully following the decision of the Coordinate Bench of the Tribunal rendered in the assessee's own case on an identical issue. The Tribunal, after examining the nature of the receipts, had categorically held that the sale of empty containers and scrap generated during the manufacturing process forms an integral part of the business operations of the eligible undertaking and that the profits arising therefrom qualify for deduction under the relevant provisions of the Act [Para 9.5]

■

It is noteworthy that the revenue has not brought on record any material demonstrating a change either in the factual matrix or in the legal position prevailing during the year under consideration. Nor has any distinguishing feature been pointed out which would justify taking a view different from that consistently adopted in the assessee's own case. In the absence of any such distinguishing circumstance, the principles of judicial discipline and consistency require that the view already taken by the Coordinate Bench be followed. [Para 9.6]

■

Accordingly, respectfully following the binding precedent rendered in the assessee's own case for the earlier assessment years, no infirmity is found in the order of the CIT(A) allowing deduction under sections 80-IB, 80-IC and 80-IE in respect of profits arising from the sale of scrap/empty containers generated during the manufacturing process. Therefore, the order of the CIT(A) on this issue is upheld. Consequently, Ground No. 3 raised by the Revenue stands dismissed. [Para 9.7]

HEADNOTE: V. Section  80-IC  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 – Deductions – Special provisions in respect of certain undertakings or enterprises in certain special category States (Scrap income) – Assessment years  2014-15 to 2016-17  – Assessee-company included scrap income generated by its eligible manufacturing undertaking at Baddi while computing deduction under section 80-IC – Assessing Officer held that scrap income did not constitute profits derived from industrial undertaking and excluded same from eligible profits – It was noted that generation of scrap was an inevitable incident of manufacturing process and identical issue stood covered in favour of assessee by decisions rendered in assessee's own case for earlier years – Whether scrap income generated during manufacturing operations of eligible industrial undertaking formed an integral part of profits derived from such undertaking, generation of scrap being an inevitable incident of manufacturing activity – Held, yes – Whether, therefore, deduction under section 80-IC was allowable in respect of scrap income earned by eligible industrial undertaking – Held, yes [Paras 116, 123 and 127] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company included scrap income generated by its eligible manufacturing undertaking at Baddi while computing deduction under section 80-IC.

■

The Assessing Officer held that scrap income did not constitute profits derived from the industrial undertaking and excluded such income from eligible profits while computing deduction under section 80-IC for assessment years 2014-15 to 2016-17.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that generation of scrap was an inevitable incident of the manufacturing process and directed inclusion of scrap income while computing deduction under section 80-IC.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The rival submissions, assessment order, appellate findings and judicial precedents relied upon by the assessee have been carefully considered. The orders passed by the Ahmedabad Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case for assessment years 2008-09 to 2010-11 in ITA Nos. 1366/Ahd/2015 & 1780/Ahd/2015, for assessment year 2011-12 in ITA Nos. 1184/Ahd/2018 & 1225/Ahd/2018 and for assessment years 2012-13, 2013-14, 2020-21 and 2022-23 in Deputy CIT v. Reckitt Benckiser Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. [2025] 176 taxmann.com 573 (Ahmedabad - Trib.) have also been examined. Upon careful examination of the issue from the perspective of section 80-IC and the settled principles governing interpretation of the expression "derived from", no infirmity is found in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 114]

■

The identical issue now stands squarely covered in favour of the assessee by consistent decisions rendered by the Ahmedabad Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case for earlier years. [Para 115]

■

In the assessee's own case for assessment years 2008-09 to 2010-11 in Reckitt Benckiser Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. v. ACIT (ITA Nos. 1366/Ahd/2015 & 1780/Ahd/2015), the Co-ordinate Bench examined the allowability of deduction under section 80-IC in respect of scrap income earned by the eligible industrial undertaking. After analysing the manufacturing process and the nature of scrap generated therefrom, it was held that scrap income formed an integral part of the profits derived from the industrial undertaking and, therefore, qualified for deduction under section 80-IC. [Para 116]

■

The identical issue also arose before the Ahmedabad Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case for assessment years 2012-13, 2013-14, 2020-21 and 2022-23 in assessee's own case. The Co-ordinate Bench after considering the earlier decisions rendered in the assessee's own case, upheld the allowability of deduction under section 80-IC in respect of scrap income generated by the Baddi Unit. [Para 123]

■

It is found that the Revenue has not brought any distinguishing feature on record to demonstrate that the nature of scrap income involved in the present assessment year differs from earlier years already adjudicated upon by the Co-ordinate Bench. The principle of consistency therefore strongly supports the assessee's claim. [Para 126]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 80-I, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertakings after a certain date - Assessment years 1987-88 to 1992-93 - Assessees engaged in dismantling of damaged/unserviceable ships claimed deduction under section 80HH and 80-I - Whether legislature intended to extend benefit of deductions only to industrial undertakings manufacturing or producing articles - Held, yes - Whether as ship-breaking activity amounts to carrying out manufacturing process in reverse order, assessees were not entitled to deduction claimed - Held, yes

FACT: The assessees, engaged in the business of breaking and dismantling of damaged or unserviceable ships and selling the goods obtained therefrom to various parties, claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claims on the grounds that the assessee were not industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH and 80-I and they did not fulfil any of the conditions of those sections and that there was nothing like a process of manufacturing done by the assessees. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that ship breaking was an industrial undertaking and, accordingly, the assessees were eligible for the deductions claimed.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: The Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. This section is not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in ‘processing of goods’ not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. The ship-breaking activity involves buying of damaged and unserviceable ships which are otherwise uneconomic to run, for the purpose of breaking and scrapping and sale of various goods and scrap obtained from such breaking and dismantling of old and used ships. Process is employed for breaking ship for dismantling and selling the scrap and substantial part of the items fitted in the ship and the oil contained in the tankers are sold in the same from without carrying out any further act, except removal of same from the ship and the remaining ship, made mainly of iron and steel, is then broken into different pieces of different sizes and shapes and sold by weight. Therefore, at the end of the process employed by the assessee, what is acquired are iron bars, plating rods, bronze, gunmetal copper and non-ferrous metal which, though marketable and commercial commodities, cannot be said to be manufactured or produced articles or things. For all practical purposes it is scrap. The scrap cannot be called a manufacture product or produced article because they are no new commodities but parts of the old and discarded ship as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Delhi Iron & Steel Co. (P.) Ltd. [1995] 98 STC 202 the condemned and unserviceable ship purchased by the dealer is not a ship but re-rollable scrap in the form of an old ship for dismantling, in effect, the dealer acquires only the old materials and articles contained therein which are sold by it in the form in which they are acquired. No process whatsoever is applied to the goods, much less any process of manufacture. The issue stood squarely covered in favour of the revenue by the decision of the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asst. CIT v. Virendra & Co. [1995] 55 ITD 309 which held that ‘the meaning of manufacture and production of articles and things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or an thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken, what is obtained by the persons who are engaged in that process are the components by which the ship is constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 80J, read with section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings, ships or hotels, etc. - Assessment year 1980-81 - Business of assessee was centrifuging rubber latex - It claimed deduction under sections 80J and 80HH - Tribunal adverting to a notification of Central Government allowed claims of assessee - While doing so, Tribunal neither, adverted to relevant materials nor entered finding as to whether any manufacturing process was involved or a new commodity produced - Tribunal even diluted legal effect of its earlier decision wherein a contrary view was taken and also failed to apply proper test governing matter as laid down by Supreme Court - Whether in above circumstances, Tribunal’s approach to question was totally faulty and resultant conclusion was tainted - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, matter was to be restored to Tribunal’s file for fresh decision - Held, yes

FACT: The business of the assessee-company was centrifuging rubber latex. It claimed that the business involved manufacture or production of articles and things and so, the company was entitled to deduction under section 80J as well as under section 80HH for the relevant assessment year in respect of a unit working in a backward area. The ITO rejected the said plea. He held that the assessee did not carry on manufacturing operations nor did it produce any article. In his view, the assessee only made the latex more concentrated. The reliefs claimed under sections 80J and 80HH were denied. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the said decision. On second appeal, the Tribunal observed that the notification dated 8-7-1983 (No. 189 of 1983), considered the latex concentrate, preserved latex, etc., as manufactured goods. After adverting to the said notification it held that the Government had proclaimed that the assessee was a manufacturer and that the said notification had to be applied with equal force to the Act also and accordingly, held that the assessee was entitled to deductions under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case, the essential question to be considered was whether when normal or natural latex was converted into preserved latex by centrifuging process, any manufacturing process was involved or a new commodity produced. A finding on this was essential. Such a finding could be entered only on the basis of evidence. Technical and scientific evidence could be gathered from competent persons or after understanding the process from standard books or literature.

The Tribunal had not rendered the decision in accordance with law. There had been no proper advertence to the relevant materials. It had not posed the correct question. The proper test governing the matter, as held by the Supreme Court in Ujagar Prints v. Union of India [1989] 179 ITR 317, was not adverted to. On the other hand, it over-emphasised the effect of the said notification and completely under-estimated and diluted the legal effect of its earlier decision wherein it had held that in spite of the changes that were effected by the process of centrifuging, the end product could not be considered to be materially different from the raw material, the natural latex and that commercially no different product was produced and no production or manufacture was involved in subjecting the natural rubber latex to the centrifugal operation after obtaining preserved latex. The approach to the question was totally faulty. The resultant conclusion was tainted.

In the above circumstances, the Tribunal was directed to restore the appeal to its file and decide the matter afresh in accordance with law.
