In the show-cause notice, the Commissioner had not disclosed that ground and the assessee was never directed to meet the Commissioner’s observations that deduction under section 80HH was not permissible on account of lack of gross total income. Therefore, the impugned order under section 263 also suffered from the infirmity of not allowing proper opportunity of being heard to the assessee. [Para 21] From the assessment year 1985-86 onwards, the assessee had consistently disclosed in the computation statement that factory No. III was set up as a new industrial undertaking eligible for deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer had required the assessee to give specific information regarding establishment of the factory No. III as new industrial undertaking and also required the assessee to prove that it fulfilled the conditions laid down in sections 80HH and 80-I. The assessee furnished its explanations and documentary evidences to prove that the said factory No. III was set up as a new industrial undertaking and commenced production in March 1984 relevant to the assessment year 1985-86. The said factory No. III was given a new factory licence and central excise licence. The Central Excise authorities also certified that the first dispatch from the said factory took place only on 29-3-1984. Therefore, before the Assessing Officer in the assessment proceedings, the assessee had brought on record sufficient material and evidence to prove that a new industrial undertaking was set up during the calendar year 1984 relevant to the assessment year 1985-86. In the assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95, the deductions under sections 80-I and 80HH were allowed in respect of profits of factory No. III. Those orders were not made subject-matter of appeals or revision and the deductions allowed by the Assessing Officer had become final. In the above factual circumstances, therefore, in the succeeding assessment years on the same set of facts, the revenue authorities accepted factory No. III as new industrial undertaking eligible to deductions under sections 80-I and 80HH. On those facts, therefore, there was no justification for the Commissioner to doubt the establishment of factory No. III as new industrial undertaking only in the assessment year 1991-92. Though the principle of res judicata was not strictly applicable to revenue proceedings, yet the said principle was no stranger to the tax proceedings. If on the same set of facts the revenue authorities in the later years allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to factory No. III treating it as an industrial undertaking set up in the assessment year 1985-86, then there was no reason for the Commissioner to disturb the finding of the Assessing Officer in the assessment year 1991-92 as the Commissioner did not bring on record any specific evidence to prove contrary. Therefore, the Commissioner was not justified in doubting the establishment of factory No. III as new industrial undertaking during 1985-86. [Para 23]

During the assessment year 1985-86, the deduction under section 80HH was permissible to a newly established undertaking if it was situated in any of the districts specified in the eighth schedule. By Notification dated 19-12-1986, the Central Government notified list of backward districts and District Udaipur was included therein. The Raj Samund Block of Udaipur District, where factory No. III was situated, was in excluded category of the said notification. However, the CBDT in its circular No. 484 dated 1-5-1987 had clarified that all areas specified in the Eighth Schedule continued to enjoy the benefit of section 80HH if the industrial undertaking had begun manufacture before 10-9-1986. Therefore, factory No. III situated in Raj Samund Block of Udaipur District was eligible for deduction under section 80HH since it began production in March 1984 as certified by the Central Excise authorities. [Para 24]

According to the Commissioner, factory No. III merely represented expansion of the assessee’s existing business and, therefore, not eligible for beneficial deductions as no new business was set up. However, this proposition has not been accepted by the Supreme Court as well as by the various High Courts. In the assessee’s own case for the assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95, the department had allowed deduction under sections 80-I and 80HH in respect of profits derived by factory No. III. Therefore, the order of the Assessing Officer, allowing deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I considering factory No. III as new industrial undertaking was supported by various judicial decisions wherein it was held that for claming the deductions it was not necessary to manufacture a new or different product. Therefore, the order of the Assessing Officer on this issue could not be considered as erroneous. [Para 25]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas (Condition precedent) - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether what becomes entitled to claim exemption under section 80HH is an industrial undertaking and once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial whether it is manufacturing, or producing or processing - Held, yes - Whether assessee, an industrial undertaking engaged in activity of converting cotton pieces known as cops into yarn, would be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]IT : Once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial for purpose of allowing deduction under section 80HH whether it is manufacturing or producing or processing

FACT: The assessee was an industrial undertaking engaged in the activity of converting cotton pieces known as cops into yarn., depending upon the customer requirement. It claimed deduction under section 80HH.

The Assessing Officer held that no process of manufacture was undertaken by assessee and, therefore, it was not entitled to claim deduction under section 80HH.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee's claim.

The Tribunal dismissed the revenue's appeal.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: In the context of section 80HH, the Parliament guardedly used the expression 'manufacturing process, or manufacture, or produce articles' in sub-section (4) and other parts thereof. [Para 11]

What becomes entitled to claim exemption under section 80HH, is an industrial undertaking, as is evident from the very heading of the section, than the nature of activity taken up by it. Once the assessee answers the description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial whether it is manufacturing, or producing or processing. The amount that qualifies for deduction is the profits and gains of such an undertaking to the extent of 20 per cent. Things would have been different altogether, had the deduction been restricted only to the activity of manufacturing. [Para 12]

There is no ground to interfere with the order passed by the Tribunal. [Para 16]

The appeal is accordingly dismissed. [Para 17]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether activity of breaking or dismantling a ship or ships can be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactures or produces articles so as to be entitled to get deduction under sections 80HHA and 80-I - Held, no

FACT: The assessee, involved in breaking of ships and selling the parts and its other articles, claimed to be an industrial undertaking engaged in the manufacture of articles or things and, thus, entitled to deduction under sections 80HHA and 80-I. Such claim was rejected by the Assessing Officer but allowed by the first appellate authority.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: After the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412 the concept of adopting a liberal interpretation has been reconsidered and now as per the Supreme Court the principles of adopting a liberal interpretation which advances the purpose and object of beneficial provisions cannot be carried to the extent of doing violence to the plain and simple language used in the enactment. It would not be reasonable or permissible for the court to re-write the section or substitute words of its own for the actual words employed by the Legislature in the name of giving effect to the supposed underlying object.

The meaning of `manufacture’ and ‘production of articles or things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary, plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or a thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken what is obtained by the person or persons who are engaged in that process are those components by which the ship was constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or a thing is being manufactured or produced.

Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling a ship could not be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deductions under sections 80HHA and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the income-tax act, 1961-Deductions-Profits and 
gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward 
areas-For assessment year 1977-78, assessee-company was allowed 
weighted deduction under section 35b and was also eligible for 
section 80hh relief-whether for computing section 80hh relief, 
profits should be arrived at after deducting only the actual 
expenses for export markets development, and not weighted deduc-
tion-Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was eligible for relief under section 80HH. It had also been granted weighted deduction in respect of export development expenditure under section 35B. For the assessment year 1977-78, the assessee was allowed relief under section 80HH on the profit of the manu-facturing unit after deducting the extra weighted deduction under section 35B, as against its claim that profit for this purpose was the profit as understood in the normal commercial sense, and should be arrived at after deducting actual expenses and not the weighted allowance.

On second appeal :

HELD: The phrase ‘profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking’ has not been defined in the Act. Hence, its meaning has to be understood in the general commercial sense. In order to arrive at the profit from an under-taking, only the actual expenses are deducted and not the notional expenses. Hence, the profits of an undertaking can mean the amount arrived at after deduction of actual expenses only and without deduction of the notional expenses like the relief under section 35B: This is really not an expense that goes out of the pocket of the assessee, and cannot, therefore, go to reduce the commercial profit, though it may reduce the taxable profit.

Accordingly, the assessee should be allowed relief under section 80HH before deducting the extra weighted deduction allowed under the section.

43A including development rebate under section 33 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company claimed relief under section 80HH in respect of the profits of a new industrial undertaking in backward area in the assessment year 1974-75. The said profits, it claimed, were to be arrived at without deduction of development rebate. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee's plea and his order was confirmed by the appellate authority and the Tribunal.

On appeal under section 260A : HELD: Section 80HH begins with the words 'where the gross total income of an assessee includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking'. The expression 'gross total income' is defined under section 80B(5) to mean the total income computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act, before making any deduction under Chapter VI-A. Therefore, what is included in the gross total income in such a case is not only the category of such income included in the gross total income but also the quantum of the income so included. This is the basic test which needs to be applied to answer the question raised by the assessee in this appeal. In the case of Distributors (Baroda) (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [1985] 155 ITR 120/ 22 Taxman 49, the Supreme Court has categorically laid down that the expression 'gross total income' in section 80B(5) would mean the total income computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act before making any deductions under Chapter VI-A and what is included in the gross total income is a particular quantum of income belonging to a specified category. Therefore, the words 'such income by way of profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking referred to in section 80HH', must be referable not only to the category of income but also to the quantum of income included in the gross total income and, therefore, such income belonging to a specified category and forming part of the gross total income is required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Therefore, on a bare reading of the provisions of section 80HH, along with section 80B(5), it is clear that even prior to the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1980, Parliament had clearly intended to say that what is included in the gross total income is not only a specified category of income, but also a particular quantum of income belonging to that specified category. In Court's opinion, therefore, the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1980, has merely made the position, which was implicit, explicit. Therefore, section 80AB is clearly declaratory in nature like section 80AA and it merely declares what the correct position has always been. In fact, in the concurring judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Distributors (Baroda) (P.) Ltd. (supra), Sen, J. has observed that section 80AA was clearly declaratory in nature and it merely declared what the correct position has always been and, therefore, there was no question of imposition of any fresh tax with retrospective effect by virtue of the said section. It may be pointed out that the Supreme Court has reversed its own judgment in the case of Cloth Traders (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 243/ 1 Taxman 335, vide judgment in the case of Distributors (Baroda) (P.) Ltd. (supra). At this stage, it may be mentioned that in the case of H.H. Sir Rama Varma v. CIT [1994] 205 ITR 433/[1993] 71 Taxman 237, the Supreme Court has held that section 80AB was enacted to declare the law as it always stood in relation to the deductions to be made in respect of the income specified under Chapter VI-A. Therefore, it is clear that even without section 80AB, the profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking referred to in section 80HH have to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43A and in any event since section 80AB has been held to be retrospective by the Supreme Court in H.H. Sir Rama Varma's case (supra), it was not open to the assessee to say that the said section is prospective as stated above.

On a bare reading of the judgment of the Bombay High Court in the case of CIT v. Albright Morarji & Pandit Ltd. [1999] 236 ITR 914/ 103 Taxman 168, it is clear that the said judgment is based on review of the various provisions of the Act both with and de hors section 80AB. In the said judgment, it has been laid down that section 80AB, though inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1980 with effect from 1-4-1981, was merely declaratory.

Accordingly, the appeal stood rejected.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc. in backward areas [Computation of deduction] - Assessee-company had been carrying on two activities; one was business of manufacturing cement and second was mining operation of lime - Lime was used as raw material in manufacturing cement - Assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH from whole of business income - Same was disallowed on ground that assessee had been carrying on business of mining operation - Whether mining activity of assessee was distinct and independent from cement manufacturing activities and segregation of profit of two different business activities was permissible under law - Held, yes - Whether segregation of profit derived from cement manufacturing activity was permitted by law in order to find out profit derived from mining activities and, thus, deduction under section 80HH would be available only on profit derived from cement manufacturing activity - Held, yes [Paras 6 to 11] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee had two separate and distinct undertaking, one for manufacturing cement and another for mining of lime that was to be used in cement manufacturing, profit only from manufacturing of cement would be eligible for deduction under section 80HH

FACT: The assessee-company had been carrying on business of manufacturing cement and also carrying on mining operation of lime which was used as a raw material in manufacturing cement.

The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH and the same was disallowed by Assessing Officer on the ground that assessee had been carrying on business of mining operation.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction by observing that the assessee carried business of manufacturing cement.

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee could be said to have been running two industrial undertakings. The assessee's main business of manufacturing of cement, was entitled to deduction under section 80HH in respect of items manufactured or produced, and it would not cease to be entitled to claim the deduction if the industrial undertaking is engaged in mining. The Tribunal, therefore, allowed deduction with respect to profit attributable to manufacturing cement.

On assessee's appeal to High Court :

HELD: From the records the Court find, as has been rightly contended by revenue that in the previous assessment years, namely 1984-85 and 1985-86, the Tribunal found on fact that the assessee has been running two industrial undertakings, one is mining of lime and another is manufacturing of cement. It is an admitted position further that against the aforesaid findings, no appeal has been preferred. Hence, the Court have to proceed on the premise that the mining activity of the assessee is distinct and independent from the cement manufacturing activity. Now the question remains is whether the use of the entire product of lime, extracted from mining operation for manufacturing of cement, looses its marketable value in order to ascertain the profit or not. [Para 6]

The argument of the assessee is that a manufacturer cannot trade with itself. Therefore, unless there is a factual sale in the market, no profit can be derived from this mining operation. In order to derive the entire profit, the cement manufacturing unit has to be taken into account and the product has to be sold in the market and then the profit will be ascertained. This submission, at the first blush, sounds logic, but while keeping in view the matter, this logic does not have any basis. It is the admitted position that lime is one of the raw materials in manufacturing cement and in order to manufacture the finished products, raw material is essential and the cost thereof is one of the factors for cost price of the finished goods. Therefore, in the manufacturing activity of cement unit, the cost of the finished product has to be ascertained and in that process, the cost of lime has also to be taken into consideration. In the case on hand, the lime, being a raw material, is not procured from open market and it has got its own indigenous supply. Therefore, the cost of the lime extracted from mining operation has to be ascertained from the cost price and it is found, while doing so, that the cost of lime of its own source (ordinarily it happens) is lesser than the market price. Therefore, the difference between the cost price of indigenous source and the market price is obviously the profit. Moreover, once lime is used from its indigenous source to manufacture the finished products and by virtue of sale of such finished products if there is any profit, then obviously that profit is also related to the mining operation. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Section 32A of the Income-tax Act, 1961-Investment allowance-
Whether, assessee was entitled to investment allowance under
section 32A in respect of machinery and plant installed in cold
storage-Held, no

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961-Deductions-Profits and 
gains from newly established industrial undertaking in backward
areas-Whether, assessee was entitled to relief in respect of cold 
storage, which was situated in backward area, under section 80HH-
Held, no

FACT: The assessee, being an owner of a cold storage situated in a backward area wherein potatoes were kept in the relevant assessment year, claimed investment allowance under section 32A on machinery and plant installed in the cold storage on the ground that the cold storage involved ‘manufac-turing’. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that a cold storage involved only processing and not manufacture or production of an article or thing. He also disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH, On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal;

HELD: Section 32 A uses the expression ‘business of manufacture or production of any article or thing’. The expression used in section 80HH is similar, namely, ‘to manufacture or produce articles’. There is no reference to ‘processing’ as used in the definition of ‘industrial company’ under section 2(7)(d) of the Finance Act, 1966, and the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1967. Again, unlike section 80J(4)(iii), reference is not made in section 32A or 80HH to the operation of a cold storage plant. This would show that mere processing (even if the potatoes were held to undergo processing in a cold storage) is not recognised under sections 32A and 80HH to amount to manufacture or production of any article or thing. The same expression is used in section 80HHA and 80-I(2)(iii). Again, section 35C, which deals with agricultural development allowance, refers to a company or a co-operative society being engaged in the manufacture or processing of a relevant article or thing There-fore, as neither section 32A nor section 80HH refers to processing of any article or thing, the lower authorities were justified in rejecting the claims of the assessee.

 can be adjusted against revenue expenditure of like nature - Held, yes - Whether for determining profits and gains ‘derived from any business of industrial undertaking’, manufacturing or producing any article or thing includes sale proceeds of such article or thing or scrap generated during course of such manufacturing activity which amounts to increase in sale consideration - Held, yes - Whether since assessee was under business obligation to have security deposit with ‘D’ Ltd. and its associates and as such deposits were given in consideration of providing bank guarantee, organizing finance and providing franchise to set up industry by assessee-company, there was a direct and proximate nexus between interest earned on such deposits and interest paid on funds borrowed for running of business of industrial undertaking and, therefore, assessee was eligible for deduction on such interest earning under section 80-IA - Held, yes - Whether, even otherwise, since interest payment during year was more than interest received, in effect, there was no income on account of interest included in profits of business of industrial undertaking required to be reduced for computing deduction under section 80-IA - Held, yes - Whether, sale of empty drums/containers and sale of useless materials could not be ignored as it was closely and directly connected with outcome of manufacturing process itself and there was a direct nexus between sale of those items and carrying on of business of industrial undertaking - Held, yes.

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment years 1985-86 and 1986-87 - Assessee used to purchase potable spirit and by processing it produced IMFLs like brandy, whisky and rum etc. by adding certain percentage of water, colour and essence - Whether there is any difference between potable spirit and brandy or whisky - Held, no - Whether, therefore, no distinct article or thing could be said have been produced by assessee as alcohol remained alcohol throughout processing stage till it was marketed - Held, yes - Whether therefore, activities of assessee involved no manufacturing but only processing and, thus, it was disentitled to benefit of section 80HH - Held, yes
Words & phrases - 'industrial undertaking' occurring in section 80HH(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

SECTION 41(1) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-REMISSION OR CESSATION OF 
TRADING LIABILITY-WHETHER IN VIEW OF THE FACTS MENTIONED UNDER 
CAPTION 'DEDUCTION - IN RESPECT OF PROFITS AND GAINS OF INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING, ETC., IN BACKWARD AREAS', SECTION 41(1) WAS NOT 
APPLICABLE INTO PROFITS DERIVED BY ASSESSEE PROM SALE OF SCRAP AND 
DRUMS-HELD, YES

IV. Section 80-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profit and gains from infrastructure undertakings (Scrap sale) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee had credited an amount under head 'scrap sales' and claimed deduction under section 80-IA on same - Assessing Officer denied same holding that said income was not derived from manufacturing activity of industrial undertaking - It was noted that scrap sold was related to unserviceable spared retrieved from plant - Cost of new spares replaced in place of damaged spares was fully charged to profit and loss account - Spares sold resulted reduction in cost of new spares purchased and, hence, led to higher manufacturing profits to assessee - Merely because scrap sale or sale of spares was shown separately, it did not tantamount to a new source of income - Whether, on facts, profits commensurate with scrap sold was said to be directly earned from manufacturing activity of assessee and, therefore, assessee was entitled to claim deduction under section 80-IA on same - Held, yes [Para 38] [In favour of assessee]

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - In respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment year 1983-84 - Assessee having an industrial unit in backward area received a sum on account of job charges for twisting of yarn - Whether absence of separate balance sheet in respect of new unit would disentitle assessee from claiming deduction - Held, no - Whether assessee could be said to be engaged in manufacture - Held, yes - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction - Held, yes

V. Section  80-IC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deductions -  Special provisions in respect of certain undertakings or enterprises in certain special category States (Computation of deduction) - Assessment years 2012-13 and 2013-14 - Assessee-company had claimed deduction under section 80 - IC in respect of profits of its Baddi unit including income arising from sale of scrap - Assessing Officer questioned allowability of deduction on such income and called upon assessee to justify its inclusion in eligible profits for purpose of deduction under section 80 - IC - It was noted that assessee had duly explained that scrap was a by-product arising directly from manufacturing process undertaken at Baddi unit, and thus formed an integral part of its business receipts - Assessee had consistently included such scrap income as part of eligible profits for deduction under section 80 - IC in preceding years - Whether therefore, scrap income was derived from industrial undertaking and eligible for deduction under section 80 - IC - Held, yes [Para 9.4] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee-company while computing profits derived from its two new industrial undertakings claimed deduction under section 80HH, including marketing receipts and interest which was derived from marketing activities carried on by it - Whether since marketing activities carried on by assessee were independent of activities of industrial undertaking, in such circumstances, amount of marketing receipts and interest could not be included for purpose of computing deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

Sections 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings, etc. in backward areas - Three units belonging to assessee were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges - Further, assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets for each unit - Whether barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes and, therefore, barytes powder is an article produced from barytes - Held, yes - Whether sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate division of profits and gains in respect of a unit and Assessing Officer may compute such profits and gains under section 80HH on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit - Held, yes - Whether when industrial units satisfied other critiera laid down under sections 80HH and 80-I, assessee was entitled to deduction - Held, yes

Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings (Manufacture) - Assessee was engaged in activity of segregation and processing of metal scrap - Assessee's claim for deduction under section 80-IB was rejected by Assessing Officer holding that activities undertaken by assessee did not amount to manufacturing activity - Tribunal, however, allowed assessee's claim - Whether in view of fact that assessee put imported scrap to series of manual and mechanical processes and thereby brought into existence entirely new, distinct and different commodities which were marketable, Tribunal rightly concluded that said process amounted to 'manufacturing' and, therefore, assessee's claim for deduction was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 20] [In favour of assessee]IT: Where assessee put imported scrap to series of manual and mechanical processes and thereby brought into existence entirely new and distinct commodity which was marketable, it was to be regarded as 'manufacturing' activity and, thus, assessee's claim for deduction under section 80-IB was to be allowed

Section 80HH, read with section 32A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of certain incomes of hotels or industries in backward areas - Assessment year 1978-79 - Assessee-firm took over assets of a firm which carried on business of selling diesel engines in a backward area -Assessee-firm subsequently purchased machinery for manufacturing fuel injection pipes for diesel engines by making nipples and giving shapes at both ends of tubes which were used as raw material in process and claimed deduction under section 80HH - Whether unit of assessee having new machinery amounted to 'industrial undertaking' and process of making fuel injection pipes amounted to manufacture so as to make assessee eligible for deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1980-81 - Assessee, engaged in business of centrifuging rubber latex, claimed deduction under section 80HH - ITO rejected claim on the ground that assessee was not an industrial company manufacturing or producing any article or thing - Whether centrifuging process could be said to have resulted in manufacture or production of a marketable commodity and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH of the Act - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc., in backward areas - Whether where income from industrial undertaking was only source of income of assessee, unexplained cash credits could be treated as profits of industrial undertaking for purpose of computation of deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I - Held, yes - Whether assessee will be entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I even if part of production process is got done by third parties - Held, yes

Section 80-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from infrastructure undertakings - Assessment year 1997-98 - Assessee had a factory in a backward area where it produced automobile filter elements which were further used for manufacture of automobile filters by an automobile manufacturer - Assessee's claim for deduction under section 80-IA was disallowed on ground that process carried out by it did not yield commercially any new or different commodity - On appeal, Tribunal discussed nature of raw materials used by assessee and applying well-known test, recorded a finding that process undertaken by assessee involved manufacture - It, therefore, allowed assessee's claim for deductions under section 80-IA - Whether any substantial question of law did arise from Tribunal's order - Held, no

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits of new industrial undertaking in backward areas - Whether processing of raw seeds whereby seeds which can be consumed by human beings and animals, after being subjected to process, are no longer edible and can be used only for cultivation, amounts to manufacture for purpose of claiming deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture and sale of portable gensets and water pumps - It imported certain spare parts and components and additionally imported gensets of a certain capacity which were not being manufactured in India - Assessee claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I - Assessing Officer disallowed claim in respect of profits earned from both sale of spare parts and components as well as sale of imported gensets on ground that profits therefrom could not be considered to be income derived from activity of industrial undertaking which was manufacture of gensets - Whether Assessing Officer was justified - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1991-92 - Whether if a new industrial undertaking fulfils conditions laid down in sections 80HH and 80-I, deduc-tions are permissible under both sections - Held, yes - Whether where on 
 same set of facts, revenue authorities in later years allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to a factory treating it as new industrial undertaking, deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I could be denied in relevant assessment year on ground that said factory was not new industrial undertaking - Held, no - Whether for claiming deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I, it is necessary to manufacture a product different from products which assessee was already manufacturing - Held, no

III. Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1995-96 - Whether where freight-collection was at par with job work receipts and was part and parcel of operation of business of assessee and connected to priority industry of assessee, assessee was entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on freight collection on depot sales - Held, yes

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95 - Whether assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80HH in respect of interest recovered from debtors for late payment of sale price, interest received from bank on deposits pledged with it for obtaining letter of credit/bank guarantee, interest received from IDBI on deposits pledged with it as required under section 32AB, interest from sarafi and bank deposits out of initial/surplus funds, insurance claim receipts for reimbursement of losses, interest from bank on short-term loans and interest on fixed deposits with banks, interest from Electricity Board from electricity deposit, dividend income, income from hire charges and interest on income-tax refund - Held, yes - Whether as far as sale of spare parts and of raw material and other misc. receipts is concerned, if it was a sale as an ‘after sale service’ condition or sale is of own manufactured spare parts or receipt has arisen in course of manufacture or production, it would be income derived from industrial undertaking; on other hand, if it is an independent activity not conditioned to sale or manufacture or production, it would not be an income derived from industrial undertaking even though it might be income attributable to industrial undertaking - Held, yes

Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings [Manufacture] - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with help of machines and then end product was rubber crumb, which was sold to tyre manufacturing company - It claimed deduction under section 80-IB - Whether assessee was engaged in manufacturing of rubber crumb and hence eligible to deduction under section 80-IB - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with help of machines and then end product was rubber crumb, assessee was engaged in manufacturing of rubber crumb and hence eligible to deduction under section 80-IB

II. Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings (Sale of scrap) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Whether deduction under section 80-IB is given on profits derived from manufacturing process, being undertaken by assessee which qualify for deduction - Held, yes - Whether where assessee set up an industrial undertaking for purpose of manufacture of steel forging, transmission gears and part and accessories of motor vehicles, receipts of sale of scrap being part and parcel of activity of manufacturing of forging items and being proximate thereto would be within ambit of 'profits derived from industrial undertaking' for purpose of computing deduction under section 80-IB - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

V. Section  80-IC  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 – Deductions – Special provisions in respect of certain undertakings or enterprises in certain special category States (Scrap income) – Assessment years  2014-15 to 2016-17  – Assessee-company included scrap income generated by its eligible manufacturing undertaking at Baddi while computing deduction under section 80-IC – Assessing Officer held that scrap income did not constitute profits derived from industrial undertaking and excluded same from eligible profits – It was noted that generation of scrap was an inevitable incident of manufacturing process and identical issue stood covered in favour of assessee by decisions rendered in assessee's own case for earlier years – Whether scrap income generated during manufacturing operations of eligible industrial undertaking formed an integral part of profits derived from such undertaking, generation of scrap being an inevitable incident of manufacturing activity – Held, yes – Whether, therefore, deduction under section 80-IC was allowable in respect of scrap income earned by eligible industrial undertaking – Held, yes [Paras 116, 123 and 127] [In favour of assessee]

Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1993-94 - Whether only that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with industrial undertaking, will be taken into consideration for calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I - Held, yes - Whether where main business of assessee was to manufacture and sell soyabeen oil, income earned by assessee from sale of old gunny bags could be treated as an income earned from industrial undertaking within meaning of section 80HH/80-I - Held, no

Section 80-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from Industrial undertakings, etc., after certain dates/infrastructure undertakings (Manufacture) - Assessment year 1997-98 - Assessee, a private limited company, was repairing and manufacturing transformers - It claimed 100 per cent deduction in respect of transformer oil, scrap and labour charges for sale of scrap - Transformer oil had been purchased by assessee from market and centrifuging i.e., processing, had been done by centrifugal machine in order to make it usable in transformer - In substance, no new articles or things had emerged from said processing, but only some special processing or treatment had been given to transformer oil through a particular method and, thus, it was a sort of processing only and could not be termed as manufacture of centrifuged transformer oil - Whether since there was no change in substance and no new article had come out, assessee was not entitled deduction under section 80-IA - Held, yes [Paras 26 and 27] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where transformer oil had been purchased by assessee from market and centrifuging i.e., processing had been done by centrifugal machine in order to make it usable in transformer and no articles or things had emerged from said processing, assessee was not entitled to benefits of 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - New industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether assessee’s claim, that technical service charges representing cost of the ‘brain’ - Component of electric typewriter manufactured by it, though billed separately for purposes of excise duty, was to be included as part of profit of undertaking for deduction under section 80HH, had to be allowed -Held, yes.

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1982-83 - Whether sales of waste material, export incentive, duty drawback and import licence premium shall have also to be included in profits of business for computing deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes.

Section 80J, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertaking , ships or hotels - Assessment year 1987-88 - Assessee-firm carried on business of manufacturing water/air pollution control plant at site of its customers, and its claim for deductions under sections 80J and 80HH was being allowed since its inception - Whether assessee was an industrial undertaking, engaged in manufacturing or producing an article in shape of air/water control plant in a backward area, and Commissioner committed an error in setting aside Assessing Officer’s order allowing deductions under sections 80J and 80HH - Held, yes - Whether since very year of inception of assessee’s business, position had continuously remained same and in absence of any new fact coming to his knowledge or any separate enquiry having been made, it was permissible for Commissioner to start afresh from admitted position of parties on a particular point - Held, no

II. Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee was generating and selling electricity - Assessee's claim for deduction under section 80-IB was disallowed in respect of receipt by way of sale of scrap and credit balances written off on ground that said income could not be said to have been derived from business of generation of power - It was noted from records that each and every item of credit balances written back and sale of scrap had not been examined by revenue authorities to ascertain as to whether those items had any direct link with business operation of assessee's industrial undertaking - Whether in aforesaid circumstances, matter was to be restored back to file of Assessing Officer for his fresh adjudication after examining all details thereof - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1977-78 - Whether assessee buying shrimps, peeling them and freezing them could be said to be engaged in manufacture or production, in absence of material on record to indicate what was done by assessee and how it was done, so as to eligible for allowance under section 80HH - Held, no

Section 80HH,  read with section 32A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1994-95 - Whether, in order to constitute an industrial undertaking, be it under section 32A or under section 80HH, important criterion to be applied by Assessing Officer is to identify item in question, process undertaken by it and resultant output - Held, yes - During relevant assessment year, assessee-hospital having made investment in plant and machinery, claimed deduction under section 80HH - Assessing Officer rejected assessee's claim holding that it was not an industrial undertaking - Commissioner (Appeals) as well as Tribunal allowed assessee's claim - Whether since there was no identification of items installed in hospital by Tribunal, it was not possible to express any opinion as to whether assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, matter was to be remitted to Tribunal for deciding case de novo in accordance with law - Held, yes

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether assessee carrying on business of ship breaking could be said to be an industrial undertaking so as to be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes.

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether there must be, for application of words 'derived from' as used in section 80HH, a direct nexus between profits and gains and industrial undertaking - Held, yes - Assessee industrial undertaking exported processed sea food and under Export Promotion Scheme was entitled to import entitlements which it could sell - Whether receipt from sale of import entitlement could not constitute profit and gain derived from assessee's undertaking and same could not be included in income of assessee for computing deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether assessee carrying on business of ship breaking could be said to be an industrial undertaking so as to be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

Section 80HHA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether activity of breaking or dismantling a ship or ships can be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactures or produces articles so as to be entitled to get deduction under sections 80HHA and 80-I - Held, no

Section 80HH, read with  section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1979-80 and 1980-81 - Whether business of tyre retreading does not amount to production of new article entitling assessee to relief under sections 80HH and 80J - Held, yes

Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee's industrial undertaking was set up for purpose of manufacture of steel, forging, transmission gears and parts, and accessories of motor vehicles - It claimed deduction under section 80-IB on its gross receipts which, apart from goods sales, also included scrap sales, labour charges and job work charges - Assessing Officer held that deduction under section 80-IB could not be permitted on sale of scrap, job work and labour charges as same were not derived from assessee's industrial undertaking - Whether activity of forging undertaken by assessee was 'manufacturing' within ambit of section 80-IB and when assessee was entitled to claim exemption in respect of income derived from such processes doing for itself, there was no reason to deny deduction on job work charges and labour charges merely because raw material component was being supplied by other customers for whom assessee was doing job - Held, yes - Whether since manufacturing activity of type of material being undertaken by assessee would also generate scrap in process of manufacturing receipts of sale of scrap being part and parcel of activity and being proximate thereto would also be within ambit of gains derived from industrial undertaking for purpose of computing deduction under section 80-IB - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with  section 80J, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits of new industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment years 1983-84 and 1984-85 - Whether amounts of cash assistance, duty drawback as also value of import licence nomination, can be taken as profits derived from industrial undertaking for purpose of determining amount in respect of which deduction under section 80HH could be allowed - Held, no

III. Section  80-IB , read with sections  80-IC  and  80-IE , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deductions  -  Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings (Sale of scrap/empty containers)  - Assessment years  2013-14 and 2015-16 to 2017-18  - Assessee had multiple eligible units claiming deduction under sections 80IB/80IC/80IE and earned receipts from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing - AO held such receipts were merely incidental, not profits derived from eligible undertakings, and excluded them while computing deductions - CIT(A), noting that scrap and empty containers arose from manufacturing process of eligible units and following Tribunal’s orders in assessee’s own case for earlier years, allowed receipts as part of eligible profits - Whether since revenue had not brought on record any material demonstrating a change either in factual matrix or in legal position prevailing during year under consideration, impugned order of CIT(A) allowing deduction under sections 80IB, 80IC and 80IE in respect of profits arising from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing process was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 9.7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas (Condition precedent) - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether what becomes entitled to claim exemption under section 80HH is an industrial undertaking and once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial whether it is manufacturing, or producing or processing - Held, yes - Whether assessee, an industrial undertaking engaged in activity of converting cotton pieces known as cops into yarn, would be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]IT : Once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial for purpose of allowing deduction under section 80HH whether it is manufacturing or producing or processing

Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1988-89 and 1989-90 - Whether, where assessee was engaged in business of fire works on job work basis and was supplied with raw materials by its customers and had engaged 200 labourers for producing end- product of crackers, it could be said that assessee had satisfied test of manufacturer as well as an industrial undertaking - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with sections 80AB and 260A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Newly established industrial undertakings or hotels in backward areas - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee-company had two separate units, one of which showed profits while other incurred losses - Claim of assessee-company for deduction under section 80HH with reference to profits of particular unit without setting off loss of other unit was rejected by Assessing Officer by recomputing deduction with reference to net profit after setting off loss in question - Whether deduction contemplated is to be allowed with reference to particular industrial undertaking and not with reference to total income of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in accepting assessee's claim and no substantial question of law arose from its order - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of newly established industrial undertaking in backward areas - Whether assessee engaged in business of rearing and development of chicks into broilers, could be said to be 'manufacturing' a product - Held, no

facts.text:
The assessee-company, carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc., set-up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH in respect of profit on sale of scrap which resulted in the manufacturing process. The ITO disallowed that claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim. On further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order.

On reference :

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

The assessee-company, an industrial undertaking, had claimed deduction under section 80HH on sale of scrap. The Assessing Officer held that the deduction could be available only on the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and not from income incidental to the activity of industrial undertaking. Therefore, for the purpose of determining the deduction, the income shown from sale of scrap should be excluded. In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the generation of scrap was independent to manufacturing activity and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim of deduction under section 80HH and the action of the Assessing Officer was confirmed.

On second appeal :

The assessee established three industrial units in backward areas. The units were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges. The Assessing Officer held that mere crushing of barytes was not a manufacturing activity nor the powder produced could be called a new article. He further found that the assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets in respect of each unit. He, therefore, disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal found that the barytes powder so produced got its marketability for its use for the purposes totally different from that of barytes. It further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no division of account, still they were entitled for the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I as having satisfied the conditions laid down thereunder.

On reference :

While computing deduction under section 80HH, the Assessing Officer excluded income from the sale of scrap by xerographic equipment unit and toner, developer, photocopier unit holding that income from the scrap could not be said to be income derived from the industrial undertaking.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to take income from sale of scrap as income derived from industrial undertaking.

The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee-company, which was retreader and established its plant in a backward area, claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80J. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article and that, therefore, the assessee was entitled to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference:

The assessee had set up a small-scale industrial unit in the backward industrial area. It was the case of the assessee that it purchased tea leaves powder/granules and dispatched same to the blend master, who after going through his own process, suggested the mixing ratio and process of mixing for making the perfect blend of tea, and the activity of blending of different types of leaves obtained from different gardens in a definite ratio resulted in production of a commodity having its own identity and though it might not amount to manufacture, it amounted to production. Therefore, it being an industrial undertaking set up in the backward industrial area and fulfilling all other conditions, was entitled to avail the benefit of deduction under section 80-IA/80-IB. The Assessing Officer, by holding that even after blending, tea remained tea and blending did not bring out a distinct marketable commodity and it did not amount to manufacture or production of article or thing for the purpose of claiming benefit of deduction under section 80-IA/80-IB, disallowed the claim of the assessee.

On appeal :

■

The assessee had claimed deduction under section 80-IC in respect of the profits of its Baddi Unit, including income arising from sale of scrap.

■

The Assessing Officer held that the income from scrap was merely incidental or ancillary in nature, not forming a core part of the manufacturing operation. He, thus, disallowed the claim of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), directed deletion of the disallowance, holding that the scrap income was derived from the industrial undertaking and eligible for deduction under section 80-IC.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee-company claimed relief under section 80HH in respect of the profits of a new industrial undertaking in backward area in the assessment year 1974-75. The said profits, it claimed, were to be arrived at without deduction of development rebate. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee's plea and his order was confirmed by the appellate authority and the Tribunal.

On appeal under section 260A :

The assessee-company was carrying on the business of manufacture of tyres and tubes. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I in respect of profit derived from factory No. III. The Assessing Officer allowed the claim after being satisfied that the conditions laid down in sections 80HH and 80-I were fulfilled by the assessee. However, the Commissioner, in exercise of his power under section 263, directed the Assessing Officer to withdraw relief allowed under sections 80HH and 80-I holding that the undertaking situated in the backward area was not entitled to simultaneous reliefs under two sections, i.e., 80HH and 80-I; that although in the impugned assessment, the Assessing Officer had made addition on account of understatement of sale of tyres to close business associate, yet he accepted the working of profits of the new industrial undertaking as made by the assessee which resulted in determination of excessive profit relatable to eligible undertaking; that the assessee was already in the business of manufacture of tyres and tubes for the past several years and, therefore, the third unit could not be said to be newly established industrial undertaking qualifying for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I; and that no deduction was permissible under sections 80HH and 80-I in view of the inadequacy of the profits of the said industrial undertaking.

The assessee's industrial undertaking was set up for the purpose of manufacture of steel, forging, transmission gears and parts, and accessories of motor vehicles. During the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under section 80-IB on its gross receipts which, apart from goods sales, also included scrap sales, labour charges and job work charges. The Assessing Officer held that the deduction under section 80-IB could not be allowed on sale of scrap, job work and labour charges as the same were attributable to the business carried on by the assessee, but not derived from the profits of industrial undertaking. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed deduction under section 80-IB on the scrap sales holding that the scrap generation at various stages of manufacturing process was part of the manufacturing activity of an industrial unit and, thus, profits and gains derived on that account were from the industrial undertaking. However, with regard to the claim of deduction on job work and labour charges, the Commissioner (Appeals) disallowed the appeal of the assessee and held that the job charges and labour charges not derived from the exports, were to be categorized as independent income and had to be deducted from gross profits to calculate profits derived from the exports. On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed deduction under section 80-IB on job work charges and labour charges also holding that job works/labour charges income received by the assessee, by utilizing its plant and machinery installed in the undertaking, gave rise to income which had a direct nexus with the assessee's industrial undertaking, and, thus, was entitled to claim of deduction under section 80-IB.

The sale of scrap generated in the printing work was a result of the main work of printing and had to be treated as a profit derived from an industrial undertaking. The earning of those receipts had a near and proximate nexus with that of the industrial undertaking.
