On reference:

The assessee-company, engaged in the manufacture of cooling towers, had set-up one unit at ‘O’ in the year 1985 for manufacturing of certain components required for round bottle (RB series) cool- ing towers. During the financial year 1991-92, the assessee had set-up a new unit at ‘C’ in order to revamp its business activities and ente- red into collaboration agreement with a foreign company ‘G’ and obtained technical know-how for making ‘cross flow’ (XE series) and ‘counter flow’ (CM series) cooling towers. The assessee had also closed down its original unit situated at ‘O’ during the year 1992 and plant and machinery and moulds from the ‘O’ unit were transferred to the new unit at ‘C’. As per the assessee the total extent of such items transferred was 11.60 per cent of the total investment in new plant in terms of cost and 0.63 per cent in terms of WDV. Most of the employees of the old unit were also transferred to the new unit and certain new employees were also recruited. The assessee thereafter started manufacturing in the new unit, certain components required for cooling towers, i.e., RB series, XE series and CM series. The modus operandi of the assessee in carrying out business was that on receipt of enquiries from the clients, it designed the cooling tower as per requirement of the clients and the quotations were forwarded to the clients along with detailed analysis of the said towers. The assessee on receipt of the orders from the clients manufactured the basic compo-nents required for the said cooling towers in its unit and certain items/components like electric motors, fans, etc., were purchased from the market. As per the assessee, these items were tested and checked in the factory of the assessee. The said components, i.e., manufactured and bought out items were transferred to the site of the customers and two separate invoices were prepared, one for in-house manufactured components on which excise duty was paid and another for the bought out components and, accordingly, the sales were shown under the head ‘Manufactured items and bought out components’. The assembly of the unit and erection of the same was carried out at the customer’s site and the assessee in addition raised the bill for installation charges, forwarding charges and service charges, which were booked under the respective heads in the books of account. For the relevant assessment years, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80-IA on the total turnover of the manufactured items during the year, including sale of bought out components, installation charges, forwarding charges and service charges. The Assessing Officer held that the new unit set-up by the assessee manufactured the items required for XE and CM type cooling towers only and the machinery, which had been shifted from the old unit, manufactured the parts required for round bottle cooling towers; and that since the moulds required for manufacturing the round bottle and CM/XE type cooling towers were independent and totally different and the assessee started manufacturing both under one roof for the sake of convenience and the old equipment was acquired in the year 1985 while the new equipment was purchased in 1992, the profits arising from the sale of items manufactured by the assessee for round bottle cooling towers were not eligible for deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer further held that bought out components purchased by the assessee from the market were never integrated at the assessee’s factory into the cooling tower and tested and, therefore, the assessee was not manufacturing the cooling tower but manufacturing only certain parts required for cooling towers and assembling the cooling tower at the clients’ place as per the requirement of the clients. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the profit earned by the assessee on the bought out components did not have any nexus with the manufacturing activity carried out by the assessee in its factory and the said profit could not be treated as profits of industrial undertaking for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer in respect of the forwarding charges, installation charges and service charges held that the assessee had incurred expenditure on account of transport, labour charges both for loading/unloading and assembling, which were not adjusted against the receipts and, therefore, all these charges did not have any connection with the manufacturing activity of the assessee and, accordingly, the profit earned by the assessee on the said charges was not eligible for deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA only in respect of profits arising from sale of components manufactured by the assessee required for XE and CM cooling towers. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the impugned order.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company, a small-scale industrial undertaking, was carrying on the business of manufacturing ‘Jarda’ from raw tobacco in a backward area. The processing operations employed by the assessee were that raw tobacco (angad) was stripped off the midrib by manual labour. It was then sand-screened to control the moisture content. The raw tobacco was fed into a vibratory feeder and it was conveyed into a pneumatic pick up duct where heavy stems and stones would drop down. In the pick up duct, the tobacco was lifted up by suction and discharged into first tower classifier. In this tower classifier, the heavier tobacco flakes were separated from lighter ones and left behind. The lighter flakes were carried by air into second tower classifier. Here, the tobacco dust and flakes were differentiated. Finally, the lamina was sent to a sleeve chamber where it was cut and graded to suit the requirement of beedi manufacturer. The pure tobacco flakes came out after the dust was sucked out in the dust collecting unit. The end-product was called ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’. The assessee claimed reliefs under sections 32A, 80HH and 80-I for the assessment years 1984-85 and 1985-86. The assessee also claimed that it should be charged at a concessional rate treating it as an industrial company as defined under section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1985. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claims on the ground that the assessee was not manufacturing or producing any article or any thing. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance.

On second appeal:

The assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with the help of machines and then the end product was rubber crumb, which was sold to the tyre manufacturing company. It claimed deduction under section 80-IB.

The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) disallowed the claim of deduction.

On second appeal, the Tribunal found that the end product of the assessee was different from its raw material and secondly it was commercially known to be different in the market. It, therefore, held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IB.

On appeal to High Court:

The assessee was a manufacturer of commutators. It also manufactured certain goods on sub-contract basis for others and received services/job charges and besides receipts from sale of copper scrap. They claimed deduction under section 80HHC including the said receipts. The assessing authority held that the receipts from the sub-contract receipts and scrap fell within the Explanation ( baa) to section 80HHC and, therefore, the same could not be included. Aggrieved by the said order, the assessee preferred an appeal. The appellate authority held that as there was a direct nexus between the receipts from special contract as well as sale of scrap material, it did not fall within the Explanation ( baa) and the assessee was entitled to include the said receipts in the income from the business and profits. The revenues appeal to the Tribunal came to be dismissed.

The assessee-company was an ‘industrial undertaking’ engaged in the manufacturing activity of de-humidifiers. During the course of such activity, the assessee had made earnings on account of engineering designing fee which was related only to the articles manufactured and produced by it and not for professional advice to others. The Tribunal allowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80-I on such earnings. The Tribunal had also allowed benefit of section 80-I on income derived from rent, interest, scrap, difference in exchange rate, etc.

On application under section 256(2) :

During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noticed that the scrap sale declared by the assessee of the packing material was out of the manufacturing activity and therefore, the same was business receipt and accordingly, he disallowed said amount while computing amount of deduction under section 80-IC.

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the revenue received from the sale of the scrap material would reduce the sale consideration/cost of raw material and therefore it would reduce the profit of the undertaking. It was held that there was a direct nexus between the sale activities and the profit from the eligible business. He thus set aside disallowance made by Assessing Officer.

The revenue filed instant appeal contending that the first degree nexus was not with respect to amount received from the sale of scrap and therefore, it was not the part of the manufacturing activities of the assessee. The revenue relied upon the judgment of the High Court of Madras in the case of CIT v. Shiva Distilleries Ltd.[2007] 293 ITR 108.

The assessee ran a cold storage and had claimed that it was an industrial undertaking in a backward area and since it had satisfied all the conditions laid down in section 80HH(2), it was entitled to the benefit of the aforesaid section. The ITO rejected its claim as according to him the assessee was not engaged in the manufacture of articles and hence the necessary conditions were not satisfied and, therefore, the claim could not be allowed. On appeal, the Commissioner upheld the order of the assessing authority, which order had been confirmed in further appeal by the Tribunal.

On reference :

The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of Single Super Phosphate (SSP) fertiliser. The Assessing Officer dis- allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on enhanced income by way of excessive subsidy showing bogus purchases and sales in its books of account as it was not earned out of the industrial activities carried out by the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On second appeal, however, the Tribunal held that if an assessee is found to have involved itself in earning unaccounted money, it cannot be held disentitled from claiming the other statutory benefits which are available to it at that time for its carrying on the business in the backward area.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of portable generators sets. While completing the assessments, the Assessing Officer noted that the turnover of the industrial undertaking included sale of imported spare parts and tools and imported portable generating sets. He held that the profits earned on those items could not be considered eligible for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I, as it could not be said that same were derived from the industrial undertaking as required by the sections. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I in respect of the profits from the sale of the spare parts and components and disallowed deduction in respect of the profits from the sale of the imported gensets.

On cross appeal :

The assessee, a leading manufacturer of moulded luggage under the brand name of ‘VIP’, had set up a new industrial undertaking in addition to the existing undertaking for manufacturing some moulded luggage by installing new machines. The installed capacity for manufacturing moulded luggage, consequent to the installation of the new machines had substantially increased and its production had also increased as a result of increase on the investment and thus, the assessee claimed benefit under section 80-I. The claim was rejected by Assessing Officer on the ground that the action of installing a new capacity by purchasing new machines was merely an expansion of the existing unit and no expansion of the existing unit and no new industrial undertaking came into existence. It was further held that no new product was manufactured in the new industrial undertaking and the assessee was simply manufacturing old type of luggage. Therefore, the Assessing Officer came to the conclusion that the action of the assessee in installing new machinery in different years was only with a view to expansion of the existing industrial capacity and no new industrial undertaking came into existence for which deduction under section 80-I was admissible and this view was upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On second appeal :

The assessee furnished details of installation of the injection moulding machines indicating the capacity in metric tonnes and number of machines installed and the value in rupees and contended that the assessee had in fact installed a new industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80-I, and it was entitled to the permissible deduction.

held.text:
Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

While giving the relief under section 80HH, value of closing stock of scrap would also have to be included. The sale proceeds of drums used for storing water and which had become useless could not, however, be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manufactur-ing activity in which the assessee was involved. This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

Section 80HH is meant to give a tax rebate to certain categories of assessees and one, who wants to claim such a relief, must strictly satisfy the requirements prescribed therein. He must establish that his profits and gains are derived from his industrial undertaking or the business of hotel. Axiomatic proposition of law is that it is not sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits earned and the industrial undertaking and the law requires that such profits must have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The industrial undertaking itself must be the source of that profit. The business of the industrial undertaking must strictly yield that profit. It must be the direct source of profit and not a means to earn any other profit.

In the instant case, in the industrial undertaking for the manufacture of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products, certain scrap materials resulted, which had a saleable value. To say that the scrap materials had no direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking, could not at all be expected to commend acceptance, especially, on the facts and in the circumstances of the instant case. The scrap materials came within the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking in the manufacture of certain products such as V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and certain rubber moulded products, etc. In that view of the matter, profits and gains from the sale of scrap materials were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, inasmuch as such gains or profits were derived from the industrial undertaking and includible in the gross total income of the assessee and the question relatable to the profit on the sale of scrap was answered in favour of the assessee.

Section 80HH provides for deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas subject to fulfilment of the conditions specified therein. The authorities had not come to the conclusion that the assessee did not fulfil the said conditions, as in view of their decision, the said question did not arise for consideration. The Tribunal, proceeded on the basis that the end-product of the assessee would not be an article.

An article would, inter alia, mean a particular object or substance, a material, thing or a class of things, material or tangible object.

Nobody manufactures a dam or a tunnel. A dam or tunnel is constructed, but the question, which arose for consideration, was although a tunnel or a dam would not be an article, which is capable of being manufactured, but whether the intermediate products may be considered to come within the purview of manufacturing activity/industrial undertaking within the meaning thereof. The question, which had not been gone into by the Tribunal was, if at all the gross total income of assessee included any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking, by reason of manufacture of intermediate product and not necessarily end-product, whether the benefit under the aforementioned provisions could be derived by the assessee-company.

Section 80J provides for deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established undertakings or ships or hotel business in certain cases. Sub-section (4) of the said section declares that the same would apply to any industrial undertaking, which fulfils the conditions laid down therein; clause (iii) whereof refers to manufacture or production of articles.

Section 32A refers to an investment allowance, inter alia, in respect of a plant specified in sub-section (2) thereof, which is owned by the assessee and is wholly used for the purpose of business carried on by him, whereas clause (a) of sub-section (2) lays down a qualification to the effect that the assessee should be engaged in the business of operation of ships or aircraft; no such qualification has been laid down in clause (b) thereof. Sub-clause (iii) of clause (b ) of section 32A refers to any other industrial undertaking for the purpose of business of construction, manufacture or production of any article or thing, not being an article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule. The said provision refers to construction and not to a construction company. It categorically refers to manufacture or production.

The question as to whether the companies, which undertake such composite business of manufacturing and constructions are entitled to the benefits of the aforementioned provisions in the light of the decisions relied upon by assessee was essentially question of fact which had not been considered by the Tribunal. It mainly proceeded on the basis of the end-product doctrine.

In the instant case, the assessee had not claimed benefit in respect of the entire profit earned by it, but was only asking for the relief to the extent to which it would have otherwise been entitled to, had it been held to be an ‘industrial company’ for the purpose of manufacture of the intermediate products, which it was required to manufacture for the purpose of utilization thereof in construction of dams and tunnels, etc. Therefore, it was obligatory on the part of the department to go into the said question. Such question was specifically raised by the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) as also before the Tribunal, but the same had not been considered in its proper perspective.

Having regard to the fact that the question as to whether the assessee was an ‘industrial company’ or not itself had been directed to be determined by the Assessing Officer by the Tribunal, the matter required fresh consideration at the hands of the Tribunal.

The decision of the Apex Court as also the other High Courts must, therefore, be considered while taking into the account the fact situation obtaining in each case. The interest of justice would be sub-served if the contention of the parties, which was the crux of the matter, to the effect that whether in relation to the intermediate products, the assessee-company fulfilled the criteria of ‘an industrial undertaking or not’ should be determined by the Tribunal in the light of the observations made herein before and on the basis thereof necessary reliefs could be granted in terms thereof.

EDITOR’S NOTE

Following the decision of I.T.C. No. 5 of 1998 in Hydel Construction (P.) Ltd. v. CIT, it was held that it would be appropriate to direct the Tribunal to re-hear the appeal and to find out, on facts, as to whether or not 51 per cent of the total income was attributable to manufacturing, processing and mining activities.

Like in section 33, so also in section 80HH, the word 'manufacture' or 'produce' appear. While both the words appear in clause (i ) of sub-section (2) of section 80HH only the word 'manufacturing' appears in clause (iv ) of that sub-section. The benefit of section 80HH is available whenever anew industrial undertaking is started in a backward area and that undertaking begins to manufacture or produce articles. The facts that section 80HH(2)(iv ) refers to the manufacturing process alone does not mean that production process is excluded. Every manufacturing process naturally involves production process for the object of manufacture is the production of goods.

It processed or frozen fish and fish products can be regarded as articles manufactured or produced' for the purpose of the development rebate, it was the Legislature intent to attribute the same meaning to the identical expression appearing in another provision of the same statute, the object of which is to confer a benefit in the newly established industrial undertaking with a view to the advancement of the backward areas. In the instant case, the Tribunal understood the various stages through which prawns were prepared for export and held that process involved production or manufacture. Therefore, its finding was not perverse and was perfectly in harmony with the Legislature intent as disclosed by the scheme of the relevant provision of the statute. Hence, the assessee was rightly allowed the deduction under section 80HH.

P.K.R. Menon for the Applicant. G. Sivarajan for the Respondent.

and judgments of the Tribunal and keeping in view the findings recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals), it could be concluded in the instant case that the deposits given by the assessee were out of business compulsion and the interest earned thereon, even though not derived from industrial undertaking, was having direct and proximate connection with the business of industrial undertaking of the assessee. The assessee was, therefore, eligible for deduction under section 80-IA on the interest earning. [Para 15] Further, the assessee was under compulsion to provide such deposits for availing the financial assistance for running its industrial undertaking on which the assessee, in turn, had paid substantial interest. The interest payment during the year was much more than the interest received. With regard to the proposition of netting off the interest, when profit is determined under the head ‘Profits and gains of business or profession’, what are included in it are the net receipts/payments of the various components that go to make the profit under that head. Thus, if the profits of business include certain receipts which have corresponding costs, or if the profits include certain credits and the business has also debits of the same nature and, if these are not netted out against each other, the profit of business will present a distorted picture and may lead to injustice while implementing an incentive provision. In the instant case, the receipt and payment of interest being of the same geneses, the interest earning had merely gone to reduce the net interest burden of the assessee-company. Thus, in effect, there was no income on account of interest included in the profits of the business of industrial undertaking, so no reduction whatsoever was called for while computing deduction under section 80-IA. While computing profit of the business of an industrial undertaking under section 80-IA, revenue receipts can be adjusted against revenue expenditure of the like nature. In the instant case, revenue receipt in the form of interest went to reduce the revenue expenditure of interest, because funds were borrowed for the purpose of business of industrial undertaking and funds were kept in deposit for the purpose of business of the assessee’s industrial undertaking. Thus, interest income or expenditure was inextricably linked and was having direct and proximate connection with the business of industrial undertaking. [Para 16]

In view of the above and keeping in view the findings recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals), there was no reason to interfere with his order. [Para 19]

In respect of other miscellaneous income, arising from sale of empty drums/containers and sale of useless materials,all the sale proceeds were only out of the business of industrial undertaking of the assessee. Therefore, even for determining the profits and gains ‘derived from any business of industrial undertaking’, manufacturing or producing any article or thing includes sale proceeds of such article or thing or scrap generated during the course of such manufacturing activity which amounts to increase in the sale consideration. After all what is to be determined is the profits and gains of business of industrial undertaking and there is no warrant to stop for the above purpose at sale of main products only. The controversy was not when manufacturing activity of the assessee was over, but what was the profit and gains of the business of the industrial undertaking and how was it to be determined. For determining the profits of business of industrial undertaking, it was not possible to ignore the said sales which were closely and directly connected with the outcome of the manufacturing process itself. Thus, there was a direct nexus between the sale of those items and carrying on of the business of industrial undertaking. [Para 20]

In the result, all the appeals of the revenue were to be dismissed. [Para 21]

The undisputed facts of the instant case were that the assessee purchased potable spirit from the distilleries as per agreement. This potable spirit was already manufactured and did not require any further manufacturing. Only some processing was required to produce IMFLs like brandy, whisky and rum etc. by adding certain percentage of water, colour, essence and, for safe marketing, required bottling. Generally manufacturing means consumption of one article for production of another. But, in the instant case, no article or thing was consumed for production of another. Alcohol remained alcohol. There was only reduction of degree of alcohol content because of addition of water to potable alcohol and stirring it. This action at best could be said to be processing and not manufacturing. There should also be transformation of article or thing if manufacturing is involved for the same. But, in the instant case no such transformation had taken place as alcohol remained alcohol both in the beginning and after processing also. In case of manufacturing also, article or thing should be distinct and separate. In the instant case, no new product had come as a by-product which could be said to be distinct and separate from the original one and alcohol remained alcohol with reduced content of alcohol because of the addition of water. There was also no change in its basic identity. Generally in case of manufacturing there will be change which is considerable and substantial but in the instant case it was not so. In order to encourage industrial activity in backward areas, section 80HH grants deduction to an assessee, whose total income includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking (other than a mining undertaking) or the business of a hotel in a notified backward area. Section 80GG(1) defines the word 'derived' from an industrial undertaking. The meaning of the term 'derived' has been construed to have a definite narrow and restrictive meaning compared to the word 'attributable' or 'referable to'. The industrial undertaking must itself be the source of the profits and gains and it would not be sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits and gains earned and the industrial undertaking. From section 80HH(2) it is clear that the Act has not given any definition of the expression 'industrial undertaking'. The requirement of section 80HH(2) is that to be eligible, the industrial undertaking should be one which is engaged in the manufacture or production of an article or thing. Therefore, the expression can be understood by looking upto the meaning as understood in common parlance or by making a reference to its definition in cognate legislation.

In the instant case, the alcohol in the beginning and after processing also remained alcohol. No distinct article or thing had been produced. Alcohol remained alcohol throughout the processing stage till it was marketed. There is no difference between potable spirit and whisky or brandy except in the process of production, water and certain essences have been added to them. Therefore, although it had undergone a degree of processing, it
must be regarded as still retaining its original identity. The original commodity was alcohol and the commodity produced had also remained alcohol. Therefore, it would be said that no commodity was consumed in the manufacture of another in the instant case. Therefore, there was no essential difference between the potable spirit and the bottled IMFLs. The dealer and the consumer both regard it as alcohol. The only difference was that in potable spirit some water and essences were added and bottled up nicely to make it presentable for marketing. Therefore the above discussion clearly showed that the bottled IMFLs and potable spirit must be held to possess the same character, identity as the original before its bottling. Hence, the activities of the assessee did not involved any manufacturing but only processing and, therefore, it was not entitled to the benefit of section 80HH.

The assessee in his explanation had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware of the fact that inside the guns, there was brass scrap which was removed. Thus, it was clear from the reply that brass was not an ingredient used in the process of manufacture in industrial undertaking of the assessee. The brass scrap had no direct nexus with the appellant’s industrial undertaking. It could not be said that brass scrap was a profit or gain which directly flowed, neither it had close connection with undertaking of the assessee. By removal of brass scrap which was not useful for steel rerolling work no different and distinct article came into existence, it was only incidental as was apparent from the assessee’s reply. [Paras 13 and 14]

Further, composition of brass scrap was not at all changed, that was only removed as that was not useful to the assessee for the activity of manufacturing which he was carrying on. It was only a fortuitous circumstance that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee had purchased the guns without the knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in the process of manufacture. There was no nexus between brass and activity of steel rerolling. Brass was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25]

Thus, there was no nexus between the brass scrap obtained on dismantling of the guns and the main activity of the assessee of steel rerolling. Gun was not an essential raw material of appellants’ industrial unit, in any case, brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling. Thus, separation of brass could not be said to be in the process of manufacture or a product or a by-product of the activity of the assessee’s industrial undertaking. There was no direct nexus between the separation of the brass from the guns and the main activity. Thus, considering the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, it could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking. Thus, deductions on profits and gains under sections 80HH and 80-I were not admissible and had been rightly disallowed by the Tribunal. [Para 28]

Resultantly, the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 29]

The Supreme Court, in the case of Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa AIR 1978 SC 548, has laid down that where there is (i) systematic activity, (ii) organised by co-operation between employer and employees, (iii) for the production and/or distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes, prima facie, there is an industry. Absence of profit motive or gainful object is irrelevant. This view of the Supreme Court has been followed by the jurisdictional High Court in the case of CIT v. J.B. Kharwar & Sons [1987] 163 ITR 394 and by Karnataka High Court in the case of Shankar Construction Co. v. CIT [1991] 189 ITR 463. In the case before the Karnataka High Court, the business of constructing dams and channels was taken as that of ‘industrial undertaking’ entitled to investment allowance; while in the case of J.B. Kharwar & Sons (supra) before the Gujarat High Court, the business was that of printing and dyeing of cloths and the work was taken as manufacturing work for the entitlement of deduction under section 80J. On the basis of the above case law, the working of the assessee-firm which was involved in the work of designing, erection and commissioning of water and air pollution control plants, would certainly be falling in the category of an ‘industrial undertaking’, and the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ as used in sections 80HH and 80J.

In the instant case, the activities of the assessee-firm were that of manufacturing or that of producing an article as they were constructing water/air pollution plants. Thus, the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ and was engaged in manufacturing or producing an article in the shape of air/water pollution control. That the assessee was manufacturing or producing the plant in backward area, was one of the requirements of the claim under section 80HH. The contention of the assessee was that only 11.45 per cent of the total receipt had been taken for deduction under section 80HH as that work alone was done in backward area and it was not expected from the assessee to have its office or plant in backward area. The crux of the case laws is that if an industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce outside in any backward area, it is entitled to deduction under section 80HH. The assessee-firm set up its own industrial undertaking at the site of its customers for whom water/air pollution control plant was manufactured and of the places which were falling under the backward area declared under the Act, then, naturally the assessee should be getting benefit of the same and the computation made by the assessee-firm of the same was correct one.

Thus the assessee-firm had been able to make out a case in its favour on the guidelines referred to above for qualifying its claim under sections 80HH and 80J and the ITO was justified in allowing its claim from the assessment year 1982-83 onwards till the year under consideration and the Commissioner committed an error in concluding otherwise and the order of Commissioner was to be quashed on this point.

The second argument of the assessee-firm was that the Assessing Officer examined the case of the assessee in assessment year 1982-83, the first year of its business and for that necessary enquiries as posed by the Commissioner to himself while passing the order under section 263 were raised by the ITO and necessary correspondence held in between the ITO and the assessee-firm. The assessee had made available all the informations required by Assessing Officer who went through the same, examined the same and then found force in the plea of the assessee and allowed its claim under sections 80HH and 80J for the assessment year 1982-83 and that pattern was followed till the year under consideration and now the Commissioner was not justified to pass an order in question as no new fact had emerged out nor any change of circumstances took place to show that findings of ITO were in any way perverse of contrary to legal position.

The above contention of the assessee had got force as since the assessment year 1982-83, the position had been continuously the same and the Commissioner had not given out any reason to show that order of the ITO was in any way perverse nor any new fact came into his knowledge nor any separate enquiry had been made to differ from the earlier stand and, thus, it was not permissible for the Commissioner to start a fresh litigation from admitted positions of the parties on particular point. Thus, the case of the assessee was rightly processed by the Assessing Officer and there was no justification for the Commissioner to make an order under section 263 with direction to the ITO to withdraw the deduction made in favour of the assessee under said sections.

New ships are not meant for demolition or breaking. It is after the operative and useful life of the ship is over that they are scheduled to be sold for demolition. The procedure for demolition of a ship is not just a private affair and involves permission of the authorities under the law to transfer them for demolition. Merely because the ship is able to sail on its own up to the shore where it is to be demolished, it cannot be said that such ship which is sold for demolition is a new ship. Remaining afloat is not a sure test for a ship to be called new, because a condemned ship is not always a sunk ship. An old ship sold for demolition that manages to remain afloat cannot be said to be a new ship. The distinction made on that count is a distinction attempted without any real difference between the old ships which are sold for demolition, for the purpose of considering whether the ship breaking activity is a manufacturing or production activity. [Para 22]

By the nature of its very setting, one has to construe the expression ‘manufacture or produce articles’ in sub-section (2)(i ) of section 80HH and the expression ‘manufactures or produces any article or thing not being any article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule’, appearing in section 80-I(2)(iii) in the context of the fact that the deduction under section 80HH is meant to encourage establishment of new industrial undertakings in backward areas when such industrial undertaking ‘has begun or begins to manufacture or produce articles’ and in context of the fact that section 80-I is designed to encourage industrial undertakings to manufacture or produce ‘any articles or thing not being article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule’.

Provisions of section 80HH or 80-I are meant for the benefit of industrial undertakings that carry out the activity of manufacture or production of articles or things and not for the scrap merchants who trade in buying old articles or things and take out their parts to sell them separately. All large scale junk dealers in discarded old and scrapped vehicles who might fish out a horn in working condition from such vehicle or pull out its steering wheel or part of its engine that may have a demand in the market of second hand spares will proclaim themselves to be manufacturers or producers of articles or things. No such startling result is intended by the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, having regard to their underlying purpose of encouraging industries for being set up for manufacturing or production of new articles or things. In fact, industrial undertaking formed by transfer of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose is disentitled to such benefits both under sections 80HH(2)(iii) and 80-I(2)(iii). [Para 23]

The ships imported for breaking up are obviously old ships, purchased to retrieve the material, particularly steel plates, for disposal in the market for re-rolling or re-cycling purposes which is the activity done by these ship breakers in the process of ship breaking.

Thus, there is nothing whatsoever in the process of ship breaking activity which can be termed as manufacture or production of any article or thing. The dismantled material is already existing as a component of the old ship. The process of extracting steel plates from it while dismantling the ship will not make such extraction of existing material an activity of manufacture or production of such material nor will the process of cutting extracted steel plates for convenient disposal be manufacture or production of such steel plates. Merely because the ship breaking is considered as an industry, it would not be an industry engaged in manufacture or production of any article or thing. Benefit of the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I is clearly not intended for such ship breaking activities which do not result in bringing into existence any new article or thing. The word ‘manufacture’ in the context of sections 80HH and 80-I would mean making of articles or things. While dismantling, the ship steel plates are not made but only removed which is not the same thing as making of steel plates. The word ‘production’ in context of these provisions would mean the action of making or manufacturing from components or raw materials an article or thing and not just removing of an existing article or cutting it.

In the instant case, application of mechanical methods only removed the steel plates and other objects which were existing on the ships, which would not mean that the assessee produced those existing articles or things by the process of removing and cutting them. [Para 27]

The word ‘production’ or ‘produce’ when used in juxtaposition with word ‘manufacture’ takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. The principle of adopting a liberal interpretation which advances the purpose and object of beneficial provisions cannot be carried out to the extent of doing violence to the plain and simple language of the enactment. [Para 27.1]

In Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT (No. 2) [2000] 241 ITR 803, the Madras High Court expressed the view that the scrap materials has direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, profit from the sale of the scrap materials should be eligible for deduction under section 80HH. Following that decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the relief under section 80HH was allowable to the assessee on profit on sale of scrap. [Para 13]

INTERPRETATION : PRINCIPLES : OBJECT AND PURPOSE :

A plain reading of the provisions of sections 32A, 80HH and 80J clearly indicates from the very scheme that these are really in the form of incentives for industrial growth and development. The object cannot be overlooked while interpreting the statute. A construction, which advances the object, is to be preferred to that which is opposed to it. [Para 5]

SECTIONS 32A, 80HH, 80J : PRODUCTION : MEANING OF :

Section 32A provides for certain deduction in the computation of the income from the profits and gains from the business by way of investment allowance. Similar benefit is allowed further under section 80HH when such industrial undertaking is operating in backward areas. Further, similar incentive was allowed to new industrial undertaking under section 80J. Admittedly, the assessee had its industrial undertaking in the A&N Island, which was admittedly a backward area. The industrial undertaking of the assessee was established on 27-1-1977 whereas the cut off date of eligibility was 31-3-1976. Thus, factually the assessee, a new industrial undertaking, operating in a backward area having invested within the meaning of section 32AB, qualified for the test to come within the scope and ambit of the said three sections. But, in order to obtain the benefit, the business of the assessee must be that of an industrial undertaking owned by the assessee and engaged in a business operation in relation to manufacture and production of an article or thing. The entitlement of the assessee cannot be disputed or denied if it is established that the assessee is industrial undertaking and that the industrial undertaking operating in a backward area is engaged in manufacture or production of an article or a thing, and was established after 31-3-1976 and had made the investment. [Para 6.1]

ASSESSEE : WHETHER INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING :

The establishment of the assessee was definitely an industrial undertaking when it was engaged in production of certain commodities or things. Admittedly, the assessees’ establishment employed more than 20 persons and carried on the operation with the aid of power. The industrial undertaking has not been defined in the Act. Therefore, it must be given the ordinary meaning of an industry. [Para 6.3]

ELIGIBILITY OF DEDUCTION : WHETHER SATISFIED :

However, each and every industrial undertaking would not be eligible for the said deductions. An industrial undertaking which is engaged in manufacture and production of an article or thing would be eligible for the deduction under section 32AB; it would be eligible for the deduction under section 80HH if situated in backward area; it would, if established after 31-3-1976, be eligible for the deduction allowed under section 80J. In the instant case, all the ingredients were undisputedly satisfied. [Para 6.4]

PRODUCTION : MEANING OF :

In the instant case, the relief was claimed on the ground that the establish-ment of the assessee was engaged in the production of logs. Trees cannot be sold in the open market with all their branches and leaves even if felled, as a whole. The branches are slopped, the trunk is cut into pieces and then converted into logs which primarily involves effort or exercise or enterprising or undertaking of some process. The conversion of trunk into logs is the first step towards extraction of timber for which human efforts are necessary. In order to make it a saleable commercial article, the logs are seasoned. The commercial activity that the assessee undertook was the sale of logs, the main purpose of the assessee’s business. The enterprise undertaken in the industrial undertaking of the assessee was to produce commercially saleable logs out of the felled trees. Thus, the production of logs, though may not involve manufacture, is yet a production within the meaning of sections 32AB, 80HH and 80J respectively. [Para 6.5]

The conversion of logs would not amount to manufacture since no article other than wood is brought out and no change in the characteristics is effected. Conversion of tree into logs would not change the character, which remains wood as before. Admittedly, in the instant case, the assessee did not claim conversion of felled tree to log as manufacture. An establishment, which is engaged in production of something is an industrial undertaking eligible under the provisions of sections 32A, 80HH and 80J. [Para 6.8]

Sub-section (2) of section 80HH lays down certain conditions, one of which is that the industrial undertaking should manufacture or produce articles in any backward area and another condition is that it should employ 10 or more workers in the manufacturing process carried on with the aid of power. It was not the case of the revenue that any of these conditions were not fulfilled. Their only case was that the entire manufacturing activity from beginning to end was not carried on in the backward area and an initial part of it had been entrusted to the contractors who carried on that part of the activity outside the backward area. The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5]

Sub-section (7) of section 80HH provides for this contingency by stating that where it appears to the Assessing Officer that owing to the close connection between the assessee carrying on the business to which this section applies and any other person, the business between them is so arranged that it produces to the assessee more than the ordinary profit, the profits and gains of this industrial undertaking may be reasonably estimated. In the instant case also, if the Assessing Officer had carefully scrutinised the accounts of the assessee and drawn the inference that because of the entrustment of the initial part of the contract process to contractors, the income from the industrial undertaking was likely to be inflated, with reference to the profit derived from the backward area, he could have reasonably estimated the profit instead of accepting the profit as shown by the assessee. That estimate, he failed to do at the time of the assessment and he sought to do the same by reopening the assessment. The question was whether he could do it by stating that there was an omission on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts. In the case of Parashuram Pottery Works Co. Ltd. v. ITO [1977] 106 ITR 1, the Supreme Court stated that the duty of an assessee in any case does not extend beyond making a true and full disclosure of primary facts. Once he has done that, his duty ends. It is for the ITO to draw the correct inference from the primary facts. It is no responsibility of the assessee to advise the ITO with regard to the inference, which he should draw from the primary facts. If an ITO draws an inference which appears subsequently to be erroneous, mere change of opinion with regard to that inference would not justify initiation of action for reopening assessments. In the instant case, the ITO failed to draw an inference that because of the entrustment of the initial manufacturing activity to contractors, the income derived from the industrial undertaking with reference to the backward area could be inflated and to that extent the income had to be estimated for confining the deduction to that profit which could be said to have been derived only from the backward area. Failing to draw that inference, blame could not be put on the assessee, when at the time of assessment the list of contractors, the quantity of beedies manufactured and the amount paid had been disclosed by the assessee. That disclosure was admitted in the counter affidavit. The ITO was not able to specify what extra information was required by him to have applied his mind to draw that inference for reducing the deduction to which the assessee was entitled. As long as it was not possible for the ITO to specify the exact information which was required and which was not disclosed, it was not possible to accept the claim that there was no true and full disclosure in the case. When that jurisdictional fact was not established, the ITO could not issue a notice under section 147(a). In the circumstances, the impugned notices were quashed. [Paras 6 & 7]

The writ petition was allowed. [Para 7]

As per the law laid down by the Supreme Court in several decisions, the expression 'derived from' is to be given restricted meaning in section 80HH/80-I while interpreting the section in which this expression is used. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the main and only business of the assessee, for which the plant was set up in the backward area, was to manufacture and to sell soya oil. Hence, all incomes derived from sale of soya oil would be income derived from an industrial undertaking for the purpose of calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I.

The income earned by the assessee out of sale of gunny bags could not be kept at par or alike the income derived from sale of soya bean oil due to following reasons - Sale of gunny bags was not the main or even ancillary business activity of the assessee; it was not regular or continuous business activity; no investment was made by the assessee for their sale. The gunny bags were never manufactured by the assessee in its plant and merely because some gunny bags were lying in the factory as surplus or unused or as waste material for any reason and such bags were sold to earn income, then it could not be a ground to hold that for the purpose of section 80HH/80-I, such income was the income actually derived from the assessee's industrial undertaking. [Para 16]

In order to derive income from industrial undertaking, the assessee must show that it was earned by sale of goods/commodity which were manufactured/produced in the said industrial undertakings as a part of its main and day-to-day business activity. Only then, the income earned by sale of such goods can be termed as income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I. It is for this reason that it has a direct or immediate nexus with the assessee's industrial undertaking established in the backward area. This necessarily follows that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking, alone will be taken into consideration for calculating the deduction under section 80HH/80-I, ibid. Such was not the case in the instant case, because the income earned from sale of gunny bags was not the result of direct or immediate nexus with the business of assessee carried on in the industrial undertaking. [Para 17]

Hence, the Tribunal fell in error in holding that the income earned by the assessee from sale of gunny bags was an income earned from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and, accordingly, the assessee was entitled to claim deduction from total income. That view was to be reversed and order of the Tribunal was to be set aside. [Para 21]

cause notice and the assessee was never given an opportunity of being heard on that issue. In the show-cause notice, the Commissioner had not disclosed that ground and the assessee was never directed to meet the Commissioner’s observations that deduction under section 80HH was not permissible on account of lack of gross total income. Therefore, the impugned order under section 263 also suffered from the infirmity of not allowing proper opportunity of being heard to the assessee. [Para 21] From the assessment year 1985-86 onwards, the assessee had consistently disclosed in the computation statement that factory No. III was set up as a new industrial undertaking eligible for deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer had required the assessee to give specific information regarding establishment of the factory No. III as new industrial undertaking and also required the assessee to prove that it fulfilled the conditions laid down in sections 80HH and 80-I. The assessee furnished its explanations and documentary evidences to prove that the said factory No. III was set up as a new industrial undertaking and commenced production in March 1984 relevant to the assessment year 1985-86. The said factory No. III was given a new factory licence and central excise licence. The Central Excise authorities also certified that the first dispatch from the said factory took place only on 29-3-1984. Therefore, before the Assessing Officer in the assessment proceedings, the assessee had brought on record sufficient material and evidence to prove that a new industrial undertaking was set up during the calendar year 1984 relevant to the assessment year 1985-86. In the assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95, the deductions under sections 80-I and 80HH were allowed in respect of profits of factory No. III. Those orders were not made subject-matter of appeals or revision and the deductions allowed by the Assessing Officer had become final. In the above factual circumstances, therefore, in the succeeding assessment years on the same set of facts, the revenue authorities accepted factory No. III as new industrial undertaking eligible to deductions under sections 80-I and 80HH. On those facts, therefore, there was no justification for the Commissioner to doubt the establishment of factory No. III as new industrial undertaking only in the assessment year 1991-92. Though the principle of res judicata was not strictly applicable to revenue proceedings, yet the said principle was no stranger to the tax proceedings. If on the same set of facts the revenue authorities in the later years allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to factory No. III treating it as an industrial undertaking set up in the assessment year 1985-86, then there was no reason for the Commissioner to disturb the finding of the Assessing Officer in the assessment year 1991-92 as the Commissioner did not bring on record any specific evidence to prove contrary. Therefore, the Commissioner was not justified in doubting the establishment of factory No. III as new industrial undertaking during 1985-86. [Para 23]

During the assessment year 1985-86, the deduction under section 80HH was permissible to a newly established undertaking if it was situated in any of the districts specified in the eighth schedule. By Notification dated 19-12-1986, the Central Government notified list of backward districts and District Udaipur was included therein. The Raj Samund Block of Udaipur District, where factory No. III was situated, was in excluded category of the said notification. However, the CBDT in its circular No. 484 dated 1-5-1987 had clarified that all areas specified in the Eighth Schedule continued to enjoy the benefit of section 80HH if the industrial undertaking had begun manufacture before 10-9-1986. Therefore, factory No. III situated in Raj Samund Block of Udaipur District was eligible for deduction under section 80HH since it began production in March 1984 as certified by the Central Excise authorities. [Para 24]

According to the Commissioner, factory No. III merely represented expansion of the assessee’s existing business and, therefore, not eligible for beneficial deductions as no new business was set up. However, this proposition has not been accepted by the Supreme Court as well as by the various High Courts. In the assessee’s own case for the assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95, the department had allowed deduction under sections 80-I and 80HH in respect of profits derived by factory No. III. Therefore, the order of the Assessing Officer, allowing deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I considering factory No. III as new industrial undertaking was supported by various judicial decisions wherein it was held that for claming the deductions it was not necessary to manufacture a new or different product. Therefore, the order of the Assessing Officer on this issue could not be considered as erroneous. [Para 25]

It is well-settled that if there is nexus between the receipt of income and the industrial undertaking, it has to be treated as income derived from the industrial undertaking. In the instant case, the immediate source of job charges received was the industrial undertaking itself. Therefore, the job work charges had to be treated as income derived from the industrial undertaking. The conversion charges might not have any nexus with export or other activity. But, said charges had a direct nexus with the manufacturing activity of the assessee, since the assessee did the job work by utilizing the very same machinery and labourers. Therefore, the income had to be considered as derived from the industrial undertaking and was eligible for deduction under section 80-IB. In view of the above, there was no infirmity in the order of the lower authority. [Para 6]

As regards profit on the sale of scrap, it was not in dispute that the scrap was generated during the course of manufacturing activity. Therefore, the profit on sale of the scrap material had a direct nexus with the manufacturing activity of the assessee and receipt of income. In other words, unless the assessee manufactured the goods, the scrap would not have been generated at all. Therefore, the income from sale of scrap was derived from the industrial undertaking and was eligible for deduction under section 80-IB. The income received from sale of scrap might not have any relation with export of goods and it might not be eligible for deduction under section 80HHC. However, it had a direct nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, it was eligible for deduction under section 80-IB. [Para 10]

As regards interest on delayed payments, in view of decision of the Madras High Court in CIT v. Rane (Madras) Ltd. [1999] 238 ITR 377/ 102 Taxman 284 it was to be held that said interest was directly related to industrial undertaking and, therefore, was eligible for deduction. [Para 11]

In the result, the revenue's appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 12]

The word "derived from" under section 80-HH has to be understood as something which has immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking. In the instant case, the scrap generated from the concerned units has direct and immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking since the said scrap has been generated from the manufacturing process itself. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal have committed no error in allowing the benefit of section 80-HH to the assessee on the aforesaid income. [Para 15]

of businesses and some of them are industrial undertakings and some of them are not industrial undertaking for example deduction is allowable in case of hotels or operation of ship or for development of housing project, multiplex theatres etc. which cannot be called industrial undertaking. Similarly deduction under section 80-IB (11A) is for the eligible business and specifically for the 'integrated business' of handling, storage and transportation of foodgrains which cannot be called industrial undertaking. [Para 56] Before considering the addition of new plant & Machinery, the contention regarding discarding of machines is being considered for which a certificate has been filed from an Engineer and C.A. However, during the course of hearing it was noticed from the schedule of fixed assets that it does not show any discarding of machines because the assessee has claimed depreciation on all the plant & Machinery. Therefore further enquiry proceeds on assumption that no machinery was discarded. When this was confronted to the assessee, he admitted that actual new purchase of machinery was started in Financial year 2005-06 itself, therefore Assessment year 2006-07 may be taken to be the first year of the new project.[Para 57]

Reasoning for deduction in Assessment year 2006-07 as the first year is that mega project has been sanctioned by the Govt. of Punjab on 6.9.2005 and admittedly the project was implemented over a period of time. Therefore, Assessment year 2006-07 should have been reckoned as the first year for the purpose of eligibility of deduction under section 80-IB(11A). However, no such deduction has been claimed but that itself will not hinder the claim of deduction in the later years.[Para 58]

The revenue had raised the objection that the assessee had made contradictory statement in the sense that before the Assessing officer and the Commissioner(Appeals) it was claimed that industrial undertaking was started in Assessment year 2008-09 whereas before the Bench he has conceded that the industrial undertaking was started in Assessment year 2006-07. There was no force in this objection because it was clear that the mega project was sanctioned in 2005 thereafter the assessee started acquiring new land, building and machinery in the financial year 2005-06 onwards. Moreover the assessee conceded that the project was started in Assessment year 2006-07 then the assessee is likely to loose the deduction for first two years, therefore it is rather against the assessee than in favour of the assessee. Otherwise also as pointed out by the assessee that there cannot be any estoppel against the law. When the question whether the project is formed by splitting old machinery is to be considered then obviously the WDV of the old machinery is to be considered. This is so because in some cases old machinery may be very old and may not have any value and if the gross value was to be taken the distorted results may be obtained.[Para 60]

There was one more objection that control devices should not be reckoned into new plant & Machinery because the assessee has claimed 100 per cent depreciation on these items and therefore new plant & Machinery would be only Rs. 9.85 crore. Even this objection cannot be upheld because the idea in section 80 IB(2)(i) is to compare the purchase of new machinery with the value of old machinery, therefore value of the control devices cannot be ignored simply because the assessee has claimed 100 per cent depreciation on the control devices which have been installed before 30-9-2005. In this regard it was held that for considering the meaning of reconstruction the value of old machinery may not be considered at all. [Para 61]

Now when the value of old machinery is compared to the value of new machinery in Assessment year 2006-07, it becomes clear that the value of old machinery is about 18.14 per cent and therefore same is within the limit given in section 80-IB(2)(i). Therefore, the assessee has not violated the conditions laid down in section 80-IB((2)(i).[Para 63]

The Assessing officer has raised one more objection that no deduction has been claimed in the return filed by the assessee and therefore no deduction can be allowed. Perusal of the statement of income clearly show that deduction was claimed in the return of income perhaps some mistake was committed during the processing of return and that is why the assessee had applied for rectification of mistake and this mistake was rectified in the order under section 154, therefore this allegation of the Assessing officer is totally incorrect.[Para 64]

The submission of the assessee was that since power in the form of steam was generated by the captive power plant and consumed in the manufacture of PVC and Ilmenite, the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA.
