(Per Lord Hoffman) 1.5 Contradiction between AS-2 and AS-6/AS-26, if any - The prescribed accountancy treatment of including depreciation on assets used in production in the cost of closing stock came up for judicial scrutiny. The revenue’s objection was that this prescribed treatment conflicts with the principle "the depreciable amount of a tangible fixed asset must be allocated on a systematic basis over its [i.e., the asset’s] useful economic life" (see AS-6 and AS-26) inasmuch as it has the effect of "depreciating the asset over a longer period than this - effectively a period ending only when the trading stock whose value is debited with part of the depreciation charge is finally sold or written down.". The cost of fixed assets used in production is, thus, charged as an expense over the period during which they are generating revenue (i.e., over the period during which the stock produced by the assets is sold), rather than over the period during which their value is written off in the balance sheet. One consequence is a deferral of the point at which such depreciation is charged as an expense in the profit and loss account (assuming that not all the stock produced in a given year is sold in the same year). The deferral is for a particularly long period in the Scotch whisky industry, because stocks are held for many years as they mature. Stock which remains unsold at the end of the accounting period forms part of the company’s current assets; and the figure at which the stock is stated in the balance sheet is normally its cost, including the depreciation forming part of that cost. Depreciation on production assets is, therefore, said, in accountancy parlance, to be ‘carried to stock’; and it normally remains in the balance sheet, under the heading of ‘current assets’, unless and until the stock in question is sold, at which point the depreciation is charged as an expense in the profit and loss account under the heading of ‘cost of sales’.

The House unanimously upheld the validity of the prescribed accountancy treatment of including depreciation on assets used in production in the cost of closing stock notwithstanding the result, i.e., depreciation gets charged off to the profit and loss account over a period longer than the asset’s useful life. The House held that this does not militate against the true and fair view of the profit and loss account. Lord Hope of Craighed held that "When depreciation is to be taken into account to show a true and fair view of the profit or loss for each financial year is in the end a question of timing. If, in order to show a true and fair view according to currently accepted accounting principles, part of the depreciation has in fact been carried forward, that must be treated as fact..." Lord Hoffman pointed out that the requirement to carry forward a part of depreciation on assets used in production as part of closing stock is an exception to the general rule that" depreciable amount of a tangible fixed asset must be allocated on a systematic basis over its [i.e., the asset’s] useful economic life". He observed that "Obviously any reduction in balance sheet value for depreciation must at some time be reflected in a profit and loss account deduction, but there is nothing to say that they must coincide".

CHALLENGES AND FUTURE UNCERTAINTY

While MOOWR is a beneficial scheme, these challenges are hindering its performance.

Complex compliance: Filing multiple BOEs for each DTA sale is time-consuming and complex.

No depreciation is allowed when capital goods are sold in the domestic market—duty is on full import value.

No RODTEP or Drawback: MOOWR-based exports are less competitive given they are not eligible for RODTEP scrips or Drawback. Typically benefits RODTEP and Drawback would be in the range of 4-5% of the value of exported good, which is significant for a lot of exporters.

New concern: The Finance Act 2024 empowered the Government of India to exclude certain goods or operations from the applicability of MOOWR scheme. This adds unpredictability, making long-term planning difficult for businesses relying on this scheme and creating an unease in doing business.

Takeaways

If you are importing raw materials or machinery regularly, consider obtaining a MOOWR license.

Be prepared for higher compliance costs.

Evaluate if loss of RODTEP/Drawback is offset by duty deferment benefits.

MOOWR is one of the most flexible and cash-flow-friendly customs schemes available in India. It's ideal for businesses that import raw material or machinery and sell their finished goods either in domestic market or export market.

Small and Mid-sized manufacturers initially hesitate to register under MOOWR because of compliance worries. But once they set up the systems, the cash flow benefits are too significant to ignore.

CENTRAL EXCISE - TREATMENT OF WASTE

1. We have two factories registered under central excise with the following details —

1st Factory - Manufacturer of fine chemicals falling under Chapter 34

2nd Factory - Declared as job worker (a bottling plant) of first factory.

We sent 100 Kgs. of chemicals to be packed in 100 gms. bottles to bottling plant. After completion of packing in small packs we received only 90 Kgs. chemicals packed in small container. What would be the treatment of non-collectible waste of 10% (10 Kgs. out of every lot of 100 kgs.) ?

It is clearly stated by you that both the factories are registered separately. In this case the manufacturing factory is clearing 100 Kgs. to job-worker and receiving back the same in entirety (subject to processing loss). The process loss of 10% will not be chargeable to duty, only if the same is normal process loss.

The benefit may be claimed under rule 21 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, as —

the same is due to natural causes or unavoidable reasons, and

is incurred prior to removal of finished goods from the factory.

An alternative view may be that only 90 Kg. is the manufactured product, because manufacture under section 2(f) is complete only after the completion of all incidental or ancillary processes, which include packing/bottling.

In any case, the duty can be levied only on 90 Kgs.

CENTRAL EXCISE - WHETHER IN CASE OF EXPORT UNDER CLAIM OF REBATE, EXCISE DUTY MAY BE PAID THROUGH CENVAT CREDIT

2. We are exporters of a final product. Export is made under claim of rebate. Please clarify whether we can set-off/adjust excise duty payable under the option of "Export under claim of Rebate" through Cenvat credit or not ? Whether rebate would be allowed even in that case ?

As per rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, credit is allowed of duty or tax paid on inputs or input services or capital goods used in factory/manufacture purposes.

The said credit may be used to pay duty on final product. Goods exported under claim of rebate are cleared on payment of duty and said duty can very well be paid by using Cenvat credit as per rule 3(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In fact, Form ARE-1 itself in Part A provides for certification as follows —

Certified that 1. duty has been paid by debit entry in the Personal Ledger Account No. .........and/or CENVAT Account Entry No. .……or recorded as payable in Daily Stock Account, on the goods described overleaf.

(Emphasis Supplied)

Therefore, for purpose of export under claim of rebate, duty may be paid using balance in Cenvat Credit Account.

CENVAT CREDIT - ROTARY MILL AND WOODEN BALL - CAPITAL GOODS V. INPUT

3. We are availing of credit of duty paid on Rotary Mill and Wooden Ball falling under Tariff Items 44219050 and 44219050, respectively, and use it for grinding Propellant Powder as input. The said goods are machinery and are being capitalized in our financial accounts and depreciation is being claimed. Whether Cenvat credit availed by us is in order ?

The query has been replied in two parts —

Part - I : Input v. Capital Goods

Taking classification put forth by you to be correct, since the goods are classifiable under Chapter 44, they are not listed in any of the categories of capital goods as provided in rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. However, if —

they are purchased as 'components or spares or accessories' of some other machinery ; and

such other machinery is a capital goods under rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004,

then the said mill/ball would be classifiable as capital goods under rule 2(a)(A)(iii) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In any other event the same would be eligible for credit as an 'input', as the same is presumably used within the factory.

Part - II : Relevant treatment under Financial Accounts

The classification and treatment under financial accounts is not relevant for the purpose of deciding eligibility to Cenvat credit.

In other words, even if the said goods are inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, they may be 'fixed assets' under the accounting standards issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and would, accordingly, be eligible for depreciation.

The two things must be viewed separately.

Withdraw amendment denying depreciation on goodwill; or the amendment may be made prospective, and grandfathering be allowed for pre-existing goodwill The Government in the Finance Act 2021 made a far-reaching amendment of denying depreciation on goodwill. Though the amendment is slated to be effective prospectively, in substance it has the effect of denying depreciation on past transactions. Such retrospective amendments create hardship for taxpayers, and also impact the investment climate.

Also, denial of depreciation on purchased goodwill arising in non-tax neutral transactions (such as where the seller has paid appropriate tax on a slump sale or simpliciter sale of goodwill) is against the principle of tax neutrality.

Therefore, it is recommended that the amendment be withdrawn, or that specific kinds of goodwill (arising on a slump sale/simpliciter purchase) be allowed to be amortized over 4-5 years. Alternatively, the amendment may be made prospective, and pre-existing goodwill in the block of assets as on 1 April 2020 can be grandfathered.

4. Limitation of Interest Benefit – Section 94B

Section 94B provides a capping of 30% of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization ("EBITDA") on the interest deduction that can be claimed by an entity in respect of funds borrowed from non-resident associated enterprises ("AE").

(a)

In terms of sub-section (2) of section 94B, 'excess interest' is defined to mean an amount of total interest paid or payable in excess of 30% of EBITDA of the borrower, or interest paid or payable to AE for that previous year, whichever is less. Since the expression used in sub-section (2) is 'total interest', a question arises as to whether it would include only foreign interest, or both foreign and domestic interest, paid by the entity. If domestic interest is also to be included, then, it would result in a higher disallowance of foreign interest compared to the normal scenario where there is no domestic borrowing. Hence, it is recommended to clarify that interest may be restricted only to foreign AE interest and not total interest.

(b)

In the event of borrowing by an infrastructure company from outside India, it often happens that foreign lenders insist on a joint guarantee by a parent company and SPV for the project. In this regard, the current reading of section 94B provides that debt issued by a non-resident lender (being non-AE) to a resident subsidiary under the guarantee of a resident parent (being an AE) would be covered under the provision. Hence, limit on interest deduction leads to additional disallowance in the hands of subsidiary, even when the transaction is entered into with non-AE, thereby discouraging funding to such sectors from outside India, which does not appear to be in line with government's policy of attracting foreign funds for key debt-intensive sectors. Hence, it is recommended that the restriction be applicable only in the case of borrowing from AEs.

(c)

Furthermore, the infrastructure sector generally warrants high capital requirement, especially in the initial years. Hence, it is recommended that considering the sector-specific requirement, a higher limit (i.e. a higher percentage of EBITDA) ought to apply in case of infrastructure companies, at least in the first 8-10 years.

5. Allow deduction for CSR expenditure in the nature of Covid-19 relief expenditure

(a)

Presently, CSR expenditure is not allowed as business expenditure and there is a lack of clarity with respect to the deductibility of expenditure on employee welfare. Therefore, it is recommended that such expenditure incurred towards COVID-19 relief, whether it is made in cash or in kind, or whether it is capital or revenue in nature, may be allowed as deductible expenditure while computing total income.

(b)

Recently, it was clarified that donations made to the PM CARES Fund will be allowed as deductions under section 80G of the Act. However, companies opting for the new regime of concessional tax rate will not be entitled to avail such deduction under section 80G of the Act. Therefore, it is recommended that the deduction may be extended to such companies opting for the concessional tax rate.

(c)

Section 11 of the Act may be amended to provide that the amount spent towards COVID-19 relief shall be considered as application of income for computing exemption under section 11 of the Act.

6. Increase wage limit for new employee deduction under section 80JJAA

Under section 80JJAA, deduction is available for additional employees whose monthly salary is up to INR 25,000. The definition of employee also includes managerial and administrative persons. Accordingly, for managerial persons the limit of INR 25,000 is not in line with the industry standards and is considered quite low.

Therefore, it is recommended that the aforesaid wage limit of INR 25,000 may be revised upward to align it with the current pay structure of the industry, which will in turn facilitate enterprises in claiming the benefit of weighted deductions.

Background

1. In industries like pharmaceuticals and agro-chemicals many times near-about expired goods, defective goods or damaged goods (for the sake of convenience let us say "defective goods") are sent again by various marketing depots (not registered under excise) for reprocessing. Usually it happens that the original goods have been manufactured by let us say factory A, B and C but the defective goods are returned to only one factory, let us say factory D for reprocessing. This is so because it will be impractical to send the defective goods for reprocessing to the very same factory which had manufactured the original goods due to logistical costs as well as difficulties in identifying them on one-to-one basis.

In such scenario, only document available will be copy of excise invoice issued by the original factory. Had the defective goods been returned to the same factory, manufacturer could have easily claimed CENVAT credit on the basis of originally issued invoice (as the excise invoice was issued by the same factory). However, here the case is different. Factory D wants to claim CENVAT credit of returned defective goods on the basis of excise invoice issued by other factories.

Critical Issues

2. Following critical issues arise in this set-up:

2.1 Whether CENVAT credit can be claimed by factory D when the invoices on the basis of which credit will be claimed has been issued by factory A, B and C ?

2.2 W.e.f. 11-07-2014, third proviso has been added to rule 4(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which provides that credit cannot be claimed after a period of six months from the date of issuance of any document (in our case excise invoice) on the basis of which credit is claimed. In our case, as we are dealing with near-expired or defective goods, in all likelihood excise invoice issued by original manufacturer would have been dated beyond statutory period of six months. Issue is whether the third proviso will apply to the present case ?

2.3 What are the procedures one needs to follow to claim the said credit ?

3. Legal Analysis

3.1 To answer the first question, i.e., whether factory D can avail CENVAT credit on the basis of invoices issued by factory A, B and C for defective goods which are received back, one has to refer to rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. Relevant extract is reproduced below for ready reference:

"Rule 16. Credit of duty on goods brought to the factory.—(1) Where any goods on which duty had been paid at the time of removal thereof are brought to any factory for being re-made, refined, re-conditioned or for any other reason, the assessee shall state the particulars of such receipt in his records and shall be entitled to take CENVAT credit of the duty paid as if such goods are received as inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and utilize this credit according to the said rules.

(2) If the process to which the goods are subjected before being removed does not amount to manufacture, the manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the CENVAT credit taken under sub-rule (1) and in any other case the manufacturer shall pay duty on goods received under sub-rule (1) at the rate applicable on the date of removal and on the value determined under sub-section (2) of section 3 or section 4 or section 4A of the Act, as the case may be.

[Explanation.—The amount paid under this sub-rule shall be allowed as CENVAT credit as if it was a duty paid by the manufacturer who removes the goods.]

3.2 Careful reading of above rule provides that CENVAT credit will be available of any goods on which duty has been paid and are brought to any factory for re-making, refining, re-conditioning or for any other reason as inputs. Thus, only condition to be fulfilled for claiming credit is that duty should have been paid on said goods. It is not necessary that goods should be received back in the same factory. It can be received in any factory. Further, goods can be brought back for reprocessing under rule 16 even if shelf life has expired (CCE v. Rako Agrochem (P.) Ltd. 2010 (260) ELT 479 (Trib. - Delhi)). Thus, credit can be claimed of goods received by factory D on the basis of invoices issued by original manufacturers. One may also refer to Board's Circular 607/44/2001-CX, dated 13-12-2001 which confirms the above view. Thus, CENVAT credit can be claimed on basis of manufacturers invoice available with depot to the extent of quantity received by factory D.

Further, the process of deemed export drawback is complicated inasmuch as the supplier has to produce all the duty paying documents to the satisfaction of DGFT for fixation of Brand Rate of duty drawback.

Alternatively, an assessee may prefer to avail of the benefit of "Advance Intermediate Authorization" for procuring inputs without payment of duty. However, in such situation, it will have to carry out double compliance in the form of "Deemed Export Drawback" in respect of the service tax paid on the input services which are used in manufacture of goods supplied against Advance Authorization and also the compliance for obtaining and closure of "Advance Intermediate Authorization".

Therefore, effectively on account of lack of clarity in policies between the two Ministries of the Central Government, a manufacturer in India would have to unnecessarily carry out either double compliances or incur excessive cost to avail of the refund of duties, which could have been easily granted exemption from reversal under rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Further, such escalated cost and tiresome compliance would also effect the interest and efficiency of the business and pose a direct contradiction to the very intention of the Central Governments programme of 'Make in India' or 'Ease of Doing Business'.

Alternatively, supply against an Advance Authorization shall be allowed to avail of the benefit of Terminal Excise Duty under the erstwhile FTP, 2009-14.

3.0 FAQ's

3.1 Whether amendment to rule 3(5B) of the CCR, 2004 has a retrospective impact? - Rule 3(5B) of the CCR, 2004 as amended vide Notification No. 3/2011 C.E. (N.T.) with effect from 1 March, 2011 provides for reversal of the CENVAT credit even when inputs are partially written off or provision for partial write-off is made.

Since the amendment has come into effect only with effect from 1 March, 2011, partial write-off and provision for partial write-off of inputs prior to such date would not attract reversal of credit under rule 3(5B) of the CCR, 2004.

3.2 Whether semi-finished and finished goods are covered? - Inputs and capital goods have been defined under rule 2(k) and rule 2(a) respectively, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. With respect to applicability of rule 3(5B) to WIP/FG, clarification has been issued by the CBEC vide Circular No. 907/27/2009-CX. As per the circular, if the goods have been manufactured a manufacturer is liable to pay excise duty, unless duty is remitted under rule 21. Therefore, if the value of finished goods is written off, the manufacturer would be liable to pay excise duty or he would be required to reverse the credit on the inputs used, if duty has been remitted on finished goods.

As regards writing off work-in-progress (WIP), it is stated that if the WIP has reached the stage, when it can be considered as manufactured goods, in that case, the same treatment as is applicable to finished goods will be applicable. However, if the activity carried out on the WIP goods cannot be considered as amounting to manufacture, the said goods should be considered as inputs and the treatment for reversal of credit applicable to inputs would be applicable.

Rule 3(5) of the CCR, 2004 provides that if the inputs or capital goods on which CEVNAT credit is taken are removed as such, the CENVAT credit so taken has to be reversed.

Alternatively, where inputs are used in the manufacturing process and are removed as manufactured scrap, the company shall pay applicable excise duty and CENVAT shall not be reversed.

3.3 Whether write down of Inventory as per AS-2 attracts rule 3(5B)? - Write down in common business parlance represents restating the value with a lower amount, while write off generally results in permanent 'de-recognizing' or bringing down to Zero or negligible amount with no intention of writing back; unless situation otherwise warrants, write down is temporary reduction in value. On the other hand, in the case of provision, it is shown as a deduction from gross amount in the books of account. While rule 3(5B) covers write off provision, write down is not covered within the scope.

Backdrop

The economic slow-down, the rise in unemployment, fall in production and the general pessimism creeping in the country called for some substantial steps to be taken. The corporate tax rates in some of the neighboring and other relevant jurisdictions also necessitated a review of tax rates in India so that the arbitrages could be evened out and India emerges as a competitive regime for undertaking business activities, specially manufacturing.

In order to put more money in the hands of the private sector which would in turn translate into fresh investment and economic activity, as well as offer India as an attractive destination for making it a manufacturing hub thereby increasing employment and consumption, the Government has taken a bold step in substantially reducing the tax rates for companies.

Reduction in Tax Rates!

On September 20, 2019, the Union Finance Minister in a press conference announced that tax rates w.e.f. April 1, 2019, subject to certain conditions, for:

-

all existing and new companies, incorporated in India, shall be slashed to 22%^- Effective rate 25.168%; and

-

new manufacturing companies incorporated in India, on or after October 1, 2019 and commencing production on or before March 31, 2023, shall be 15%^.- Effective rate 17.16%

Companies opting to be governed in the above regime are not liable to pay Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT).

For existing corporates and other corporates not opting for the aforesaid regime, the MAT rate has been slashed from existing 18.5%^ to 15%^.- Effective MAT rate 16.692/ 17.472% depending on whether the quantum of book profits is upto INR 100 million or higher.

Conditions for applying the regime with reduced tax rates

I.

Following deductions cannot be claimed:

Deduction under section 10AA – available to a SEZ unit in respect of exports;

Additional Depreciation under clause (iia) of sub-section (1) of section 32 i.e. additional depreciation of 20%/35% on new plant and machinery;

Investment allowance of 15% of cost for undertakings/enterprises for manufacture or production of any article or thing, on or after the April 1, 2015 in any notified backward area under section 32AD;

Deduction under section 33AB in respect of deposits in special/ deposit account by entities growing and manufacturing tea, rubber, coffee;

^ Applicable surcharge and cess in addition

Deduction under section 33ABA in respect of deposits in Site Restoration account by entities carrying on business consisting of the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, petroleum or natural gas or both in India;

Deduction for sums paid to approved research organizations/ companies, etc. (100%-150%) under section 35 – Incurring of research expenditure on its own (revenue or capital) can still be claimed as a deduction in accordance with the said section;

Deduction of capital expenditure for specified businesses under section 35AD;

Expenditure on agriculture extension project under section 35CCC;

Expenditure on skill development project under section or section 35CCD;

Deduction under any provisions of Chapter VI-A under the heading "C.—Deductions in respect of certain incomes" viz. sections 80H – 80RRB. – Deduction under section 80JJAA on account of salaries/wages to new employees would however is permitted.

II.

Any loss carried forward from earlier years which is attributable to deductions referred to in I above will not be allowed to be set-off and the same would be deemed to have been give full effect and no further deduction of such losses would be allowed in any subsequent year.

III.

Depreciation other than additional depreciation referred to in I above, would be allowed in the manner prescribed.

IV.

The reduced tax rate shall be applicable, only if opted in return filed for period ending on or after March 31, 2020 and shall be applicable from the year in which it is so opted. The companies opting for above option are not liable to pay minimum alternative tax (MAT).

Once the option is exercised, it cannot be withdrawn. Companies can evaluate and choose to opt for the new regime after they have exhausted the deductions, benefits under the existing regime.

V.

Where a new company is incorporated on or after October 1, 2019 to undertake manufacturing activity, in addition to the above, it should

-

not be formed by splitting up or reconstruction of an existing business;

-

not use old plant and machinery (other than which is imported) beyond 20% of the value of total plant and machinery;

-

not use any building previously used as hotel or a convention center;

-

accelerated depreciation and loss on account of specified incentives/ holiday:

Companies with high capex/expansion in past years and having huge carried forward losses on account of accelerated depreciation, which would lapse if they opt for the concessional tax regime, should also undertake a cost benefit analysis of which regime to follow and at what time.

Similarly, companies that have availed tax holidays/ incentives in the past and are having carried forward losses on this account should also undertake a cost benefit analysis of which regime to follow. While the industry is analysing the benefits of the beneficial tax regime, the new law also requires some clarifications and ambiguities, which require immediate attention and clarity:

1.

Method of computation of depreciation: Concessional tax regimes provide that depreciation (other than accelerated depreciation) should be computed in the manner as may be prescribed. The Government is yet to prescribe this method of computation of depreciation and it would be interesting to see if it prescribes anything new in this regard.

2.

Disallowance of past-accelerated depreciation: Indian tax law allows accelerated depreciation on plant and machinery. When this accelerated depreciation is allowed, the written down value of the relevant block of such plant and machinery is also correspondingly reduced. In the concessional tax regime, the unabsorbed accelerated depreciation of the past years is disallowed. However, there is no corresponding amendment to provide that the written down value of the relevant block of plant and machinery should be increased by the above disallowance. In the absence of the above, taxpayers will be denied from claiming full depreciation on the acquisition cost of the plant and machinery they purchase.

The above corporate tax rate amendments as introduced through an Ordinance, needs to be approved by the Parliament within 6 weeks of reassembly. The Winter Session of the Parliament will commence on 18 November and the above ordinance being an Industry favouring one is likely to be passed by the Parliament in this session. It would be pertinent to see if the Ordinance is approved by the Parliament on as is basis and if any amendments are issued on it to bring in clarity and remove ambiguities.

If any waste is not marketable, the same shall not be dutiable - CCE v. Indian Tube Co. Ltd. 1995 (77) ELT 21 (SC); Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd.’s case (supra). For example, refuse, rubbish and ashes thrown up in the course of manufacture are not goods even if they may fetch some prices - CCE v. Tata Iron & Steels Co. Ltd. 2004 (165) ELT 386 (SC). If the resultant waste (after process of a waste) is same having almost identical chemical and physical properties, resultant waste could not be said as manufactured waste - Indian Organic Chemicals Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (88) ELT 644 (SC).

Waste and scrap is dutiable only when it is a manufactured product and not otherwise - Elphinstone Metal Rolling Mills v. CCE 2004 (167) ELT 481 (SC)

A by-product is something of value, which is produced in making main product or it is a substance obtained in the course of a specific process, but it is not the primary product. If it is not marketable (although sold in market in few occasions), the same will not be dutiable - Gujarat State Fertilizers Co. Ltd. v. CCE 1997 (90) ELT 149 (Trib. - New Delhi). For example, by-product obtained during the course of processing of rice in the rice mill, not fit for human consumption, does not fall within the ambit of definition of ‘vegetable oil’ contained in section 3(h) of the National Oil Seeds and Vegetable Oil Development Board Act - A.P. Rice Bran Solvent Extractors Association v. Union of India 1998 (103) ELT 481 (SC).

And waste and scrap arising out of manufacture of exempted goods are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise vide Notification No. 89/95-CE, dated May 18, 1995, provided that in such factory, any other excisable goods (other than exempted goods) shall not be manufactured - see also E.P. 1965, only sales made in nature of any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure or any sales in connection with or ancillary to such trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure were taxable. Thus, intention of doing the business measured by volume, frequency, continuity or regularity as well as profit motive was essential to tax a sale transaction. Any sale of goods done without intention of doing a business in those goods or without profit motive was not taxable. In this context Apex Court in the case of State of Gujarat v. Raipur Manufacturing Co. Ltd. [1967] 19 STC 1 had taken a view that to bring ancillary sales under tax net it must be shown by the revenue that they were made with an intention to do business and earn profit. It relied on its own decision in the case of State Of Andhra Pradesh v. Abdul Bakhi and Bros AIR 1965 SC 531. It was held that when a person in the course of carrying on a business is required to dispose of what may be called his fixed assets or his discarded goods acquired in the course of the business, an inference that he desired to carry on the business of selling his machinery or fixed assets or discarded goods would not ordinarily arise. Hence, the same will not be taxable.

Legislators amended the definition of 'business' by providing that any sale made in the nature of any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure; whether or not there was intention of makingany gain or profit; as well as sales in connection with or incidental orancillary to such trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure shall be covered.

First important decision on the issue post the amendment was rendered by the Hon. Supreme Court in the case of State of Tamil Nadu v. Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Co of India Ltd. [1973] AIR 1045. In this case the respondent under the Factories Act had to supply tea and edibles to its workmen for the Canteen established by it. It also supplied to its distributors calendars, purses and key chains. They also periodically sold items such as scraps, unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, rims, etc., Issue before the Court was whether these sales were 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' to the business ?

Before the above case, the Hon. Madras High Court in the case of Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. Sri Thirumagal Mills Limited [1967] 20 STC 287 had taken a view that even if by way of amendment to the definition of 'business' profit motive is deleted as an ingredient, still the ancillary activity has to be of commercial nature. It should still partake the nature of 'trade, commerce, manufacture, etc.' specified in the first limb and only then it can be taxed. Hence, it was held that turnover of fair price shop run for the employees will not be leviable to tax.

The Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court on the contrary in the case of Hyderabad Asbestos Cement Products Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh [1969] 24 STC 487 (SC) had taken a view that for an ancillary sale to be taxed it is not required that the same must be done with an intention of doing business. Any ancillary sale connected with the business shall be taxable.

The Hon. Supreme Court in the case of Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Co. of India Ltd. (supra) did not agree with the decision of the Hon. Madras High Court and affirmed the ratio decided by the Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court.

It held that the Hon. Madras High Court had not paid sufficient attention to word 'such' as appearing in clause 'any transaction in connection with, or incidental or ancillary to, such trade, commerce, manufacture,adventure or concern'. Hence, it held that after the omission of profitmotive, any sale which is ancillary to business whether or not made with an intention to do business of such ancillary goods shall be taxable. The Hon. Supreme Court thus held that once a transaction is covered within the ambit of terms 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' the same shall be taxable, whether or not there was any intention to do business in the commercial sense of 'business' in these ancillary goods.

In the given case the Apex Court held that whether sale of scrap such unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, etc, is ancillary to the business is a finding of fact. However, it observed that as the respondent was an oil company, all those items were parts of the business activity of trading in oil and, hence, the same were taxable. In respect of marketing items like calendars, wallets, etc. it was observed that such goods were given to dealers for increasing the sales. Hence, the same were also ancillary to business. With regard to canteen sales it was observed that Government Order specifically provided for exemption to sales made by canteen and, hence, the same must be considered by lower authorities.

In the case of Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd.’s case (supra), the Division Bench accepted the revenue’s argument that transportation did not come within the scope of clearance, which was not different from the view taken in the instant case. In the result it was held that the outward transportation of final products after their clearance from factory, in that case was not a service used, directly or indirectly, in the clearance of the goods from the factory. uThe question then arose as to whether such transportation could be said to be a service used, directly or indirectly, in relation to the clearance of the goods from the factory. That question did not appear to have been answered in Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd.’s case (supra) nor was it considered in CCE v NHK Springs India Ltd. [2007] 9 STT 548 (New Delhi - CESTAT) ‘Input service’ as defined under rule 2(l)(ii) is any service used, directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal. The revenue had noted the conjunction ‘and’ used in the definition and argued that any service to qualify as input service should be shown to have been used in relation to both manufacture and clearance of final products. That argument could not be accepted for at least two reasons. Firstly, manufacture and clearance are separate and different activities, one posterior to the other. A service used in or in relation to manufacture may not necessarily be used or useful for clearance. Secondly, the above argument of the revenue was incongruent with a situation where the place of removal was not the factory. Where the place of removal of final products is, say, a depot, transportation of the goods from factory to the depot is an input service as it is used in relation to clearance of the goods from the depot. Without such transportation, the final products cannot be cleared from the depot. On the other hand, obviously, such transportation has nothing to do with the anterior process, viz., ‘manufacture’ which was completed in the factory, and, hence, cannot be said to be used in relation to the manufacture of the goods. Therefore, the word ‘and’ used in rule 2(l)( ii) has got to be understood in the disjunctive sense, which is compatible with the differences between ‘manufacture’ and ‘clearance’ as also with the definition of ‘place of removal’ under section 4(3)(c) of the Central Excise Act.

uThe expression ‘in relation to’ has been similarly used in the definition of the term ‘input’ in rule 2(k). ‘Input’ means goods (with certain exceptions) used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products, whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. The expression was used in the same manner under the erstwhile provisions (rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944) also and the same has been considered and construed by the Tribunal in a large number of cases. There was a time when lubricating oils and greases, used in plant and machinery (capital goods), were not specified as capital goods under rule 57Q of the CER, 1944 nor as inputs under rule 57A. A doubt arose as to whether they should be considered as inputs or capital goods for Modvat credit and that was cleared by a Larger Bench of the Tribunal [Vide CCE v. Modi Rubber Ltd. 2000 (38) RLT 718 (CEGAT)] which held that such lubricants were to be considered as inputs used in relation to the manufacture of final products. That view was taken after noting that lubrication of machinery was essential for smooth conduct of the manufacturing activity. The lubricants did not enter into the process of manufacture and, therefore, there was no chance of their being contained in the final product. Nevertheless, it was found that they aided the manufacturing activity by lubricating the capital goods. There are also cases in which even effluent treatment chemicals used by certain industries were held to be inputs for Modvat credit under rule 57A. Those chemicals were also held to have been used in relation to the manufacture of final products. Whenever any good (other than capital goods) used by a manufacturer in his factory was found to have at least a remote relation to the manufacture of final product, it was held to be input used in relation to such manufacture. The expression ‘indirectly’ employed in the definition was understood as indicative of such relation. The expression ‘in relation to’ used in the definition of ‘input service’ has to be understood in the same sense as it has the definition of ‘input’. When it has to be determined whether a given service has been used, directly or indirectly, in relation to the clearance of final products from the place of removal, the test is whether the service has remotedly aided the clearance of the final products or whether the clearance of the final products would have been facile in the absence of the service and outward transportation of final products from the place of removal, being an activity posterior to the clearance of the goods, as in the instant case, cannot pass the test.

Cenvat credit relating to service provided at the residential colony outside the assessee’s factory 5.4 In the case of CCE v. Manikgarh Cement Works [2010] 24 STT 1 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee availed the Cenvat credit of service tax paid on (a) construction service, (b) repair and maintenance service, (c) manpower recruitment service, and (d) cleaning service, all of which were provided by the respective service providers at the residential colony outside the assessee’s factory. The employees of the assessee reside in the said colony. The residential buildings were constructed, old residential buildings were repaired and maintained, security guards for the colony were recruited by a manpower recruiting agency and the residential premises was cleaned by another agency. The adjudicating authority held the said services to be outside the purview of the definition of ‘input service’ given under rule 2(l) and, accordingly, disallowed the Cenvat credit to the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the Cenvat credit.

On appeal, the Tribunal held as under :

u The Supreme Court in the case of Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54 has considered the definition of ‘input’ given under rule 2(k) to be divisible into three parts; (1) specific part (main or substantive part); (2) inclusive part; (3) place of use and laid down an important ruling to the effect that, where the inclusive part of a definition provides a list of items, any such item should also satisfy the quintessential ingredients of the main part of the definition. In other words, the definition has to be considered in its entirety. The inclusive part is not independent of the main part. It is not a ‘stand-alone’ provision. This ruling is applicable to the definition of ‘input service’, given under rule 2(l). There is nothing in the said definition to indicate that the legislative intent behind it is different from the one underlying the definition of ‘input’. Accordingly, any service which is apparently covered by the parameters of the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ should also satisfy the quintessential requirements of the main part of the definition and, accordingly, any person claiming the benefit of Cenvat credit on input service in terms of the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ should establish that such service was used, directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of his final products or the clearance of such products from his factory.

u The assessee had sought to distinguish the decision of the Supreme Court rendered in the case of Maruti Suzuki Ltd. (supra) from the decision of the Bombay High Court rendered in the case of Coca Cola India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 130, wherein the Court examined the scope of the definition of ‘input service’ given in section 2(1) and argued that the Supreme Court’s decision relating to ‘input’ could not be applied to ‘input service’. The argument was not acceptable whether it be input or input service. The main part of the definition contains the quintessential ingredients and the inclusive part provides a non-exhaustive list of items each of which should satisfy the requirements of the main part. The assessee had pointed out that, in the case of definition of ‘input’, ‘place of use’ was the third part of the definition, which was conspicuously absent in the definition of ‘input service’. It had been argued that an input service need not necessarily be rendered within the factory premises whereas an input should normally be used within the factory. Broadly, this distinction sounds valid. But, again, it does not offer an answer to the question whether the service (which is rendered within the factory or outside) satisfies other essential requirements laid down in the main part of the definition. Even if it be held that there is no ‘place of use’ in relation to input service, the basic requirement remains to be that anything mentioned as an input service in the inclusive part of the definition should be shown to have been used in or in relation to the manufacture or clearance of final products, whether directly or indirectly.

u Accordingly, as the assessee had not established nexus between any of the four services and the manufacture or clearance of excisable goods, the benefit of Cenvat credit in respect of such services could not be allowed. However, in a case of this nature, the assessee should not be penalized. The instant case involves rival interpretations of a provision of law. In typical cases of interpretative nature, penalties have been waived by the Tribunal. In this view of the matter, the order-in-original was sustained except in respect of penalty imposed by the original authority.

On 20 September 2019, the government amended the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) vide The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019 (the Ordinance). The primary purpose of the Ordinance was to bring India's corporate tax rate at par with key competing economies. In addition to reducing the cost of capital, the reduced tax rate was also intended to act as a catalyst for companies to make fresh investments and consequently generate new avenues for employment.

Amongst other things, the Ordinance provided for reduced corporate tax rate of 15% under section 115BAB of the Act to new manufacturing companies which are not availing specified tax exemptions/incentives. The move was seen as a push towards the government's "Make in India" initiative and making India a US $5 trillion economy by 2024-25.

New manufacturing companies have been defined to mean companies which are formed after 1 October 2019 and begin to manufacture article or thing by 31 March 2023. While there are various conditions that a company needs to satisfy for claiming the lower tax rate, the main condition which is the subject matter of discussion in this article is as under:

"the company is not engaged in any business other than the business of manufacture or production of any article or thing and research in relation to, or distribution of, such article or thing manufactured or produced by it"

However, the term 'manufacture' or 'production' has not been defined under section 115BAB for the purpose of availing the reduced tax rate. Hence, it is generally understood that the definition of the term 'manufacture' as prescribed under section 2(29BA) of the Act may be relied upon while interpreting section 115BAB.

Section 2(29BA) of the Act defines the term 'manufacture' as follows:

"manufacture", with its grammatical variations, means a change in a non-living physical object or article or thing,—

(a)

resulting in transformation of the object or article or thing into a new and distinct object or article or thing having a different name, character and use; or

(b)

bringing into existence of a new and distinct object or article or thing with a different chemical composition or integral structure;

The government has on 25 November 2019 tabled the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2019 in the Lok Sabha. Amongst other things, the Amendment Bill seeks to clarify that business of 'development of computer software in any form or in any media' would not be regarded as a manufacturing activity for the purpose of section 115BAB.

It seems that the intention of the government is to only allow the reduced corporate tax rate to traditional manufacturing of physical goods generating large scale employment of unskilled and semi-skilled work-force, aka blue-collar jobs. Nevertheless, specifically excluding software development from the ambit of the section 115BAB could have more adverse consequences than originally anticipated.

Key arguments in favour of retaining software development within the ambit of 'manufacture' are discussed in the ensuing paragraphs.

Employment generation

As of 2018, the Information Technology (IT) industry employed nearly 39 lakh people in India. The industry is expected to add over 250,000 new jobs in 2019. [Source: Ibef.org]

It should be noted here that employment generation has been one of the major goal of the government to arrest the sliding economy. While traditional heavy manufacturing has a potential for employment generation, software development industry has also played a significant role in employment generation, albeit in white-collar jobs.

Impetus to Investments in IT industry

Because fresh investments have a cascading effect on various facets like employment generation and increase in disposable income etc, the government has taken various steps to attract investment, especially foreign investments. The liberalization of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) norms in manufacturing and more specifically related to contract manufacturing is a testament to this.

In this regard, it should be noted here that the computer software and hardware sector in India attracted cumulative FDI inflows worth US $37.23 billion between April 2000 and March 2019 and ranks second in inflow of FDI, as per data released by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)

This is despite the fact that India's share in the global software product market, which is valued at US $438 billion, is miniscule and the country continues to be a net importer of software products. The total software business in India stands at US $8.2 billion, out of which exports amount to a mere US $2 billion.

Views taken by Courts in taxation matter:

Keeping software development out of the ambit of manufacturing is also disconcerting since over the years, various Courts/Tribunals have held software development activity to be manufacturing under various provisions of the Act.

it has to be determined whether a given service has been used, directly or indirectly, in relation to the clearance of final products from the place of removal, the test is whether the service has remotedly aided the clearance of the final products or whether the clearance of the final products would have been facile in the absence of the service and outward transportation of final products from the place of removal, being an activity posterior to the clearance of the goods, as in the instant case, cannot pass the test. uHad the ‘place of removal’ of final products been other than factory for purposes of section 4 of the Central Excise Act, the transportation of the goods out of the factory up to the place of removal would have qualified to be ‘input service’ under rule 2(l)(ii ) for, in such a situation, transportation is anterior to clearance from the place of removal and passes the test. The clearance of final products from the place of removal (depot/warehouse) would not have been possible without their transportation upto such place from the factory. In other words, the transportation aids the clearance of the goods from the place of removal and can be said to have been used, directly or indirectly, in relation to such clearance.

uThe inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ is an exhaustive list of services which appeared to have a bearing on the scope of the main part of the definition. Some of the listed services are of a kind used (directly or indirectly) in relation to the manufacture of final products, while others are of a kind used (directly or indirectly) in relation to the clearance of final products from the place of removal. Services relating to setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of factory are in the first category, and so are those relating to procurement of inputs and inward transportation of inputs/capital goods. Services relating to sales promotion and market research can be identified as services of the second category, i.e., services used (directly or indirectly) in relation to the clearance of final products from the place of removal. The eye-catcher in this category is outward transportation upto the place of removal. This expression juxtaposed with ‘inward transportation of inputs or capital goods’ can only mean outward transportation of final products upto the place of removal. Obviously, ‘inward transportation of inputs/capital goods’ means transportation of these goods into the factory. ‘Outward’ being the antonym of ‘inward’, can only mean transportation out of the factory. What is transported from factory to depot or warehouse (place of removal) for clearance is not input or capital goods but final product. Such transportation of final products only upto the place of removal has been recognized as ‘input service’ under rule 2(l) as held by the coordinate Bench in Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd.’s case (supra).

uThe assessees’ opposition to taking aid from the inclusive part of the definition was not justifiable. Neither any rule of interpretation nor any judicial authority had tabooed it. Whether to take such aid for understanding the scope of the main part of the definition will depend on the text and context of the definition. The main part of the definition of ‘input service’ under rule 2(l)( ii) deals with service used in the manufacture or clearance of final products as also with service used in relation to the manufacture or clearance of final products. Any service used in the manufacture or clearance of final products is easily identifiable, whereas any service used in relation to the manufacture or clearance of final product is required to be determined, for which a ‘relation’ - whether direct or indirect, proximate or remote - has to be established between the service and manufacture or clearance, as the case may be. The services specified in the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ pertain to activities performed either in relation to manufacture of final products or in relation to clearance of such goods. They can, definitely, be of aid to the determination of the scope of the expression, ‘in relation to’, used in the main part of the definition. This is not to say generally that the inclusive part of the definition is expansive or restrictive. But one thing which can be said with certainty is that, insofar as transportation of final products is concerned, the inclusive part of the definition is restrictive as it permits such transportation upto the place of removal only as input service. The scope of the expression ‘in relation to’ used in the main part of the definition of ‘input service’ vide rule 2(l)(ii ) must be understood as circumscribed by the limiting factor as regards transportation of final products.

The sections 115BAA and 115BAB start with a non-obstante clause and overrides the other provisions of the Act. However, the sections are subject to the provisions of Chapter XII.

Owing to manner in which the sections have been introduced in the Act, certain issues have emerged which would need clarification, which are briefly discussed here-in-below:

1. Applicable tax rate on Long-term capital gains, short-term capital gains on listed securities and income under other heads

The sections do not override the provisions of Chapter XII of the Act i.e. provisions contained in the said chapter would hold forte. Hence special rates mentioned in sections 111A, 112, 112A, etc. would continue to apply.

Having regard to the language used in the sections, in our view, companies having income from House Property, Short-term capitals gains (other than on listed securities) and Income from Other Sources viz. bank interest, etc. should be taxed at 17.16%/ 25.168% if the reduced tax rate regime is opted for. A new manufacturing company holding sizeable rent yielding real estate and fixed deposits would stand to benefit (on account of lower tax rate of 17.16%) as compared to any other company having similar sources of income. The tax authorities may however, seek to dispute the adoption of section 115BAB by such companies by contending that the intention is not to extend benefit of lower taxes to non-business income.

2. Whether past MAT credit would be allowed

Sub-section 5A of section 115JB has been amended stating that provisions of section 115JB would not apply to companies which have exercised option to be governed by the aforesaid regime. It may be noted that no amendment has been made in section 115JAA of the Act which deals with utilization of MAT credit on account of MAT paid in earlier years. A plain reading of the provisions, in our view, suggest that past MAT credit available to an existing company should be allowed as a set-off against the tax liability under section 115BAA. There is no express prohibition in section 115BAA to deny MAT credit unlike several other deductions and losses specifically mentioned.

In our view, the MAT credit to be allowed in a year should be limited to the difference between the tax liability under section 115BAA and that under section 115JB which would have been payable. The fact that provisions of section 115JB are not applicable should not impact the computation of the credit which is separately provided in section 115JAA(5) and is an independent exercise for the purpose of determining and granting MAT credit only.

However, considering that the section seeks to override all the provisions of the Act, there may be litigation on the issue.

4.4 Certain additional issues on which the Rangachary Committee has opined but which have not been covered in Circular No.1 4.4.1 Issue No.1- Whether hiring of new employees is a condition for eligibility to claim deduction under section 10AA?

4.4.1.1 BACKGROUND AND RANGACHARY COMMITTEE'S VIEWS - Post the introduction of the sunset clause of the erstwhile section 10A provisions in the Finance Act, 2010, STPI units are no longer eligible to claim any tax benefit. On the other hand, SEZ units in software development segment enjoy a 15 year tax holiday under the provisions of section 10AA. The revenue denies benefits of section 10AA in certain cases where old employees are transferred from STPI unit to SEZ unit, stating that there should be a certain percentage of new employees in the new SEZ units to enable the units the tax holiday benefit.This contention of revenue is widely opposed by the industry experts in the absence of specific provisions in the income-tax statute on this issue. The Rangachary Committee endorses the industry's view in this matter and advocates that in the absence of specific conditions on employing new employees, denial of deduction under this section by insisting upon the employment of new employees is unwarranted. The Committee also recommends the insertion of prospective amendment to the income-tax provisions to set the qualification criteria in this regard.

4.4.2 Issue No.2 - Reduction in tax holiday owing to absence of parity in treatment of the terms 'export turnover' and 'total turnover'.

4.4.2.1 BACKGROUND AND RANGACHARY COMMITTEE'S VIEWS - In the absence of a definition of the term 'total turnover', the revenue while computing export turnover, excludes freight and insurance charges, in view of the fact that a specific exclusion of such charges is mandated in the Income-tax Act but does not exclude the above expenses while computing the value of 'total turnover'. This results in the reduction of the tax holiday available to the IT companies. The Committee recommends that whenever certain items of expenses or receipts are removed from export turnover, the same items of expenses or receipts should also be removed from the total turnover to ensure parity between the numerator and denominator.

In case of the above two issues, the recommendations of the Rangachary Committee are supporting the industry's views and an absence of any clarification being offered in Circular No. 1 issued by the tax department on the above two matters shows that the department holds its stand iterated in the legal precedents on the above two issues.

6.5 Statutory requirement

6.5-1 In Hero Motocorp Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (285) ELT 218 (Tri. - Delhi) - The Tribunal held that on bare reading of Rule 2(k) it was clear that 'input' meant and included accessories of final product cleared along with final product. Rule 138(4)(b) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1989 made it incumbent on driver of every vehicle to carry the tool kit prescribed by the manufacturer. Since carrying of the tool kit in the vehicle was obligatory for the driver, it could be safely inferred that tool kit was necessary accessory of the motor vehicle because driving of the vehicle without those accessories would be violative of Rule 138(4)(b) of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989. Thus, the Tribunal was of the view that the appellants had supplied the tool kit as per the statutory requirements under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 as accessories to be used in relation to the manufacture of vehicle. Thus 'tool kit' was squarely covered by the definition of 'input' under Rule 2(k)(i) of the CENVAT credit Rules and that the appellants had rightly availed of the CENVAT credit in relation to tool kit.

2. The export documents, viz., ARE and Export Promotion Copy relating to excisable goods exported by us under claim for rebate were misplaced by CHA. The following points will explain the position of law and remedies available —

A. Rebate is a form of refund as defined in section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and, therefore, time-bar stated in said section (except as otherwise stated) is applicable. Accordingly, the due date for filing rebate claim was 1-11-2012 + 1 year = 1-11-2013. The refund claim in this case is late by 3.5 months.

B. The date of filing of refund claim is the date on which it is filed along with all requisite documents. Therefore, even if you had filed an incomplete claim on 1-11-2012, the same would have been rejected as incomplete. However, in that case you would have an option to challenge rejection in appeal and you could have produced documents in appeal, as Commissioner (Appeals) has power to admit additional evidence as per rule 5 of the Central Excise (Appeals) Rules. Therefore, in similar cases arising in future, we would advise you to file refund claim in time even if some documents have been misplaced.

C. Even if the ARE and Export Promotion Copy were lost, it was always within your rights to file an additional certified copy thereof to the Department and then file rebate claim with requisite undertaking to the satisfaction of the Department. Therefore, it appears that you have not availed of requisite options.

D. Since all the aforestated options are outside the time-limit now, we would advise you to challenge rejection of rebate claim vide writ jurisdiction of the High Court. Only that may provide you relief, if any (grant of relief is within extraordinary powers of the High Court and discretionary). Though section 11B(3) bars refund contrary to section 11B, but in extraordinary circumstances faced by you, the High Court may consider your case.

Inclusive Part

5. The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

In Indo Rama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (219) ELT 122 (Bom.), the High Court held that the credit of duty paid on the goods or fuel used in the generation of electricity is available, provided the electricity is used for the manufacture of final product. The use of electricity must have nexus with goods manufactured in the factory.

5.1 Primary packing material - In Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 201 (Punj. & Har.), it was held that it is not a matter of dispute that chewing gum/bubble gums manufactured by the assessees are directly or primarily packed with the printed aluminium foils without tattoos. It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

Introduction

1. In September 2014 as part of a wider set of nation-building initiatives, the Central Government had launched a programme called as 'Make in India', to market India's image as a global manufacturing and export hub. For the said goal to be achieved, the first and foremost important thing would be to have Economic, Tax, etc., policies guiding and motivating the interests of business organizations. It is further an endeavour of all the Ministries of the Central Government that their policy framework shall be in complete synchronization with one another towards achieving the common goal and to ensure "Ease of Doing Business" in India. In present article, we will address one such issue wherein there appears to be conflict of policy and a tussle between two Ministries of the Central Government.

Chapter 7 of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015-20 ('FTP') issued by the Ministry of Commerce enlists various supplies which are considered as deemed exports and prescribes incentives for the domestic manufacturers carrying out such deemed exports. One of such supplier is supplying intermediate goods against an Advance Authorization. The benefits available for effecting such deemed export as enlisted in Para 7.03 of FTP are as under:

(a)

Refund of Terminal Excise Duty, if exemption is not available

(b)

Refund of duty by way of Deemed Export Drawback

(c)

Availing of the benefit of Advance Intermediate Authorization.

Similar provisions also existed in the erstwhile Foreign Trade Policy, 2009-14. However, vide Policy Circular No. 16, dated 15-3-2013, the DGFT had clarified that the benefit of deemed export in the form of "Terminal Excise Duty" shall not be available in respect of supplies which are entitled to an ab-initio exemption. It is to be noted that the above referred to Public Notice was challenged before various High Courts on ground of being unconstitutional and was later on was quashed for being unconstitutional and in contradiction to the Foreign Trade Policy, 2009-14.

The intent behind the Policy Circular dated 15-3-2013, was to ensure that the refund of excise duty collected by the Ministry of Finance, shall not be granted by DGFT. Hence, the aforesaid policy circular was specifically incorporated in the FTP by introducing Para 7.05 which had specifically denied the benefit of "Terminal Excise Duty" in respect of supplies entitled to an ab initio exemption.

An example

2. Now let us assume a situation where the supplies against an Advance Authorization are entitled to ab inito exemption under Notification No. 44/01-C.E-(N.T). As per Para 7.05 of FTP, a domestic supplier carrying out deemed exports cannot opt for availing of the benefit of Terminal Excise Duty for supplying of goods against an Advance Authorization and has to compulsorily clear the goods without payment of duty by availing of the benefit of exemption notification in force.

However, considering the fact that the domestic supplier is availing of the benefit of Notification No. 44/2001-C.E-(N.T) for effecting the exempted clearances, it is also required to reverse the proportionate CENVAT credit as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 inasmuch as the inputs/input services commonly received are also used in the manufacture of exempted goods which are cleared by availing of the benefit of Notification No. 44/01-C.E-(N.T). Moreover, the domestic supplier would also not be entitled for availing of the CENVAT credit of duty suffered on the inputs exclusively used in the manufacture of exempted goods which are supplied against an Advance Authorization as per provisions of rule 6(1).

Rule 6 issues under the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004

3. In the above regard, the attention is invited to rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which has an overriding effect over the provisions of sub-rules (1), (2), (3), & (4) of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Rule 6(6) has prescribed certain supplies, wherein reversal of the CENVAT credit will not apply even if the goods are cleared without payment of duty. Rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 covers all such supplies which are qualifying as deemed exports and also entitled to avail of the benefit of ab initio exemption, viz., supply to an EOU, supply to an ICB, etc., which are also covered by Para 7.05 of FTP, except supplies against an Advance Authorization.

622. CIT v. Cement Distributors Ltd. [1994] 208 ITR 355 (Delhi)

The word 'derived' has to be assigned a restricted meaning as compared to the words 'attributable to' or 'referable to' and, therefore, to avail of a rebate under section 80HH, an assessee must establish that he has derived profits or gains from an industrial undertaking.

♦♦

A.M. Moosa, Bharath Sea Food v. CIT [1996] 135 CTR (Ker.) 110

The law that the amount in regard to which exemption is sought must be relatable to an industrial undertaking, as the amount which would be understood to be 'derived from' is more than settled.

♦♦

CIT v. Pandian Chemicals Ltd. [1998] 233 ITR 497 (Mad.)

A restricted meaning is given when the Legislature uses the expression, 'derived from'. There is no justification to give the expression 'derived from' a wider meaning to cover every receipt connected with the industrial undertaking.

♦♦

Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT 1998 Tax LR 927 (Mad.)

The expression 'derived from' used in section 80HH implies that section 80-HH is confined only to profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and cannot be attributed to the original source of product.

♦♦

Pandian Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [2003] 129 Taxman 539/262 ITR 278 (SC)

It is clear that the words 'derived from' in section 80HH must be understood as something which has direct or immediate nexus with an industrial undertaking.

♦♦

Dy. CIT v. Vindhya Telelinks Ltd. [1997] 63 ITD 127 (Jab. - Trib.)

An income can be said to be derived from an industrial undertaking only if it is directly related to the running of the industrial undertaking itself. The scope of the expression 'derived from' is much narrower than the expression 'attributable to'.

♦♦

CIT v. Alpine Solvex Ltd. [2005] 144 Taxman 67/276 ITR 92 (MP)

The words 'derived from' as used in section 80HH/80-I have got to be given restricted meaning.

♦♦

BIO Pharma v. Dy. CIT [2003] 85 ITD 575/[2002] 75 TTJ 486 (Ahd. - Trib.)

The expression 'derived from' has a definite but narrow meaning and it cannot receive a flexible or wider concept. The phrase 'profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking' has been judicially interpreted as meaning that direct and immediate source of receipt is the industrial undertaking and the nexus is of the first degree in the genealogical tree. The correct connotation of the expression 'derived from', as laid down and explained by the Supreme Court in various decisions does not leave any doubt or ambiguity that interest from fixed deposits does not directly flow from an industrial undertaking and cannot be treated as derived from the industrial undertaking.

♦♦

CIT v. Modi Xerox Ltd. [2014] 50 taxmann.com 201/226 Taxman 152 (Mag.)/365 ITR 200 (All.)

The word 'derived from' under section 80HH has to be understood as something which has immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking. When the scrap generated from the concerned units has direct and immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking since the said scrap has been generated from the manufacturing process itself, benefit under section 80HH is available.

♦♦

Deccan Cements Ltd. v. CIT [2014] 41 taxmann.com 536/223 Taxman 194 (Mag.)/360 ITR 444/268 CTR 212 (AP)

The words 'profit derived from' and not 'attributable to'. Therefore, what is the import of the words 'derived from' has been explained by the Supreme Court in the case of Liberty India v. CIT [2009] 317 ITR 218/183 Taxman 349. Therein the Supreme Court had made it clear that the connotation of the words 'derived from' is narrower as compared to that of the words 'attributable to'. Hence, while reading the provision of section 80HH, the profit derived from the cement manufacturing activity is deductible thereunder and not otherwise.

◆ Accordingly, after the amendment, in the illustration considered above, the deduction under section 80HHC would be Rs. 70 and the aggregate deduction would be Rs.100. It may be mentioned that the provision does not require that from the amount of deduction under section 80HHC of Rs. 90, the amount of deduction under section 80-IA of Rs. 30 be reduced and restrict the amount of deduction under section 80HHC to Rs. 60.

◆ An assessee carries on two activities. One activity is manufacture of an article or a thing in an Industrial Undertaking eligible for deduction under section 80IA. The other activity is Trading Export, entitled to deduction under section 80HHC. The businesses are not interlinked. In other words, no exports are effected of the goods manufactured in the Industrial Undertaking. In that case, there may be a controversy about the applicability of the new sub-section. Its profits from the Industrial Undertaking is Rs. 100; its profits from Trading Export is Rs. 500; and the total income, accordingly, is Rs. 600. It is entitled to 30% deduction under section 80-IA.

Based on the language of the provision, can it be said that an assessee would get deduction under section 80-IA of Rs.30, and deduction under section 80HHC only to the extent of Rs.70? Having regard to the Explanation given in the Memorandum, the language of the provision and above illustration and the analysis, it is evident that the provisions of new sub-section (9A) would apply only where a deduction is claimed with reference to profit of the Industrial Undertaking, which is also entitled to deduction under other provision. However when a claim is made with reference to other profits, the restriction cannot apply. Accordingly, the assessee would be entitled to a deduction of Rs. 30 under section 80-IA and Rs. 500 under section 80HHC.

◆ In case of an assessee, which has a number of industrial units entitled to deductions under section 80-IA, whether full or partial, and also has exports, from the same Units and also otherwise, including trading and also, has project income eligible for deduction under section 80HHB, how would one give effect to provisions of section 80HHD(7) or 80-IA (9A)? It seems, the principles to be applied would be the same as discussed above, namely :

- The restriction imposed is not with reference to computation of deductions under the other provisions; and

- Where profits do not form part of profit or income on which the other deduction is claimed, the restriction should not operate.

Apart from the above, where exports are from the Industrial Undertakings, one may have to apply mathematical formula for finding out what are the export profits relating to those undertakings. Such attributable profits, which also form part of profit of industrial undertaking and are entitled to deduction under section 80-IA, the deduction U/s. 80HHC could be subject to the restrictions and/or limitations placed by section 80-IA (9A). However, the other export profits would not be subject to same discipline or limitations. Similarly, a deduction under section 80HHB cannot be curtailed inasmuch as it is not claimed with reference to profits of an Industrial Undertaking.
