rewritten_query: Can a new industrial undertaking claim the backward-area deduction on profits from manufacturing scrap as well as on proceeds from discarded water-storage drums?

case_summary.text: INCOME TAX : Where assessee set up an industrial undertaking for purpose of manufacture of steel forging, transmission gears and part and accessories of motor vehicles, receipts of sale of scrap being part and parcel of activity of manufacturing of forging items and being proximate thereto would be within ambit of 'profits derived from industrial undertaking' for purpose of computing deduction under section 80-IB

INCOME TAX : Where income generated from sale of spares as scrap actually only reduced cost of new spares purchased and, thus, leads to higher manufacturing profits to assessee, profits commensurate with scrap sold was said to be directly earned from manufacturing activity of assessee and, accordingly, assessee was entitled to claim deduction under section 80-IA on such income generated from sale of spares

IT: Where assessee put imported scrap to series of manual and mechanical processes and thereby brought into existence entirely new and distinct commodity which was marketable, it was to be regarded as 'manufacturing' activity and, thus, assessee's claim for deduction under section 80-IB was to be allowed

IT : Where assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with help of machines and then end product was rubber crumb, assessee was engaged in manufacturing of rubber crumb and hence eligible to deduction under section 80-IB
IT: Income from sale of scrap generated from manufacturing process of industrial undertaking has to be included for purpose of benefit of section 80HH
IT-II: Profits and gains from sale of scraps resulting in manufacturing process were eligible for deduction under section 80-IC
Converting scrap into an entirely new product to be treated as manufacturing activity for sec. 80-IB relief
IT : Scrap being bi-product of manufacturing activity, there are no expenses which could be excluded from sale of scrap for computing deduction under section 80HHC
INCOME TAX : Profits and gains from scraps resulting in manufacturing process were eligible for deduction under section 80-IC
Scrap income generated during manufacturing process would be eligible for deduction under section 80-IC: HC

INCOME TAX : Sale of scrap cannot be considered as part of 'total turnover' for purpose of calculation of deduction under section 80HHC in case of assessee engaged in manufacturing of industrial boilers

INCOME TAX : Where scrap was generated from production process and assessee was not in business of sale of scrap, any income from such scrap would tantamount to recoupment of cost of raw material/production and, therefore, was includible in 'profits of business' for purpose of section 80HHC

IT : Where assessee after using material, had sold packing materials/scrap and aggregate amount of scrap sale was credited to profit and loss account (thereby reducing cost of material), amount derived by sale of scrap was eligible for deduction under section 80-IC
IT : Income on account of sale of various items of scrap is to be included for purpose of calculation of deduction under sections 80-IA and 80HH

IT-III : Sale of scrap being part and parcel of activities of assessee-undertaking, gains derived from said activity was required to be taken into consideration for purposes of computation of deduction under section 80-IC
IT: For purpose of computation of deduction under section 80HHC proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover'

IT: When assessee undertakes manufacturing or production activity and in process it results in any scrap, since said scrap attracts nexus between profits and gains derived from export business, income arising from sale of it is eligible for benefit of section 10B
INCOME TAX : Scrap income generated during manufacturing process would be eligible for deduction under section 80-IC

IT : Where assessee imported metal scrap and after segregating such scrap, produced various articles including graded brass metal, metal vires, etc., entire process came within meaning of 'manufacture or produce'
INCOME TAX : Income from sale of scraps is an eligible income in calculating deduction under section 80-IC

INCOME TAX: Where a reopening notice was issued for reason that assessee had derived income from damaged goods claim and discount and that these incomes had no nexus and were not derived by assessee from manufacturing activities, hence, same could not have been allowed while computing eligible profits for claim of deduction under section 80IC, since there was nothing on record to suggest that sale of damaged stock had not been derived from an industrial activity and, therefore,
IT : Receipts from sale of scrap cannot be included in total turnover for computing deduction under section 80HHE
Profit arising from sale of scrap resulting out of manufacturing process would be eligible for sec. 80-IC relief

INCOME TAX : Profit from sale of slag, which was a by-product in manufacture of pig iron, was to be considered as profit from business of industrial undertaking engaged in manufacture and sale of pig iron for purpose of deduction under section 80-IB
IT : Assessee, engaged in manufacturing card boxes, was entitled to deduction under section 80-IB in respect of income arising from sale of scrap

IT: For purpose of computation of deduction under section 80HHC of manufacturer and exporter of stainless steel utensils, proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover'

IT: For purpose of computation of deduction under section 80HHC in case of firm dealing in trading and manufacturing of cycle parts, proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover'
IT : Sale proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in total turnover for purpose of deduction under section 80HHC
IT : Where assessee dismantled old plant and used same at new industrial unit but old plant constituted less than 20 per cent. of cost of new plant, deduction under section 80-I could not be denied

IT : While computing deduction under section 80-IA exchange rate difference should be treated to be derived from industrial undertaking whereas duty drawback should not be treated as derived form Industrial Undertaking
IT : Scrap sale is to be excluded from total turnover while computing deduction under section 80HHC
Generation of brass alloys and metal wires from metal scrap to be deemed as manufacture for sec. 10B relief
Income arising to EOU on sale of scrap generated during manufacture was eligible for sec. 10B relief
IT : Once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial for purpose of allowing deduction under section 80HH whether it is manufacturing or producing or processing
Sec. 80-IB deduction allowable to card box manufacturer on income arising from sale of scrap

IT : Where assessee's industrial undertaking was located in an industrially backward area, there was no need to fulfil requirement of SSI for claiming deduction under section 80-IB, even though it manufactured article specified in Eleventh Schedule
IT : Scrap sales is not to be included in total turnover for purpose of computing deduction under section 80HHC

IT : Where assessee claimed deduction on income earned from excess provision written back, as said amount was not an income but a reduced amount of eligible deduction in computation of profits derived from eligible enterprises, deduction claimed under section 80-IA would be allowed
Processing of unfinished handicrafts goods amounts to manufacture eligible for sec. 10AA relief

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing pickles, spices, paste and chutney, since process of manufacturing pickles from raw vegetables and fruits, masala and other ingredients had different marketable commodities than raw materials which were a different value addition, and a new product emerged therefrom, assessee was eligible for deduction under section 10B

IT : Deduction under section 80-IB is admissible to all small scale industrial undertakings/industrial undertakings set up in a declared industrially backward State/Union Territory, even if it is engaged in production of articles or things listed in XIth Schedule
IT : Assessee eligible for deduction under section 80-IC on account of sale of scrap.
IT : Where assessee did not establish any new industrial unit and had only improved existing unit by adding new machineries, deduction claimed under sections 80HH and 80-I were not allowable
INCOME TAX : For purpose of section 80HHC, proceeds of sale of scrap would not form part of 'total turnover'

INCOME TAX : Process of sieving carried out by assessee in its SEZ unit in order to separate dust particles from raw material such as silicon, sand and waste before reselling same as semi finished product in market amounted to 'manufacturing' and, thus, assessee was eligible to claim exemption under section 10AA

IT : Where assessee, a hundred per cent export oriented undertaking, claimed deduction under section 80-IB in respect of entire business profits including duty drawback receipt, duty drawback receipt was includible in computation of deduction under section 80-IB, only if it had first degree nexus with profits of assessee's industrial undertaking

Excise & Customs : Where re-processing of returned 'defective finished goods' results in scrap, duty is payable on such scrap at rate applicable to scrap and asessee cannot be asked to pay back entire credit taken on return of defective finished goods
IT: Where cotton waste disposed of by assessee was reused by purchaser was used for manufacture of lower count of cotton yarn, it would not come under meaning of 'scrap' as defined in section 206C

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a pharmaceutical company, had two units eligible for deduction under section 80-IC and 80-IB, assessee was eligible for deduction under section 80-IC in respect of income arising from sale of scrap
DEPB and duty drawback not eligible as profits derived from industrial undertaking for sec. 80-IB deduction:HC

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: SECTION 80HH OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-DEDUCTIONS-PROFITS AND 
GAINS FROM NEWLY ESTABLISHED INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS ETC., IN BACK- 
WARD AREAS-ASSESSEE WAS ENGAGED IN MANUFACTURE AND SALE OF 
DIFFERENT VARIETIES OF METALLIC WIRES AND IN COURSE OF SUCH MANUFAC-TURING ACTIVITY, WASTE MATERIAL, VIZ., SCRAP METAL, WAS OBTAINED-
WHETHER ASSESSEE WAS ENTITLED TO DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH IN 
RESPECT OF PROFITS FROM SALE OF SUCH SCRAP METAL-HELD, YES-
WHETHER ASSESSEE COULD ALSO CLAIM DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH IN RESPECT OF PROFITS DERIVED FROM SALE OF DRUMS, USED FOR STORING 
WATER, WHICH HAD BECOME USELESS-HELD, NO

SECTION 41(1) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-REMISSION OR CESSATION OF 
TRADING LIABILITY-WHETHER IN VIEW OF THE FACTS MENTIONED UNDER 
CAPTION 'DEDUCTION - IN RESPECT OF PROFITS AND GAINS OF INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING, ETC., IN BACKWARD AREAS', SECTION 41(1) WAS NOT 
APPLICABLE INTO PROFITS DERIVED BY ASSESSEE PROM SALE OF SCRAP AND 
DRUMS-HELD, YES

SECTION 41(2) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-BALANCING CHARGE-
WHETHER IN VIEW OF FACTS MENTIONED UNDER CAPTION 'DEDUCTIONS - IN 
RESPECT OF PROFITS AND GAINS OF INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING, ETC., IN 
BACKWARD AREAS', SECTION 41(2) WAS NOT ATTRACTED TO PROFITS FROM 
SALE OF SCRAP BUT WAS APPLICABLE TO PROFITS FROM SALE OF DRUMS-
HELD, YES

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

HELD: Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking. While giving the relief under section 80HH, value of closing stock of scrap would also have to be included. The sale proceeds of drums used for storing water and which had become useless could not, however, be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manufactur-ing activity in which the assessee was involved. This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings in backward area - Assessee-company had set up an industrial undertaking in a backward area and was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc. - Whether profits and gains from sale of scrap material resulting in manufacturing process were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, since scrap materials came within manufacturing process of industrial undertaking set-up by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc., set-up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH in respect of profit on sale of scrap which resulted in the manufacturing process. The ITO disallowed that claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim. On further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order.

On reference :

HELD: Section 80HH is meant to give a tax rebate to certain categories of assessees and one, who wants to claim such a relief, must strictly satisfy the requirements prescribed therein. He must establish that his profits and gains are derived from his industrial undertaking or the business of hotel. Axiomatic proposition of law is that it is not sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits earned and the industrial undertaking and the law requires that such profits must have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The industrial undertaking itself must be the source of that profit. The business of the industrial undertaking must strictly yield that profit. It must be the direct source of profit and not a means to earn any other profit.

In the instant case, in the industrial undertaking for the manufacture of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products, certain scrap materials resulted, which had a saleable value. To say that the scrap materials had no direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking, could not at all be expected to commend acceptance, especially, on the facts and in the circumstances of the instant case. The scrap materials came within the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking in the manufacture of certain products such as V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and certain rubber moulded products, etc. In that view of the matter, profits and gains from the sale of scrap materials were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, inasmuch as such gains or profits were derived from the industrial undertaking and includible in the gross total income of the assessee and the question relatable to the profit on the sale of scrap was answered in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels and industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether deduction under section 80HH is allowable on profit from sale of scrap in case of an industrial undertaking - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, an industrial undertaking, had claimed deduction under section 80HH on sale of scrap. The Assessing Officer held that the deduction could be available only on the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and not from income incidental to the activity of industrial undertaking. Therefore, for the purpose of determining the deduction, the income shown from sale of scrap should be excluded. In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the generation of scrap was independent to manufacturing activity and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim of deduction under section 80HH and the action of the Assessing Officer was confirmed.

On second appeal :

HELD: In Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT (No. 2) [2000] 241 ITR 803, the Madras High Court expressed the view that the scrap materials has direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, profit from the sale of the scrap materials should be eligible for deduction under section 80HH. Following that decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the relief under section 80HH was allowable to the assessee on profit on sale of scrap. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: II. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas (Computation of deduction) - Assessment years 1993-94 and 1994-95 - Whether scrap generated from manufacturing process has direct and immediate nexus with industrial undertaking and any income from sale of such scrap has to be included for purpose of benefit of section 80HH - Held, yes [Para 15] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: While computing deduction under section 80HH, the Assessing Officer excluded income from the sale of scrap by xerographic equipment unit and toner, developer, photocopier unit holding that income from the scrap could not be said to be income derived from the industrial undertaking.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to take income from sale of scrap as income derived from industrial undertaking.

The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: The word "derived from" under section 80-HH has to be understood as something which has immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking. In the instant case, the scrap generated from the concerned units has direct and immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking since the said scrap has been generated from the manufacturing process itself. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal have committed no error in allowing the benefit of section 80-HH to the assessee on the aforesaid income. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1994-95 - Assessee, engaged in running of steel and iron re-rolling mill, derived income from sale of brass scrap which he obtained from dismantling certain guns purchased in auction and which could not be used for re-rolling - He claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on such income which was denied as it was not considered as income arising from industrial undertaking - Assessee had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware that inside guns, there was brass scrap which was removed - Thus, it was only a fortuitous circumstance that, in relevant assessment year, assessee had purchased guns without knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in process of manufacture - Whether since brass was not an essential raw material of industrial unit, in question and brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling, there was no nexus between brass scrap obtained on dismantling of guns and main activity of assessee of steel re-rolling and, therefore, separation of brass could not be said to be in process of manufacture or a product or by-product of activity of assessee’s industrial undertaking - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, profit on sale of brass scrap could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking so as to be entitled to deduction under sections 80HHC and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the manufacture of re-rolled products of iron and steel in his re-rolling mill, filed his return of income which was accepted as such. In the course of the survey conducted under section 133A, the assessee had offered to pay tax on Rs. 10 lakhs. When required to explain the surrender, the assessee submitted that he had purchased certain guns in auction and certain quantity of brass scrap was obtained from breaking and dismantling those guns and the balance was iron scrap. It was contended that the said activity tantamounted to production of goods and, hence, income from industrial undertaking. The Assessing Officer, however, did not consider the income from sale of brass scrap as arising from industrial undertaking for purposes of allowing deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I and allowed the claim only in respect of other income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s submission. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal reversed the impugned order and allowed the revenue’s appeal. It accepted the plea that the assessee had purchased guns and the income from brass scrap which could not be used for re-rolling, thus, was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: The assessee in his explanation had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware of the fact that inside the guns, there was brass scrap which was removed. Thus, it was clear from the reply that brass was not an ingredient used in the process of manufacture in industrial undertaking of the assessee. The brass scrap had no direct nexus with the appellant’s industrial undertaking. It could not be said that brass scrap was a profit or gain which directly flowed, neither it had close connection with undertaking of the assessee. By removal of brass scrap which was not useful for steel rerolling work no different and distinct article came into existence, it was only incidental as was apparent from the assessee’s reply. [Paras 13 and 14]

Further, composition of brass scrap was not at all changed, that was only removed as that was not useful to the assessee for the activity of manufacturing which he was carrying on. It was only a fortuitous circumstance that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee had purchased the guns without the knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in the process of manufacture. There was no nexus between brass and activity of steel rerolling. Brass was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25]

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether income from sale of scrap not being relatable to industrial activities of assessee-company, could not be allowed for deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee-company claimed deduction under section 80HH on income from sale of scrap. The Tribunal disallowed the claim of the assessee on ground that income from sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee.

On reference :

HELD: This Court in a case concerning the same assessee in Pandian Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 254 ITR 562, had held, inter alia, that scrap not being a necessary by product in the process of manufacturer, the income from the sale of scrap could not be regarded as income derived from the industrial undertaking.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the income from the sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee for the purpose of section 80HH.

HEADNOTE: Section 80-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings, etc., after certain dates/infrastructure undertakings - Assessment years 1995-96 to 1998-99 - Assessee-company had a franchise for manufacturing Dabur products with ‘D’ Ltd. - Assessing Officer rejected assessee’s claim for deduction under section 
80-IA in respect of interest income earned by it and miscellaneous income arising from sale of empty drums/containers and useless materials - Interest income was earned on deposits made by it with ‘D’ Ltd. 
and its associates - Whether all sorts of income which are inextricably 
related to carrying on of business of industrial undertaking 
are to be considered for computing deduction under section 
80-IA - Held, yes - Whether while computing profit of business of 
an industrial undertaking under section 80-IA, revenue receipts 
 can be adjusted against revenue expenditure of like nature - Held, yes - Whether for determining profits and gains ‘derived from any business of industrial undertaking’, manufacturing or producing any article or thing includes sale proceeds of such article or thing or scrap generated during course of such manufacturing activity which amounts to increase in sale consideration - Held, yes - Whether since assessee was under business obligation to have security deposit with ‘D’ Ltd. and its associates and as such deposits were given in consideration of providing bank guarantee, organizing finance and providing franchise to set up industry by assessee-company, there was a direct and proximate nexus between interest earned on such deposits and interest paid on funds borrowed for running of business of industrial undertaking and, therefore, assessee was eligible for deduction on such interest earning under section 80-IA - Held, yes - Whether, even otherwise, since interest payment during year was more than interest received, in effect, there was no income on account of interest included in profits of business of industrial undertaking required to be reduced for computing deduction under section 80-IA - Held, yes - Whether, sale of empty drums/containers and sale of useless materials could not be ignored as it was closely and directly connected with outcome of manufacturing process itself and there was a direct nexus between sale of those items and carrying on of business of industrial undertaking - Held, yes.

FACT: The Assessing Officer found that the assessee had claimed deduction under section 80-IA in respect of interest earned by it and miscellaneous income arising out of sale of empty drums/containers and useless materials. As per the Assessing Officer, section 80-IA provided for deduction when the gross total income of an assessee included any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking. Therefore, he declined the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80-IA in respect of above items. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee-company had a franchise for manufacturing Dabur products with ‘D’ Ltd. For manufacturing of those products the machineries were financed by ‘D’ Finance Ltd., whereas the interest income was earned from ‘D’ Ltd., and ‘C’ Ltd., with whom the assessee made agreement for providing financial assistance to it and such arrangement was backed by stipulation of making security deposits in the course of business. It was further observed that the assessee was obliged to keep deposits with those companies in the course of its business and interest earned thereon was having direct nexus with its business. In respect of miscellaneous income, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the miscellaneous income arising out of sale of empty drums/containers, etc., was the outcome of the manufacturing process of the assessee-company. Therefore, the same was also held to be an integral part of the business of the industrial undertaking of the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) also held that interest expenditure incurred was much more than the interest income earned from the very same source and, therefore, ultimately there was no interest earning and, thus, deduction under section 80-IA could not be denied qua interest income.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: Only the income derived from business of industrial undertaking is eligible for deduction under section 80-IA. On the other hand, under section 80-I, the deduction is to be restricted to income which is derived from industrial undertaking. Thus, in the earlier section 80-I, the statute had used the expression ‘derived from’ with a view to give a restricted meaning to the income of the industrial undertaking. However, in section 80-IA, expression used is ‘profits and gains derived from any business of industrial undertaking’. It clearly shows that the intention of the Legislature, while inserting the additional words in section 80-IA, i.e., ‘any business of’, was to give benefit of deduction not only to the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking but also to give benefit of deduction in resect of the income having a close and direct nexus with the profits and gains of the industrial undertaking. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Sections 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings, etc. in backward areas - Three units belonging to assessee were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges - Further, assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets for each unit - Whether barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes and, therefore, barytes powder is an article produced from barytes - Held, yes - Whether sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate division of profits and gains in respect of a unit and Assessing Officer may compute such profits and gains under section 80HH on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit - Held, yes - Whether when industrial units satisfied other critiera laid down under sections 80HH and 80-I, assessee was entitled to deduction - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee established three industrial units in backward areas. The units were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges. The Assessing Officer held that mere crushing of barytes was not a manufacturing activity nor the powder produced could be called a new article. He further found that the assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets in respect of each unit. He, therefore, disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal found that the barytes powder so produced got its marketability for its use for the purposes totally different from that of barytes. It further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no division of account, still they were entitled for the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I as having satisfied the conditions laid down thereunder.

On reference :

HELD: Sections 80HH and 80-I do not contemplate the division of profits and gains in respect of a unit, provided the industrial undertaking satisfies the criteria laid down under section 80HH. The proviso of section 80HH(c ) itself provides that if in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the computation of the profits and gains of industrial undertaking presents exceptional difficulties, the officer may compute such profits and gains on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit. In other words, it empowers the Assessing Officer to ascertain the profits and gains of a particular unit and make assessment. Therefore, the assessee was entitled to the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I, provided the criteria laid down were satisfied.

It is not disputed that the barytes were made into powder by using power and the powder is a distinct and separate article from barytes and the use of barytes powder is in the manufacturing of paints while the barytes are used in a different form for different purposes.

Further, the barytes powder is marketed as such. Therefore, barytes are distinct not only in form and name but also in use from barytes powder and barytes powder is distinct and separate article produced from barytes. Therefore, it cannot be said that barytes powder is not an article produced from barytes. As a result, the assessee was entitled to deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I.

J.V. Prasad for the Applicant.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment years 1985-86 and 1986-87 - Assessee used to purchase potable spirit and by processing it produced IMFLs like brandy, whisky and rum etc. by adding certain percentage of water, colour and essence - Whether there is any difference between potable spirit and brandy or whisky - Held, no - Whether, therefore, no distinct article or thing could be said have been produced by assessee as alcohol remained alcohol throughout processing stage till it was marketed - Held, yes - Whether therefore, activities of assessee involved no manufacturing but only processing and, thus, it was disentitled to benefit of section 80HH - Held, yes
Words & phrases - 'industrial undertaking' occurring in section 80HH(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on business of manufacturing different brands of IMFL products. The business of the assessee was to process raw alcohol and sell the same with a new brand name. According to it, production of potable liquor involved dilution of the alcohol which was the raw material with de-mineralised water to prepare an admixture of alcohol and the same had to be properly blended with the right amount of essence and colouring substance by which an entirely new product emerged which had got a different name like brandy, whisky and rum etc. in the market and, therefore, it was entitled to the benefit of deduction under section 80HH. On the other hand, the revenue submitted that by mere blending of spirit and bottling the same, there, was no change in the commodity and, hence, the process of blending did not amount to manufacture; further, the quality of the original remained in the end products also.

HELD: The undisputed facts of the instant case were that the assessee purchased potable spirit from the distilleries as per agreement. This potable spirit was already manufactured and did not require any further manufacturing. Only some processing was required to produce IMFLs like brandy, whisky and rum etc. by adding certain percentage of water, colour, essence and, for safe marketing, required bottling. Generally manufacturing means consumption of one article for production of another. But, in the instant case, no article or thing was consumed for production of another. Alcohol remained alcohol. There was only reduction of degree of alcohol content because of addition of water to potable alcohol and stirring it. This action at best could be said to be processing and not manufacturing. There should also be transformation of article or thing if manufacturing is involved for the same. But, in the instant case no such transformation had taken place as alcohol remained alcohol both in the beginning and after processing also. In case of manufacturing also, article or thing should be distinct and separate. In the instant case, no new product had come as a by-product which could be said to be distinct and separate from the original one and alcohol remained alcohol with reduced content of alcohol because of the addition of water. There was also no change in its basic identity. Generally in case of manufacturing there will be change which is considerable and substantial but in the instant case it was not so. In order to encourage industrial activity in backward areas, section 80HH grants deduction to an assessee, whose total income includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking (other than a mining undertaking) or the business of a hotel in a notified backward area. Section 80GG(1) defines the word 'derived' from an industrial undertaking. The meaning of the term 'derived' has been construed to have a definite narrow and restrictive meaning compared to the word 'attributable' or 'referable to'. The industrial undertaking must itself be the source of the profits and gains and it would not be sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits and gains earned and the industrial undertaking. From section 80HH(2) it is clear that the Act has not given any definition of the expression 'industrial undertaking'. The requirement of section 80HH(2) is that to be eligible, the industrial undertaking should be one which is engaged in the manufacture or production of an article or thing. Therefore, the expression can be understood by looking upto the meaning as understood in common parlance or by making a reference to its definition in cognate legislation.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with  section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1979-80 and 1980-81 - Whether business of tyre retreading does not amount to production of new article entitling assessee to relief under sections 80HH and 80J - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, which was retreader and established its plant in a backward area, claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80J. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article and that, therefore, the assessee was entitled to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference:

HELD: The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such, comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.

Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles, which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production new words are not being added to section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved, that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture, would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. In view of aforesaid, it could not be said that retreading of tyres resulted in the production of an article for the purpose of section 80HH.

Hence, the Tribunal was not right in holding that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article entitling the assessee to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - In respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment year 1983-84 - Assessee having an industrial unit in backward area received a sum on account of job charges for twisting of yarn - Whether absence of separate balance sheet in respect of new unit would disentitle assessee from claiming deduction - Held, no - Whether assessee could be said to be engaged in manufacture - Held, yes - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction - Held, yes

Section 80-I of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Priority industries - Assessment year 1983-84 - Whether in view of facts given under heading ‘Deductions - In respect of profits of new industrial undertaking in backward areas’, assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee had installed an industrial unit at a notified backward area. During the year in appeal the assessee received a sum on account of job charges for twisting of yarn during the year. The claim of the assessee under sections 80HH and 80-I was rejected by the assessing officer on the ground that separate balance sheet in respect of the unit had not been filed; that the assessee had done job work and was not manufacturing goods on his own account and that, the twisting of year did not amount to manufacturing of goods for the purposes of sections 80HH and 80-I claims. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled to a deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal:

HELD: The fact that the assessee had not filed the balance sheet was not a valid reason for the disallowance of the claim. Further, the assessee’s claim was rejected on the ground that the assessee was doing job work and was not involved in the manufacture of goods owned by him. In view of the decision of the Gujarat High Court in the case of CIT v. J.B. Kharwar & Sons [1987] 30 Taxman 225 this objection could not be sustained. On the question whether the twisting of yarn by a chemical process did not amount to manufacturing of goods, the Tribunal in N.(P.) Ltd. v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 927 (Ahd.) of 1982] has held that when the flat yarn is physically twisted under mechanical process in chemicals, a different commercial commodity than the flat yarn is produced and as such the processing of the flat yarn amounts to manufacturing of goods. Since no contrary decision had been brought to the Tribunal’s notice, the decision of the Ahmedabad Bench of the Tribunal that the processing of flat yarn by a mechnical process and by twisting several threads together, a different commercial commodity is produced, was to be followed.

Thus, the assessee was entitled to deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 80J, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertaking , ships or hotels - Assessment year 1987-88 - Assessee-firm carried on business of manufacturing water/air pollution control plant at site of its customers, and its claim for deductions under sections 80J and 80HH was being allowed since its inception - Whether assessee was an industrial undertaking, engaged in manufacturing or producing an article in shape of air/water control plant in a backward area, and Commissioner committed an error in setting aside Assessing Officer’s order allowing deductions under sections 80J and 80HH - Held, yes - Whether since very year of inception of assessee’s business, position had continuously remained same and in absence of any new fact coming to his knowledge or any separate enquiry having been made, it was permissible for Commissioner to start afresh from admitted position of parties on a particular point - Held, no

FACT: For the assessment year 1987-88, the assessee-firm claimed deduction under sections 80J and 80HH and the Assessing Officer allowed the same in the assessment order framed under section 143(3). The Commissioner set aside the assessment order by invoking the provisions of section 263, on the ground that the conditions laid down for allowing deductions under sections 80J and 80HH had not been fulfilled by the assessee.

On appeal:

HELD: The Supreme Court, in the case of Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa AIR 1978 SC 548, has laid down that where there is (i) systematic activity, (ii) organised by co-operation between employer and employees, (iii) for the production and/or distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes, prima facie, there is an industry. Absence of profit motive or gainful object is irrelevant. This view of the Supreme Court has been followed by the jurisdictional High Court in the case of CIT v. J.B. Kharwar & Sons [1987] 163 ITR 394 and by Karnataka High Court in the case of Shankar Construction Co. v. CIT [1991] 189 ITR 463. In the case before the Karnataka High Court, the business of constructing dams and channels was taken as that of ‘industrial undertaking’ entitled to investment allowance; while in the case of J.B. Kharwar & Sons (supra) before the Gujarat High Court, the business was that of printing and dyeing of cloths and the work was taken as manufacturing work for the entitlement of deduction under section 80J. On the basis of the above case law, the working of the assessee-firm which was involved in the work of designing, erection and commissioning of water and air pollution control plants, would certainly be falling in the category of an ‘industrial undertaking’, and the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ as used in sections 80HH and 80J.

In the instant case, the activities of the assessee-firm were that of manufacturing or that of producing an article as they were constructing water/air pollution plants. Thus, the assessee-firm was an ‘industrial undertaking’ and was engaged in manufacturing or producing an article in the shape of air/water pollution control. That the assessee was manufacturing or producing the plant in backward area, was one of the requirements of the claim under section 80HH. The contention of the assessee was that only 11.45 per cent of the total receipt had been taken for deduction under section 80HH as that work alone was done in backward area and it was not expected from the assessee to have its office or plant in backward area. The crux of the case laws is that if an industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce outside in any backward area, it is entitled to deduction under section 80HH. The assessee-firm set up its own industrial undertaking at the site of its customers for whom water/air pollution control plant was manufactured and of the places which were falling under the backward area declared under the Act, then, naturally the assessee should be getting benefit of the same and the computation made by the assessee-firm of the same was correct one.

Thus the assessee-firm had been able to make out a case in its favour on the guidelines referred to above for qualifying its claim under sections 80HH and 80J and the ITO was justified in allowing its claim from the assessment year 1982-83 onwards till the year under consideration and the Commissioner committed an error in concluding otherwise and the order of Commissioner was to be quashed on this point.

be an activity of an Industrial Company, but it was another thing to say that such benefits were being claimed by a company not for its end-product, but for its intermediate products. Once it was held, the assessee contended, that the assessee-company was so entitled as it was an ‘Industrial company’, it would also be entitled to the investment allowance.

The assessee submitted that construction companies, thus, are also entitled to the benefit of the aforementioned provisions in relation to the intermediate products. HELD: Section 80HH provides for deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas subject to fulfilment of the conditions specified therein. The authorities had not come to the conclusion that the assessee did not fulfil the said conditions, as in view of their decision, the said question did not arise for consideration. The Tribunal, proceeded on the basis that the end-product of the assessee would not be an article.

An article would, inter alia, mean a particular object or substance, a material, thing or a class of things, material or tangible object.

Nobody manufactures a dam or a tunnel. A dam or tunnel is constructed, but the question, which arose for consideration, was although a tunnel or a dam would not be an article, which is capable of being manufactured, but whether the intermediate products may be considered to come within the purview of manufacturing activity/industrial undertaking within the meaning thereof. The question, which had not been gone into by the Tribunal was, if at all the gross total income of assessee included any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking, by reason of manufacture of intermediate product and not necessarily end-product, whether the benefit under the aforementioned provisions could be derived by the assessee-company.

Section 80J provides for deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established undertakings or ships or hotel business in certain cases. Sub-section (4) of the said section declares that the same would apply to any industrial undertaking, which fulfils the conditions laid down therein; clause (iii) whereof refers to manufacture or production of articles.

Section 32A refers to an investment allowance, inter alia, in respect of a plant specified in sub-section (2) thereof, which is owned by the assessee and is wholly used for the purpose of business carried on by him, whereas clause (a) of sub-section (2) lays down a qualification to the effect that the assessee should be engaged in the business of operation of ships or aircraft; no such qualification has been laid down in clause (b) thereof. Sub-clause (iii) of clause (b ) of section 32A refers to any other industrial undertaking for the purpose of business of construction, manufacture or production of any article or thing, not being an article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule. The said provision refers to construction and not to a construction company. It categorically refers to manufacture or production.

The question as to whether the companies, which undertake such composite business of manufacturing and constructions are entitled to the benefits of the aforementioned provisions in the light of the decisions relied upon by assessee was essentially question of fact which had not been considered by the Tribunal. It mainly proceeded on the basis of the end-product doctrine.

In the instant case, the assessee had not claimed benefit in respect of the entire profit earned by it, but was only asking for the relief to the extent to which it would have otherwise been entitled to, had it been held to be an ‘industrial company’ for the purpose of manufacture of the intermediate products, which it was required to manufacture for the purpose of utilization thereof in construction of dams and tunnels, etc. Therefore, it was obligatory on the part of the department to go into the said question. Such question was specifically raised by the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) as also before the Tribunal, but the same had not been considered in its proper perspective.

Having regard to the fact that the question as to whether the assessee was an ‘industrial company’ or not itself had been directed to be determined by the Assessing Officer by the Tribunal, the matter required fresh consideration at the hands of the Tribunal.

The decision of the Apex Court as also the other High Courts must, therefore, be considered while taking into the account the fact situation obtaining in each case. The interest of justice would be sub-served if the contention of the parties, which was the crux of the matter, to the effect that whether in relation to the intermediate products, the assessee-company fulfilled the criteria of ‘an industrial undertaking or not’ should be determined by the Tribunal in the light of the observations made herein before and on the basis thereof necessary reliefs could be granted in terms thereof.

EDITOR’S NOTE

Following the decision of I.T.C. No. 5 of 1998 in Hydel Construction (P.) Ltd. v. CIT, it was held that it would be appropriate to direct the Tribunal to re-hear the appeal and to find out, on facts, as to whether or not 51 per cent of the total income was attributable to manufacturing, processing and mining activities.

venth Schedule’, appearing in section 80-I(2)(iii) in the context of the fact that the deduction under section 80HH is meant to encourage establishment of new industrial undertakings in backward areas when such industrial undertaking ‘has begun or begins to manufacture or produce articles’ and in context of the fact that section 80-I is designed to encourage industrial undertakings to manufacture or produce ‘any articles or thing not being article or thing specified in the list in the Eleventh Schedule’. Provisions of section 80HH or 80-I are meant for the benefit of industrial undertakings that carry out the activity of manufacture or production of articles or things and not for the scrap merchants who trade in buying old articles or things and take out their parts to sell them separately. All large scale junk dealers in discarded old and scrapped vehicles who might fish out a horn in working condition from such vehicle or pull out its steering wheel or part of its engine that may have a demand in the market of second hand spares will proclaim themselves to be manufacturers or producers of articles or things. No such startling result is intended by the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, having regard to their underlying purpose of encouraging industries for being set up for manufacturing or production of new articles or things. In fact, industrial undertaking formed by transfer of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose is disentitled to such benefits both under sections 80HH(2)(iii) and 80-I(2)(iii). [Para 23]

The ships imported for breaking up are obviously old ships, purchased to retrieve the material, particularly steel plates, for disposal in the market for re-rolling or re-cycling purposes which is the activity done by these ship breakers in the process of ship breaking.

Thus, there is nothing whatsoever in the process of ship breaking activity which can be termed as manufacture or production of any article or thing. The dismantled material is already existing as a component of the old ship. The process of extracting steel plates from it while dismantling the ship will not make such extraction of existing material an activity of manufacture or production of such material nor will the process of cutting extracted steel plates for convenient disposal be manufacture or production of such steel plates. Merely because the ship breaking is considered as an industry, it would not be an industry engaged in manufacture or production of any article or thing. Benefit of the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I is clearly not intended for such ship breaking activities which do not result in bringing into existence any new article or thing. The word ‘manufacture’ in the context of sections 80HH and 80-I would mean making of articles or things. While dismantling, the ship steel plates are not made but only removed which is not the same thing as making of steel plates. The word ‘production’ in context of these provisions would mean the action of making or manufacturing from components or raw materials an article or thing and not just removing of an existing article or cutting it.

In the instant case, application of mechanical methods only removed the steel plates and other objects which were existing on the ships, which would not mean that the assessee produced those existing articles or things by the process of removing and cutting them. [Para 27]

The word ‘production’ or ‘produce’ when used in juxtaposition with word ‘manufacture’ takes in bringing into existence new goods by a process which may or may not amount to manufacture. The principle of adopting a liberal interpretation which advances the purpose and object of beneficial provisions cannot be carried out to the extent of doing violence to the plain and simple language of the enactment. [Para 27.1]

Therefore, ship breaking is not an activity which gives rise to manufacture and production of altogether new commercial articles or things. The assessees were not entitled to claim deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I and the Tribunal committed an error in upholding such deductions. [Para 27.2]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 32A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of certain incomes of hotels or industries in backward areas - Assessment year 1978-79 - Assessee-firm took over assets of a firm which carried on business of selling diesel engines in a backward area -Assessee-firm subsequently purchased machinery for manufacturing fuel injection pipes for diesel engines by making nipples and giving shapes at both ends of tubes which were used as raw material in process and claimed deduction under section 80HH - Whether unit of assessee having new machinery amounted to 'industrial undertaking' and process of making fuel injection pipes amounted to manufacture so as to make assessee eligible for deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: A partnership firm KB carried on business of selling diesel engines at a backward area in the State of Maharashtra. The business was carried on in the trade name of 'CD' up to 30-9-1976. The business assets of 'CD' were valued at Rs. 35,066. The assessee-firm was formed by a deed of partnership dated 1-10-1976. It took over the said business and assets and carried on the business of selling diesel engines. It subsequently purchased machinery worth Rs. 79,726 for manufacturing fuel injection pipes for diesel engines by making nipples and giving shapes at both the ends of the tubes which were used as raw material in the process. For the assessment year 1978-79, the assessee-firm claimed deductions under (i) section 32A and (ii) section 80HH. The ITO disallowed both the deductions. On appeal, the AAC affirmed the order of the ITO. On second appeal, the Tribunal, however, allowed the deduction on both the counts.

On reference, the revenue contended that section 80HH was not attracted because (i) there existed no industrial undertaking, (ii) the industrial undertaking did not either manufacture or produce any article, (iii) it was formed by splitting up or reconstruction of a business already in existence and/or by the transfer to a new business of machinery previously used.

HELD: Section 80HH is intended to encourage setting up new industrial enterprises and, hence, will have to be construed liberally in a broad commercial sense keeping its object in view. The Act does not define the expression 'industrial undertaking'. Therefore, reference to its definition in similar enactments or adoption of its ordinary meaning is inevitable.

In the instant case, 'CD', when taken over by the assessee, had neither any machinery nor was it making fuel injection pipes. It was carrying on only the business of selling diesel engines. The assessee made investment to the tune of Rs. 79,726 in purchasing new machinery for the purposes of making fuel injection pipes for diesel engines by making nipples and giving shape at both ends of the tubes. Tube was the raw material and the fuel injection pipe was the produce. Tube had undergone change as a result of operation performed on it by men and machine and a new identifiably different commercial and saleable commodity had emerged The Tribunal was satisfied after seeing the raw material and the demonstration of process of making the produce, that manufacturing activity was involved in the endeavour, and there was nothing on record to hold that this finding was in any way perverse.

Further, in the instant case, the revenue had not challenged the deduction under section 32A. The basic concepts of 'industrial undertaking', 'manufacture', 'produce' occur even in section 32A. If the unit having new machinery amounted to industrial undertaking and the process amounted to manufacture for the purposes of section 32A, it was difficult to see how any different legislative intent could be attributed to the identical expressions used in section 80HH.

Sub-section (2) of section 80HH refers to ‘industrial undertaking' and not to the assessee or his other business. There was no question in the instant case of formation of 'industrial undertaking', by splitting up of the business activity already in existence since there was no such activity before, or by transfer to a new business of machinery previously used for any purpose. Hence, condition Nos. (i) and (iii) in sub-section (2) were also fulfilled. The conclusion was inevitable that the assessee was entitled to deduction also under section 80HH.

Therefore, the Tribunal was correct in holding that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH.

HEADNOTE: SECTION 80HH OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961 - DEDUCTIONS-PROFITS AND
GAINS FROM NEWLY ESTABLISHED INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS IN BACKWARD AREAS - ASSESSEE CARRIED ON BUSINESS OF PURCHASING FORESTS, FELLING
TREES THEREON AND CONVERTING WOOD INTO USEFUL TIMBER IN BACKWARD
AREA - WHETHER ASSESSEE’S CLAIM FOR DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH IN RESPECT OF PROFITS FROM SAID INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING WAS ALLOWABLE - HELD, YES

FACT: The assessee, a private trust, carried on the business of purchasing forests, felling the trees and converting them into logs and, subsequently, sawing them into timber of various sizes and varieties fit to be used in construction of buildings and also for being put to other uses inclusive Of manufacture of furniture. The business operations of the assessee were carried on in a backward area. The ITO allowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of the profits and gains derived from the said industrial undertaking. However, the Commissioner held that all the activities of the assessee did not represent manufacturing activities. Accor-dingly, he set aside the assessment under section 263 and directed the ITO to examine each activity and allow deduction under section 80HH only in respect of those activities, which actually represented manufacturing of commodities.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: It is clear from the decision of the Calcutta High Court in Shaw Bros. & Co. v. State of West Bengal [1963] 14 STC 878 that sawing of planks from timber or sizing the same, amounts to manufacture. The activities of the assessee, in the instant case, could be taken to be manufacturing activities inasmuch as, commercially viable commodities had emerged out of the same and, therefore, there was an industrial undertaking as required for the purpose of the deduc-tion under section 80HH. Therefore, the claim for deduction under section

80HH in respect of the profits of the industrial undertaking was allowable and the Commissioner’s order under section 263 was not justified.

HEADNOTE: I. Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee-company while computing profits derived from its two new industrial undertakings claimed deduction under section 80HH, including marketing receipts and interest which was derived from marketing activities carried on by it - Whether since marketing activities carried on by assessee were independent of activities of industrial undertaking, in such circumstances, amount of marketing receipts and interest could not be included for purpose of computing deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, which had two new industrial undertakings, while computing the profits derived from the new industrial undertakings, claimed deduction under section 80HH, including the marketing receipts and interest which was derived from marketing activities carried on by it. While computing the deduction under section 80HH, the Assessing Officer, however, excluded the gross marketing receipts and interest. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed said order.

On second appeal :

HELD: The deduction under section 80HH is granted to an industrial undertaking on profits and gains derived by an industrial undertaking. The term ‘derived from’ is narrower than the term ‘attributable to’ as settled by the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Sterling Foods [1999] 234 ITR 579, therefore, it is only the profits of an industrial undertaking which are eligible for deduction under section 80HH. The assessee may be engaged in multiple business activities and the profits from such activities cannot become eligible for deduction under section 80HH merely because these are the business profits. The marketing activities carried on by the assessee were independent of the activities of the industrial undertaking. Thus, the net marketing receipts, i.e., gross receipts less expenses incurred/allocable to earning of such marketing receipts had been rightly excluded from the profits and gains of industrial undertaking by the Commissioner (Appeals). Hence, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue was confirmed.

HEADNOTE: Section 32A, read with sections 80HH and 80J, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Investment allowance - Assessment years 1983-84 and 1985-86 - Whether de-embarking and seasoning tree trunks and converting same into logs would amount to production of a new commercial article or thing within meaning of sections 32A, 80HH and 80J - Held, yes - Whether assessee engaged in business of felling trees, cutting them into pieces and converting pieces into logs to make commercially saleable article was entitled to benefit of said deductions - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of felling trees, cutting them into pieces and converting the pieces into logs to make commercially saleable article. The Tribunal denied the relief claimed by the assessee under sections 32A, 80HH and 80J on the ground that the establishment did not engage in manufacture of an article or thing.

On appeal :

HELD: INTERPRETATION : PRINCIPLES : OBJECT AND PURPOSE :

A plain reading of the provisions of sections 32A, 80HH and 80J clearly indicates from the very scheme that these are really in the form of incentives for industrial growth and development. The object cannot be overlooked while interpreting the statute. A construction, which advances the object, is to be preferred to that which is opposed to it. [Para 5]

SECTIONS 32A, 80HH, 80J : PRODUCTION : MEANING OF :

Section 32A provides for certain deduction in the computation of the income from the profits and gains from the business by way of investment allowance. Similar benefit is allowed further under section 80HH when such industrial undertaking is operating in backward areas. Further, similar incentive was allowed to new industrial undertaking under section 80J. Admittedly, the assessee had its industrial undertaking in the A&N Island, which was admittedly a backward area. The industrial undertaking of the assessee was established on 27-1-1977 whereas the cut off date of eligibility was 31-3-1976. Thus, factually the assessee, a new industrial undertaking, operating in a backward area having invested within the meaning of section 32AB, qualified for the test to come within the scope and ambit of the said three sections. But, in order to obtain the benefit, the business of the assessee must be that of an industrial undertaking owned by the assessee and engaged in a business operation in relation to manufacture and production of an article or thing. The entitlement of the assessee cannot be disputed or denied if it is established that the assessee is industrial undertaking and that the industrial undertaking operating in a backward area is engaged in manufacture or production of an article or a thing, and was established after 31-3-1976 and had made the investment. [Para 6.1]

ASSESSEE : WHETHER INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING :

The establishment of the assessee was definitely an industrial undertaking when it was engaged in production of certain commodities or things. Admittedly, the assessees’ establishment employed more than 20 persons and carried on the operation with the aid of power. The industrial undertaking has not been defined in the Act. Therefore, it must be given the ordinary meaning of an industry. [Para 6.3]

ELIGIBILITY OF DEDUCTION : WHETHER SATISFIED :

However, each and every industrial undertaking would not be eligible for the said deductions. An industrial undertaking which is engaged in manufacture and production of an article or thing would be eligible for the deduction under section 32AB; it would be eligible for the deduction under section 80HH if situated in backward area; it would, if established after 31-3-1976, be eligible for the deduction allowed under section 80J. In the instant case, all the ingredients were undisputedly satisfied. [Para 6.4]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1980-81 - Assessee, engaged in business of centrifuging rubber latex, claimed deduction under section 80HH - ITO rejected claim on the ground that assessee was not an industrial company manufacturing or producing any article or thing - Whether centrifuging process could be said to have resulted in manufacture or production of a marketable commodity and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH of the Act - Held, yes

Section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertakings, ships or hotels - Assessment year 1980-81 - Whether in view of the facts stated under ‘Deductions - Profits and gains 
from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in 
backward areas’ assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80J of the Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a closely held company deriving income from the business of centrifuging rubber latex. For the assessment year 1980-81, it claimed deduction under sections 80J and 80HH which was rejected by the Assessing Officer on the ground that the assessee was not an industrial company manufacturing or producing any article or thing. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) followed the Tribunal’s decision dated 23-12-1983 in the assessee’s own case for the assessment years 1977-78 and 1978-79 and dismissed the appeal. He further held that as the assessee was not employing ten persons on the average it would not be entitled to deductions under section 80J or 80HH, even if it was engaged in manufacturing operations. On second appeal, the Tribunal distin- guished its earlier decision on the ground that the notification dated 8-7-1983 (189 of 1983) passed under the Central Excise and Salt Act, which considered latex concentrate, preserved latex etc., as manufac- tured goods, was not brought to the notice of the Tribunal at the time of earlier appeal. It, therefore, took the view that by means of centrifuging process normal latex is converted into preserved latex which is entirely a different commercial product. Thus, it upheld the assessee’s claim. On reference by the revenue, the High Court observed that the Tribunal over- emphasised the effect of the notification dated 8-7-1983 (supra) and completely under-estimated and diluted the legal effect of its earlier decision and, therefore, the resultant conclusion was tainted. It was further observed that the essential question to be considered was whether when normal and natural latex is converted into preserved latex by centrifuging process, any manufacturing process is involved or a new commodity produced. The Tribunal’s decision was, therefore, held to be not according to law and it was directed to restore the appeal to its file and decide the matter afresh according to law.

On reconsideration of the decisions of various courts, and other materials on record:

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1993-94 - Whether only that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with industrial undertaking, will be taken into consideration for calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I - Held, yes - Whether where main business of assessee was to manufacture and sell soyabeen oil, income earned by assessee from sale of old gunny bags could be treated as an income earned from industrial undertaking within meaning of section 80HH/80-I - Held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling soyabean oil. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on the amount realized by it from sale of the old gunny bags (packing material). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim holding that the said income could not be treated as an income derived from an industrial undertaking. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted deduction as claimed by the assessee. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that the amount earned by the assessee from the sale of old gunny bags was an income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and was eligible for deduction.

HELD: As per the law laid down by the Supreme Court in several decisions, the expression 'derived from' is to be given restricted meaning in section 80HH/80-I while interpreting the section in which this expression is used. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the main and only business of the assessee, for which the plant was set up in the backward area, was to manufacture and to sell soya oil. Hence, all incomes derived from sale of soya oil would be income derived from an industrial undertaking for the purpose of calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I.

The income earned by the assessee out of sale of gunny bags could not be kept at par or alike the income derived from sale of soya bean oil due to following reasons - Sale of gunny bags was not the main or even ancillary business activity of the assessee; it was not regular or continuous business activity; no investment was made by the assessee for their sale. The gunny bags were never manufactured by the assessee in its plant and merely because some gunny bags were lying in the factory as surplus or unused or as waste material for any reason and such bags were sold to earn income, then it could not be a ground to hold that for the purpose of section 80HH/80-I, such income was the income actually derived from the assessee's industrial undertaking. [Para 16]

In order to derive income from industrial undertaking, the assessee must show that it was earned by sale of goods/commodity which were manufactured/produced in the said industrial undertakings as a part of its main and day-to-day business activity. Only then, the income earned by sale of such goods can be termed as income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I. It is for this reason that it has a direct or immediate nexus with the assessee's industrial undertaking established in the backward area. This necessarily follows that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking, alone will be taken into consideration for calculating the deduction under section 80HH/80-I, ibid. Such was not the case in the instant case, because the income earned from sale of gunny bags was not the result of direct or immediate nexus with the business of assessee carried on in the industrial undertaking. [Para 17]

Hence, the Tribunal fell in error in holding that the income earned by the assessee from sale of gunny bags was an income earned from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and, accordingly, the assessee was entitled to claim deduction from total income. That view was to be reversed and order of the Tribunal was to be set aside. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: V.
