Therefore, it is clear that even without section 80AB, the profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking referred to in section 80HH have to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43A and in any event since section 80AB has been held to be retrospective by the Supreme Court in H.H. Sir Rama Varma's case (supra), it was not open to the assessee to say that the said section is prospective as stated above.

On a bare reading of the judgment of the Bombay High Court in the case of CIT v. Albright Morarji & Pandit Ltd. [1999] 236 ITR 914/ 103 Taxman 168, it is clear that the said judgment is based on review of the various provisions of the Act both with and de hors section 80AB. In the said judgment, it has been laid down that section 80AB, though inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1980 with effect from 1-4-1981, was merely declaratory.

Accordingly, the appeal stood rejected.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc. in backward areas [Computation of deduction] - Assessee-company had been carrying on two activities; one was business of manufacturing cement and second was mining operation of lime - Lime was used as raw material in manufacturing cement - Assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH from whole of business income - Same was disallowed on ground that assessee had been carrying on business of mining operation - Whether mining activity of assessee was distinct and independent from cement manufacturing activities and segregation of profit of two different business activities was permissible under law - Held, yes - Whether segregation of profit derived from cement manufacturing activity was permitted by law in order to find out profit derived from mining activities and, thus, deduction under section 80HH would be available only on profit derived from cement manufacturing activity - Held, yes [Paras 6 to 11] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee had two separate and distinct undertaking, one for manufacturing cement and another for mining of lime that was to be used in cement manufacturing, profit only from manufacturing of cement would be eligible for deduction under section 80HH

FACT: The assessee-company had been carrying on business of manufacturing cement and also carrying on mining operation of lime which was used as a raw material in manufacturing cement.

The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH and the same was disallowed by Assessing Officer on the ground that assessee had been carrying on business of mining operation.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction by observing that the assessee carried business of manufacturing cement.

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee could be said to have been running two industrial undertakings. The assessee's main business of manufacturing of cement, was entitled to deduction under section 80HH in respect of items manufactured or produced, and it would not cease to be entitled to claim the deduction if the industrial undertaking is engaged in mining. The Tribunal, therefore, allowed deduction with respect to profit attributable to manufacturing cement.

On assessee's appeal to High Court :

HELD: From the records the Court find, as has been rightly contended by revenue that in the previous assessment years, namely 1984-85 and 1985-86, the Tribunal found on fact that the assessee has been running two industrial undertakings, one is mining of lime and another is manufacturing of cement. It is an admitted position further that against the aforesaid findings, no appeal has been preferred. Hence, the Court have to proceed on the premise that the mining activity of the assessee is distinct and independent from the cement manufacturing activity. Now the question remains is whether the use of the entire product of lime, extracted from mining operation for manufacturing of cement, looses its marketable value in order to ascertain the profit or not. [Para 6]

The argument of the assessee is that a manufacturer cannot trade with itself. Therefore, unless there is a factual sale in the market, no profit can be derived from this mining operation. In order to derive the entire profit, the cement manufacturing unit has to be taken into account and the product has to be sold in the market and then the profit will be ascertained. This submission, at the first blush, sounds logic, but while keeping in view the matter, this logic does not have any basis. It is the admitted position that lime is one of the raw materials in manufacturing cement and in order to manufacture the finished products, raw material is essential and the cost thereof is one of the factors for cost price of the finished goods. Therefore, in the manufacturing activity of cement unit, the cost of the finished product has to be ascertained and in that process, the cost of lime has also to be taken into consideration. In the case on hand, the lime, being a raw material, is not procured from open market and it has got its own indigenous supply. Therefore, the cost of the lime extracted from mining operation has to be ascertained from the cost price and it is found, while doing so, that the cost of lime of its own source (ordinarily it happens) is lesser than the market price. Therefore, the difference between the cost price of indigenous source and the market price is obviously the profit. Moreover, once lime is used from its indigenous source to manufacture the finished products and by virtue of sale of such finished products if there is any profit, then obviously that profit is also related to the mining operation. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Section 32A of the Income-tax Act, 1961-Investment allowance-
Whether, assessee was entitled to investment allowance under
section 32A in respect of machinery and plant installed in cold
storage-Held, no

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961-Deductions-Profits and 
gains from newly established industrial undertaking in backward
areas-Whether, assessee was entitled to relief in respect of cold 
storage, which was situated in backward area, under section 80HH-
Held, no

FACT: The assessee, being an owner of a cold storage situated in a backward area wherein potatoes were kept in the relevant assessment year, claimed investment allowance under section 32A on machinery and plant installed in the cold storage on the ground that the cold storage involved ‘manufac-turing’. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that a cold storage involved only processing and not manufacture or production of an article or thing. He also disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH, On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal;

HELD: Section 32 A uses the expression ‘business of manufacture or production of any article or thing’. The expression used in section 80HH is similar, namely, ‘to manufacture or produce articles’. There is no reference to ‘processing’ as used in the definition of ‘industrial company’ under section 2(7)(d) of the Finance Act, 1966, and the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1967. Again, unlike section 80J(4)(iii), reference is not made in section 32A or 80HH to the operation of a cold storage plant. This would show that mere processing (even if the potatoes were held to undergo processing in a cold storage) is not recognised under sections 32A and 80HH to amount to manufacture or production of any article or thing. The same expression is used in section 80HHA and 80-I(2)(iii). Again, section 35C, which deals with agricultural development allowance, refers to a company or a co-operative society being engaged in the manufacture or processing of a relevant article or thing There-fore, as neither section 32A nor section 80HH refers to processing of any article or thing, the lower authorities were justified in rejecting the claims of the assessee.

Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture and sale of portable gensets and water pumps - It imported certain spare parts and components and additionally imported gensets of a certain capacity which were not being manufactured in India - Assessee claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I - Assessing Officer disallowed claim in respect of profits earned from both sale of spare parts and components as well as sale of imported gensets on ground that profits therefrom could not be considered to be income derived from activity of industrial undertaking which was manufacture of gensets - Whether Assessing Officer was justified - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1991-92 - Whether if a new industrial undertaking fulfils conditions laid down in sections 80HH and 80-I, deduc-tions are permissible under both sections - Held, yes - Whether where on 
 same set of facts, revenue authorities in later years allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to a factory treating it as new industrial undertaking, deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I could be denied in relevant assessment year on ground that said factory was not new industrial undertaking - Held, no - Whether for claiming deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I, it is necessary to manufacture a product different from products which assessee was already manufacturing - Held, no

III. Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1995-96 - Whether where freight-collection was at par with job work receipts and was part and parcel of operation of business of assessee and connected to priority industry of assessee, assessee was entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on freight collection on depot sales - Held, yes

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95 - Whether assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80HH in respect of interest recovered from debtors for late payment of sale price, interest received from bank on deposits pledged with it for obtaining letter of credit/bank guarantee, interest received from IDBI on deposits pledged with it as required under section 32AB, interest from sarafi and bank deposits out of initial/surplus funds, insurance claim receipts for reimbursement of losses, interest from bank on short-term loans and interest on fixed deposits with banks, interest from Electricity Board from electricity deposit, dividend income, income from hire charges and interest on income-tax refund - Held, yes - Whether as far as sale of spare parts and of raw material and other misc. receipts is concerned, if it was a sale as an ‘after sale service’ condition or sale is of own manufactured spare parts or receipt has arisen in course of manufacture or production, it would be income derived from industrial undertaking; on other hand, if it is an independent activity not conditioned to sale or manufacture or production, it would not be an income derived from industrial undertaking even though it might be income attributable to industrial undertaking - Held, yes

Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings [Manufacture] - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with help of machines and then end product was rubber crumb, which was sold to tyre manufacturing company - It claimed deduction under section 80-IB - Whether assessee was engaged in manufacturing of rubber crumb and hence eligible to deduction under section 80-IB - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with help of machines and then end product was rubber crumb, assessee was engaged in manufacturing of rubber crumb and hence eligible to deduction under section 80-IB

II. Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings (Sale of scrap) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Whether deduction under section 80-IB is given on profits derived from manufacturing process, being undertaken by assessee which qualify for deduction - Held, yes - Whether where assessee set up an industrial undertaking for purpose of manufacture of steel forging, transmission gears and part and accessories of motor vehicles, receipts of sale of scrap being part and parcel of activity of manufacturing of forging items and being proximate thereto would be within ambit of 'profits derived from industrial undertaking' for purpose of computing deduction under section 80-IB - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

V. Section  80-IC  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 – Deductions – Special provisions in respect of certain undertakings or enterprises in certain special category States (Scrap income) – Assessment years  2014-15 to 2016-17  – Assessee-company included scrap income generated by its eligible manufacturing undertaking at Baddi while computing deduction under section 80-IC – Assessing Officer held that scrap income did not constitute profits derived from industrial undertaking and excluded same from eligible profits – It was noted that generation of scrap was an inevitable incident of manufacturing process and identical issue stood covered in favour of assessee by decisions rendered in assessee's own case for earlier years – Whether scrap income generated during manufacturing operations of eligible industrial undertaking formed an integral part of profits derived from such undertaking, generation of scrap being an inevitable incident of manufacturing activity – Held, yes – Whether, therefore, deduction under section 80-IC was allowable in respect of scrap income earned by eligible industrial undertaking – Held, yes [Paras 116, 123 and 127] [In favour of assessee]

Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1993-94 - Whether only that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with industrial undertaking, will be taken into consideration for calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I - Held, yes - Whether where main business of assessee was to manufacture and sell soyabeen oil, income earned by assessee from sale of old gunny bags could be treated as an income earned from industrial undertaking within meaning of section 80HH/80-I - Held, no

Section 80-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from Industrial undertakings, etc., after certain dates/infrastructure undertakings (Manufacture) - Assessment year 1997-98 - Assessee, a private limited company, was repairing and manufacturing transformers - It claimed 100 per cent deduction in respect of transformer oil, scrap and labour charges for sale of scrap - Transformer oil had been purchased by assessee from market and centrifuging i.e., processing, had been done by centrifugal machine in order to make it usable in transformer - In substance, no new articles or things had emerged from said processing, but only some special processing or treatment had been given to transformer oil through a particular method and, thus, it was a sort of processing only and could not be termed as manufacture of centrifuged transformer oil - Whether since there was no change in substance and no new article had come out, assessee was not entitled deduction under section 80-IA - Held, yes [Paras 26 and 27] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where transformer oil had been purchased by assessee from market and centrifuging i.e., processing had been done by centrifugal machine in order to make it usable in transformer and no articles or things had emerged from said processing, assessee was not entitled to benefits of 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - New industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether assessee’s claim, that technical service charges representing cost of the ‘brain’ - Component of electric typewriter manufactured by it, though billed separately for purposes of excise duty, was to be included as part of profit of undertaking for deduction under section 80HH, had to be allowed -Held, yes.

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1982-83 - Whether sales of waste material, export incentive, duty drawback and import licence premium shall have also to be included in profits of business for computing deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes.

Section 80J, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertaking , ships or hotels - Assessment year 1987-88 - Assessee-firm carried on business of manufacturing water/air pollution control plant at site of its customers, and its claim for deductions under sections 80J and 80HH was being allowed since its inception - Whether assessee was an industrial undertaking, engaged in manufacturing or producing an article in shape of air/water control plant in a backward area, and Commissioner committed an error in setting aside Assessing Officer’s order allowing deductions under sections 80J and 80HH - Held, yes - Whether since very year of inception of assessee’s business, position had continuously remained same and in absence of any new fact coming to his knowledge or any separate enquiry having been made, it was permissible for Commissioner to start afresh from admitted position of parties on a particular point - Held, no

II. Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee was generating and selling electricity - Assessee's claim for deduction under section 80-IB was disallowed in respect of receipt by way of sale of scrap and credit balances written off on ground that said income could not be said to have been derived from business of generation of power - It was noted from records that each and every item of credit balances written back and sale of scrap had not been examined by revenue authorities to ascertain as to whether those items had any direct link with business operation of assessee's industrial undertaking - Whether in aforesaid circumstances, matter was to be restored back to file of Assessing Officer for his fresh adjudication after examining all details thereof - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1977-78 - Whether assessee buying shrimps, peeling them and freezing them could be said to be engaged in manufacture or production, in absence of material on record to indicate what was done by assessee and how it was done, so as to eligible for allowance under section 80HH - Held, no

Section 80HH,  read with section 32A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1994-95 - Whether, in order to constitute an industrial undertaking, be it under section 32A or under section 80HH, important criterion to be applied by Assessing Officer is to identify item in question, process undertaken by it and resultant output - Held, yes - During relevant assessment year, assessee-hospital having made investment in plant and machinery, claimed deduction under section 80HH - Assessing Officer rejected assessee's claim holding that it was not an industrial undertaking - Commissioner (Appeals) as well as Tribunal allowed assessee's claim - Whether since there was no identification of items installed in hospital by Tribunal, it was not possible to express any opinion as to whether assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, matter was to be remitted to Tribunal for deciding case de novo in accordance with law - Held, yes

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether assessee carrying on business of ship breaking could be said to be an industrial undertaking so as to be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes.

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether there must be, for application of words 'derived from' as used in section 80HH, a direct nexus between profits and gains and industrial undertaking - Held, yes - Assessee industrial undertaking exported processed sea food and under Export Promotion Scheme was entitled to import entitlements which it could sell - Whether receipt from sale of import entitlement could not constitute profit and gain derived from assessee's undertaking and same could not be included in income of assessee for computing deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether assessee carrying on business of ship breaking could be said to be an industrial undertaking so as to be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

Section 80HHA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether activity of breaking or dismantling a ship or ships can be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactures or produces articles so as to be entitled to get deduction under sections 80HHA and 80-I - Held, no

Section 80HH, read with  section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1979-80 and 1980-81 - Whether business of tyre retreading does not amount to production of new article entitling assessee to relief under sections 80HH and 80J - Held, yes

Section 80-IB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee's industrial undertaking was set up for purpose of manufacture of steel, forging, transmission gears and parts, and accessories of motor vehicles - It claimed deduction under section 80-IB on its gross receipts which, apart from goods sales, also included scrap sales, labour charges and job work charges - Assessing Officer held that deduction under section 80-IB could not be permitted on sale of scrap, job work and labour charges as same were not derived from assessee's industrial undertaking - Whether activity of forging undertaken by assessee was 'manufacturing' within ambit of section 80-IB and when assessee was entitled to claim exemption in respect of income derived from such processes doing for itself, there was no reason to deny deduction on job work charges and labour charges merely because raw material component was being supplied by other customers for whom assessee was doing job - Held, yes - Whether since manufacturing activity of type of material being undertaken by assessee would also generate scrap in process of manufacturing receipts of sale of scrap being part and parcel of activity and being proximate thereto would also be within ambit of gains derived from industrial undertaking for purpose of computing deduction under section 80-IB - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with  section 80J, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits of new industrial undertaking in backward areas - Assessment years 1983-84 and 1984-85 - Whether amounts of cash assistance, duty drawback as also value of import licence nomination, can be taken as profits derived from industrial undertaking for purpose of determining amount in respect of which deduction under section 80HH could be allowed - Held, no

III. Section  80-IB , read with sections  80-IC  and  80-IE , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deductions  -  Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings (Sale of scrap/empty containers)  - Assessment years  2013-14 and 2015-16 to 2017-18  - Assessee had multiple eligible units claiming deduction under sections 80IB/80IC/80IE and earned receipts from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing - AO held such receipts were merely incidental, not profits derived from eligible undertakings, and excluded them while computing deductions - CIT(A), noting that scrap and empty containers arose from manufacturing process of eligible units and following Tribunal’s orders in assessee’s own case for earlier years, allowed receipts as part of eligible profits - Whether since revenue had not brought on record any material demonstrating a change either in factual matrix or in legal position prevailing during year under consideration, impugned order of CIT(A) allowing deduction under sections 80IB, 80IC and 80IE in respect of profits arising from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing process was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 9.7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas (Condition precedent) - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether what becomes entitled to claim exemption under section 80HH is an industrial undertaking and once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial whether it is manufacturing, or producing or processing - Held, yes - Whether assessee, an industrial undertaking engaged in activity of converting cotton pieces known as cops into yarn, would be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]IT : Once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial for purpose of allowing deduction under section 80HH whether it is manufacturing or producing or processing

Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1988-89 and 1989-90 - Whether, where assessee was engaged in business of fire works on job work basis and was supplied with raw materials by its customers and had engaged 200 labourers for producing end- product of crackers, it could be said that assessee had satisfied test of manufacturer as well as an industrial undertaking - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with sections 80AB and 260A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Newly established industrial undertakings or hotels in backward areas - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee-company had two separate units, one of which showed profits while other incurred losses - Claim of assessee-company for deduction under section 80HH with reference to profits of particular unit without setting off loss of other unit was rejected by Assessing Officer by recomputing deduction with reference to net profit after setting off loss in question - Whether deduction contemplated is to be allowed with reference to particular industrial undertaking and not with reference to total income of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in accepting assessee's claim and no substantial question of law arose from its order - Held, yes

Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of newly established industrial undertaking in backward areas - Whether assessee engaged in business of rearing and development of chicks into broilers, could be said to be 'manufacturing' a product - Held, no

facts.text:
The assessee-company, carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc., set-up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH in respect of profit on sale of scrap which resulted in the manufacturing process. The ITO disallowed that claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim. On further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order.

On reference :

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

The assessee-company, an industrial undertaking, had claimed deduction under section 80HH on sale of scrap. The Assessing Officer held that the deduction could be available only on the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and not from income incidental to the activity of industrial undertaking. Therefore, for the purpose of determining the deduction, the income shown from sale of scrap should be excluded. In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the generation of scrap was independent to manufacturing activity and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to claim of deduction under section 80HH and the action of the Assessing Officer was confirmed.

On second appeal :

The assessee established three industrial units in backward areas. The units were crushing barytes into powder for hire and receiving crushing charges. The Assessing Officer held that mere crushing of barytes was not a manufacturing activity nor the powder produced could be called a new article. He further found that the assessee had not prepared separate profit and loss accounts and balance sheets in respect of each unit. He, therefore, disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal found that the barytes powder so produced got its marketability for its use for the purposes totally different from that of barytes. It further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no division of account, still they were entitled for the benefit of sections 80HH and 80-I as having satisfied the conditions laid down thereunder.

On reference :

While computing deduction under section 80HH, the Assessing Officer excluded income from the sale of scrap by xerographic equipment unit and toner, developer, photocopier unit holding that income from the scrap could not be said to be income derived from the industrial undertaking.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to take income from sale of scrap as income derived from industrial undertaking.

The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee-company, which was retreader and established its plant in a backward area, claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80J. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article and that, therefore, the assessee was entitled to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference:

The assessee had set up a small-scale industrial unit in the backward industrial area. It was the case of the assessee that it purchased tea leaves powder/granules and dispatched same to the blend master, who after going through his own process, suggested the mixing ratio and process of mixing for making the perfect blend of tea, and the activity of blending of different types of leaves obtained from different gardens in a definite ratio resulted in production of a commodity having its own identity and though it might not amount to manufacture, it amounted to production. Therefore, it being an industrial undertaking set up in the backward industrial area and fulfilling all other conditions, was entitled to avail the benefit of deduction under section 80-IA/80-IB. The Assessing Officer, by holding that even after blending, tea remained tea and blending did not bring out a distinct marketable commodity and it did not amount to manufacture or production of article or thing for the purpose of claiming benefit of deduction under section 80-IA/80-IB, disallowed the claim of the assessee.

On appeal :

■

The assessee had claimed deduction under section 80-IC in respect of the profits of its Baddi Unit, including income arising from sale of scrap.

■

The Assessing Officer held that the income from scrap was merely incidental or ancillary in nature, not forming a core part of the manufacturing operation. He, thus, disallowed the claim of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), directed deletion of the disallowance, holding that the scrap income was derived from the industrial undertaking and eligible for deduction under section 80-IC.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee-company claimed relief under section 80HH in respect of the profits of a new industrial undertaking in backward area in the assessment year 1974-75. The said profits, it claimed, were to be arrived at without deduction of development rebate. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee's plea and his order was confirmed by the appellate authority and the Tribunal.

On appeal under section 260A :

The assessee-company was carrying on the business of manufacture of tyres and tubes. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I in respect of profit derived from factory No. III. The Assessing Officer allowed the claim after being satisfied that the conditions laid down in sections 80HH and 80-I were fulfilled by the assessee. However, the Commissioner, in exercise of his power under section 263, directed the Assessing Officer to withdraw relief allowed under sections 80HH and 80-I holding that the undertaking situated in the backward area was not entitled to simultaneous reliefs under two sections, i.e., 80HH and 80-I; that although in the impugned assessment, the Assessing Officer had made addition on account of understatement of sale of tyres to close business associate, yet he accepted the working of profits of the new industrial undertaking as made by the assessee which resulted in determination of excessive profit relatable to eligible undertaking; that the assessee was already in the business of manufacture of tyres and tubes for the past several years and, therefore, the third unit could not be said to be newly established industrial undertaking qualifying for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I; and that no deduction was permissible under sections 80HH and 80-I in view of the inadequacy of the profits of the said industrial undertaking.

The assessee's industrial undertaking was set up for the purpose of manufacture of steel, forging, transmission gears and parts, and accessories of motor vehicles. During the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under section 80-IB on its gross receipts which, apart from goods sales, also included scrap sales, labour charges and job work charges. The Assessing Officer held that the deduction under section 80-IB could not be allowed on sale of scrap, job work and labour charges as the same were attributable to the business carried on by the assessee, but not derived from the profits of industrial undertaking. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed deduction under section 80-IB on the scrap sales holding that the scrap generation at various stages of manufacturing process was part of the manufacturing activity of an industrial unit and, thus, profits and gains derived on that account were from the industrial undertaking. However, with regard to the claim of deduction on job work and labour charges, the Commissioner (Appeals) disallowed the appeal of the assessee and held that the job charges and labour charges not derived from the exports, were to be categorized as independent income and had to be deducted from gross profits to calculate profits derived from the exports. On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed deduction under section 80-IB on job work charges and labour charges also holding that job works/labour charges income received by the assessee, by utilizing its plant and machinery installed in the undertaking, gave rise to income which had a direct nexus with the assessee's industrial undertaking, and, thus, was entitled to claim of deduction under section 80-IB.

On the revenue's appeal :

■

The assessee had multiple eligible units claiming deduction under sections 80IB/80IC/80IE and earned receipts from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing.

■

The AO held such receipts were merely incidental, not profits derived from the eligible undertakings, and excluded them while computing deductions (e.g., disallowance around Rs. 36.24 lakhs in AY 2013-14 and similar disallowances in later years for specified units).

■

The CIT(A), noting that the scrap and empty containers arose from the manufacturing process of the eligible units and following the Tribunal’s orders in the assessee’s own case for earlier years, allowed the receipts as part of eligible profits.

■

On the revenue’s appeals to the Tribunal.

The assessee was a 100 per cent Export Oriented Undertaking ('EOU' for short) engaged in the manufacturing of X-Ray tubes, High Voltage Tanks, CT detectors used in CT Scanners and X-ray equipments.

For relevant assessment years, the assessee filed its return claiming deduction under section 10B.

The Assessing Officer restricted the claim of deduction on the ground that the turnover on account of export of spares/components was not to be included in the eligible profits to determine the deduction under section 10B of the Act.

The Assessing Officer further disallowed assessee's claim for inclusion of amount representing the sale of scraps in the company's profits for calculating the deduction under section 10B.

The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer holding that income on sale of spare parts was not eligible profit for the purpose of computing deduction under section 10B.

Insofar as sale of scraps was concerned, relying on the order of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case in earlier assessment year 2001-02, the Tribunal granted relief under section 10B in respect of sale of scraps.

On appeal:

The assessee-company was an industrial undertaking set up in a backward area, for the purpose of repairs of barges. It was following the financial year as its accounting year. For the assessment year 1976-77, its claim for deduction under section 80HH was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that its activities commenced prior to 31-12-1970 as was evident from the facts that it was allowed deduction under section 80J for the assessment year 1971-72 and that it had receipts from repairing charges during that year. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that the only receipt dur-ing that year being from repairing activity, no manufacturing activity commenced during that year but only in the next year and, hence, the assessee was entitled to the impugned relief.

On second appeal:

■

The assessee-company included scrap income generated by its eligible manufacturing undertaking at Baddi while computing deduction under section 80-IC.

■

The Assessing Officer held that scrap income did not constitute profits derived from the industrial undertaking and excluded such income from eligible profits while computing deduction under section 80-IC for assessment years 2014-15 to 2016-17.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that generation of scrap was an inevitable incident of the manufacturing process and directed inclusion of scrap income while computing deduction under section 80-IC.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee, engaged in the manufacture of re-rolled products of iron and steel in his re-rolling mill, filed his return of income which was accepted as such. In the course of the survey conducted under section 133A, the assessee had offered to pay tax on Rs. 10 lakhs. When required to explain the surrender, the assessee submitted that he had purchased certain guns in auction and certain quantity of brass scrap was obtained from breaking and dismantling those guns and the balance was iron scrap. It was contended that the said activity tantamounted to production of goods and, hence, income from industrial undertaking. The Assessing Officer, however, did not consider the income from sale of brass scrap as arising from industrial undertaking for purposes of allowing deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I and allowed the claim only in respect of other income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s submission. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal reversed the impugned order and allowed the revenue’s appeal. It accepted the plea that the assessee had purchased guns and the income from brass scrap which could not be used for re-rolling, thus, was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal to the High Court :

The assessee-company was engaged in the process of printing of continuous and non-continous stationery required by corporate sectors. In addition, the company was also having income by way of sale of waste paper, kasar, courier charges, labour income and miscellaneous income. It claimed deduction under section 80-I on all of those incomes. The Assessing Officer was satisfied with the assessee’s claim with regard to its printing activity and, accordingly, allowed deduction under section 80-IA. With regard to income by way of net courier charges, sale of scrap and job charges, he held that it could not be said to be profit derived from activity of manufacture or production of articles or thing by the industrial undertaking as required and defined under section 80-I and, therefore, declined the assessee’s claim for deduction on such income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that since the contract for printing was part and parcel of the distribution of the share application forms, the courier charges had to be taken as part of the printing and, therefore, were to be taken as derived from an industrial undertaking. Further, the labour charges were for printing work and though they bore the nomenclature of labour charges, they were in fact job work for printing and, therefore, income derived from industrial undertaking. The sale of scrap generated in the printing work was a result of the main work of printing and had to be treated as a profit derived from an industrial undertaking. The earning of those receipts had a near and proximate nexus with that of the industrial undertaking. He, therefore, directed the Assessing Officer to allow deduction under section 80-IA on those receipts also.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee-company was engaged in manufacture and sale of high tensile fasteners, cold extruded parts, etc., in Padi. It had a unit at 'k', a notified backward area, which manufactured fasteners and sockets. The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH in respect of forging work done in 'k' unit on products manufactured in Padi, which it called as 'sub-contract receipts'. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim for deduction in respect of 'k' unit. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to allow relief in accordance with law. Aggrieved, the revenue went in appeal before the Tribunal, which was allowed by a common order holding that the receipt on sub-contract could not be treated as income derived from the industrial undertaking for the purpose of granting relief under section 80HH.

On assessee's appeal :

The assessee, a Punjab Government undertaking, undertook substantial expansion programme for raising the production of tractors from 12,000 units to 25,000 units, which involved creation of a new industrial unit with substantial investment in plant and machinery, totalling to Rs. 40.90 crores. Since the product of both the old and new units was tractor and sold at uniform market price, profits of new industrial undertaking were computed on proportionate basis, as the assessee had not maintained separate books of account. On the basis of such proportionate working, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80-I in respect of the new industrial unit.

However, the Assessing Officer was not satisfied with the working of profits of the new unit. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that no separate books of account had been maintained and the working of profit derived from new industrial unit was not possible as the assessee had included many items of income, which could not strictly fall in the category of profit ‘derived from’ an industrial undertaking. The assessee had claimed deduction by including following incomes - interest received from bank on deposits, loans to employees, interest on income-tax refund, interest on HDFC bonds, recovery of insurance claims and profit on sale of fixed assets. The Assessing Officer held that these incomes did not relate to industrial activity and, therefore, not includible for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80-I. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer and concluded that no new industrial unit had come into existence and the entire exercise was undertaken for modernizing and expansion of the manufacturing capacity of existing unit.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling soyabean oil. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on the amount realized by it from sale of the old gunny bags (packing material). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim holding that the said income could not be treated as an income derived from an industrial undertaking. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted deduction as claimed by the assessee. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that the amount earned by the assessee from the sale of old gunny bags was an income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and was eligible for deduction.

The assessee-company, which had two new industrial undertakings, while computing the profits derived from the new industrial undertakings, claimed deduction under section 80HH, including the marketing receipts and interest which was derived from marketing activities carried on by it. While computing the deduction under section 80HH, the Assessing Officer, however, excluded the gross marketing receipts and interest. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed said order.

On second appeal :

The assessee, a private limited company, was repairing and manufacturing transformers. It claimed deduction under section 80-IA in respect of transformer oil, scrap and labour charges for sale of scrap.

The Assessing Officer noticed that company had been engaged in repairing of old transformer and it did not manufacture new transformer.

The assessee submitted that company had been manufacturing aluminium HT/LT Leg Coils which were used in old burnt transformers and on the basis of the said manufacturing, the assessee had claimed 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA(2)(iv)(c).

The Assessing Officer had held that assessee had not manufactured or produced transformer oil and scrap, rather had purchased the T/oil from market and only centrifuging i.e., processing had been done, but no new article or thing had been produced/manufactured. Finally, the Assessing Officer had turned down the plea of the assessee of 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled for the benefits under section 80-IA.

On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed deduction under section 80-IA on transformer oil, which was not sold, but was a part of assembly of transformer, and disallowed deduction under section 80-IA on scrap and the labour charges for the sale of scrap.

On further appeal:

The petitioner-company, which was carrying on the business of manufacturing and sale of beedies, set up a factory in a backward area. Some of the raw beedies were entrusted to contractors for being manufactured and with that along with raw beedies manufactured by the assessee itself in the industrial undertaking, the further processes of heating, ringing, belleying, wrapping and packing were carried on with the consequence that the finished product was made in the factory which was in the backward area. The petitioner claimed deduction under section 80HH. Deduction was allowed for some years by the ITO, for some years by the Commissioner (Appeals) and for some years by the Tribunal. On the ground that a part of the manufacturing activity was carried on outside the backward area, notices were issued alleging that the petitioner had failed to disclose fully and truly all the material facts for making the assessment. Petitioner questioned the issue of notices contending that they lacked jurisdiction inasmuch as the facts had been disclosed before the assessments were made.

On petition :

The assessee had installed an industrial unit at a notified backward area. During the year in appeal the assessee received a sum on account of job charges for twisting of yarn during the year. The claim of the assessee under sections 80HH and 80-I was rejected by the assessing officer on the ground that separate balance sheet in respect of the unit had not been filed; that the assessee had done job work and was not manufacturing goods on his own account and that, the twisting of year did not amount to manufacturing of goods for the purposes of sections 80HH and 80-I claims. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled to a deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal:

The assessee filed return and claimed deduction under section 80-IB for one of its industrial undertakings which was engaged in manufacture of pig iron. The Assessing Officer computed the deduction under section 80-IB only on the profits arising from sale of pig-iron, without considering the profit arising on sale of 'slag' which, according to the assessee, was a by-product in the manufacturing of pig iron.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that any profit earned on sale of such slag, had to be considered as part of the profits derived from the business of the industrial undertaking manufacturing pig iron for purpose of deduction under section 80IB.

On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the profit arising from the sale of 'slag' was not derived from the business of the industrial undertaking. Thus, it denied the deduction under section 80IB in respect of profit on sale of slag.

On the assessee's appeal to the High court:

The assessee, a private trust, carried on the business of purchasing forests, felling the trees and converting them into logs and, subsequently, sawing them into timber of various sizes and varieties fit to be used in construction of buildings and also for being put to other uses inclusive Of manufacture of furniture. The business operations of the assessee were carried on in a backward area. The ITO allowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of the profits and gains derived from the said industrial undertaking. However, the Commissioner held that all the activities of the assessee did not represent manufacturing activities. Accor-dingly, he set aside the assessment under section 263 and directed the ITO to examine each activity and allow deduction under section 80HH only in respect of those activities, which actually represented manufacturing of commodities.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

In the accounting year relevant to assessment year 1997-98, the assessee-company set up an industrial undertaking for the manufacture of applique/indexes for watch dials in a backward area. The assessee filed return of income declaring ‘nil income’ which inter alia included a claim for deduction under section 80-IA the deduction had been claimed at the rate of 100 per cent of the income earned. The Assessing Officer examined the details of plant and machinery, record of production of finished goods for year under consideration as well as for the previous year and found that the assessee had begun production of finished goods as on 4-10-1995, and that taking into account the value of plant and machinery in use as on that date, the total value of the machinery or plant previously used and transferred to the industrial undertaking of the assessee by its principal company ‘KDDL’, exceeded 20 per cent of the total value of the plant and machinery of industrial undertaking and, therefore, the assessee did not qualify the condition as laid down in Explanation 2 to section 80-IA(3)(ii). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the stand of the Assessing Officer.

In appeal, the assessee contended that it started its commercial production on 1-1-1996, and that the production carried out for the period 4-10-1995 to 1-1-1996 was only a trial production and that too did not involve the complete manufacturing process, and thus, the condition stipulated in Explanation 2 to section 80-IA(3) had to be examined on the basis of value of plant & machinery on 1-1-1996.

The assessee company set up a new unit at Sansarpur Terrace, Himachal Pradesh, for manufacture and sale of lamination tordials cores and transformers etc. It was claimed by the assessee that said unit was located in industrially backward area, therefore, the profits and gains of the said unit were eligible for 100 per cent deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer allowed partial deduction.

On appeal, the same was upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals). However, the Tribunal had allowed entire claim of the assessee.

On appeal:

The Assessing Officer found that the assessee had claimed deduction under section 80-IA in respect of interest earned by it and miscellaneous income arising out of sale of empty drums/containers and useless materials. As per the Assessing Officer, section 80-IA provided for deduction when the gross total income of an assessee included any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking. Therefore, he declined the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80-IA in respect of above items. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee-company had a franchise for manufacturing Dabur products with ‘D’ Ltd. For manufacturing of those products the machineries were financed by ‘D’ Finance Ltd., whereas the interest income was earned from ‘D’ Ltd., and ‘C’ Ltd., with whom the assessee made agreement for providing financial assistance to it and such arrangement was backed by stipulation of making security deposits in the course of business. It was further observed that the assessee was obliged to keep deposits with those companies in the course of its business and interest earned thereon was having direct nexus with its business. In respect of miscellaneous income, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the miscellaneous income arising out of sale of empty drums/containers, etc., was the outcome of the manufacturing process of the assessee-company. Therefore, the same was also held to be an integral part of the business of the industrial undertaking of the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) also held that interest expenditure incurred was much more than the interest income earned from the very same source and, therefore, ultimately there was no interest earning and, thus, deduction under section 80-IA could not be denied qua interest income.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee, set up a factory in a industrially backward area/State as specified in the VIII Schedule. The factory was a registered small scale industrial unit engaged in spinning of yarn for the manufacture of waste cotton yarn. The assessee purchased coarse cotton waste from various cotton mills, and got the job of cleaning and opening of cotton from an outside agency ‘S.U.’ by paying processing and labour charges. The end products was sold to handloom industries for making dusters and durries.

The assessee claimed deduction under section 80-IA that included the sum paid to the said outside agency. The Assessing Officer took up the assessment for scrutiny under section 142(1) and after considering details about that outside agency held that the assessee’s unit was an industrial undertaking. However, the Commissioner exercising his powers under section 263 held that the order of the Assessing Officer allowing deduction under section 80-IA was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. He held so mainly on the ground that the major expenditure paid to said outside agency was on process charges whereas the expenditure incurred by the assessee in its own factory was less than that. Consequently, he directed the Assessing Officer to reconsider the claim under section 80-IA.

On appeal :

The assessee claimed deduction under section 80-IB(1) read with section 80-IB(4) at hundred per cent of its profit stating that it was engaged in the manufacture of electrical power distribution and control equipments [electrical control panels] at its undertaking located at Daman (UT), a backward area.

The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of deduction on the grounds that (i) the assessee's workers were mounting bought out components on the panel and wiring them and, therefore, the processes involved, though loosely termed as 'manufacture', was essentially only an assembly job, (ii) the assessee was procuring goods on a contract basis from the contractors, who supplied electric control panels as assembled by them at their own premises located at Kalyan, Thane and Mumbai, as the case may be, (iii) there was low power consumption, and (iv) there was low quantum of plant and machinery.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim of deduction.

On second appeal:

The assessee had set-up its industrial undertaking in an industrially backward district. It was engaged in production of ‘cattle and poultry feed’ in its said establishment. The cattle and poultry feed was produced from raw materials, purchased by it like maize, soya and other ingredients. For the relevant assessment years, the assessee claimed benefit of deduction under section 80-IB(5) which was allowed. Subsequently, the Assessing Officer, taking a view that the production of ‘cattle and poultry feed’ could not be classified as manufacture, initiated reassessment proceedings. The assessee filed instant writ petition challenging the validity of the reassessment proceedings.

The assessee established a new industrial undertaking in a backward area and claimed deductions under section 80HH of Rs. 55,518 and section 80J of Rs. 62,515, respectively, for the assessment year 1981-82. The Assessing Officer allowed deductions of Rs. 55,518 under section 80HH in full and Rs. 6,997 (Rs. 62,515 less Rs. 55,518) under section 80J. The Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal allowed full deduction as claimed by the assessee under sections 80HH and 80J.

On reference :

During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1977-78, assessee-firm entered into an agreement with another company for processing of scrap material by the another company's labour in the assessee's factory. The factory of assessee was used exclusively by the other party. The workers were also engaged by the said company and the work was done under the direct supervision and control of the officers of the said company. The raw material consumed in the manufacturing process also belonged to the said company. The only work carried out in the factory was the processing of the scrap material of the other company for which assessee received certain remuneration described as 'labour charges'. In its assessment for the assessment year 1977-78, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80J in respect of the above amount claiming it to be profits and gains of the newly established industrial undertaking. The ITO rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that section 80J was not attracted. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that section 80J was applicable as processing and manufacturing work was done in the factory of the assessee - wherein more than 10 persons were employed and it was immaterial whether the workers were paid and employed by the assessee or the company whose scrap material was processed therein. On appeal by the revenue, the Tribunal affirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On reference:

■

The assessee included scrap sales income in computing profits eligible for deduction under section 80IA.

■

The Assessing Officer noted no explanation was furnished to show a direct nexus with the eligible business and proposed exclusion of the amount from eligible profits.

■

The DRP did not issue a specific direction on this item, and the Assessing Officer, in the final order, excluded scrap sale from profits eligible for section 80IA.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal

The assessee-company was engaged in manufacture and sale of rubberized coir products like mattresses, pillows, railway and bus seats. It had four industrial units one of which was a new one and was located in a backward area. The assessee claimed that it was entitled to get deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I in respect of said unit before allowing deduction under section 35(2). However, the Assessing Officer first granted eligible deduction under section 35(2) on the capital expenditure in research and development and on the gross total income so arrived at, he granted deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I from the gross total income before granting deduction under section 35(2). The Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal :

A partnership firm KB carried on business of selling diesel engines at a backward area in the State of Maharashtra. The business was carried on in the trade name of 'CD' up to 30-9-1976. The business assets of 'CD' were valued at Rs. 35,066. The assessee-firm was formed by a deed of partnership dated 1-10-1976. It took over the said business and assets and carried on the business of selling diesel engines. It subsequently purchased machinery worth Rs. 79,726 for manufacturing fuel injection pipes for diesel engines by making nipples and giving shapes at both the ends of the tubes which were used as raw material in the process. For the assessment year 1978-79, the assessee-firm claimed deductions under (i) section 32A and (ii) section 80HH. The ITO disallowed both the deductions. On appeal, the AAC affirmed the order of the ITO. On second appeal, the Tribunal, however, allowed the deduction on both the counts.

On reference, the revenue contended that section 80HH was not attracted because (i) there existed no industrial undertaking, (ii) the industrial undertaking did not either manufacture or produce any article, (iii) it was formed by splitting up or reconstruction of a business already in existence and/or by the transfer to a new business of machinery previously used.

The assessee, engaged in the business of rearing of chicks to broilers, a saleable product, by applying scientific process and technology, established an industrial unit in the backward area and claimed deduction under section 80HH and section 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the claim. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal, however, set aside the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) and affirmed that of the Assessing Officer.

The assessees, engaged in the business of breaking and dismantling of damaged or unserviceable ships and selling the goods obtained therefrom to various parties, claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claims on the grounds that the assessee were not industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH and 80-I and they did not fulfil any of the conditions of those sections and that there was nothing like a process of manufacturing done by the assessees. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that ship breaking was an industrial undertaking and, accordingly, the assessees were eligible for the deductions claimed.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee company was a newly established industrial undertaking set up in a backward area. It claimed deduction under section 80HH. The ITO, however, held that the business loss, unabsorbed investment allowance and the depreciation carried forward from the earlier years should first be deducted and the deduction under section 80HH should be allowable only on the net income of the business.

However, on second appeal, the Tribunal held that the deduction under section 80HH should be given on the gross profit of the newly established industrial undertaking without setting off the earlier losses provided in the Act for the computation of business income. In so far as the assessment year 1980-81 was concerned, the Tribunal directed the ITO to recompute the relief depending upon the computation of income for the earlier assessment year 1979-80.

On reference:

The assessee-company, engaged in the manufacture of cooling towers, had set-up one unit at ‘O’ in the year 1985 for manufacturing of certain components required for round bottle (RB series) cool- ing towers. During the financial year 1991-92, the assessee had set-up a new unit at ‘C’ in order to revamp its business activities and ente- red into collaboration agreement with a foreign company ‘G’ and obtained technical know-how for making ‘cross flow’ (XE series) and ‘counter flow’ (CM series) cooling towers. The assessee had also closed down its original unit situated at ‘O’ during the year 1992 and plant and machinery and moulds from the ‘O’ unit were transferred to the new unit at ‘C’. As per the assessee the total extent of such items transferred was 11.60 per cent of the total investment in new plant in terms of cost and 0.63 per cent in terms of WDV. Most of the employees of the old unit were also transferred to the new unit and certain new employees were also recruited. The assessee thereafter started manufacturing in the new unit, certain components required for cooling towers, i.e., RB series, XE series and CM series. The modus operandi of the assessee in carrying out business was that on receipt of enquiries from the clients, it designed the cooling tower as per requirement of the clients and the quotations were forwarded to the clients along with detailed analysis of the said towers. The assessee on receipt of the orders from the clients manufactured the basic compo-nents required for the said cooling towers in its unit and certain items/components like electric motors, fans, etc., were purchased from the market. As per the assessee, these items were tested and checked in the factory of the assessee. The said components, i.e., manufactured and bought out items were transferred to the site of the customers and two separate invoices were prepared, one for in-house manufactured components on which excise duty was paid and another for the bought out components and, accordingly, the sales were shown under the head ‘Manufactured items and bought out components’. The assembly of the unit and erection of the same was carried out at the customer’s site and the assessee in addition raised the bill for installation charges, forwarding charges and service charges, which were booked under the respective heads in the books of account. For the relevant assessment years, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80-IA on the total turnover of the manufactured items during the year, including sale of bought out components, installation charges, forwarding charges and service charges. The Assessing Officer held that the new unit set-up by the assessee manufactured the items required for XE and CM type cooling towers only and the machinery, which had been shifted from the old unit, manufactured the parts required for round bottle cooling towers; and that since the moulds required for manufacturing the round bottle and CM/XE type cooling towers were independent and totally different and the assessee started manufacturing both under one roof for the sake of convenience and the old equipment was acquired in the year 1985 while the new equipment was purchased in 1992, the profits arising from the sale of items manufactured by the assessee for round bottle cooling towers were not eligible for deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer further held that bought out components purchased by the assessee from the market were never integrated at the assessee’s factory into the cooling tower and tested and, therefore, the assessee was not manufacturing the cooling tower but manufacturing only certain parts required for cooling towers and assembling the cooling tower at the clients’ place as per the requirement of the clients. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the profit earned by the assessee on the bought out components did not have any nexus with the manufacturing activity carried out by the assessee in its factory and the said profit could not be treated as profits of industrial undertaking for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer in respect of the forwarding charges, installation charges and service charges held that the assessee had incurred expenditure on account of transport, labour charges both for loading/unloading and assembling, which were not adjusted against the receipts and, therefore, all these charges did not have any connection with the manufacturing activity of the assessee and, accordingly, the profit earned by the assessee on the said charges was not eligible for deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA only in respect of profits arising from sale of components manufactured by the assessee required for XE and CM cooling towers. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the impugned order.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company, a small-scale industrial undertaking, was carrying on the business of manufacturing ‘Jarda’ from raw tobacco in a backward area. The processing operations employed by the assessee were that raw tobacco (angad) was stripped off the midrib by manual labour. It was then sand-screened to control the moisture content. The raw tobacco was fed into a vibratory feeder and it was conveyed into a pneumatic pick up duct where heavy stems and stones would drop down. In the pick up duct, the tobacco was lifted up by suction and discharged into first tower classifier. In this tower classifier, the heavier tobacco flakes were separated from lighter ones and left behind. The lighter flakes were carried by air into second tower classifier. Here, the tobacco dust and flakes were differentiated. Finally, the lamina was sent to a sleeve chamber where it was cut and graded to suit the requirement of beedi manufacturer. The pure tobacco flakes came out after the dust was sucked out in the dust collecting unit. The end-product was called ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’. The assessee claimed reliefs under sections 32A, 80HH and 80-I for the assessment years 1984-85 and 1985-86. The assessee also claimed that it should be charged at a concessional rate treating it as an industrial company as defined under section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1985. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claims on the ground that the assessee was not manufacturing or producing any article or any thing. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance.

On second appeal:

The assessee was engaged in purchasing old and used tyres/rubber scrap, which were cut into small pieces and thereafter grinded with the help of machines and then the end product was rubber crumb, which was sold to the tyre manufacturing company. It claimed deduction under section 80-IB.

The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) disallowed the claim of deduction.

On second appeal, the Tribunal found that the end product of the assessee was different from its raw material and secondly it was commercially known to be different in the market. It, therefore, held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IB.

On appeal to High Court:

The assessee was a manufacturer of commutators. It also manufactured certain goods on sub-contract basis for others and received services/job charges and besides receipts from sale of copper scrap. They claimed deduction under section 80HHC including the said receipts. The assessing authority held that the receipts from the sub-contract receipts and scrap fell within the Explanation ( baa) to section 80HHC and, therefore, the same could not be included. Aggrieved by the said order, the assessee preferred an appeal. The appellate authority held that as there was a direct nexus between the receipts from special contract as well as sale of scrap material, it did not fall within the Explanation ( baa) and the assessee was entitled to include the said receipts in the income from the business and profits. The revenues appeal to the Tribunal came to be dismissed.

The assessee-company was an ‘industrial undertaking’ engaged in the manufacturing activity of de-humidifiers. During the course of such activity, the assessee had made earnings on account of engineering designing fee which was related only to the articles manufactured and produced by it and not for professional advice to others. The Tribunal allowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80-I on such earnings. The Tribunal had also allowed benefit of section 80-I on income derived from rent, interest, scrap, difference in exchange rate, etc.

On application under section 256(2) :

During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noticed that the scrap sale declared by the assessee of the packing material was out of the manufacturing activity and therefore, the same was business receipt and accordingly, he disallowed said amount while computing amount of deduction under section 80-IC.

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the revenue received from the sale of the scrap material would reduce the sale consideration/cost of raw material and therefore it would reduce the profit of the undertaking. It was held that there was a direct nexus between the sale activities and the profit from the eligible business. He thus set aside disallowance made by Assessing Officer.

The revenue filed instant appeal contending that the first degree nexus was not with respect to amount received from the sale of scrap and therefore, it was not the part of the manufacturing activities of the assessee. The revenue relied upon the judgment of the High Court of Madras in the case of CIT v. Shiva Distilleries Ltd.[2007] 293 ITR 108.

The assessee ran a cold storage and had claimed that it was an industrial undertaking in a backward area and since it had satisfied all the conditions laid down in section 80HH(2), it was entitled to the benefit of the aforesaid section. The ITO rejected its claim as according to him the assessee was not engaged in the manufacture of articles and hence the necessary conditions were not satisfied and, therefore, the claim could not be allowed. On appeal, the Commissioner upheld the order of the assessing authority, which order had been confirmed in further appeal by the Tribunal.

On reference :

The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of Single Super Phosphate (SSP) fertiliser. The Assessing Officer dis- allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on enhanced income by way of excessive subsidy showing bogus purchases and sales in its books of account as it was not earned out of the industrial activities carried out by the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On second appeal, however, the Tribunal held that if an assessee is found to have involved itself in earning unaccounted money, it cannot be held disentitled from claiming the other statutory benefits which are available to it at that time for its carrying on the business in the backward area.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of portable generators sets. While completing the assessments, the Assessing Officer noted that the turnover of the industrial undertaking included sale of imported spare parts and tools and imported portable generating sets. He held that the profits earned on those items could not be considered eligible for deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I, as it could not be said that same were derived from the industrial undertaking as required by the sections. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I in respect of the profits from the sale of the spare parts and components and disallowed deduction in respect of the profits from the sale of the imported gensets.

On cross appeal :

The assessee, a leading manufacturer of moulded luggage under the brand name of ‘VIP’, had set up a new industrial undertaking in addition to the existing undertaking for manufacturing some moulded luggage by installing new machines. The installed capacity for manufacturing moulded luggage, consequent to the installation of the new machines had substantially increased and its production had also increased as a result of increase on the investment and thus, the assessee claimed benefit under section 80-I. The claim was rejected by Assessing Officer on the ground that the action of installing a new capacity by purchasing new machines was merely an expansion of the existing unit and no expansion of the existing unit and no new industrial undertaking came into existence. It was further held that no new product was manufactured in the new industrial undertaking and the assessee was simply manufacturing old type of luggage.
