Cenvat credit relating to service provided at the residential colony outside the assessee’s factory 5.4 In the case of CCE v. Manikgarh Cement Works [2010] 24 STT 1 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee availed the Cenvat credit of service tax paid on (a) construction service, (b) repair and maintenance service, (c) manpower recruitment service, and (d) cleaning service, all of which were provided by the respective service providers at the residential colony outside the assessee’s factory. The employees of the assessee reside in the said colony. The residential buildings were constructed, old residential buildings were repaired and maintained, security guards for the colony were recruited by a manpower recruiting agency and the residential premises was cleaned by another agency. The adjudicating authority held the said services to be outside the purview of the definition of ‘input service’ given under rule 2(l) and, accordingly, disallowed the Cenvat credit to the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the Cenvat credit.

On appeal, the Tribunal held as under :

u The Supreme Court in the case of Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54 has considered the definition of ‘input’ given under rule 2(k) to be divisible into three parts; (1) specific part (main or substantive part); (2) inclusive part; (3) place of use and laid down an important ruling to the effect that, where the inclusive part of a definition provides a list of items, any such item should also satisfy the quintessential ingredients of the main part of the definition. In other words, the definition has to be considered in its entirety. The inclusive part is not independent of the main part. It is not a ‘stand-alone’ provision. This ruling is applicable to the definition of ‘input service’, given under rule 2(l). There is nothing in the said definition to indicate that the legislative intent behind it is different from the one underlying the definition of ‘input’. Accordingly, any service which is apparently covered by the parameters of the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ should also satisfy the quintessential requirements of the main part of the definition and, accordingly, any person claiming the benefit of Cenvat credit on input service in terms of the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ should establish that such service was used, directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of his final products or the clearance of such products from his factory.

u The assessee had sought to distinguish the decision of the Supreme Court rendered in the case of Maruti Suzuki Ltd. (supra) from the decision of the Bombay High Court rendered in the case of Coca Cola India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 130, wherein the Court examined the scope of the definition of ‘input service’ given in section 2(1) and argued that the Supreme Court’s decision relating to ‘input’ could not be applied to ‘input service’. The argument was not acceptable whether it be input or input service. The main part of the definition contains the quintessential ingredients and the inclusive part provides a non-exhaustive list of items each of which should satisfy the requirements of the main part. The assessee had pointed out that, in the case of definition of ‘input’, ‘place of use’ was the third part of the definition, which was conspicuously absent in the definition of ‘input service’. It had been argued that an input service need not necessarily be rendered within the factory premises whereas an input should normally be used within the factory. Broadly, this distinction sounds valid. But, again, it does not offer an answer to the question whether the service (which is rendered within the factory or outside) satisfies other essential requirements laid down in the main part of the definition. Even if it be held that there is no ‘place of use’ in relation to input service, the basic requirement remains to be that anything mentioned as an input service in the inclusive part of the definition should be shown to have been used in or in relation to the manufacture or clearance of final products, whether directly or indirectly.

u Accordingly, as the assessee had not established nexus between any of the four services and the manufacture or clearance of excisable goods, the benefit of Cenvat credit in respect of such services could not be allowed. However, in a case of this nature, the assessee should not be penalized. The instant case involves rival interpretations of a provision of law. In typical cases of interpretative nature, penalties have been waived by the Tribunal. In this view of the matter, the order-in-original was sustained except in respect of penalty imposed by the original authority.

On 20 September 2019, the government amended the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) vide The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019 (the Ordinance). The primary purpose of the Ordinance was to bring India's corporate tax rate at par with key competing economies. In addition to reducing the cost of capital, the reduced tax rate was also intended to act as a catalyst for companies to make fresh investments and consequently generate new avenues for employment.

Amongst other things, the Ordinance provided for reduced corporate tax rate of 15% under section 115BAB of the Act to new manufacturing companies which are not availing specified tax exemptions/incentives. The move was seen as a push towards the government's "Make in India" initiative and making India a US $5 trillion economy by 2024-25.

New manufacturing companies have been defined to mean companies which are formed after 1 October 2019 and begin to manufacture article or thing by 31 March 2023. While there are various conditions that a company needs to satisfy for claiming the lower tax rate, the main condition which is the subject matter of discussion in this article is as under:

"the company is not engaged in any business other than the business of manufacture or production of any article or thing and research in relation to, or distribution of, such article or thing manufactured or produced by it"

However, the term 'manufacture' or 'production' has not been defined under section 115BAB for the purpose of availing the reduced tax rate. Hence, it is generally understood that the definition of the term 'manufacture' as prescribed under section 2(29BA) of the Act may be relied upon while interpreting section 115BAB.

Section 2(29BA) of the Act defines the term 'manufacture' as follows:

"manufacture", with its grammatical variations, means a change in a non-living physical object or article or thing,—

(a)

resulting in transformation of the object or article or thing into a new and distinct object or article or thing having a different name, character and use; or

(b)

bringing into existence of a new and distinct object or article or thing with a different chemical composition or integral structure;

The government has on 25 November 2019 tabled the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2019 in the Lok Sabha. Amongst other things, the Amendment Bill seeks to clarify that business of 'development of computer software in any form or in any media' would not be regarded as a manufacturing activity for the purpose of section 115BAB.

It seems that the intention of the government is to only allow the reduced corporate tax rate to traditional manufacturing of physical goods generating large scale employment of unskilled and semi-skilled work-force, aka blue-collar jobs. Nevertheless, specifically excluding software development from the ambit of the section 115BAB could have more adverse consequences than originally anticipated.

Key arguments in favour of retaining software development within the ambit of 'manufacture' are discussed in the ensuing paragraphs.

Employment generation

As of 2018, the Information Technology (IT) industry employed nearly 39 lakh people in India. The industry is expected to add over 250,000 new jobs in 2019. [Source: Ibef.org]

It should be noted here that employment generation has been one of the major goal of the government to arrest the sliding economy. While traditional heavy manufacturing has a potential for employment generation, software development industry has also played a significant role in employment generation, albeit in white-collar jobs.

Impetus to Investments in IT industry

Because fresh investments have a cascading effect on various facets like employment generation and increase in disposable income etc, the government has taken various steps to attract investment, especially foreign investments. The liberalization of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) norms in manufacturing and more specifically related to contract manufacturing is a testament to this.

In this regard, it should be noted here that the computer software and hardware sector in India attracted cumulative FDI inflows worth US $37.23 billion between April 2000 and March 2019 and ranks second in inflow of FDI, as per data released by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)

This is despite the fact that India's share in the global software product market, which is valued at US $438 billion, is miniscule and the country continues to be a net importer of software products. The total software business in India stands at US $8.2 billion, out of which exports amount to a mere US $2 billion.

Views taken by Courts in taxation matter:

Keeping software development out of the ambit of manufacturing is also disconcerting since over the years, various Courts/Tribunals have held software development activity to be manufacturing under various provisions of the Act.

it has to be determined whether a given service has been used, directly or indirectly, in relation to the clearance of final products from the place of removal, the test is whether the service has remotedly aided the clearance of the final products or whether the clearance of the final products would have been facile in the absence of the service and outward transportation of final products from the place of removal, being an activity posterior to the clearance of the goods, as in the instant case, cannot pass the test. uHad the ‘place of removal’ of final products been other than factory for purposes of section 4 of the Central Excise Act, the transportation of the goods out of the factory up to the place of removal would have qualified to be ‘input service’ under rule 2(l)(ii ) for, in such a situation, transportation is anterior to clearance from the place of removal and passes the test. The clearance of final products from the place of removal (depot/warehouse) would not have been possible without their transportation upto such place from the factory. In other words, the transportation aids the clearance of the goods from the place of removal and can be said to have been used, directly or indirectly, in relation to such clearance.

uThe inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ is an exhaustive list of services which appeared to have a bearing on the scope of the main part of the definition. Some of the listed services are of a kind used (directly or indirectly) in relation to the manufacture of final products, while others are of a kind used (directly or indirectly) in relation to the clearance of final products from the place of removal. Services relating to setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of factory are in the first category, and so are those relating to procurement of inputs and inward transportation of inputs/capital goods. Services relating to sales promotion and market research can be identified as services of the second category, i.e., services used (directly or indirectly) in relation to the clearance of final products from the place of removal. The eye-catcher in this category is outward transportation upto the place of removal. This expression juxtaposed with ‘inward transportation of inputs or capital goods’ can only mean outward transportation of final products upto the place of removal. Obviously, ‘inward transportation of inputs/capital goods’ means transportation of these goods into the factory. ‘Outward’ being the antonym of ‘inward’, can only mean transportation out of the factory. What is transported from factory to depot or warehouse (place of removal) for clearance is not input or capital goods but final product. Such transportation of final products only upto the place of removal has been recognized as ‘input service’ under rule 2(l) as held by the coordinate Bench in Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd.’s case (supra).

uThe assessees’ opposition to taking aid from the inclusive part of the definition was not justifiable. Neither any rule of interpretation nor any judicial authority had tabooed it. Whether to take such aid for understanding the scope of the main part of the definition will depend on the text and context of the definition. The main part of the definition of ‘input service’ under rule 2(l)( ii) deals with service used in the manufacture or clearance of final products as also with service used in relation to the manufacture or clearance of final products. Any service used in the manufacture or clearance of final products is easily identifiable, whereas any service used in relation to the manufacture or clearance of final product is required to be determined, for which a ‘relation’ - whether direct or indirect, proximate or remote - has to be established between the service and manufacture or clearance, as the case may be. The services specified in the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ pertain to activities performed either in relation to manufacture of final products or in relation to clearance of such goods. They can, definitely, be of aid to the determination of the scope of the expression, ‘in relation to’, used in the main part of the definition. This is not to say generally that the inclusive part of the definition is expansive or restrictive. But one thing which can be said with certainty is that, insofar as transportation of final products is concerned, the inclusive part of the definition is restrictive as it permits such transportation upto the place of removal only as input service. The scope of the expression ‘in relation to’ used in the main part of the definition of ‘input service’ vide rule 2(l)(ii ) must be understood as circumscribed by the limiting factor as regards transportation of final products.

The sections do not override the provisions of Chapter XII of the Act i.e. provisions contained in the said chapter would hold forte. Hence special rates mentioned in sections 111A, 112, 112A, etc. would continue to apply.

A new manufacturing company holding sizeable rent yielding real estate and fixed deposits would stand to benefit (on account of lower tax rate of 17.16%) as compared to any other company having similar sources of income. The tax authorities may however, seek to dispute the adoption of section 115BAB by such companies by contending that the intention is not to extend benefit of lower taxes to non-business income.

2. Whether past MAT credit would be allowed

Sub-section 5A of section 115JB has been amended stating that provisions of section 115JB would not apply to companies which have exercised option to be governed by the aforesaid regime. It may be noted that no amendment has been made in section 115JAA of the Act which deals with utilization of MAT credit on account of MAT paid in earlier years. A plain reading of the provisions, in our view, suggest that past MAT credit available to an existing company should be allowed as a set-off against the tax liability under section 115BAA. There is no express prohibition in section 115BAA to deny MAT credit unlike several other deductions and losses specifically mentioned.

In our view, the MAT credit to be allowed in a year should be limited to the difference between the tax liability under section 115BAA and that under section 115JB which would have been payable. 4.4.1.1 BACKGROUND AND RANGACHARY COMMITTEE'S VIEWS - Post the introduction of the sunset clause of the erstwhile section 10A provisions in the Finance Act, 2010, STPI units are no longer eligible to claim any tax benefit. On the other hand, SEZ units in software development segment enjoy a 15 year tax holiday under the provisions of section 10AA. The revenue denies benefits of section 10AA in certain cases where old employees are transferred from STPI unit to SEZ unit, stating that there should be a certain percentage of new employees in the new SEZ units to enable the units the tax holiday benefit.This contention of revenue is widely opposed by the industry experts in the absence of specific provisions in the income-tax statute on this issue. The Rangachary Committee endorses the industry's view in this matter and advocates that in the absence of specific conditions on employing new employees, denial of deduction under this section by insisting upon the employment of new employees is unwarranted. The Committee also recommends the insertion of prospective amendment to the income-tax provisions to set the qualification criteria in this regard.

4.4.2 Issue No.2 - Reduction in tax holiday owing to absence of parity in treatment of the terms 'export turnover' and 'total turnover'.

4.4.2.1 BACKGROUND AND RANGACHARY COMMITTEE'S VIEWS - In the absence of a definition of the term 'total turnover', the revenue while computing export turnover, excludes freight and insurance charges, in view of the fact that a specific exclusion of such charges is mandated in the Income-tax Act but does not exclude the above expenses while computing the value of 'total turnover'. This results in the reduction of the tax holiday available to the IT companies. The Committee recommends that whenever certain items of expenses or receipts are removed from export turnover, the same items of expenses or receipts should also be removed from the total turnover to ensure parity between the numerator and denominator.

inform the department about the said shifting and keep the said goods separate in the factory. It would be better if a separate registration as depot is taken in respect of certain earmarked premises within the Guntur factory/plant.

alternatively, if rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 is applicable, the procedure envisaged therein may be followed. If circumstances of rule 16 are applicable, then depot must issue Cenvatable invoices in the name of Guntur factory and the factory may take credit based thereupon.

2. The export documents, viz., ARE and Export Promotion Copy relating to excisable goods exported by us under claim for rebate were misplaced by CHA. The Department has rejected the said claim as time-barred. Please advise us in this respect.

The following points will explain the position of law and remedies available —

A. Rebate is a form of refund as defined in section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and, therefore, time-bar stated in said section (except as otherwise stated) is applicable. Accordingly, the due date for filing rebate claim was 1-11-2012 + 1 year = 1-11-2013. The refund claim in this case is late by 3.5 months.

B. The date of filing of refund claim is the date on which it is filed along with all requisite documents. Therefore, even if you had filed an incomplete claim on 1-11-2012, the same would have been rejected as incomplete. However, in that case you would have an option to challenge rejection in appeal and you could have produced documents in appeal, as Commissioner (Appeals) has power to admit additional evidence as per rule 5 of the Central Excise (Appeals) Rules. Therefore, in similar cases arising in future, we would advise you to file refund claim in time even if some documents have been misplaced.

C. Even if the ARE and Export Promotion Copy were lost, it was always within your rights to file an additional certified copy thereof to the Department and then file rebate claim with requisite undertaking to the satisfaction of the Department. Therefore, it appears that you have not availed of requisite options.

D. Since all the aforestated options are outside the time-limit now, we would advise you to challenge rejection of rebate claim vide writ jurisdiction of the High Court. Only that may provide you relief, if any (grant of relief is within extraordinary powers of the High Court and discretionary). Though section 11B(3) bars refund contrary to section 11B, but in extraordinary circumstances faced by you, the High Court may consider your case.

Tulsyan NEC Ltd. 2007 (207) ELT 209 (Kar.), it has been held that an assessee is entitled to claim CENVAT credit on the inputs destroyed in a fire accident; but in the event of settlement by the insurance company they would remit the benefit back to the department.

Inclusive Part

5. The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

In Indo Rama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (219) ELT 122 (Bom.), the High Court held that the credit of duty paid on the goods or fuel used in the generation of electricity is available, provided the electricity is used for the manufacture of final product. The use of electricity must have nexus with goods manufactured in the factory.

5.1 Primary packing material - In Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 201 (Punj. & Har.), it was held that it is not a matter of dispute that chewing gum/bubble gums manufactured by the assessees are directly or primarily packed with the printed aluminium foils without tattoos. It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

Introduction

1. In September 2014 as part of a wider set of nation-building initiatives, the Central Government had launched a programme called as 'Make in India', to market India's image as a global manufacturing and export hub. For the said goal to be achieved, the first and foremost important thing would be to have Economic, Tax, etc., policies guiding and motivating the interests of business organizations. It is further an endeavour of all the Ministries of the Central Government that their policy framework shall be in complete synchronization with one another towards achieving the common goal and to ensure "Ease of Doing Business" in India. In present article, we will address one such issue wherein there appears to be conflict of policy and a tussle between two Ministries of the Central Government.

Chapter 7 of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015-20 ('FTP') issued by the Ministry of Commerce enlists various supplies which are considered as deemed exports and prescribes incentives for the domestic manufacturers carrying out such deemed exports. One of such supplier is supplying intermediate goods against an Advance Authorization. The benefits available for effecting such deemed export as enlisted in Para 7.03 of FTP are as under:

(a)

Refund of Terminal Excise Duty, if exemption is not available

(b)

Refund of duty by way of Deemed Export Drawback

(c)

Availing of the benefit of Advance Intermediate Authorization.

Similar provisions also existed in the erstwhile Foreign Trade Policy, 2009-14. However, vide Policy Circular No. 16, dated 15-3-2013, the DGFT had clarified that the benefit of deemed export in the form of "Terminal Excise Duty" shall not be available in respect of supplies which are entitled to an ab-initio exemption. It is to be noted that the above referred to Public Notice was challenged before various High Courts on ground of being unconstitutional and was later on was quashed for being unconstitutional and in contradiction to the Foreign Trade Policy, 2009-14.

The intent behind the Policy Circular dated 15-3-2013, was to ensure that the refund of excise duty collected by the Ministry of Finance, shall not be granted by DGFT. Hence, the aforesaid policy circular was specifically incorporated in the FTP by introducing Para 7.05 which had specifically denied the benefit of "Terminal Excise Duty" in respect of supplies entitled to an ab initio exemption.

An example

2. Now let us assume a situation where the supplies against an Advance Authorization are entitled to ab inito exemption under Notification No. 44/01-C.E-(N.T). As per Para 7.05 of FTP, a domestic supplier carrying out deemed exports cannot opt for availing of the benefit of Terminal Excise Duty for supplying of goods against an Advance Authorization and has to compulsorily clear the goods without payment of duty by availing of the benefit of exemption notification in force.

However, considering the fact that the domestic supplier is availing of the benefit of Notification No. 44/2001-C.E-(N.T) for effecting the exempted clearances, it is also required to reverse the proportionate CENVAT credit as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 inasmuch as the inputs/input services commonly received are also used in the manufacture of exempted goods which are cleared by availing of the benefit of Notification No. 44/01-C.E-(N.T). Moreover, the domestic supplier would also not be entitled for availing of the CENVAT credit of duty suffered on the inputs exclusively used in the manufacture of exempted goods which are supplied against an Advance Authorization as per provisions of rule 6(1).

Rule 6 issues under the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004

3. In the above regard, the attention is invited to rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which has an overriding effect over the provisions of sub-rules (1), (2), (3), & (4) of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Rule 6(6) has prescribed certain supplies, wherein reversal of the CENVAT credit will not apply even if the goods are cleared without payment of duty. Rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 covers all such supplies which are qualifying as deemed exports and also entitled to avail of the benefit of ab initio exemption, viz., supply to an EOU, supply to an ICB, etc., which are also covered by Para 7.05 of FTP, except supplies against an Advance Authorization.

Deduction in respect profits and gains from business of collecting and processing bio-degradable waste

6.3 A new section 80JJA has been inserted with effect from assessment year 1999-2000 to provide for deduction in respect profits and gains from business of collecting and processing bio-degradable waste.

The section provides that “Where the gross total income of an assessee includes any profits and gains derived from the business of collecting and processing or treating of bio-degradable waste for generating power, producing bio-gas, making pellets or briquettes for fuel or organic manure, there shall be allowed, in computing the total income of the assessee, a deduction from such profits and gains of an amount equal to the whole of such income, or five lakh rupees, whichever is less.”

6.3-1 Analysis of new provision : Note the following

◆ The deduction is available to all assessees.

◆ On a plain reading of the section, the deduction is available only if the assessee is engaged in the business of collecting as well as processing or treating bio-degradable waste. It is not available if the assessee is engaged in only collection or only processing/treating.

◆ The deduction is available only in respect of profit and gains of processing or treatment for generating power, producing bio-gas , making pellets or briquettes for fuel or organic manure. It is not available in respect of profits and gains of processing or treating for other purposes.

◆ The deduction is available to all entities, whether new or old. In other words unlike section 80-IA it is not restricted to new units.

Deduction in respect of employment of new workmen

6.4 In order to encourage the employers to further generate more employment opportunities, a new section 80JJAA has been inserted (with effect from 1-4-1999) to provide an incentive in the form of a special deduction against business profits of a company.

6.4-1 Conditions to be fulfilled - The following conditions have to be fulfilled in order to be eligible to the deduction provided in the section :

◆ the assessee should be an Indian company.

◆ its gross total income should include profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking.

◆ the industrial undertaking should be engaged in the manufacture or production of any article or thing.

◆ the industrial undertaking should not have been formed by splitting up of an existing undertaking.

◆ the industrial undertaking should not have been formed by reconstruction of an existing undertaking.

◆ the industrial undertaking should not have been formed by amalgamation with an existing undertaking.

◆ the assessee furnishes alongwith the return of income a report of an accountant.

◆ in case of a new industrial undertaking, in the first previous year, it employs more than 100 regular workmen.

◆ in the case of an existing industrial undertaking, the number of regular workers employed during the relevant previous year is equal to at least 110% of the regular workmen employed in such undertaking as on the last day of the preceding year.

The provisions relating to aforesaid conditions are elaborately explained in subsequent paragraphs.

6.4-2 Quantum of deduction - See para 6.4-11

6.4-3 Indian company - The section is applicable only if the assessee is an Indian company as defined in section 2(26) of the Act. Hence, it does not apply to other entities like foreign companies, firms, HUFs, etc.

6.4-4 Profits and gains derived - The term ‘derived’ has been explained in a number of judgments involving interpretation of section 80J/80-I/80-IA etc.,

It may be noted, however, that unlike other sections, section 80JJAA does not link the deduction to quantum of profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking. For the purpose of this section , it is sufficient that the gross total income includes profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and once this condition is satisfied, the ultimate deduction is based on wages paid.

Again, it could also be argued that in the absence of a specific prohibition, the deduction under this section could exceed the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking, as long as the deductions under Chapter VIA of the Act do not exceed the gross total income [section 80A(2)].

6.4-5 Industrial undertaking - The term industrial undertaking has not been defined in the section. In the context of section 15C, of the Income-tax Act, 1922 (corresponding to s. 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961), the Supreme Court in Textile Machinery Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 107 ITR 195, had elaborately dealt with the expression industrial undertaking. It appears that the interpretation of the term “industrial undertaking” given by the Supreme Court would be equally relevant for section 80JJAA.

Similarly, a deduction under section 80HHB cannot be curtailed inasmuch as it is not claimed with reference to profits of an Industrial Undertaking.

6.1 The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 has amended the following provisions in Chapter VIA of the Act so as to extend the deductions and/or enlarge the provisions and/or to provide for the deductions in certain cases.

Section 80-IA has been amended with effect from assessment year 2005-06 to provide for :—

Extension of the deduction in case of substantial renovation and modernization ('the renovation') of the existing network of transmission or distribution lines ('the net-work') [by inserting sub-clause (c) in sub-section (4)(iv)], as also enabling such undertaking to claim deduction for 10 out of 15 years beginning from the year in which the undertaking undertakes the renovation of the network [by an amendment in sub-section (2)].

Sub-section (3) provides for fulfilment of certain conditions by a power undertaking. The said conditions have now been made applicable to telecom sector also.

A proviso is inserted below sub-section (3)(ii) so as to relax the conditions relating to formation upon reconstruction, etc., and/or transfer of machinery or plant previously used, pursuant to splitting up or reconstruction or reorganisation of State Electricity Board.

Sub-section (1) is amended to confer deduction in respect of profits derived from the operation and maintenance of hospital in a rural area and a new sub-section (11B) is inserted in section 80-IB, to lay down the conditions thereof.

Sub-section (4) enables deduction to an industrial undertaking established in backward States provided the operations start before 31-3-2004. Sub-section (11A) provides for deduction to an undertaking engaged in the integrated business of handling, storage and transportation of foodgrains. The provision is amended to extend it also to the business of processing, preservation and packaging of fruits or vegetables.

Sub-section (14) provides for various definitions for the purpose of the section and in that:

Definition of "built-up area" is inserted; and

The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to Section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions, and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production, new words are not being added to Section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. In view of the aforesaid, it could not be said that retreading of tyres resulted in the production of an article[CIT v. Madurai Pandian Engineering Corpn. Ltd. [1999] 239 ITR 375 (Mad.) affirmed in Tamil Nadu State Transport Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [2001] 252 ITR 883 (SC)].

9.4-4c Article or thing - The word "article" is not defined in the Act or the Rules. It must, therefore, be understood in its normal connotation, the sense in which it is understood in the commercial world. The word "articles" in Section 80HH is preceded by the words "it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce". The word "articles" occurring in Section 80HH(2)(i) does not comprehend and take within its ambit a dam, a bridge and so on. If a dam is an article, so would be a bridge, a road, an underground canal and a multi-storeyed building. To say that all of them fall within the meaning of the word "articles" is to overstrain the language beyond its normal and ordinary meaning. It is equally difficult to say that the process of constructing a dam is a process of manufacture or a process of production. It is true that a dam is composed of several articles, viz., stones, concrete, cement, etc. But to say that the end product, the dam, is an article is to be unfaithful to the normal connotation of the word. A dam is constructed; it is not manufactured or produced. The expressions "manufacture" and "produce" are normally associated with movables - articles and goods, big and small - but they are never employed to denote the construction activity of the nature involved in the construction of a dam or for that matter a bridge, a road or a building [CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 70 Taxman 312 (SC)]

A question arises whether the amendment would be applicable to such an undertaking, which has claimed and has been allowed the deduction?

As per one view, such an undertaking may not be eligible to claim the deduction from assessment year 2005-06 and thereafter, since the undertaking will have to satisfy the conditions in respect of each and every assessment year.

As per the other view, the amendment is effective from assessment year 2005-06, which implies that the condition would apply to any undertaking, which is established in the financial year 2004-05, and if it is formed by splitting up or reconstruction of any business already in existence for transfer of plant and machinery, then, it would not be eligible for the deduction. 4.6-2 Withdrawal of restrictions in respect of new industrial undertakings set up in backward States - In the Finance Act, 1993, a five-year tax holiday was given under section 80-IA, to new industrial undertakings located in backward States. For availing the tax deduction, the new industrial undertaking (other than a small scale industrial undertaking) should not manufacture or produce certain articles specified in the Eleventh Schedule. The Government felt that this restriction is inconsistent with the urgent need to promote the growth of industry and employment in the backward States. Accordingly, section 80-IA has been amended to provide that the condition -that the deduction will be allowed only if the industrial unit did not manufacture any item listed in the Eleventh Schedule - will not apply to units set up in backward State.

In effect, a new industrial unit, whether small-scale or not, located in a backward State, will get the full tax holiday for five years beginning from the assessment year relevant to the year of commencement of production and, thereafter, will be allowed the deduction under section 80-IA at normal rate and for the residual period as may be applicable (see para 4.6-3), even if it produces an item listed in the Eleventh Schedule. The amendment is effective from assessment year 1994-95. Relaxation of the condition relating to manufacture in case of an undertaking located in backward State is partially retrospective and applies even to the recently concluded previous year on 31st March, 1994. Thus, any undertaking located in a backward State which has commenced manufacture after 1st April, 1993 would be able to claim the tax holiday.

Although, tax holiday is extended to an undertaking located in a backward district, it is not on par with an undertaking located in a backward State, inasmuch as an undertaking (not being a small scale undertaking) located in a backward district and engaged in the manufacture of any article specified in the Eleventh Schedule would not be entitled to the tax holiday.

MANUFACTURE/PRODUCTION* General tests - Manufacture and processing are not clearly demarcated fields. The test of manufacture lies in the answer to the question whether what is processed or produced as the end-product is commercially known as a different product from the materials out of which it is so produced. Therefore, if the product has a different name and is identified by the buyers and sellers as a different product and is bought and sold as a distinct product from its raw materials, one can say that it is a manufactured product. There may be some room for debate as to whether this test is fully satisfied by edibles that come as end-products from the raw materials out of which they are made. But the expression 'produce' has to be taken in a more liberal sense than manufacture. If the end-product is different, that by itself would suffice to meet the requirement of 'producing'. Hence, an exclusive catering unit of a hotel supplying eatables in bulk for consumption by air passengers will be eligible for relief - CIT v. East India Hotels Ltd. [1994] 209 ITR 854 (Cal.).

Department should study actual process undertaken by assessee - Section 80-IA comes in Chapter VI-A. That Chapter, in any way, is a code by itself. It provides for special deductions. Broadly, these special deductions are incentives provided for setting up industrial undertakings in backward areas, for earning profits in foreign exchange, for setting up hotels, etc. It is in this background that one has to interpret the meaning of the expression 'manufacture or processing of goods'. One more aspect needs to be highlighted. Technological advancement in computer science makes knowledge as of today obsolete tomorrow. One needs to move with the times. At the same time, one needs to take note of the fact that unlimited deductions are not permissible under Chapter VI-A. Therefore, in each case, where an issue of this nature arises for determination, the department should study the actual process undertaken by the assessee - CIT v. Oracle Software India Ltd. [2010] 187 Taxman 275 (SC).

Tyre retreading is not 'manufacture' - Tyre retreading does not amount to manufacture. - Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [2001] 252 ITR 883 (SC).

Ginning of cotton is a process - Ginning of cotton is also a process of manufacture, and hence, a ginning factory is an 'industrial undertaking' entitled to deduction - Poonam Chand Prem Raj v. CIT [1994] 207 ITR 895 (Raj.).

Packing of tea is not covered - The words 'manufacture' and 'production' apply to a case which brings into existence something different from its components. Where the assessee's business consisted of buying different types of tea from the market, blending them in different proportions, and thereafter selling the tea in the market, the assessee cannot be said to be engaged in the manufacture or production of an article so as to be eligible for relief - Appeejay (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1994] 77 Taxman 208 (Cal.).

Conversion of boulders into stones is manufacture - Conversion of boulders into small stones with the aid of machinery is a manufacturing process, and an assessee engaged in such process is entitled to the deduction - CIT v. M.R. Gopal [1965] 58 ITR 598 (Mad.).

Activity of converting boulder into grits/stone chips/powder may not be a manufacturing activity, but since such activity produces grits/stone chips/powder, same would be production for purpose of deduction under section 80-IB - CIT v. Mallikarjun Georesources Associates [2011] 201 Taxman 86 (Mag.)/12 taxmann.com 439 (Uttarakhand).

Conversion of limestone into limestone powder - Converting limestone into limestone powder is a manufacturing activity for purposes deduction under section 80-IA/80-IB - CIT v. Janak Raj Bansal [2010] 229 CTR (HP) 89.

Mining of limestone/marble blocks does not amount to 'manufacture' - Mere mining of limestone and marble, and cutting the same before it is sold in the market could not be considered to be a manufacturing process - Lucky Minmat (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 245 ITR 830 (SC).

4.6-1a Eligible undertakings, amount of deduction and conditions - Following points need be noted:

There must be, for the application of the words 'derived from', a direct nexus between the profits and gains and the industrial undertaking. In the instant case, the nexus is not direct but only incidental. The industrial undertaking exports processed sea food. By reason of such export, the Export Promotion Scheme applies. Thereunder, the assessee is entitled to import entitlements, which it can sell. Sterling Foods [1999] 104 Taxman 204 (SC).

Sub-section (5) has overriding effect - Section 80-IA(5) is a distinct and separate provision which lays down the special method of computing the profits and gains entitled to deduction under section 80-IA of the Act. Moreover, this provision is of overriding nature providing specifically that during each of the assessment years in the tax holiday period, this provision will be applied as if the industrial unit is an independent unit and is the one and only source of income possessed by the assessee. The Assessing Officer would be wrong, if he adjusts the losses from the other units against the profits of the eligible unit and then allow reduced deduction under section 80-IA - CIT v. Dewan Kraft System (P.) Ltd. [2008] 297 ITR 305 (Delhi).

Interest received on investment of income - Section 80-I should not be stretched to the limit where income derived from the industrial undertaking is reinvested by the assessee in a non-industrial undertaking for the purpose of earning income from the non-industrial undertaking. Depreciation - Depreciation has to be reduced while computing deduction under section 80-IA - Plastiblends India Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2017] 86 taxmann.com 137/251 Taxman 188 (SC).

'Article' - The mere fact that the dictionary meaning of 'article' includes 'a piece of property' has no impelling force to conclude that the word also denotes an immovable like a building. In popular acceptance of the word 'article', it would be ludicrous to suggest that an immovable property is an article. In common parlance, 'article' only refers to a movable property. Hence, the activity of construction of multi-storeyed buildings consisting of flats does not amount to manufacture and production of articles - CIT v. Madgul Udyog [1994] 208 ITR 541 (Cal.).

Expressions 'manufacture' and 'produce' are normally associated with movable articles and goods, and they are never employed to denote construction activity of nature involve in construction of a dam and as such word 'article' occurring in section 80HH(2)(i) does not take within its ambit a dam - CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 70 Taxman 312 (SC).

SPLITTING UP OR 'RECONSTRUCTION' - Reconstruction of business involves the idea of substantially the same persons carrying on substantially the same business. Where the new industrial undertakings are separate and independent production units in the sense that the commodities produced or the results achieved are commercially tangible products and the undertakings can be carried on separately without complete absorption and losing their identity in the old business, they are not to be treated as business formed by reconstruction of the old business. Use by the assessee of the articles produced in its existing business or the concept of expansion are not decisive tests. The fact that an assessee by establishment of a new industrial undertaking expands his existing business would not on that score deprive him of the benefit. Every new creation in business is some kind of expansion and advancement. The true test is not whether the new industrial undertaking connotes expansion of the existing business of the assessee but whether it is all the same a new and identifiable undertaking separate and distinct from the existing business. There must be a new emergence of a physically separate unit which may exist on its own as a viable industrial unit. An undertaking is formed out of the existing business if the physical identity with the old unit is preserved. The new activity may produce the same commodities of the old business or it may produce some other distinct marketable products, even commodities which may feed the old business. These products may be consumed by the assessee in his old business or may be sold in the open market. One thing is certain that the new undertaking must be an integrated unit by itself - Textile Machinery Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 107 ITR 195 (SC)/CIT v. Orient Paper Mills Ltd. [1989] 176 ITR 110 (SC). [See also CIT v. Mahaan Foods Ltd. [2009] 177 Taxman 274 (Delhi).]

The Government felt that this restriction is inconsistent with the urgent need to promote the growth of industry and employment in the backward States.

Thus, any undertaking located in a backward State which has commenced manufacture after 1st April, 1993 would be able to claim the tax holiday.

Although, tax holiday is extended to an undertaking located in a backward district, it is not on par with an undertaking located in a backward State, inasmuch as an undertaking (not being a small scale undertaking) located in a backward district and engaged in the manufacture of any article specified in the Eleventh Schedule would not be entitled to the tax holiday.

1.2-6 Manufacture of any item is permitted - Additional depreciation would be available to any undertaking including those manufacturing items listed in Eleventh Schedule. This is unlike section 80-IB which provides that the deduction under that section is not available to any undertaking other than a small scale undertaking if it manufactures or produces any article or thing specified in the Eleventh Schedule.

1.2-7 ‘Not formed by transfer to a new business of old machinery’ - The section defines a new industrial undertaking as an undertaking which is not formed by the transfer to a new business of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose. Similar expression is found in section 10A/10B/80-IA/80-IB. However, in those sections it is provided that if the value of machinery or plant transferred does not exceed 20% of the total value of the machinery or plant used in the business then the condition prohibiting transfer of old machinery should be deemed to be complied with. Now, a similar exception is not provided in the provision relating to additional depreciation. Does this mean that transfer of machinery of any insignificant value will disentitle the assessee from the grant of additional depreciation? In this context the meaning of the word ‘formed’ as given by the Supreme Court in Bajaj Tempo Limited v. CIT [1992] 196 ITR 188 becomes relevant.

In that case, the new industrial undertaking for which deduction under section 15C of the Income-tax Act, 1922 was claimed had taken a building on lease and some tools and implements valued at Rs. 3,500. The Assessing Officer argued that the undertaking was formed by transfer of the building and machinery previously used in another business.

The Supreme Court held as follows :

“The word ‘form’ according to the dictionary has different meanings. In the context in which it has been used it was intended to connote that the body of the company or its shape did not come up in consequence of transfer of machinery and plant used previously for business purpose. Use of the negative before the word ‘formed’ further strengthens it. In other words, machinery and plant used previously in other business should not result in the undertaking being formed by it. The transfer to take out the new undertaking out of the purview of the provision must be such that but for transfer the new undertaking could not have come into being.”

It observed that since on the facts, the part played by taking the building on lease was not dominant, the undertaking was not formed by such transfer.

Applying the ratio of the aforesaid judgment, it is submitted that transfer of machinery (of any insignificant value or otherwise) which does not result in formation of the industrial undertaking or without which the undertaking could have come into being should not disentitle the assessee from the grant of additional depreciation.

1.2-8 Eligible assessee - The benefit is available only if the machinery or plant is acquired and installed by an assessee engaged in the business of manufacture or production of an article or thing. Hence, the deduction will not be available to any assessee who is not engaged in a business of manufacture or production.

1.2-6 Manufacture of any item is permitted - Additional depreciation would be available to any undertaking including those manufacturing items listed in Eleventh Schedule. This is unlike section 80-IB which provides that the deduction under that section is not available to any undertaking other than a small scale undertaking if it manufactures or produces any article or thing specified in the Eleventh Schedule.

1.2-7 ‘Not formed by transfer to a new business of old machinery’ - The section defines a new industrial undertaking as an undertaking which is not formed by the transfer to a new business of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose. Similar expression is found in section 10A/10B/80-IA/80-IB. However, in those sections it is provided that if the value of machinery or plant transferred does not exceed 20% of the total value of the machinery or plant used in the business then the condition prohibiting transfer of old machinery should be deemed to be complied with. Now, a similar exception is not provided in the provision relating to additional depreciation. Does this mean that transfer of machinery of any insignificant value will disentitle the assessee from the grant of additional depreciation? In this context the meaning of the word ‘formed’ as given by the Supreme Court in Bajaj Tempo Limited v. CIT [1992] 196 ITR 188 becomes relevant.

In that case, the new industrial undertaking for which deduction under section 15C of the Income-tax Act, 1922 was claimed had taken a building on lease and some tools and implements valued at Rs. 3,500. The Assessing Officer argued that the undertaking was formed by transfer of the building and machinery previously used in another business.

The Supreme Court held as follows :

“The word ‘form’ according to the dictionary has different meanings. In the context in which it has been used it was intended to connote that the body of the company or its shape did not come up in consequence of transfer of machinery and plant used previously for business purpose. Use of the negative before the word ‘formed’ further strengthens it. In other words, machinery and plant used previously in other business should not result in the undertaking being formed by it. The transfer to take out the new undertaking out of the purview of the provision must be such that but for transfer the new undertaking could not have come into being.”

It observed that since on the facts, the part played by taking the building on lease was not dominant, the undertaking was not formed by such transfer.

Applying the ratio of the aforesaid judgment, it is submitted that transfer of machinery (of any insignificant value or otherwise) which does not result in formation of the industrial undertaking or without which the undertaking could have come into being should not disentitle the assessee from the grant of additional depreciation.

5.5-1 Scheme of section 80-IA - A recapitulation - To recapitulate, various provisions/conditions of section 80-IA are as follows: An industrial undertaking is entitled to certain deduction provided it fulfils the following conditions (including the conditions imposed by amendments):

■ It is not 'formed' by:

- splitting up, or reconstruction of a business already in existence [Section 8O-IA(2)(i)]; and

- transfer to a new business of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose [Section 80-IA(2)(ii)].

■ In case of a small scale industrial undertaking it manufactures or produces any article or thing [Proviso to section 80-IA(2)(iii)];

■ In case of units other than a small scale industrial undertaking, it manufactures or produces any article or thing not specified in Eleventh Schedule [Section 80-IA(2)(iii)].

■ It begins the relevant activity anytime during:

- 1-4-1993 to 31-1-1998 in case of a Power Undertaking/State Undertaking [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(b) - the amended clause]; and

- 1-4-1991 to 31-3-1995 in case of other undertaking (This period can be extended by the Central Government by a Notification) [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(a)].

■ It employs requisite number of workers [Section 80-IA (2)(v)].

The conditions and the amendments, may now be examined in the light of the Scheme of section 80-IA.

5.5-2 Analysis of the amendments The amendments lay down certain conditions or attributes of State undertaking or Power undertaking, which will entitle it to a higher deduction.

5.5-2a State undertaking - In respect of a State undertaking it lays down that:

■ It should be located in an industrially backward State specified in the Eighth Schedule; and

■ It begins to manufacture or produce article or thing, or begins to operate a cold storage plant at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

5.5-2b Power undertaking - In respect of a power undertaking, it lays down that:

■ It may be set up in any part of India for the generation or generation and distribution of power; and

■ It commences generation of power at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

The amendments only classify industrial undertakings for:

■ prescribing period during which the relevant activity has to commence; and

■ conferring higher amount of relief to certain undertakings.

The amendments do not lay down qualifying conditions for claiming a deduction under section 80-IA. Thus, any undertaking claiming a deduction under section 80-IA will, in any case, have to comply with the other condition laid down in section 80-IA(2) including clause (iii) thereof.

From the language of the amended clause, in relation to a State undertaking, it would be observed that it omits 'Union Territory', whereas the Eighth Schedule, Finance Minister's speech. Notes on clauses, and Memorandum explaining the Bill refers to 'Union Territories'. This seems to be a slip.

5.5-2c Initial assessment year - The higher deduction is available for initial five assessment years. 'Intitial assessment year' is defined by section 80-IA(12)(c) as follows:

‘initial assessment year’ means the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce articles or things, or to operate its cold storage plant or plants or the ship is first brought into use or the business of the hotel starts functioning".

From the definition it would be noticed that the previous year in which the prescribed activity commences is to be regarded as a starting point and the relevant assessment year relating thereto would be the initial assessment year.

13.3 Scientific Research expenditure [Section 35]

Under section 35(2AB) of the Act, weighted deduction of 200% is allowed to a company engaged in the business of biotechnology or manufacturing of goods (except items specified in Schedule XI) for the expenditure (not being expenditure in the nature of cost of any land or building) incurred on scientific research carried out in an approved in-house research and development facility. For availing this weighted deduction, the company is required to enter into an agreement with the Secretary, Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) and also required to obtain his approval. The Secretary, DSIR is required to send the report regarding approval to DGIT (Exemption) in prescribed Form who generally does not have jurisdiction over the assessee company. Further, the company is required to maintain separate books of account for approved R&D facility and is also required to get the account audited. However, the copy of audit report is required to be submitted to the DSIR only.

The Comptroller and Auditor General of India in its report on performance audit of pharmaceuticals sector recommended for rationalisation of the provision relating to monitoring of this weighted deduction.

In order to have a better and meaningful monitoring mechanism for weighted deduction allowed under section 35(2AB) of the Act, the provisions of section 35(2AB) of the Act have been amended to provide that deduction under the said section shall be allowed if the company enters into an agreement with the prescribed authority for cooperation in such research and development facility and fulfils prescribed conditions with regard to maintenance and audit of accounts and also furnishes prescribed reports.

The Finance Act, 2015 has also inserted reference of the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner in section 35(2AA) and section 35(2AB) of the Act so that the report referred to therein may be sent to the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner having jurisdiction over the company claiming the weighted deduction under the said section.

Therefore, even if the undertaking is established by transfer of building, plant or machinery, but it is not formed a result of such transfer, the assessee could not be denied the benefit.".

(i) The assessee may continue to produce the same kind of article as hitherto but that is not a relevant factor at all to consider whether the section is attracted. What is relevant is that the industrial unit set up must be new. In that sense, though new plant and machinery are erected for producing either the same commodities or some distinct commodities, it should not be a case of reconstruction of the old business. The assessee will have to plead and establish that a new unit has come into existence which independently produces articles of whatsoever nature and that this new unit is not dependent upon the old existing unit, in the sense that the new unit cannot be equated as an expansion of the old unit [Canara Wire & Wire Products Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 196 ITR 426 (Kar.)].

(j)

The true test is not whether the new industrial undertaking connotes expansion of the existing business of the assessee, but whether it is all the same a new and identifiable undertaking, separate and distinct from the existing business. The reconstruction of a business or an industrial undertaking must necessarily involve the concept that the original business or undertaking is not to cease functioning, and its identity is not to be lost or abandoned. The concept essentially rests on changes, but the changes must be constructive and not destructive. There must be something positive about the whole matter as opposed to negative. The underlying idea of a reconstruction evidently must be - as is brought out by the section itself - of a 'business already in existence'. There must be a continuation of the activities and business of the same industrial undertaking, which must continue to carry on the same business, though in some altered or varied form. If the alteration and changes are substantial, there would be little scope for describing what emerges as a reconstruction of the business. From the perusal of the section, it is clear that the statute itself has envisaged and approved of a situation in which an old existing, smaller industrial undertaking is absorbed by a new and much bigger industrial undertaking. In the instant case, only capacity had been increased, and there was an expansion of the old business with some modifications. As for the reconstruction of the business, it was nowhere evident that the old industrial unit was split up or damaged or destroyed and was supposedly reconstructed as a new unit by the assessee. What the assessee had done was to set up an industrial undertaking with the latest technology and increased capacity and, of course, with a fairly good amount of fresh investment. The formation of the new undertaking was not as a consequence of the transfer of the plant or machinery of the old business. The value of the plant and machinery utilised in the new undertaking had been less than 20 per cent of the total investment. Thus, the assessee's case also did not get disqualified under this provision. Investment in new plant and machinery was Rs. 104.88 lakhs. Investment in old plant and machinery was Rs. 20.86 lakhs. In that view of the matter, the conclusion was inevitable that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA in respect of the profits of the new industrial undertaking having satisfied the requisite conditions [CIT v. Mahaan Foods Ltd. [2009] 177 Taxman 274 (Delhi)].

6.1 The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 has amended the following provisions in Chapter VIA of the Act so as to extend the deductions and/or enlarge the provisions and/or to provide for the deductions in certain cases.

Sub-section (3) provides for fulfilment of certain conditions by a power undertaking. The said conditions have now been made applicable to telecom sector also.

Sub-section (4) enables deduction to an industrial undertaking established in backward States provided the operations start before 31-3-2004. FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

HELD: Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

2. The assessee, it appears, set up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act'), in respect of (i ) profit on sale of scrap; (ii) interest earned by the industrial undertaking; and (iii) cash assistance received from the Government on account of exports made by the assessee.

3. The ITO disallowed the relief in respect of those items under section 80HH.

4. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim for deduction in regard to the profit on sale of scrap and interest earned by the industrial undertaking, but disallowed such relief in respect of the third item, namely, cash assistance received from the Government on account of exports made by the assessee.

5. On further appeal by the revenue, the Tribunal, following its order for the earlier year, reversed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in respect of the first two items, namely, profit on sale of scrap and interest earned by the industrial undertaking and allowed the revenue's appeal.

6. On the basis of the above facts, the question of law, as below, was referred for the opinion of this Court :

"Whether, on the basis of the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal is correct in holding that the assessee is not entitled to relief under section 80HH of the Income-tax Act in respect of (a) profit on sale of scrap, and (b) interest earned by the industrial undertaking ?"

7. Arguments of Mr. K. Vaitheeswaran, the learned counsel representing Subbaraya Aiyar, Padmanabhan and Ramamani, the learned counsel appearing for the assessee, and of Mr. R. Sivaraman, the learned counsel representing Mr. C.V. Rajan, the learned junior standing counsel appearing for the revenue, were heard.

8. There is no denial of the fact that the industrial undertaking had been established in a backward area. Yet another fact, about which there is no dispute, is that the said industrial undertaking manufactures V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products. One another fact, about which there is no dispute, is that in the process of manufacture of the products abovementioned, certain scrap also resulted. The resultant product of scrap materials, it is said, had also a market. The scrap materials were also sold. The scrap materials so sold were also reflected in the turnover of the industrial undertaking.

9. The moot question that arises for consideration is as to whether the assessee is entitled to deduction of an amount equal to 20 per cent on the profits earned out of the sale of scrap materials under section 80HH.

10. Sub-section (1) of section 80HH, relevant for the present purpose, reads as under :

"Deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas.—(1) Where the gross total income of an assessee includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking, or the business of a hotel, to which this section applies, there shall, in accordance with and subject to the provisions of this section, be allowed, in computing the total income of the assessee, a deduction from such profits and gains of an amount equal to twenty per cent thereof." [Emphasis supplied]

11. No dispute is raised by the revenue, as respects the conditions required to be fulfilled under sub-section (2) thereof for availing of the deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent, as contemplated by sub-section (1). What is now disputed by the revenue is that profit on sale of scrap materials can, by no stretch of imagination, be stated to have been derived from the industrial undertaking and if at all, such profits may be attributable to an industrial undertaking. This sort of a submission is further elucidated by stating that profits on sales of the manufactured products by the industrial undertaking such as V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products alone can be stated to be gains or profits derived from the industrial undertaking, in respect of which a deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent is permissible and not in respect of the profits from the sale of scrap materials, which could, if at all, be stated to be attributable to an industrial undertaking. To such sort of submission, we are unable to affix our seal of approval, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings in backward area - Assessee-company had set up an industrial undertaking in a backward area and was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc. - Whether profits and gains from sale of scrap material resulting in manufacturing process were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, since scrap materials came within manufacturing process of industrial undertaking set-up by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings, rubber moulded products, etc., set-up an industrial undertaking in a backward area. It claimed deduction of 20 per cent of net profits allowable under section 80HH in respect of profit on sale of scrap which resulted in the manufacturing process. The ITO disallowed that claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim. On further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order.

On reference :

HELD: Section 80HH is meant to give a tax rebate to certain categories of assessees and one, who wants to claim such a relief, must strictly satisfy the requirements prescribed therein. He must establish that his profits and gains are derived from his industrial undertaking or the business of hotel. Axiomatic proposition of law is that it is not sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits earned and the industrial undertaking and the law requires that such profits must have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The industrial undertaking itself must be the source of that profit. The business of the industrial undertaking must strictly yield that profit. It must be the direct source of profit and not a means to earn any other profit.

In the instant case, in the industrial undertaking for the manufacture of V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and rubber moulded products, certain scrap materials resulted, which had a saleable value. To say that the scrap materials had no direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking, could not at all be expected to commend acceptance, especially, on the facts and in the circumstances of the instant case. The scrap materials came within the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking in the manufacture of certain products such as V-belts, oil seals, O-rings and certain rubber moulded products, etc. In that view of the matter, profits and gains from the sale of scrap materials were eligible for deduction in an amount equal to 20 per cent under section 80HH, inasmuch as such gains or profits were derived from the industrial undertaking and includible in the gross total income of the assessee and the question relatable to the profit on the sale of scrap was answered in favour of the assessee.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.
