IT: Where assessee put imported scrap to series of manual and mechanical processes and thereby brought into existence entirely new and distinct commodity which was marketable, it was to be regarded as 'manufacturing' activity and, thus, assessee's claim for deduction under section 80-IB was to be allowed

The assessee had installed an industrial unit at a notified backward area. During the year in appeal the assessee received a sum on account of job charges for twisting of yarn during the year. The claim of the assessee under sections 80HH and 80-I was rejected by the assessing officer on the ground that separate balance sheet in respect of the unit had not been filed; that the assessee had done job work and was not manufacturing goods on his own account and that, the twisting of year did not amount to manufacturing of goods for the purposes of sections 80HH and 80-I claims. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was entitled to a deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal:

As per the law laid down by the Supreme Court in several decisions, the expression 'derived from' is to be given restricted meaning in section 80HH/80-I while interpreting the section in which this expression is used. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the main and only business of the assessee, for which the plant was set up in the backward area, was to manufacture and to sell soya oil. Hence, all incomes derived from sale of soya oil would be income derived from an industrial undertaking for the purpose of calculating deduction under section 80HH/80-I.

The income earned by the assessee out of sale of gunny bags could not be kept at par or alike the income derived from sale of soya bean oil due to following reasons - Sale of gunny bags was not the main or even ancillary business activity of the assessee; it was not regular or continuous business activity; no investment was made by the assessee for their sale. The gunny bags were never manufactured by the assessee in its plant and merely because some gunny bags were lying in the factory as surplus or unused or as waste material for any reason and such bags were sold to earn income, then it could not be a ground to hold that for the purpose of section 80HH/80-I, such income was the income actually derived from the assessee's industrial undertaking. [Para 16]

In order to derive income from industrial undertaking, the assessee must show that it was earned by sale of goods/commodity which were manufactured/produced in the said industrial undertakings as a part of its main and day-to-day business activity. Only then, the income earned by sale of such goods can be termed as income derived from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I. It is for this reason that it has a direct or immediate nexus with the assessee's industrial undertaking established in the backward area. This necessarily follows that income, which has a direct or immediate nexus with the industrial undertaking, alone will be taken into consideration for calculating the deduction under section 80HH/80-I, ibid. Such was not the case in the instant case, because the income earned from sale of gunny bags was not the result of direct or immediate nexus with the business of assessee carried on in the industrial undertaking. [Para 17]

Hence, the Tribunal fell in error in holding that the income earned by the assessee from sale of gunny bags was an income earned from industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH/80-I and, accordingly, the assessee was entitled to claim deduction from total income. That view was to be reversed and order of the Tribunal was to be set aside. [Para 21]

FACT: The assessee-company, a small-scale industrial undertaking, was carrying on the business of manufacturing ‘Jarda’ from raw tobacco in a backward area. The processing operations employed by the assessee were that raw tobacco (angad) was stripped off the midrib by manual labour. It was then sand-screened to control the moisture content. The raw tobacco was fed into a vibratory feeder and it was conveyed into a pneumatic pick up duct where heavy stems and stones would drop down. In the pick up duct, the tobacco was lifted up by suction and discharged into first tower classifier. In this tower classifier, the heavier tobacco flakes were separated from lighter ones and left behind. The lighter flakes were carried by air into second tower classifier. Here, the tobacco dust and flakes were differentiated. Finally, the lamina was sent to a sleeve chamber where it was cut and graded to suit the requirement of beedi manufacturer. The pure tobacco flakes came out after the dust was sucked out in the dust collecting unit. The end-product was called ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’. The assessee claimed reliefs under sections 32A, 80HH and 80-I for the assessment years 1984-85 and 1985-86. The assessee also claimed that it should be charged at a concessional rate treating it as an industrial company as defined under section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1985. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claims on the ground that the assessee was not manufacturing or producing any article or any thing. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance.

On second appeal:

HELD: The instant case was not a border line case and a firm conclusion was easily approachable. By subjecting tobacco to treatment beedi patti was produced. By ginning cotton, pure cotton is obtained or pressed cotton is produced. Raw wool subjected to processing to eliminate dirt, grease and other vegetable matter results in production of pure wool. Leather is said to be manufactured when raw hide is treated. In all these cases a different product in commercial realm is said to be produced. In the same strain, it was equally possible to say that ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’ was produced or manufactured from raw tobacco as a result of some manual or mechanical treatment, or both. Anybody could go to the market and purchase the article known as raw tobacco and it is equally possible to go and purchase in the market an article called Jarda or Jardi. The physical property in raw tobacco and Jarda or Jardi might be same. While raw tobacco is unfit for beedi manufacture in the same condition, Jarda or Jardi can ready be used in the beedi manufacture. In commercial parlance Jarda or Jardi is distinctively different from raw tobacco. For the aforesaid reasons, in the instant case, the assessee’s business was one of manufacture or production of an article or thing. The assessee’s business undertaking was in a backward area and there was no dispute about it. Then, if the assessee was manufacturing or producing an article, it must be taken that all the conditions in sub-section(2) of section 80HH were fulfilled. The assessee was having a mechanised tobacco processing plant which was even patented. It was registered as a small scale industrial unit by the Government. The most vital was the schedule of assets which formed part of the balance sheet, which showed that the cost of machinery employed was below the limit placed in Explanation to section 32A(2) or Explanation 3 to section 80-I(2), read with section 80HHA(8). The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the reliefs under sections 32A, 80HHA and 80-I. Since the assessee was found manufacturing an article it should be treated as an industrial company as defined in the Finance Act, though even processing, which the assessee was certainly doing, may be sufficient to justify a claim for concessional rate of tax. Thus, the assessee was also entitled to concessional rate of tax for both the years being an industrial company within the meaning of section 2(8)(c).

Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of newly established industrial undertaking in backward areas - Whether assessee engaged in business of rearing and development of chicks into broilers, could be said to be 'manufacturing' a product - Held, no

In the instant case, revenue receipt in the form of interest went to reduce the revenue expenditure of interest, because funds were borrowed for the purpose of business of industrial undertaking and funds were kept in deposit for the purpose of business of the assessee’s industrial undertaking. In respect of other miscellaneous income, arising from sale of empty drums/containers and sale of useless materials,all the sale proceeds were only out of the business of industrial undertaking of the assessee. Therefore, even for determining the profits and gains ‘derived from any business of industrial undertaking’, manufacturing or producing any article or thing includes sale proceeds of such article or thing or scrap generated during the course of such manufacturing activity which amounts to increase in the sale consideration. After all what is to be determined is the profits and gains of business of industrial undertaking and there is no warrant to stop for the above purpose at sale of main products only. The controversy was not when manufacturing activity of the assessee was over, but what was the profit and gains of the business of the industrial undertaking and how was it to be determined. For determining the profits of business of industrial undertaking, it was not possible to ignore the said sales which were closely and directly connected with the outcome of the manufacturing process itself. HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment years 1983-84 to 1987-88 - Whether process of processed (including frozen) fish and fish products should be regarded as an activity of manufacture or production of an article, or thing entitled to benefit of section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacture or production of frozen sea foods from shrimps obtained from the sea. The catch obtained from the sea was cleaned, beheaded, deskinned, sorted, frozen and was converted or produced into frozen sea foods which were exported in packs to foreign countries. The assessee claimed that it was an industrial undertaking engaged in the business of manufacture or production of frozen sea food and, thus, claimed deduction under section 80HH. The ITO allowed the said claim of the assessee. The Commissioner, however, exercising his powers under section 263, disallowed the said deduction.

On appeal :

HELD: In section 80HH the words ‘manufacture’ or ‘produce’ appear. The same words appear in section 33 of the Act which relates to grant of relief of development rebate to the assessee. It is implicit in section 33(1)(b )(B)(i ) that processed (frozen).fish and fish products produced by the assessee constituted new commercial article compared to raw fish as far as provisions in section 33 were concerned. Thus, the legislative intent under the provisions of the Act is that process of the processed (including frozen) fish and fish products should be regarded as an activity of manufacture or production of an article or thing eligible for grant of development rebate. There is no reason why the same intent should not be presumed to be present in enacting section 80HH where same words ‘manufacture’ or ‘production’ of articles have been used. Consequently, as far as the Act was concerned, processing which resulted in processed (including frozen) fish and fish products amounts to an activity of manufacture or production of an article or thing within the ambit of sections 33 and 80HH. Consequently, in the present case, the activity of the assessee would be regarded as an activity of manufacture or production of an article or thing. Accordingly, the order of Commissioner was to be set aside and that of the ITO was to be restored.

The assessee, a private trust, carried on the business of purchasing forests, felling the trees and converting them into logs and, subsequently, sawing them into timber of various sizes and varieties fit to be used in construction of buildings and also for being put to other uses inclusive Of manufacture of furniture. On appeal to the Tribunal:

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1977-78 - Whether assessee buying shrimps, peeling them and freezing them could be said to be engaged in manufacture or production, in absence of material on record to indicate what was done by assessee and how it was done, so as to eligible for allowance under section 80HH - Held, no

FACT: The assessee bought shrimps, peeled them and froze them. It claimed allowance under section 80HH on the ground that it was an industrial undertaking that manufactured/produced articles. There was no other material on the record which indicated what was done by the assessee and how it was done. The claim was rejected by the Assessing Officer but upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal. On reference, the High Court upheld the decision of the Tribunal on ground that buying and processing of shrimps involved production.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: There was, upon the record before the Court, no detailed description of what the assessee did to the shrimps it bought, other than the bald statement that it peeled and froze them. The Court could not accept the statement at the Bar that the process to which the assessee put the shrimps was the process that CIT v. Marwell Sea Foods [1987] 166 ITR 624/ 34 Taxman 52 (Ker.) used in regard to its prawns. That apart the Supreme Court in Sterling Foods v. State of Karnataka [1986] 68 STC 239, held that processed or frozen shrimps and prawns are commercially regarded as the same commodity as raw shrimps and prawns. When raw shrimps and prawns are subjected to the process of cutting of heads and tails, peeling, deveining, cleaning and freezing they do not cease to be shrimps and prawns and become other distinct commodities. There is no essential difference between raw shrimps and prawns and processed or frozen shrimps and prawns. In common parlance they remain known as shrimps and prawns. Therefore, the assessee who bought shrimps, peeled them and froze them was not entitled to the allowance under section 80HH as it did not involve in activity of manufacture or production.

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the manufacture and sale of black steel tubes and galvanised steel tubes. The assessee set up a new project consisting of a moulding plant for the manufacture of steel tubes of four inches diameter. Earlier it was manufacturing such tubes only of two inches diameter. The assessee claimed reliefs under section 80J and section 80HH. The ITO found that not only the mill compound but also the factory building were the same for both the projects. The earlier tin-shed had been extended to accommodate the new project and there was only one composite structure for both the projects. Further, he found that several machinery, plant ‘ land, building, store room, workshop, generating set and factory office were common to both the projects. The ITO rejected the assessee’s claim on the ground that no separate profit and loss account and balance sheet had been prepared in respect of that new project and it was a clear case of mere splitting of the old undertaking. He also observed that the entire borrowings and debts owed by the undertaking as a whole had to be deducted in computing the capital employed in the undertaking which in the present case exceeded the value of the assets of the undertaking. He also observed that the computation submitted by the assessee was also incorrect as it had taken the value of the assets as on the last day of the accounting year instead of their value as on the first day of the amounting year. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the ITO’s order.

On second appeal :

HELD: In view of the decision in Textile Machinery Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 107 ITR 195 ( SC), for purposes of relief under section 80J, one has to come to the conclusion that the assessee’s new project was a new industrial unit, which was separate physically from the old one, the capital of which and the profits thereon being ascertainable. The mere fact that some of the processes for the manufacture of new tubes in the instant case were carried on with the help of the old machines or there was common store room and common factory office were not fatal to the claim of the assessee. Thus, the assessee was entitled to reliefs under sections 80J and 80HH and the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in taking the contrary view.

In the accounting year relevant to assessment year 1997-98, the assessee-company set up an industrial undertaking for the manufacture of applique/indexes for watch dials in a backward area. The assessee filed return of income declaring ‘nil income’ which inter alia included a claim for deduction under section 80-IA the deduction had been claimed at the rate of 100 per cent of the income earned. The Assessing Officer examined the details of plant and machinery, record of production of finished goods for year under consideration as well as for the previous year and found that the assessee had begun production of finished goods as on 4-10-1995, and that taking into account the value of plant and machinery in use as on that date, the total value of the machinery or plant previously used and transferred to the industrial undertaking of the assessee by its principal company ‘KDDL’, exceeded 20 per cent of the total value of the plant and machinery of industrial undertaking and, therefore, the assessee did not qualify the condition as laid down in Explanation 2 to section 80-IA(3)(ii). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the stand of the Assessing Officer.

In appeal, the assessee contended that it started its commercial production on 1-1-1996, and that the production carried out for the period 4-10-1995 to 1-1-1996 was only a trial production and that too did not involve the complete manufacturing process, and thus, the condition stipulated in Explanation 2 to section 80-IA(3) had to be examined on the basis of value of plant & machinery on 1-1-1996.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of newly established industrial undertaking in backward areas - Whether assessee engaged in business of rearing and development of chicks into broilers, could be said to be 'manufacturing' a product - Held, no

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the business of rearing of chicks to broilers, a saleable product, by applying scientific process and technology, established an industrial unit in the backward area and claimed deduction under section 80HH and section 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the claim. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal, however, set aside the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) and affirmed that of the Assessing Officer.

HELD: AS HELD BY HIGH COURT

The process involved in the development of chicks into broilers is nothing but that the chicks basically remains chicks only. There is no substantial change so as to acquire new commercial identity. Chicks are smaller ones and when they are reared for sometime, they develop suitably for table purposes. Therefore, there is no change of substance. Manufacture implies a change, but every change is not manufacture and yet every change in an article is the result of treatment, labour and manipulation which does not necessarily mean that on account of certain treatment and manipulation, new identity has come to be acquired.

In the instant case, chicks were only reared up for a few days and they were developed, thereafter they became broilers. Therefore, even after rearing, they remained chicks only. Hence, the view taken by the Tribunal that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I as an industrial undertaking was correct.

AS HELD BY SUPREME COURT

It was not in dispute that the case was covered against the assessee by the judgment of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Venkateswara Hatcheries (P.) Ltd. [1999] 237 ITR 174/103 Taxman 503. The further point that was made by the assessee was that it not only reared the chicken but also dressed them for sale in the market and, therefore, a process of manufacture was carried out. But, it appeared that there was no material laid before the Tribunal in this behalf. It was, therefore, not possible to conclude in the present matter that the dressing of poultry tantamounted to manufacture.

The appeal was dismissed.

Section  80-IB , read with sections  80-IC  and  80-IE , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deductions  -  Profits and gains from industrial undertakings other than infrastructure development undertakings (Sale of scrap/empty containers)  - Assessment years  2013-14 and 2015-16 to 2017-18  - Assessee had multiple eligible units claiming deduction under sections 80IB/80IC/80IE and earned receipts from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing - AO held such receipts were merely incidental, not profits derived from eligible undertakings, and excluded them while computing deductions - CIT(A), noting that scrap and empty containers arose from manufacturing process of eligible units and following Tribunal’s orders in assessee’s own case for earlier years, allowed receipts as part of eligible profits - Whether since revenue had not brought on record any material demonstrating a change either in factual matrix or in legal position prevailing during year under consideration, impugned order of CIT(A) allowing deduction under sections 80IB, 80IC and 80IE in respect of profits arising from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing process was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 9.7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee had multiple eligible units claiming deduction under sections 80IB/80IC/80IE and earned receipts from sale of scrap/empty containers generated during manufacturing.

■

The AO held such receipts were merely incidental, not profits derived from the eligible undertakings, and excluded them while computing deductions (e.g., disallowance around Rs. 36.24 lakhs in AY 2013-14 and similar disallowances in later years for specified units).

■

The CIT(A), noting that the scrap and empty containers arose from the manufacturing process of the eligible units and following the Tribunal’s orders in the assessee’s own case for earlier years, allowed the receipts as part of eligible profits.

■

On the revenue’s appeals to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

It is found that the CIT(A) has granted relief by faithfully following the decision of the Coordinate Bench of the Tribunal rendered in the assessee's own case on an identical issue. The Tribunal, after examining the nature of the receipts, had categorically held that the sale of empty containers and scrap generated during the manufacturing process forms an integral part of the business operations of the eligible undertaking and that the profits arising therefrom qualify for deduction under the relevant provisions of the Act [Para 9.5]

■

It is noteworthy that the revenue has not brought on record any material demonstrating a change either in the factual matrix or in the legal position prevailing during the year under consideration. Nor has any distinguishing feature been pointed out which would justify taking a view different from that consistently adopted in the assessee's own case. In the absence of any such distinguishing circumstance, the principles of judicial discipline and consistency require that the view already taken by the Coordinate Bench be followed. [Para 9.6]

■

Accordingly, respectfully following the binding precedent rendered in the assessee's own case for the earlier assessment years, no infirmity is found in the order of the CIT(A) allowing deduction under sections 80-IB, 80-IC and 80-IE in respect of profits arising from the sale of scrap/empty containers generated during the manufacturing process. Therefore, the order of the CIT(A) on this issue is upheld. Consequently, Ground No. 3 raised by the Revenue stands dismissed. [Para 9.7]

6.2-6c EFFECTS OF NEW SUB-SECTION(S) - Note the following :

◆ Accordingly, after the amendment, in the illustration considered above, the deduction under section 80HHC would be Rs. 70 and the aggregate deduction would be Rs.100. Accordingly, other income of Rs. 20 would become liable to tax. It may be mentioned that the provision does not require that from the amount of deduction under section 80HHC of Rs. 90, the amount of deduction under section 80-IA of Rs. 30 be reduced and restrict the amount of deduction under section 80HHC to Rs. 60.

◆ An assessee carries on two activities. One activity is manufacture of an article or a thing in an Industrial Undertaking eligible for deduction under section 80IA. The other activity is Trading Export, entitled to deduction under section 80HHC. The businesses are not interlinked. In other words, no exports are effected of the goods manufactured in the Industrial Undertaking. In that case, there may be a controversy about the applicability of the new sub-section. Its profits from the Industrial Undertaking is Rs. 100; its profits from Trading Export is Rs. 500; and the total income, accordingly, is Rs. 600. It is entitled to 30% deduction under section 80-IA.

Based on the language of the provision, can it be said that an assessee would get deduction under section 80-IA of Rs.30, and deduction under section 80HHC only to the extent of Rs.70? Having regard to the Explanation given in the Memorandum, the language of the provision and above illustration and the analysis, it is evident that the provisions of new sub-section (9A) would apply only where a deduction is claimed with reference to profit of the Industrial Undertaking, which is also entitled to deduction under other provision. However when a claim is made with reference to other profits, the restriction cannot apply. Accordingly, the assessee would be entitled to a deduction of Rs. 30 under section 80-IA and Rs. 500 under section 80HHC.

◆ In case of an assessee, which has a number of industrial units entitled to deductions under section 80-IA, whether full or partial, and also has exports, from the same Units and also otherwise, including trading and also, has project income eligible for deduction under section 80HHB, how would one give effect to provisions of section 80HHD(7) or 80-IA (9A)? It seems, the principles to be applied would be the same as discussed above, namely :

- The restriction imposed is not with reference to computation of deductions under the other provisions; and

- Where profits do not form part of profit or income on which the other deduction is claimed, the restriction should not operate.

Apart from the above, where exports are from the Industrial Undertakings, one may have to apply mathematical formula for finding out what are the export profits relating to those undertakings. Such attributable profits, which also form part of profit of industrial undertaking and are entitled to deduction under section 80-IA, the deduction U/s. 80HHC could be subject to the restrictions and/or limitations placed by section 80-IA (9A). However, the other export profits would not be subject to same discipline or limitations. Similarly, a deduction under section 80HHB cannot be curtailed inasmuch as it is not claimed with reference to profits of an Industrial Undertaking.

HEADNOTE: V. Section  80-IC  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 – Deductions – Special provisions in respect of certain undertakings or enterprises in certain special category States (Scrap income) – Assessment years  2014-15 to 2016-17  – Assessee-company included scrap income generated by its eligible manufacturing undertaking at Baddi while computing deduction under section 80-IC – Assessing Officer held that scrap income did not constitute profits derived from industrial undertaking and excluded same from eligible profits – It was noted that generation of scrap was an inevitable incident of manufacturing process and identical issue stood covered in favour of assessee by decisions rendered in assessee's own case for earlier years – Whether scrap income generated during manufacturing operations of eligible industrial undertaking formed an integral part of profits derived from such undertaking, generation of scrap being an inevitable incident of manufacturing activity – Held, yes – Whether, therefore, deduction under section 80-IC was allowable in respect of scrap income earned by eligible industrial undertaking – Held, yes [Paras 116, 123 and 127] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company included scrap income generated by its eligible manufacturing undertaking at Baddi while computing deduction under section 80-IC.

■

The Assessing Officer held that scrap income did not constitute profits derived from the industrial undertaking and excluded such income from eligible profits while computing deduction under section 80-IC for assessment years 2014-15 to 2016-17.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that generation of scrap was an inevitable incident of the manufacturing process and directed inclusion of scrap income while computing deduction under section 80-IC.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The rival submissions, assessment order, appellate findings and judicial precedents relied upon by the assessee have been carefully considered. The orders passed by the Ahmedabad Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case for assessment years 2008-09 to 2010-11 in ITA Nos. 1366/Ahd/2015 & 1780/Ahd/2015, for assessment year 2011-12 in ITA Nos. 1184/Ahd/2018 & 1225/Ahd/2018 and for assessment years 2012-13, 2013-14, 2020-21 and 2022-23 in Deputy CIT v. Reckitt Benckiser Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. [2025] 176 taxmann.com 573 (Ahmedabad - Trib.) have also been examined. Upon careful examination of the issue from the perspective of section 80-IC and the settled principles governing interpretation of the expression "derived from", no infirmity is found in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 114]

■

The identical issue now stands squarely covered in favour of the assessee by consistent decisions rendered by the Ahmedabad Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case for earlier years. [Para 115]

■

In the assessee's own case for assessment years 2008-09 to 2010-11 in Reckitt Benckiser Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. v. ACIT (ITA Nos. 1366/Ahd/2015 & 1780/Ahd/2015), the Co-ordinate Bench examined the allowability of deduction under section 80-IC in respect of scrap income earned by the eligible industrial undertaking. [Para 116]

■

Deduction in respect profits and gains from business of collecting and processing bio-degradable waste

6.3 A new section 80JJA has been inserted with effect from assessment year 1999-2000 to provide for deduction in respect profits and gains from business of collecting and processing bio-degradable waste.

The section provides that “Where the gross total income of an assessee includes any profits and gains derived from the business of collecting and processing or treating of bio-degradable waste for generating power, producing bio-gas, making pellets or briquettes for fuel or organic manure, there shall be allowed, in computing the total income of the assessee, a deduction from such profits and gains of an amount equal to the whole of such income, or five lakh rupees, whichever is less.”

6.3-1 Analysis of new provision : Note the following

◆ The deduction is available to all assessees.

◆ On a plain reading of the section, the deduction is available only if the assessee is engaged in the business of collecting as well as processing or treating bio-degradable waste. It is not available if the assessee is engaged in only collection or only processing/treating.

◆ The deduction is available only in respect of profit and gains of processing or treatment for generating power, producing bio-gas , making pellets or briquettes for fuel or organic manure. It is not available in respect of profits and gains of processing or treating for other purposes.

◆ The deduction is available to all entities, whether new or old. In other words unlike section 80-IA it is not restricted to new units.

Deduction in respect of employment of new workmen

6.4 In order to encourage the employers to further generate more employment opportunities, a new section 80JJAA has been inserted (with effect from 1-4-1999) to provide an incentive in the form of a special deduction against business profits of a company.

6.4-1 Conditions to be fulfilled - The following conditions have to be fulfilled in order to be eligible to the deduction provided in the section :

◆ the assessee should be an Indian company.

◆ its gross total income should include profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking.

◆ the industrial undertaking should be engaged in the manufacture or production of any article or thing.

◆ the industrial undertaking should not have been formed by splitting up of an existing undertaking.

◆ the industrial undertaking should not have been formed by reconstruction of an existing undertaking.

◆ the industrial undertaking should not have been formed by amalgamation with an existing undertaking.

◆ the assessee furnishes alongwith the return of income a report of an accountant.

◆ in case of a new industrial undertaking, in the first previous year, it employs more than 100 regular workmen.

◆ in the case of an existing industrial undertaking, the number of regular workers employed during the relevant previous year is equal to at least 110% of the regular workmen employed in such undertaking as on the last day of the preceding year.

The provisions relating to aforesaid conditions are elaborately explained in subsequent paragraphs.

6.4-2 Quantum of deduction - See para 6.4-11

6.4-3 Indian company - The section is applicable only if the assessee is an Indian company as defined in section 2(26) of the Act. Hence, it does not apply to other entities like foreign companies, firms, HUFs, etc.

6.4-4 Profits and gains derived - The term ‘derived’ has been explained in a number of judgments involving interpretation of section 80J/80-I/80-IA etc.,

It may be noted, however, that unlike other sections, section 80JJAA does not link the deduction to quantum of profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking. For the purpose of this section , it is sufficient that the gross total income includes profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and once this condition is satisfied, the ultimate deduction is based on wages paid.

Again, it could also be argued that in the absence of a specific prohibition, the deduction under this section could exceed the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking, as long as the deductions under Chapter VIA of the Act do not exceed the gross total income [section 80A(2)].

6.4-5 Industrial undertaking - The term industrial undertaking has not been defined in the section. In the context of section 15C, of the Income-tax Act, 1922 (corresponding to s. 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961), the Supreme Court in Textile Machinery Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 107 ITR 195, had elaborately dealt with the expression industrial undertaking. It appears that the interpretation of the term “industrial undertaking” given by the Supreme Court would be equally relevant for section 80JJAA.

Similarly, a deduction under section 80HHB cannot be curtailed inasmuch as it is not claimed with reference to profits of an Industrial Undertaking.

HEADNOTE: Section 80-I, read with section 80HH, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertakings after a certain date - Assessment years 1987-88 to 1992-93 - Assessees engaged in dismantling of damaged/unserviceable ships claimed deduction under section 80HH and 80-I - Whether legislature intended to extend benefit of deductions only to industrial undertakings manufacturing or producing articles - Held, yes - Whether as ship-breaking activity amounts to carrying out manufacturing process in reverse order, assessees were not entitled to deduction claimed - Held, yes

FACT: The assessees, engaged in the business of breaking and dismantling of damaged or unserviceable ships and selling the goods obtained therefrom to various parties, claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claims on the grounds that the assessee were not industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80HH and 80-I and they did not fulfil any of the conditions of those sections and that there was nothing like a process of manufacturing done by the assessees. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that ship breaking was an industrial undertaking and, accordingly, the assessees were eligible for the deductions claimed.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: The Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. This section is not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in ‘processing of goods’ not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. The ship-breaking activity involves buying of damaged and unserviceable ships which are otherwise uneconomic to run, for the purpose of breaking and scrapping and sale of various goods and scrap obtained from such breaking and dismantling of old and used ships. Process is employed for breaking ship for dismantling and selling the scrap and substantial part of the items fitted in the ship and the oil contained in the tankers are sold in the same from without carrying out any further act, except removal of same from the ship and the remaining ship, made mainly of iron and steel, is then broken into different pieces of different sizes and shapes and sold by weight. Therefore, at the end of the process employed by the assessee, what is acquired are iron bars, plating rods, bronze, gunmetal copper and non-ferrous metal which, though marketable and commercial commodities, cannot be said to be manufactured or produced articles or things. For all practical purposes it is scrap. The scrap cannot be called a manufacture product or produced article because they are no new commodities but parts of the old and discarded ship as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Delhi Iron & Steel Co. (P.) Ltd. [1995] 98 STC 202 the condemned and unserviceable ship purchased by the dealer is not a ship but re-rollable scrap in the form of an old ship for dismantling, in effect, the dealer acquires only the old materials and articles contained therein which are sold by it in the form in which they are acquired. No process whatsoever is applied to the goods, much less any process of manufacture. The issue stood squarely covered in favour of the revenue by the decision of the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asst. CIT v. Virendra & Co. [1995] 55 ITD 309 which held that ‘the meaning of manufacture and production of articles and things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or an thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken, what is obtained by the persons who are engaged in that process are the components by which the ship is constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

HEADNOTE: Section 80J, read with section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings, ships or hotels, etc. - Assessment year 1980-81 - Business of assessee was centrifuging rubber latex - It claimed deduction under sections 80J and 80HH - Tribunal adverting to a notification of Central Government allowed claims of assessee - While doing so, Tribunal neither, adverted to relevant materials nor entered finding as to whether any manufacturing process was involved or a new commodity produced - Tribunal even diluted legal effect of its earlier decision wherein a contrary view was taken and also failed to apply proper test governing matter as laid down by Supreme Court - Whether in above circumstances, Tribunal’s approach to question was totally faulty and resultant conclusion was tainted - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, matter was to be restored to Tribunal’s file for fresh decision - Held, yes

FACT: The business of the assessee-company was centrifuging rubber latex. It claimed that the business involved manufacture or production of articles and things and so, the company was entitled to deduction under section 80J as well as under section 80HH for the relevant assessment year in respect of a unit working in a backward area. The ITO rejected the said plea. He held that the assessee did not carry on manufacturing operations nor did it produce any article. In his view, the assessee only made the latex more concentrated. The reliefs claimed under sections 80J and 80HH were denied. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the said decision. On second appeal, the Tribunal observed that the notification dated 8-7-1983 (No. 189 of 1983), considered the latex concentrate, preserved latex, etc., as manufactured goods. After adverting to the said notification it held that the Government had proclaimed that the assessee was a manufacturer and that the said notification had to be applied with equal force to the Act also and accordingly, held that the assessee was entitled to deductions under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case, the essential question to be considered was whether when normal or natural latex was converted into preserved latex by centrifuging process, any manufacturing process was involved or a new commodity produced. A finding on this was essential. Such a finding could be entered only on the basis of evidence. Technical and scientific evidence could be gathered from competent persons or after understanding the process from standard books or literature.

The Tribunal had not rendered the decision in accordance with law. There had been no proper advertence to the relevant materials. It had not posed the correct question. The proper test governing the matter, as held by the Supreme Court in Ujagar Prints v. Union of India [1989] 179 ITR 317, was not adverted to. On the other hand, it over-emphasised the effect of the said notification and completely under-estimated and diluted the legal effect of its earlier decision wherein it had held that in spite of the changes that were effected by the process of centrifuging, the end product could not be considered to be materially different from the raw material, the natural latex and that commercially no different product was produced and no production or manufacture was involved in subjecting the natural rubber latex to the centrifugal operation after obtaining preserved latex. The approach to the question was totally faulty. The resultant conclusion was tainted.

In the above circumstances, the Tribunal was directed to restore the appeal to its file and decide the matter afresh in accordance with law.

Therefore, factory No. III situated in Raj Samund Block of Udaipur District was eligible for deduction under section 80HH since it began production in March 1984 as certified by the Central Excise authorities. HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas (Condition precedent) - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether what becomes entitled to claim exemption under section 80HH is an industrial undertaking and once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial whether it is manufacturing, or producing or processing - Held, yes - Whether assessee, an industrial undertaking engaged in activity of converting cotton pieces known as cops into yarn, would be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]IT : Once assessee answers description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial for purpose of allowing deduction under section 80HH whether it is manufacturing or producing or processing

FACT: The assessee was an industrial undertaking engaged in the activity of converting cotton pieces known as cops into yarn., depending upon the customer requirement. It claimed deduction under section 80HH.

The Assessing Officer held that no process of manufacture was undertaken by assessee and, therefore, it was not entitled to claim deduction under section 80HH.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee's claim.

The Tribunal dismissed the revenue's appeal.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: In the context of section 80HH, the Parliament guardedly used the expression 'manufacturing process, or manufacture, or produce articles' in sub-section (4) and other parts thereof. [Para 11]

What becomes entitled to claim exemption under section 80HH, is an industrial undertaking, as is evident from the very heading of the section, than the nature of activity taken up by it. Once the assessee answers the description of an industrial undertaking, it is immaterial whether it is manufacturing, or producing or processing. The amount that qualifies for deduction is the profits and gains of such an undertaking to the extent of 20 per cent. Things would have been different altogether, had the deduction been restricted only to the activity of manufacturing. [Para 12]

There is no ground to interfere with the order passed by the Tribunal. [Para 16]

The appeal is accordingly dismissed. [Para 17]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether activity of breaking or dismantling a ship or ships can be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactures or produces articles so as to be entitled to get deduction under sections 80HHA and 80-I - Held, no

FACT: The assessee, involved in breaking of ships and selling the parts and its other articles, claimed to be an industrial undertaking engaged in the manufacture of articles or things and, thus, entitled to deduction under sections 80HHA and 80-I. Such claim was rejected by the Assessing Officer but allowed by the first appellate authority.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: After the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412 the concept of adopting a liberal interpretation has been reconsidered and now as per the Supreme Court the principles of adopting a liberal interpretation which advances the purpose and object of beneficial provisions cannot be carried to the extent of doing violence to the plain and simple language used in the enactment. It would not be reasonable or permissible for the court to re-write the section or substitute words of its own for the actual words employed by the Legislature in the name of giving effect to the supposed underlying object.

The meaning of `manufacture’ and ‘production of articles or things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary, plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or a thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken what is obtained by the person or persons who are engaged in that process are those components by which the ship was constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or a thing is being manufactured or produced.

Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling a ship could not be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deductions under sections 80HHA and 80-I.

On second appeal :

HELD: The phrase ‘profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking’ has not been defined in the Act. Hence, its meaning has to be understood in the general commercial sense. In order to arrive at the profit from an under-taking, only the actual expenses are deducted and not the notional expenses. Hence, the profits of an undertaking can mean the amount arrived at after deduction of actual expenses only and without deduction of the notional expenses like the relief under section 35B: This is really not an expense that goes out of the pocket of the assessee, and cannot, therefore, go to reduce the commercial profit, though it may reduce the taxable profit.

Accordingly, the assessee should be allowed relief under section 80HH before deducting the extra weighted deduction allowed under the section.

On appeal under section 260A : HELD: Section 80HH begins with the words 'where the gross total income of an assessee includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking'. The expression 'gross total income' is defined under section 80B(5) to mean the total income computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act, before making any deduction under Chapter VI-A. Therefore, what is included in the gross total income in such a case is not only the category of such income included in the gross total income but also the quantum of the income so included. This is the basic test which needs to be applied to answer the question raised by the assessee in this appeal. In the case of Distributors (Baroda) (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [1985] 155 ITR 120/ 22 Taxman 49, the Supreme Court has categorically laid down that the expression 'gross total income' in section 80B(5) would mean the total income computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act before making any deductions under Chapter VI-A and what is included in the gross total income is a particular quantum of income belonging to a specified category. Therefore, the words 'such income by way of profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking referred to in section 80HH', must be referable not only to the category of income but also to the quantum of income included in the gross total income and, therefore, such income belonging to a specified category and forming part of the gross total income is required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Therefore, on a bare reading of the provisions of section 80HH, along with section 80B(5), it is clear that even prior to the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1980, Parliament had clearly intended to say that what is included in the gross total income is not only a specified category of income, but also a particular quantum of income belonging to that specified category. In Court's opinion, therefore, the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1980, has merely made the position, which was implicit, explicit. Therefore, section 80AB is clearly declaratory in nature like section 80AA and it merely declares what the correct position has always been. In fact, in the concurring judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Distributors (Baroda) (P.) Ltd. (supra), Sen, J. has observed that section 80AA was clearly declaratory in nature and it merely declared what the correct position has always been and, therefore, there was no question of imposition of any fresh tax with retrospective effect by virtue of the said section. It may be pointed out that the Supreme Court has reversed its own judgment in the case of Cloth Traders (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 243/ 1 Taxman 335, vide judgment in the case of Distributors (Baroda) (P.) Ltd. (supra). At this stage, it may be mentioned that in the case of H.H. Sir Rama Varma v. CIT [1994] 205 ITR 433/[1993] 71 Taxman 237, the Supreme Court has held that section 80AB was enacted to declare the law as it always stood in relation to the deductions to be made in respect of the income specified under Chapter VI-A. Therefore, it is clear that even without section 80AB, the profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking referred to in section 80HH have to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43A and in any event since section 80AB has been held to be retrospective by the Supreme Court in H.H. Sir Rama Varma's case (supra), it was not open to the assessee to say that the said section is prospective as stated above.

On a bare reading of the judgment of the Bombay High Court in the case of CIT v. Albright Morarji & Pandit Ltd. [1999] 236 ITR 914/ 103 Taxman 168, it is clear that the said judgment is based on review of the various provisions of the Act both with and de hors section 80AB. In the said judgment, it has been laid down that section 80AB, though inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1980 with effect from 1-4-1981, was merely declaratory.

Accordingly, the appeal stood rejected.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc. in backward areas [Computation of deduction] - Assessee-company had been carrying on two activities; one was business of manufacturing cement and second was mining operation of lime - Lime was used as raw material in manufacturing cement - Assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH from whole of business income - Same was disallowed on ground that assessee had been carrying on business of mining operation - Whether mining activity of assessee was distinct and independent from cement manufacturing activities and segregation of profit of two different business activities was permissible under law - Held, yes - Whether segregation of profit derived from cement manufacturing activity was permitted by law in order to find out profit derived from mining activities and, thus, deduction under section 80HH would be available only on profit derived from cement manufacturing activity - Held, yes [Paras 6 to 11] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee had two separate and distinct undertaking, one for manufacturing cement and another for mining of lime that was to be used in cement manufacturing, profit only from manufacturing of cement would be eligible for deduction under section 80HH

FACT: The assessee-company had been carrying on business of manufacturing cement and also carrying on mining operation of lime which was used as a raw material in manufacturing cement.

The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH and the same was disallowed by Assessing Officer on the ground that assessee had been carrying on business of mining operation.

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee could be said to have been running two industrial undertakings. The Tribunal, therefore, allowed deduction with respect to profit attributable to manufacturing cement.

On assessee's appeal to High Court :

HELD: From the records the Court find, as has been rightly contended by revenue that in the previous assessment years, namely 1984-85 and 1985-86, the Tribunal found on fact that the assessee has been running two industrial undertakings, one is mining of lime and another is manufacturing of cement. It is an admitted position further that against the aforesaid findings, no appeal has been preferred. Hence, the Court have to proceed on the premise that the mining activity of the assessee is distinct and independent from the cement manufacturing activity. Now the question remains is whether the use of the entire product of lime, extracted from mining operation for manufacturing of cement, looses its marketable value in order to ascertain the profit or not. [Para 6]

The argument of the assessee is that a manufacturer cannot trade with itself. Therefore, unless there is a factual sale in the market, no profit can be derived from this mining operation. In order to derive the entire profit, the cement manufacturing unit has to be taken into account and the product has to be sold in the market and then the profit will be ascertained. This submission, at the first blush, sounds logic, but while keeping in view the matter, this logic does not have any basis. It is the admitted position that lime is one of the raw materials in manufacturing cement and in order to manufacture the finished products, raw material is essential and the cost thereof is one of the factors for cost price of the finished goods. Therefore, in the manufacturing activity of cement unit, the cost of the finished product has to be ascertained and in that process, the cost of lime has also to be taken into consideration. In the case on hand, the lime, being a raw material, is not procured from open market and it has got its own indigenous supply. Therefore, the cost of the lime extracted from mining operation has to be ascertained from the cost price and it is found, while doing so, that the cost of lime of its own source (ordinarily it happens) is lesser than the market price. Therefore, the difference between the cost price of indigenous source and the market price is obviously the profit. Moreover, once lime is used from its indigenous source to manufacture the finished products and by virtue of sale of such finished products if there is any profit, then obviously that profit is also related to the mining operation. [Para 7]

It is well-settled that if there is nexus between the receipt of income and the industrial undertaking, it has to be treated as income derived from the industrial undertaking. In the instant case, the immediate source of job charges received was the industrial undertaking itself. Therefore, the job work charges had to be treated as income derived from the industrial undertaking. The conversion charges might not have any nexus with export or other activity. But, said charges had a direct nexus with the manufacturing activity of the assessee, since the assessee did the job work by utilizing the very same machinery and labourers. Therefore, the income had to be considered as derived from the industrial undertaking and was eligible for deduction under section 80-IB. In view of the above, there was no infirmity in the order of the lower authority. [Para 6]

Therefore, the profit on sale of the scrap material had a direct nexus with the manufacturing activity of the assessee and receipt of income. In other words, unless the assessee manufactured the goods, the scrap would not have been generated at all. Therefore, the income from sale of scrap was derived from the industrial undertaking and was eligible for deduction under section 80-IB. The income received from sale of scrap might not have any relation with export of goods and it might not be eligible for deduction under section 80HHC. However, it had a direct nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, it was eligible for deduction under section 80-IB. [Para 10]

As regards interest on delayed payments, in view of decision of the Madras High Court in CIT v. Rane (Madras) Ltd. [1999] 238 ITR 377/ 102 Taxman 284 it was to be held that said interest was directly related to industrial undertaking and, therefore, was eligible for deduction. [Para 11]

In the result, the revenue's appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 12]

FACT: The assessee, being an owner of a cold storage situated in a backward area wherein potatoes were kept in the relevant assessment year, claimed investment allowance under section 32A on machinery and plant installed in the cold storage on the ground that the cold storage involved ‘manufac-turing’. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that a cold storage involved only processing and not manufacture or production of an article or thing. He also disallowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under section 80HH, On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal;

HELD: Section 32 A uses the expression ‘business of manufacture or production of any article or thing’. The expression used in section 80HH is similar, namely, ‘to manufacture or produce articles’. There is no reference to ‘processing’ as used in the definition of ‘industrial company’ under section 2(7)(d) of the Finance Act, 1966, and the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1967. Again, unlike section 80J(4)(iii), reference is not made in section 32A or 80HH to the operation of a cold storage plant. This would show that mere processing (even if the potatoes were held to undergo processing in a cold storage) is not recognised under sections 32A and 80HH to amount to manufacture or production of any article or thing. The same expression is used in section 80HHA and 80-I(2)(iii). Again, section 35C, which deals with agricultural development allowance, refers to a company or a co-operative society being engaged in the manufacture or processing of a relevant article or thing There-fore, as neither section 32A nor section 80HH refers to processing of any article or thing, the lower authorities were justified in rejecting the claims of the assessee.

As per the provision of section 80-IA, the same would be applicable to a company, which manufacture or produce any article or things. In the present case, the assessee company perform work in the nature of business for repairing and manufacturing of transformer. It has also been contended by the assessee that the company has been manufacturing aluminium HT/LT Leg Coils, which were used in old burnt transformers and in this regard, it had also submitted in detail before the assessing authority. The company did not manufacture or produce transformer oil and scrap, rather it has purchased the T/Oil from the market and only centrifuging has been done and no new article or things has been produced/manufactured, only processing has been done. In the processing scrap, it had obtained from old/burnt Transformers Coils, which were made of aluminium wires of different amperes. It also appeared from the record that the scrap has not been manufactured/produced. Certain more small parts have been purchased and have been used in manufacture of new HT/LT Leg Coils. It also appears that the assessee has purchased the transformer oil from the market and after centrifuging the transformer oil by centrifugal machine, the centrifuged transformer oil has been made useful in old/burnt transformer. It is a sort of processing only and cannot be termed as manufacture of centrifuged transformer oil. [Para 19]

It is apparent that the assessee did indulge in processing activities, but no manufacture or production of new articles or things is involved in this processing. [Para 20]

The assessee has also taken a stand that the word 'manufacture' and 'produce' has been defined in clauses (iii) and (vi) of Explanation to section 10-A(8) and clauses (iii) & (iv) of Explanation to section 10-B(7), while discussing the deductions under the said sections in relation to the 'Newly established Industrial Undertakings in Free Trade Zones' and 'newly established 100 per cent Export Oriented Undertakings' respectively. On this analogy, it has been argued that processing of articles or things done by assessee should be treated as 'Manufacture' of new article or thing. [Para 21]

The Explanations of both the above sections begin with the opening limb 'For the purpose of this section' and, therefore, it cannot be reasonably construed that this inclusive definition of 'Manufacture' or 'Produce' as enuciated and elaborated in sections 10A and 10B is applicable to provisions of section 80-I or section 80-IA because these words have been defined with a particular purpose or with reference to the limited/particular context, i.e., free trade zone and 100 per cent Export Oriented Undertakings. Although prima facie, there appears to be a discrimination yet this is a reasonable/discrimination because it is well within the competence of the legislature to define a word for specific purposes or object or section and not for general connotation wherever these words occur in the IT Act. Had this been the intention or object of the legislature/Parliament, the word 'Manufacture' world also have been defined in section 80-I or 80-IA in the same manner or a reference must have been made in section 10-A or 10-B because these sections are on the statute for the last 7-8 years or even some more years with certain new charges. [Para 22]

The Commissioner as well as Tribunal have given much emphasis on processing and held that the assessee, industrial undertaking does processing of goods and entitled for benefit under section 80-IA, just to appreciate the processing, it would be appropriate to place few more meanings of the processing even though the processing has not been defined in the Act.

On bare perusal of literal meaning of processing, it is clear that by means of continuous and regular action or succession of action taking place or carried on in a definite manner and leading to the accomplishment of some result, then only some benefits could be conferred in favour of the assessee. [Para 26]

From the aforementioned facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that definition of 'processing' would not be applicable in the present case, especially in the background that the transformer oil had been purchased by the assessee from market and centrifuging had been done by centrifugal machine in order to make it usable in Transformer, but in substance no new articles or things has emerged from the said processing, only some special processing or treatment had been given to transformer oil through a particular method. Therefore, it cannot be construed that due to this transformation or activity there was change in the substance and new article had come out. [Para 27]

In the case of CIT v. Abad Fisheries [2002] 258 ITR 641 / 125 Taxman 616, Kerala High Court held that interest earned on FDRs by utilizing surplus funds was not a profit derived from export of goods and, therefore, not entitled to deduction under section 80HHC. In the instant case also, the assessee had earned interest on FDRs by depositing the surplus funds in the bank deposits. Thus, it did not have any direct nexus between the interest income and the industrial undertaking. Therefore, that could not be considered as profit derived from an industrial undertaking. Same position would prevail with regard to interest received on income-tax refund and interest from HDFC bonds. Even the interest earned on loans given to employees did not have direct nexus with the industrial undertaking. It was only incidental to the business.

Therefore, it was held that interest on fixed deposits, interest on income-tax refund and loan to employees and interest on HDFC bonds would not be profit derived from by an industrial undertaking and, therefore, that would not be includible for the purpose of allowing deduction under section 80-I.

As regards recoveries of insurance claims, the same would bear a direct nexus as such insurance claims had been received on goods lost in transit.

Similarly, profits on sale of fixed assets would also be eligible for deduction under section 80-I because these were directly connected with the industrial undertaking. Moreover, the decision of ITAT, Delhi Bench in the case of Rollatainers Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2000] 110 Taxman 221 also supported that view. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was set aside and the Assessing Officer was directed to compute deduction under section 80-I after including these two items of income as business profits.

The assessee-company, engaged in the manufacture of cooling towers, had set-up one unit at ‘O’ in the year 1985 for manufacturing of certain components required for round bottle (RB series) cool- ing towers. During the financial year 1991-92, the assessee had set-up a new unit at ‘C’ in order to revamp its business activities and ente- red into collaboration agreement with a foreign company ‘G’ and obtained technical know-how for making ‘cross flow’ (XE series) and ‘counter flow’ (CM series) cooling towers. The assessee had also closed down its original unit situated at ‘O’ during the year 1992 and plant and machinery and moulds from the ‘O’ unit were transferred to the new unit at ‘C’. As per the assessee the total extent of such items transferred was 11.60 per cent of the total investment in new plant in terms of cost and 0.63 per cent in terms of WDV. Most of the employees of the old unit were also transferred to the new unit and certain new employees were also recruited. The assessee thereafter started manufacturing in the new unit, certain components required for cooling towers, i.e., RB series, XE series and CM series. The modus operandi of the assessee in carrying out business was that on receipt of enquiries from the clients, it designed the cooling tower as per requirement of the clients and the quotations were forwarded to the clients along with detailed analysis of the said towers. The assessee on receipt of the orders from the clients manufactured the basic compo-nents required for the said cooling towers in its unit and certain items/components like electric motors, fans, etc., were purchased from the market. As per the assessee, these items were tested and checked in the factory of the assessee. The said components, i.e., manufactured and bought out items were transferred to the site of the customers and two separate invoices were prepared, one for in-house manufactured components on which excise duty was paid and another for the bought out components and, accordingly, the sales were shown under the head ‘Manufactured items and bought out components’. The assembly of the unit and erection of the same was carried out at the customer’s site and the assessee in addition raised the bill for installation charges, forwarding charges and service charges, which were booked under the respective heads in the books of account. For the relevant assessment years, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80-IA on the total turnover of the manufactured items during the year, including sale of bought out components, installation charges, forwarding charges and service charges. The Assessing Officer held that the new unit set-up by the assessee manufactured the items required for XE and CM type cooling towers only and the machinery, which had been shifted from the old unit, manufactured the parts required for round bottle cooling towers; and that since the moulds required for manufacturing the round bottle and CM/XE type cooling towers were independent and totally different and the assessee started manufacturing both under one roof for the sake of convenience and the old equipment was acquired in the year 1985 while the new equipment was purchased in 1992, the profits arising from the sale of items manufactured by the assessee for round bottle cooling towers were not eligible for deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer further held that bought out components purchased by the assessee from the market were never integrated at the assessee’s factory into the cooling tower and tested and, therefore, the assessee was not manufacturing the cooling tower but manufacturing only certain parts required for cooling towers and assembling the cooling tower at the clients’ place as per the requirement of the clients. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the profit earned by the assessee on the bought out components did not have any nexus with the manufacturing activity carried out by the assessee in its factory and the said profit could not be treated as profits of industrial undertaking for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer in respect of the forwarding charges, installation charges and service charges held that the assessee had incurred expenditure on account of transport, labour charges both for loading/unloading and assembling, which were not adjusted against the receipts and, therefore, all these charges did not have any connection with the manufacturing activity of the assessee and, accordingly, the profit earned by the assessee on the said charges was not eligible for deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA only in respect of profits arising from sale of components manufactured by the assessee required for XE and CM cooling towers. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the impugned order.

The Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. This section is not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in ‘processing of goods’ not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. The ship-breaking activity involves buying of damaged and unserviceable ships which are otherwise uneconomic to run, for the purpose of breaking and scrapping and sale of various goods and scrap obtained from such breaking and dismantling of old and used ships. Process is employed for breaking ship for dismantling and selling the scrap and substantial part of the items fitted in the ship and the oil contained in the tankers are sold in the same from without carrying out any further act, except removal of same from the ship and the remaining ship, made mainly of iron and steel, is then broken into different pieces of different sizes and shapes and sold by weight. Therefore, at the end of the process employed by the assessee, what is acquired are iron bars, plating rods, bronze, gunmetal copper and non-ferrous metal which, though marketable and commercial commodities, cannot be said to be manufactured or produced articles or things. For all practical purposes it is scrap. The scrap cannot be called a manufacture product or produced article because they are no new commodities but parts of the old and discarded ship as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Delhi Iron & Steel Co. (P.) Ltd. [1995] 98 STC 202 the condemned and unserviceable ship purchased by the dealer is not a ship but re-rollable scrap in the form of an old ship for dismantling, in effect, the dealer acquires only the old materials and articles contained therein which are sold by it in the form in which they are acquired. No process whatsoever is applied to the goods, much less any process of manufacture. The issue stood squarely covered in favour of the revenue by the decision of the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asst. CIT v. Virendra & Co. [1995] 55 ITD 309 which held that ‘the meaning of manufacture and production of articles and things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or an thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken, what is obtained by the persons who are engaged in that process are the components by which the ship is constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

Regarding the contention of the assessee that the Government of India had recognised ship breaking as industry and, hence, the assessee was entitled to deduction claimed, there was no presumption that every industry is engaged in ‘manufacture’ or ‘production of articles or things’. Even if ship breaking is considered as an industry in the light of the definition of section 2(f) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, it will not mean that it would amount to manufacture or production so as to entitle the assessee to claim deductions under the respective sections. The assessee being governed by the Factories Act also would not change the matter in any way because that is broadly meant for welfare of labourers employed. The argument that a ship-breaking industry is labour intensive and that in the process heavy machinery like cranes and winches are employed is not relevant in absence of any manufacturing process involved. Mere application of systematic and sophisticated machines in the process would not treat an activity into manufacture. Thus, ship breaking activity amounts to carrying out the manufacturing process in a reverse order, as originally the ship is built from iron sheets and iron bars and other materials and by process of breaking the same, ship was reconverted into iron scrap and other materials. In view of the above, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) were to be reversed.
