1.2-6 Manufacture of any item is permitted - Additional depreciation would be available to any undertaking including those manufacturing items listed in Eleventh Schedule. This is unlike section 80-IB which provides that the deduction under that section is not available to any undertaking other than a small scale undertaking if it manufactures or produces any article or thing specified in the Eleventh Schedule.

1.2-7 ‘Not formed by transfer to a new business of old machinery’ - The section defines a new industrial undertaking as an undertaking which is not formed by the transfer to a new business of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose. Similar expression is found in section 10A/10B/80-IA/80-IB. However, in those sections it is provided that if the value of machinery or plant transferred does not exceed 20% of the total value of the machinery or plant used in the business then the condition prohibiting transfer of old machinery should be deemed to be complied with. Now, a similar exception is not provided in the provision relating to additional depreciation. Does this mean that transfer of machinery of any insignificant value will disentitle the assessee from the grant of additional depreciation? In this context the meaning of the word ‘formed’ as given by the Supreme Court in Bajaj Tempo Limited v. CIT [1992] 196 ITR 188 becomes relevant.

In that case, the new industrial undertaking for which deduction under section 15C of the Income-tax Act, 1922 was claimed had taken a building on lease and some tools and implements valued at Rs. 3,500. The Assessing Officer argued that the undertaking was formed by transfer of the building and machinery previously used in another business.

The Supreme Court held as follows :

“The word ‘form’ according to the dictionary has different meanings. In the context in which it has been used it was intended to connote that the body of the company or its shape did not come up in consequence of transfer of machinery and plant used previously for business purpose. Use of the negative before the word ‘formed’ further strengthens it. In other words, machinery and plant used previously in other business should not result in the undertaking being formed by it. The transfer to take out the new undertaking out of the purview of the provision must be such that but for transfer the new undertaking could not have come into being.”

It observed that since on the facts, the part played by taking the building on lease was not dominant, the undertaking was not formed by such transfer.

Applying the ratio of the aforesaid judgment, it is submitted that transfer of machinery (of any insignificant value or otherwise) which does not result in formation of the industrial undertaking or without which the undertaking could have come into being should not disentitle the assessee from the grant of additional depreciation.

1.2-8 Eligible assessee - The benefit is available only if the machinery or plant is acquired and installed by an assessee engaged in the business of manufacture or production of an article or thing. Hence, the deduction will not be available to any assessee who is not engaged in a business of manufacture or production.

Further, even in the case of such assessee who is engaged in manufacture/production, the first proviso to section 32(1)(iia) provides that the deduction shall be allowed to an industrial undertaking. Now, any deduction including depreciation (especially with the block of assets concept) is available to an assessee and not to an undertaking. Hence, the purpose/effect of this proviso is not clear; perhaps, the intention is to allow deduction only in respect of machinery or plant installed in the industrial undertaking manufacturing or producing such article or thing and not to machinery or plant which is not installed in such industrial undertaking. It may be noted that section 32A which dealt with grant of investment allowance clearly provided that the said allowance was available only in respect of machinery or plant installed in an industrial undertaking [section 32A(2)(b)].

1.2-9 Plant and machinery used outside India - Unlike other sections where use of a machinery or plant outside India does not disentitle an assessee from claiming a deduction [see Explanation 1 to section 80-IB(2), sections 10A, 10B, etc.], under this section, deduction is not allowed even if the machinery or plant is used outside India.

5.5-1 Scheme of section 80-IA - A recapitulation - To recapitulate, various provisions/conditions of section 80-IA are as follows: An industrial undertaking is entitled to certain deduction provided it fulfils the following conditions (including the conditions imposed by amendments):

■ It is not 'formed' by:

- splitting up, or reconstruction of a business already in existence [Section 8O-IA(2)(i)]; and

- transfer to a new business of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose [Section 80-IA(2)(ii)].

■ In case of a small scale industrial undertaking it manufactures or produces any article or thing [Proviso to section 80-IA(2)(iii)];

■ In case of units other than a small scale industrial undertaking, it manufactures or produces any article or thing not specified in Eleventh Schedule [Section 80-IA(2)(iii)].

■ It begins the relevant activity anytime during:

- 1-4-1993 to 31-1-1998 in case of a Power Undertaking/State Undertaking [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(b) - the amended clause]; and

- 1-4-1991 to 31-3-1995 in case of other undertaking (This period can be extended by the Central Government by a Notification) [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(a)].

■ It employs requisite number of workers [Section 80-IA (2)(v)].

The conditions and the amendments, may now be examined in the light of the Scheme of section 80-IA.

5.5-2 Analysis of the amendments The amendments lay down certain conditions or attributes of State undertaking or Power undertaking, which will entitle it to a higher deduction.

5.5-2a State undertaking - In respect of a State undertaking it lays down that:

■ It should be located in an industrially backward State specified in the Eighth Schedule; and

■ It begins to manufacture or produce article or thing, or begins to operate a cold storage plant at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

5.5-2b Power undertaking - In respect of a power undertaking, it lays down that:

■ It may be set up in any part of India for the generation or generation and distribution of power; and

■ It commences generation of power at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

The amendments only classify industrial undertakings for:

■ prescribing period during which the relevant activity has to commence; and

■ conferring higher amount of relief to certain undertakings.

The amendments do not lay down qualifying conditions for claiming a deduction under section 80-IA. Thus, any undertaking claiming a deduction under section 80-IA will, in any case, have to comply with the other condition laid down in section 80-IA(2) including clause (iii) thereof.

From the language of the amended clause, in relation to a State undertaking, it would be observed that it omits 'Union Territory', whereas the Eighth Schedule, Finance Minister's speech. Notes on clauses, and Memorandum explaining the Bill refers to 'Union Territories'. This seems to be a slip.

5.5-2c Initial assessment year - The higher deduction is available for initial five assessment years. 'Intitial assessment year' is defined by section 80-IA(12)(c) as follows:

‘initial assessment year’ means the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce articles or things, or to operate its cold storage plant or plants or the ship is first brought into use or the business of the hotel starts functioning".

From the definition it would be noticed that the previous year in which the prescribed activity commences is to be regarded as a starting point and the relevant assessment year relating thereto would be the initial assessment year.

Accordingly, the year in which the prescribed activity begins is relevant and not any other year including the year in which an industrial undertaking is located in a backward State and the year in which the power undertaking is being set up.

5.5-1 Scheme of section 80-IA - A recapitulation - To recapitulate, various provisions/conditions of section 80-IA are as follows: An industrial undertaking is entitled to certain deduction provided it fulfils the following conditions (including the conditions imposed by amendments):

■ It is not 'formed' by:

- splitting up, or reconstruction of a business already in existence [Section 8O-IA(2)(i)]; and

- transfer to a new business of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose [Section 80-IA(2)(ii)].

■ In case of a small scale industrial undertaking it manufactures or produces any article or thing [Proviso to section 80-IA(2)(iii)];

■ In case of units other than a small scale industrial undertaking, it manufactures or produces any article or thing not specified in Eleventh Schedule [Section 80-IA(2)(iii)].

■ It begins the relevant activity anytime during:

- 1-4-1993 to 31-1-1998 in case of a Power Undertaking/State Undertaking [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(b) - the amended clause]; and

- 1-4-1991 to 31-3-1995 in case of other undertaking (This period can be extended by the Central Government by a Notification) [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(a)].

■ It employs requisite number of workers [Section 80-IA (2)(v)].

The conditions and the amendments, may now be examined in the light of the Scheme of section 80-IA.

5.5-2 Analysis of the amendments The amendments lay down certain conditions or attributes of State undertaking or Power undertaking, which will entitle it to a higher deduction.

5.5-2a State undertaking - In respect of a State undertaking it lays down that:

■ It should be located in an industrially backward State specified in the Eighth Schedule; and

■ It begins to manufacture or produce article or thing, or begins to operate a cold storage plant at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

5.5-2b Power undertaking - In respect of a power undertaking, it lays down that:

■ It may be set up in any part of India for the generation or generation and distribution of power; and

■ It commences generation of power at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

The amendments only classify industrial undertakings for:

■ prescribing period during which the relevant activity has to commence; and

■ conferring higher amount of relief to certain undertakings.

The amendments do not lay down qualifying conditions for claiming a deduction under section 80-IA. Thus, any undertaking claiming a deduction under section 80-IA will, in any case, have to comply with the other condition laid down in section 80-IA(2) including clause (iii) thereof.

From the language of the amended clause, in relation to a State undertaking, it would be observed that it omits 'Union Territory', whereas the Eighth Schedule, Finance Minister's speech. Notes on clauses, and Memorandum explaining the Bill refers to 'Union Territories'. This seems to be a slip.

5.5-2c Initial assessment year - The higher deduction is available for initial five assessment years. 'Intitial assessment year' is defined by section 80-IA(12)(c) as follows:

‘initial assessment year’ means the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce articles or things, or to operate its cold storage plant or plants or the ship is first brought into use or the business of the hotel starts functioning".

From the definition it would be noticed that the previous year in which the prescribed activity commences is to be regarded as a starting point and the relevant assessment year relating thereto would be the initial assessment year.

Accordingly, the year in which the prescribed activity begins is relevant and not any other year including the year in which an industrial undertaking is located in a backward State and the year in which the power undertaking is being set up.

5.5-2C1 ISSUES CONNECTED WITH DATE OF COMMENCEMENT OF ACTIVITIES – The larger deduction is available, if the commencement of relevant activity is on or after 1-4-1993. Accordingly:

■ In a case where, the undertaking is set up or is being set up prior to 1-4-1993; but, commences manufacturing or generation or operation on or after 1-4-1993, the higher deduction would be available.

Bagasse - Bagasse is a waste of the sugar factory. This waste is a bio-degradable waste and the same is collected on consideration from the factory. There could be no universal definition of the word 'waste'. The term 'waste' has to be understood contextually, i.e., place where it arises and the manner in which it arises during the processing of some article. To incentivise investment in new plant or machinery, additional depreciation of 20% is allowed under the existing provisions of section 32(1)(iia) of the Act in respect of the cost of plant or machinery acquired and installed by certain assessees. This depreciation allowance is allowed over and above the deduction allowed for general depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) of the Act. In order to incentivise acquisition and installation of plant and machinery for setting up of manufacturing units in the notified backward area in the States of Andhra Pradesh or Bihar or Telangana or West Bengal, a new second proviso has been inserted by the Finance Act, 2015 in section 32(1)(iia) (with effect from 1-4-2016) to allow higher additional depreciation at the rate of 35% (instead of 20%) in respect of the actual cost of new machinery or plant (other than a ship and aircraft) acquired and installed by a manufacturing undertaking or enterprise which is set up in the notified backward area of the State of Andhra Pradesh or Bihar or Telangana of West Bengal on or after the 1st day of April, 2015.

This higher additional depreciation shall be available in respect of acquisition and installation of any new machinery or plant for the purposes of the said undertaking or enterprise during the period beginning on the 1-4-2015 and ending before 1-4-2020. The eligible machinery or plant for this purpose shall not include the machinery or plant which are currently not eligible for additional depreciation as per the existing proviso to section 32(1)(iia) of the Act.

Thus, following conditions need to be satisfied claim additional depreciation u/s 32(1)(iia) in case of specified states :

Investment in new plant and machinery in notified backward area in Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Telangana or West Bengal will qualify for additional depreciation at the rate of 35 per cent (instead of 20 per cent). If, however, the new plant and machinery is put to use for less than 180 days in the year of acquisition, then additional depreciation will be limited to 17.5 per cent of actual cost in that year. The balance of 17.5 per cent will be allowed in the immediately succeeding previous year.

The new plant and machinery should be acquired and installed and installed during the period beginning on 1-4-2015 and ending on 31-3-2020.

The new plant and machinery should be acquired and installed for the purpose of setting-up of an undertaking/enterprise in the above noted backward areas.

The eligible machinery or plant for this purpose shall not include the machinery or plant which is currently not eligible for additional depreciation as per the existing proviso to section 32(1)(iia).

13.3 Scientific Research expenditure [Section 35]

Under section 35(2AB) of the Act, weighted deduction of 200% is allowed to a company engaged in the business of biotechnology or manufacturing of goods (except items specified in Schedule XI) for the expenditure (not being expenditure in the nature of cost of any land or building) incurred on scientific research carried out in an approved in-house research and development facility. For availing this weighted deduction, the company is required to enter into an agreement with the Secretary, Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) and also required to obtain his approval. The Secretary, DSIR is required to send the report regarding approval to DGIT (Exemption) in prescribed Form who generally does not have jurisdiction over the assessee company. Further, the company is required to maintain separate books of account for approved R&D facility and is also required to get the account audited. However, the copy of audit report is required to be submitted to the DSIR only.

The Comptroller and Auditor General of India in its report on performance audit of pharmaceuticals sector recommended for rationalisation of the provision relating to monitoring of this weighted deduction.

In order to have a better and meaningful monitoring mechanism for weighted deduction allowed under section 35(2AB) of the Act, the provisions of section 35(2AB) of the Act have been amended to provide that deduction under the said section shall be allowed if the company enters into an agreement with the prescribed authority for cooperation in such research and development facility and fulfils prescribed conditions with regard to maintenance and audit of accounts and also furnishes prescribed reports.

The Finance Act, 2015 has also inserted reference of the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner in section 35(2AA) and section 35(2AB) of the Act so that the report referred to therein may be sent to the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner having jurisdiction over the company claiming the weighted deduction under the said section.

62 Taxman 480 (SC), it was held that "even though this decision was concerned with the clause dealing with reconstruction of an existing business, the expression "not formed" was construed to mean that the undertaking should not be a continuation of the old but emergence of a new unit. Therefore, even if the undertaking is established by transfer of building, plant or machinery, but it is not formed a result of such transfer, the assessee could not be denied the benefit.".

(i) The assessee may continue to produce the same kind of article as hitherto but that is not a relevant factor at all to consider whether the section is attracted. What is relevant is that the industrial unit set up must be new. In that sense, though new plant and machinery are erected for producing either the same commodities or some distinct commodities, it should not be a case of reconstruction of the old business. The assessee will have to plead and establish that a new unit has come into existence which independently produces articles of whatsoever nature and that this new unit is not dependent upon the old existing unit, in the sense that the new unit cannot be equated as an expansion of the old unit [Canara Wire & Wire Products Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 196 ITR 426 (Kar.)].

(j)

The true test is not whether the new industrial undertaking connotes expansion of the existing business of the assessee, but whether it is all the same a new and identifiable undertaking, separate and distinct from the existing business. The reconstruction of a business or an industrial undertaking must necessarily involve the concept that the original business or undertaking is not to cease functioning, and its identity is not to be lost or abandoned. The concept essentially rests on changes, but the changes must be constructive and not destructive. There must be something positive about the whole matter as opposed to negative. The underlying idea of a reconstruction evidently must be - as is brought out by the section itself - of a 'business already in existence'. There must be a continuation of the activities and business of the same industrial undertaking, which must continue to carry on the same business, though in some altered or varied form. If the alteration and changes are substantial, there would be little scope for describing what emerges as a reconstruction of the business. From the perusal of the section, it is clear that the statute itself has envisaged and approved of a situation in which an old existing, smaller industrial undertaking is absorbed by a new and much bigger industrial undertaking. In the instant case, only capacity had been increased, and there was an expansion of the old business with some modifications. As for the reconstruction of the business, it was nowhere evident that the old industrial unit was split up or damaged or destroyed and was supposedly reconstructed as a new unit by the assessee. What the assessee had done was to set up an industrial undertaking with the latest technology and increased capacity and, of course, with a fairly good amount of fresh investment. The formation of the new undertaking was not as a consequence of the transfer of the plant or machinery of the old business. The value of the plant and machinery utilised in the new undertaking had been less than 20 per cent of the total investment. Thus, the assessee's case also did not get disqualified under this provision. Investment in new plant and machinery was Rs. 104.88 lakhs. Investment in old plant and machinery was Rs. 20.86 lakhs. In that view of the matter, the conclusion was inevitable that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA in respect of the profits of the new industrial undertaking having satisfied the requisite conditions [CIT v. Mahaan Foods Ltd. [2009] 177 Taxman 274 (Delhi)].

9.4-6 New entity does not use old plant and machinery

The co-operative society must not use any machinery or plant previously used for any purpose. However, there are two exceptions.

9.4-6a Exception 1: 20% old machinery or plant - The condition of not using the old machinery or plant shall be deemed to have been complied with if the value of the old plant and machinery does not exceed 20% of the total value of the plant and machinery.

9.4-6b Exception 2: Imported old machinery or plant - Any plant or machinery which was used outside India by any other person shall not be treated as old machinery or plant if the following conditions are satisfied:

(a)

Before the date of installation by the assessee, such machinery or plant was not used in India;

(b)

Such machinery or plant has been imported from any country outside India; and

(c)

No deduction on account of depreciation has been allowed or allowable in respect of such machinery or plant before the date of installation by the assessee.

3.2 Bagasse held non-manufactured by Supreme Court : The Circular aforesaid was challenged successfully in Balrampur Chini Mills Ltd. v. UOI [2013] 30 taxmann.com 175 (Allahabad) and CCE v. DSCL Sugar [2014] 41 taxmann.com 64/43 GST 151 (Allahabad) and also in CCE v. KCP Sugar & Industries Corporation Ltd. - 2015 (321) ELT A223 (A.P.) on ground that even though marketable, Bagasse was non-manufactured product and therefore, not excisable and even payment under rule 6 would not be required. The Department went in appeal before Supreme Court in UOI v. DSCL Sugar Ltd. 2015 (322) E.L.T. 769, wherein it was held as follows :

Facts : Assessee was manufacturing sugarcane and molasses. In the process of manufacture of sugar, sugarcane is crushed, its juice is extracted and Bagasse emerges as residue/waste of sugarcane. Since Bagasse was liable to Nil rate of duty, department argued that it was 'exempted goods' and demanded Cenvat reversal under rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Held :

No manufacture/deemed manufacture : Bagasse is only an agriculture waste and residue and not result of any process; hence, it is not covered in definition of 'manufacture' under section 2(f) of Central Excise Act, 1944. Further, there is no Chapter note or Section note in Central Excise Tariff declaring process in respect of bagasse as amounting to manufacture.

Not excisable, even if deemed to be marketable : Hence, notwithstanding amendment in 2008 in section 2(d) ibid, creating a fiction of deemed marketability, bagasse is not excisable as it is not passing test of 'manufacture'.

Cenvat Rule 6 inapplicable [for period prior to 1-3-2015] : Since bagasse is not excisable, hence, even if NIL-rated, cenvat rule 6 is inapplicable thereto. Therefore, denial of credit on electricity on ground that bagasse is excisable exempted goods, was incorrect.

3.3 Zinc Dross also held to be non-manufactured by Bombay High Court : The Bombay High Court in Hindalco Industries Ltd. v. UOI [2015] 49 GST 429 opined that Aluminium dross and skimmings, etc. not 'manufactured' goods and not liable to duty, even if marketable/bought and sold. The facts and judgment are :

Facts : In course of manufacture of aluminium sheets/coils, aluminium dross/skimmings emerged as byproducts. Department demanded duty thereon arguing that in view of Explanation to section 2(d), said goods were marketable. Assessee argued that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' were not 'manufactured goods' and were not, therefore, liable to duty.

Held : Conditions contemplated under section 2(d) (excisable goods, movability and marketability) and section 2(f) (manufacture) have to be satisfied conjunctively in order to entail imposition of excise duty. Merely because goods satisfy test of being marketed and saleable and merely because goods are listed in tariff, it does not mean that they are 'manufactured goods'. In various judgments, Supreme Court held that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' are not manufactured goods and said view was followed in context of 'zinc dross and flux skimming'. Hence, impugned goods were not manufactured goods and could not, therefore, be charged to excise duty.

In order to set over this controversy in the above definition of ‘input’, the Legislature has clarified that even if an item is not contained in the final product still it would be classifiable as an ‘input’ under the above definition. In other words, it has been clarified by the definition of ‘input’ that the following considerations will not be relevant :

(a)Use of input in the manufacturing process be it direct or indirect; and (b)even if the input is not contained in the ‘final product’ it would still be covered by the definition.

These considerations have been made irrelevant by the use of expression ‘goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ which, as stated above, is the crucial requirement of the definition of ‘input’. In this regard, some case laws are cited hereunder :

In J.K. Cement Works v. CCE 2010 (252) ELT 249 (Trib. - Delhi), it was held that only those goods which form part of the process carried out by a manufacturer for converting raw material into finished goods can be considered as inputs and the goods which are not integrally connected with the process of manufacture resulting in utilization of such product directly or indirectly in the manufacture of finished product cannot be said to be input. Therefore, oxygen, helium and acetylene gases used for repair and maintenance of plant and machinery are not covered by the definition of ‘input’.

In Reva Electric Car Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (250) ELT 149 (Trib. - Bang.), the Tribunal held that it is unambiguously clear that the rejection was at the pre-manufacturing stage and for no reasons attributable to the appellant. Rejection at the pre-manufacturing stage is also indispensable for quality control. It can be said that any rejection of input without ulterior motive or oblique purpose may not disentitle an assessee from the benefit of law relating to CENVAT credit.

It did not appear that the car manufacturer had escaped duty. The revenue should, therefore, allow entitlement of CENVAT credit in the absence of any violation of law. Accordingly, the demand of Rs. 6,90,150 on the count of using of inputs for R&D was unsustainable in the absence of any finding to show that the R&D had not resulted in finished goods and that finished goods had escaped duty. Exercise of Research having resulted in the finished goods and that had suffered duty, CENVAT credit was admissible for which demand of Rs. 6,90,150 was set aside.

In HIM Technoforge Ltd.’s case (supra), the respondent was a manufacturer of rough forgings and forging articles of steel falling under Chapter 7326 of the CETA, 1985. They also availed CENVAT credit of inputs and capital goods. The dispute related to ‘metal band saw blades’ and ‘steel shots’ as to whether they could be considered as capital goods as contended by the department or could be treated as inputs as claimed by the respondent. The original authority after taking note of the duration of use of these items and the purpose for which they were used held that they were capital goods.

The Commissioner (Appeals) treated the above products as ‘inputs’. He held that under the CENVAT Credit Rules, the term ‘input’ has been defined to mean all goods, except HSD oil, LSD and motor spirit used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. In view of this above definition of the ‘input’ under the CENVAT Credit Rules, both the items, namely, ‘metal saw blade’ and ‘steel shots’ used by the appellants in connection with the production of goods on consumable would merit classification under inputs only and, therefore, the credit taken by them was in order.

The Tribunal held that if the role and period of usage as recorded by the original authority was taken into account, the decision of Commissioner (Appeals) had clearly held that the same were in the nature of consumables used in relation to manufacture of final products and, therefore, appropriately to be treated as inputs.

4.2 Waste and Scrap - In Tera Cables India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (258) ELT 111 (Trib. - Ahd.), a small amount of Rs. 9,456 stood denied to the appellant on the ground that the credit had been availed on the waste and scrap, which could not be considered as an input for the appellant’s final product. The lower authorities had nowhere discussed as to how the waste and scrap could not be considered as an input. The cable waste of cut length was being utilized and consumed by the appellant in its own factory in the manufacture of finished goods. The duty paid cable waste received in the factory had been accounted for in the input register and its consumption had been shown in the manufacture of the final product. The final product manufactured out of the same was accounted for in the RG-1 Part I Register, which stood cleared on payment of duty. As such to deny the benefit of waste and scrap on the ground that the same was not an input was not justified.

1. Our company took wrong cenvat credit of Rs. 100 in the month of Oct. 13 which was reversed in the month of Dec. 13. Actual Cenvat credit for the month of Dec. 13 was Rs. 150. But due to reversal of earlier wrong entry, credit was reduced to Rs. 50. Company, while filing of Service Tax Return, has shown Rs. 50 as their Cenvat credit. Now during EA 2000 Service tax Audit, department is saying that company should have claimed entire input of Rs. 150 in December 13 and should have shown Rs. 100 in other column and now department is asking us to pay Rs. 100 again and are saying that you cannot claim that Rs. 100 in current month as credit because one year has been elapsed. 3. Hurdle in expansion

Where a company buys land with an intention to earn rental income from it or to earn profit by dividing it into smaller plots, the company can be said to have been engaged in the rental business or sale of land. Where a co., after commencing the manufacturing operations, begins such activities, the option of Section 115BAB shall be withdrawn for that assessment year and for all subsequent assessment years. Where company earns huge profit from incidental activities (like, sale of scrap, interest income, etc.) it can continue to remain in new tax regime, but earning minimal profits from non-manufacturing business will render it ineligible for the new regime. The incidental income will be taxable on gross basis at the rate of 22% without claiming any deduction for any allowance or expense. According to the Export and Import Policy/Foreign Trade Policy, a Special Economic Zone is considered principally as a foreign territory when it comes to trade, duties & tariffs. The goods supplied thereto from a Domestic Tariff Area are treated as deemed exports and goods brought to a Domestic Tariff Area from there are treated as deemed imports in such a context. When materials are imported and used for the manufacture of goods that are manufactured in India and exported, a rebate called as drawback can be claimed on them. However, the difference between the 'import' and a 'deemed import' when it comes to claiming duty drawback on goods being sold by an SEZ unit to a DTA for input in export manufacture remains a question that has not been pondered upon. This article tries to understand if such a sale by SEZ is, in fact, a 'deemed import' and if duty drawback can be claimed on it by looking at the law and case citations.

Introduction

1. The Export and Import (EXIM) Policy introduced a new export promotion scheme called Special Economic Zone (SEZ) that came into force from April 1, 2000. It aimed at boosting foreign investments and expedited an internationally competitive and a hassle free atmosphere for exports. SEZ units in India operated from November 1, 2000 to February 9, 2006 under the provisions of the EXIM policy/Foreign Trade Policy and fiscal incentives were provided through the provisions of significant statutes. Five years later, the Special Economic Zone Act, 2005 was also introduced and in 2006 the Special Economic Zone Rules, 2006 were formulated through which various direct and indirect tax concessions had been granted for authorized operations to the SEZ units. The most significant feature of this scheme is that the SEZ area is considered essentially as a deemed foreign territory (within India) for the purposes of trade operations, duties & tariffs. Therefore, goods supplied to SEZ from the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) are treated as deemed exports and goods brought from SEZ to DTA are treated as deemed imports in this context. The SEZ areas have fiscal and economic laws that are additionally generous as compared to the business undertakings in the DTAs. Confusion often arises as to the scope of the exemptions. One of them is regarding applicability of drawback on goods sold by SEZ to DTA for the purpose of inputs for manufacture of export goods.

Why the confusion?

2. A drawback is a rebate of duty chargeable on any imported materials or excisable materials used in manufacture or processing of goods that are manufactured in India and exported. This scheme of drawback had been introduced by the Ministry of Finance to ensure that the exported products are revenue neutral. The Central Government is empowered to grant duty drawback under sections 74 and 75 of the Customs Act, 1962. Under section 74 of the Customs Act, duty drawback to the extent of 98 per cent of the duty paid on imported goods can be claimed for re-export, provided the goods are re-exported within 2 years of payment of import duty. Under Section 75 of the Customs Act, duty drawback is provided on imported raw materials and inputs that have gone in production of goods for exports. Section 75 presents a heavy relief to such manufacturers-exporters. In State of U.P. v. Delhi Cloth Mills1 the Supreme Court defined a drawback as: "Drawback means the repayment of duties or taxes previously charged on commodities from which they are relieved on exportation. For example, in the customs laws of some countries an allowance is made by the Government upon the duties due on imported merchandise when the importer, instead of selling it within the country, re-exports it, and then the difference of duty is refunded, if already paid."

(Per Lord Hoffman) 1.5 Contradiction between AS-2 and AS-6/AS-26, if any - The prescribed accountancy treatment of including depreciation on assets used in production in the cost of closing stock came up for judicial scrutiny. The revenue’s objection was that this prescribed treatment conflicts with the principle "the depreciable amount of a tangible fixed asset must be allocated on a systematic basis over its [i.e., the asset’s] useful economic life" (see AS-6 and AS-26) inasmuch as it has the effect of "depreciating the asset over a longer period than this - effectively a period ending only when the trading stock whose value is debited with part of the depreciation charge is finally sold or written down.". The cost of fixed assets used in production is, thus, charged as an expense over the period during which they are generating revenue (i.e., over the period during which the stock produced by the assets is sold), rather than over the period during which their value is written off in the balance sheet. One consequence is a deferral of the point at which such depreciation is charged as an expense in the profit and loss account (assuming that not all the stock produced in a given year is sold in the same year). The deferral is for a particularly long period in the Scotch whisky industry, because stocks are held for many years as they mature. Stock which remains unsold at the end of the accounting period forms part of the company’s current assets; and the figure at which the stock is stated in the balance sheet is normally its cost, including the depreciation forming part of that cost. Depreciation on production assets is, therefore, said, in accountancy parlance, to be ‘carried to stock’; and it normally remains in the balance sheet, under the heading of ‘current assets’, unless and until the stock in question is sold, at which point the depreciation is charged as an expense in the profit and loss account under the heading of ‘cost of sales’.

The House unanimously upheld the validity of the prescribed accountancy treatment of including depreciation on assets used in production in the cost of closing stock notwithstanding the result, i.e., depreciation gets charged off to the profit and loss account over a period longer than the asset’s useful life. The House held that this does not militate against the true and fair view of the profit and loss account. Lord Hope of Craighed held that "When depreciation is to be taken into account to show a true and fair view of the profit or loss for each financial year is in the end a question of timing. If, in order to show a true and fair view according to currently accepted accounting principles, part of the depreciation has in fact been carried forward, that must be treated as fact..." Lord Hoffman pointed out that the requirement to carry forward a part of depreciation on assets used in production as part of closing stock is an exception to the general rule that" depreciable amount of a tangible fixed asset must be allocated on a systematic basis over its [i.e., the asset’s] useful economic life". He observed that "Obviously any reduction in balance sheet value for depreciation must at some time be reflected in a profit and loss account deduction, but there is nothing to say that they must coincide".

SPECIAL SCENARIOS TO WATCH

Inter-Unit Transfers Allowed- Goods can be transferred from one MOOWR unit to another.

Scrap/waste disposal in the domestic market attracts duty; it's waived if exported.

Goods received from SEZs or FTWZs are treated as imports and must follow bonding formalities. Inputs received free of cost must be declared at nominal value and properly recorded.

Goods returning from testing or repairs should be handled as fresh imports or DTA inputs.

CHALLENGES AND FUTURE UNCERTAINTY

While MOOWR is a beneficial scheme, these challenges are hindering its performance.

Complex compliance: Filing multiple BOEs for each DTA sale is time-consuming and complex.

No depreciation is allowed when capital goods are sold in the domestic market—duty is on full import value.

No RODTEP or Drawback: MOOWR-based exports are less competitive given they are not eligible for RODTEP scrips or Drawback. Typically benefits RODTEP and Drawback would be in the range of 4-5% of the value of exported good, which is significant for a lot of exporters.

New concern: The Finance Act 2024 empowered the Government of India to exclude certain goods or operations from the applicability of MOOWR scheme. This adds unpredictability, making long-term planning difficult for businesses relying on this scheme and creating an unease in doing business.

Takeaways

If you are importing raw materials or machinery regularly, consider obtaining a MOOWR license.

Be prepared for higher compliance costs.

Evaluate if loss of RODTEP/Drawback is offset by duty deferment benefits.

MOOWR is one of the most flexible and cash-flow-friendly customs schemes available in India. It's ideal for businesses that import raw material or machinery and sell their finished goods either in domestic market or export market.

Small and Mid-sized manufacturers initially hesitate to register under MOOWR because of compliance worries. But once they set up the systems, the cash flow benefits are too significant to ignore.

CENTRAL EXCISE - TREATMENT OF WASTE

1. We have two factories registered under central excise with the following details —

1st Factory - Manufacturer of fine chemicals falling under Chapter 34

2nd Factory - Declared as job worker (a bottling plant) of first factory.

We sent 100 Kgs. of chemicals to be packed in 100 gms. bottles to bottling plant. After completion of packing in small packs we received only 90 Kgs. chemicals packed in small container. What would be the treatment of non-collectible waste of 10% (10 Kgs. out of every lot of 100 kgs.) ?

It is clearly stated by you that both the factories are registered separately. In this case the manufacturing factory is clearing 100 Kgs. to job-worker and receiving back the same in entirety (subject to processing loss). The process loss of 10% will not be chargeable to duty, only if the same is normal process loss.

The benefit may be claimed under rule 21 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, as —

the same is due to natural causes or unavoidable reasons, and

is incurred prior to removal of finished goods from the factory.

An alternative view may be that only 90 Kg. is the manufactured product, because manufacture under section 2(f) is complete only after the completion of all incidental or ancillary processes, which include packing/bottling.

In any case, the duty can be levied only on 90 Kgs.

CENTRAL EXCISE - WHETHER IN CASE OF EXPORT UNDER CLAIM OF REBATE, EXCISE DUTY MAY BE PAID THROUGH CENVAT CREDIT

2. We are exporters of a final product. Export is made under claim of rebate. Please clarify whether we can set-off/adjust excise duty payable under the option of "Export under claim of Rebate" through Cenvat credit or not ? Whether rebate would be allowed even in that case ?

As per rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, credit is allowed of duty or tax paid on inputs or input services or capital goods used in factory/manufacture purposes.

The said credit may be used to pay duty on final product. Goods exported under claim of rebate are cleared on payment of duty and said duty can very well be paid by using Cenvat credit as per rule 3(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In fact, Form ARE-1 itself in Part A provides for certification as follows —

Certified that 1. duty has been paid by debit entry in the Personal Ledger Account No. .........and/or CENVAT Account Entry No. .……or recorded as payable in Daily Stock Account, on the goods described overleaf.

(Emphasis Supplied)

Therefore, for purpose of export under claim of rebate, duty may be paid using balance in Cenvat Credit Account.

CENVAT CREDIT - ROTARY MILL AND WOODEN BALL - CAPITAL GOODS V. INPUT

3. We are availing of credit of duty paid on Rotary Mill and Wooden Ball falling under Tariff Items 44219050 and 44219050, respectively, and use it for grinding Propellant Powder as input. The said goods are machinery and are being capitalized in our financial accounts and depreciation is being claimed. Whether Cenvat credit availed by us is in order ?

The query has been replied in two parts —

Part - I : Input v. Capital Goods

Taking classification put forth by you to be correct, since the goods are classifiable under Chapter 44, they are not listed in any of the categories of capital goods as provided in rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. However, if —

they are purchased as 'components or spares or accessories' of some other machinery ; and

such other machinery is a capital goods under rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004,

then the said mill/ball would be classifiable as capital goods under rule 2(a)(A)(iii) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In any other event the same would be eligible for credit as an 'input', as the same is presumably used within the factory.

Part - II : Relevant treatment under Financial Accounts

The classification and treatment under financial accounts is not relevant for the purpose of deciding eligibility to Cenvat credit.

In other words, even if the said goods are inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, they may be 'fixed assets' under the accounting standards issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and would, accordingly, be eligible for depreciation.

The two things must be viewed separately.

Withdraw amendment denying depreciation on goodwill; or the amendment may be made prospective, and grandfathering be allowed for pre-existing goodwill The Government in the Finance Act 2021 made a far-reaching amendment of denying depreciation on goodwill. Though the amendment is slated to be effective prospectively, in substance it has the effect of denying depreciation on past transactions. Such retrospective amendments create hardship for taxpayers, and also impact the investment climate.

Also, denial of depreciation on purchased goodwill arising in non-tax neutral transactions (such as where the seller has paid appropriate tax on a slump sale or simpliciter sale of goodwill) is against the principle of tax neutrality.

Therefore, it is recommended that the amendment be withdrawn, or that specific kinds of goodwill (arising on a slump sale/simpliciter purchase) be allowed to be amortized over 4-5 years. Alternatively, the amendment may be made prospective, and pre-existing goodwill in the block of assets as on 1 April 2020 can be grandfathered.

4. Limitation of Interest Benefit – Section 94B

Section 94B provides a capping of 30% of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization ("EBITDA") on the interest deduction that can be claimed by an entity in respect of funds borrowed from non-resident associated enterprises ("AE").

(a)

In terms of sub-section (2) of section 94B, 'excess interest' is defined to mean an amount of total interest paid or payable in excess of 30% of EBITDA of the borrower, or interest paid or payable to AE for that previous year, whichever is less. Since the expression used in sub-section (2) is 'total interest', a question arises as to whether it would include only foreign interest, or both foreign and domestic interest, paid by the entity. If domestic interest is also to be included, then, it would result in a higher disallowance of foreign interest compared to the normal scenario where there is no domestic borrowing. Hence, it is recommended to clarify that interest may be restricted only to foreign AE interest and not total interest.

(b)

In the event of borrowing by an infrastructure company from outside India, it often happens that foreign lenders insist on a joint guarantee by a parent company and SPV for the project. In this regard, the current reading of section 94B provides that debt issued by a non-resident lender (being non-AE) to a resident subsidiary under the guarantee of a resident parent (being an AE) would be covered under the provision. Hence, limit on interest deduction leads to additional disallowance in the hands of subsidiary, even when the transaction is entered into with non-AE, thereby discouraging funding to such sectors from outside India, which does not appear to be in line with government's policy of attracting foreign funds for key debt-intensive sectors. Hence, it is recommended that the restriction be applicable only in the case of borrowing from AEs.

(c)

Furthermore, the infrastructure sector generally warrants high capital requirement, especially in the initial years. Hence, it is recommended that considering the sector-specific requirement, a higher limit (i.e. a higher percentage of EBITDA) ought to apply in case of infrastructure companies, at least in the first 8-10 years.

5. Allow deduction for CSR expenditure in the nature of Covid-19 relief expenditure

(a)

Presently, CSR expenditure is not allowed as business expenditure and there is a lack of clarity with respect to the deductibility of expenditure on employee welfare. Therefore, it is recommended that such expenditure incurred towards COVID-19 relief, whether it is made in cash or in kind, or whether it is capital or revenue in nature, may be allowed as deductible expenditure while computing total income.

(b)

Recently, it was clarified that donations made to the PM CARES Fund will be allowed as deductions under section 80G of the Act. However, companies opting for the new regime of concessional tax rate will not be entitled to avail such deduction under section 80G of the Act. Therefore, it is recommended that the deduction may be extended to such companies opting for the concessional tax rate.

(c)

Section 11 of the Act may be amended to provide that the amount spent towards COVID-19 relief shall be considered as application of income for computing exemption under section 11 of the Act.

6. Increase wage limit for new employee deduction under section 80JJAA

Under section 80JJAA, deduction is available for additional employees whose monthly salary is up to INR 25,000. The definition of employee also includes managerial and administrative persons. Accordingly, for managerial persons the limit of INR 25,000 is not in line with the industry standards and is considered quite low.

Therefore, it is recommended that the aforesaid wage limit of INR 25,000 may be revised upward to align it with the current pay structure of the industry, which will in turn facilitate enterprises in claiming the benefit of weighted deductions.

Background

1. In industries like pharmaceuticals and agro-chemicals many times near-about expired goods, defective goods or damaged goods (for the sake of convenience let us say "defective goods") are sent again by various marketing depots (not registered under excise) for reprocessing. Usually it happens that the original goods have been manufactured by let us say factory A, B and C but the defective goods are returned to only one factory, let us say factory D for reprocessing. This is so because it will be impractical to send the defective goods for reprocessing to the very same factory which had manufactured the original goods due to logistical costs as well as difficulties in identifying them on one-to-one basis.

In such scenario, only document available will be copy of excise invoice issued by the original factory. Had the defective goods been returned to the same factory, manufacturer could have easily claimed CENVAT credit on the basis of originally issued invoice (as the excise invoice was issued by the same factory). However, here the case is different. Factory D wants to claim CENVAT credit of returned defective goods on the basis of excise invoice issued by other factories.

Critical Issues

2. Following critical issues arise in this set-up:

2.1 Whether CENVAT credit can be claimed by factory D when the invoices on the basis of which credit will be claimed has been issued by factory A, B and C ?

2.2 W.e.f. 11-07-2014, third proviso has been added to rule 4(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which provides that credit cannot be claimed after a period of six months from the date of issuance of any document (in our case excise invoice) on the basis of which credit is claimed. In our case, as we are dealing with near-expired or defective goods, in all likelihood excise invoice issued by original manufacturer would have been dated beyond statutory period of six months. Issue is whether the third proviso will apply to the present case ?

2.3 What are the procedures one needs to follow to claim the said credit ?

3. Legal Analysis

3.1 To answer the first question, i.e., whether factory D can avail CENVAT credit on the basis of invoices issued by factory A, B and C for defective goods which are received back, one has to refer to rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. Relevant extract is reproduced below for ready reference:

"Rule 16. Credit of duty on goods brought to the factory.—(1) Where any goods on which duty had been paid at the time of removal thereof are brought to any factory for being re-made, refined, re-conditioned or for any other reason, the assessee shall state the particulars of such receipt in his records and shall be entitled to take CENVAT credit of the duty paid as if such goods are received as inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and utilize this credit according to the said rules.

(2) If the process to which the goods are subjected before being removed does not amount to manufacture, the manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the CENVAT credit taken under sub-rule (1) and in any other case the manufacturer shall pay duty on goods received under sub-rule (1) at the rate applicable on the date of removal and on the value determined under sub-section (2) of section 3 or section 4 or section 4A of the Act, as the case may be.

[Explanation.—The amount paid under this sub-rule shall be allowed as CENVAT credit as if it was a duty paid by the manufacturer who removes the goods.]

3.2 Careful reading of above rule provides that CENVAT credit will be available of any goods on which duty has been paid and are brought to any factory for re-making, refining, re-conditioning or for any other reason as inputs. Thus, only condition to be fulfilled for claiming credit is that duty should have been paid on said goods. It is not necessary that goods should be received back in the same factory. It can be received in any factory. Further, goods can be brought back for reprocessing under rule 16 even if shelf life has expired (CCE v. Rako Agrochem (P.) Ltd. 2010 (260) ELT 479 (Trib. - Delhi)). Thus, credit can be claimed of goods received by factory D on the basis of invoices issued by original manufacturers. One may also refer to Board's Circular 607/44/2001-CX, dated 13-12-2001 which confirms the above view. Thus, CENVAT credit can be claimed on basis of manufacturers invoice available with depot to the extent of quantity received by factory D.

Procedural amendment is retrospective - Procedural amendments generally have retrospective effect unless such (retrospective) construction is textually impossible - Jose Da Costa v. Bascora Sadashiva Sinai Narcornin AIR 1975 SC 1843. Procedural amendment to a law, in absence of anything to contrary, operates retrospectively in the limited sense that they apply to all actions after the date they come into force even though the claim on which the action is based may be of an anterior date. - Memon Abdul Karim HajiTejab v. Dy. Custodian General AIR 1964 SC 1256 as also in National Woollen Mills v. CCE 1991 (56) ELT 613 (Trib.). - similar views in NarhariShivram Shet Narvekar v. PannalalUmmediram AIR 1977 SC 164.

Substantive laws are generally not retrospective unless specified contrary by legislature. Procedural laws may be retrospective unless shown to the contrary – Rochiram & Sons v. Union of India 2008 (226) ELT 20 (SC).

In Shyam Sunder v. Ram Kumar AIR 2001 SC 2472, it was held that amending Act which affects the procedure is presumed to be retrospective unless amending Act provides otherwise – same view in Mandvi Coop Bank v. Nimesh B Thakore [2010] 98 SCL 139 (SC), SEBI v. Ajay Agarwal [2010] 98 SCL 424 (SC).

A beneficial provision should be given retrospective effect - In Bhavnagar University v. Palitana Sugar Mills (P.) Ltd. AIR 2003 SC 511, it was observed, 'It is well-settled that a beneficial provision of legislation must be liberally construed so as to fulfil the statutory purpose and not to frustrate it' – same view in Edukanti Kistamma v. S Venkatareddy [2010] 1 SCC 756.

Statute granting benefit can be retrospective – Statute conferring benefit can be held retrospective, by giving a purposive construction - CIT v. Vatika Township (P.) Ltd. [2014] 227 Taxman 121/ 49 taxmann.com 249 (SC).

What is likely impact of this amendment?

Answer – This will affect waste and scrap not mentioned in tariff. It will also affect waste and scrap mentioned in tariff but on which excise duty was not paid as it was held that the activity is not 'manufacture'. Now, on such goods, either 6% 'amount' will be payable or proportionate reversal of Cenvat credit will have to be made.

The amendment will also affect sale of generated electricity. In case of electricity sold outside, rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules shall be applicable.

Rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 covers all such supplies which are qualifying as deemed exports and also entitled to avail of the benefit of ab initio exemption, viz., supply to an EOU, supply to an ICB, etc., which are also covered by Para 7.05 of FTP, except supplies against an Advance Authorization. Therefore, effectively a domestic supplier supplying goods against an Advance Authorization would be liable to reverse the CENVAT credit in accordance with the rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, with respect to inputs and input services consumed commonly in the manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods which was/is never the intention of the Legislature. Further, said intention can also be evidenced from the provisions of rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and, hence, the corresponding rule has not been taken to logical conclusion by the Legislature.

Having said above, now the supplier is left with no economically viable option but to avail of the benefit of "Deemed Export Drawback" and avail of the refund of duties suffered on the input and input services used in relation to manufacture of goods supplied against Advance Authorization. Further, the process of deemed export drawback is complicated inasmuch as the supplier has to produce all the duty paying documents to the satisfaction of DGFT for fixation of Brand Rate of duty drawback.

Alternatively, an assessee may prefer to avail of the benefit of "Advance Intermediate Authorization" for procuring inputs without payment of duty. However, in such situation, it will have to carry out double compliance in the form of "Deemed Export Drawback" in respect of the service tax paid on the input services which are used in manufacture of goods supplied against Advance Authorization and also the compliance for obtaining and closure of "Advance Intermediate Authorization".

Therefore, effectively on account of lack of clarity in policies between the two Ministries of the Central Government, a manufacturer in India would have to unnecessarily carry out either double compliances or incur excessive cost to avail of the refund of duties, which could have been easily granted exemption from reversal under rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Further, such escalated cost and tiresome compliance would also effect the interest and efficiency of the business and pose a direct contradiction to the very intention of the Central Governments programme of 'Make in India' or 'Ease of Doing Business'.

Conclusion

4. In order to promote the "Make in India" initiative a uniform, unambiguous, stable and effective policy framework has to be established which will reduce the unwarranted cost of business in relation to compliances and ensure seamless benefit to the assessee as outlined in the respective policy. Eventually, making the manufacturing in India a profitable venture.

In the present case, considering the issue faced by the industry at large in respect of supplies against an Advance Authorization discussed hereinabove, it is expected that an appropriate amendment to rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 should be carried out to incorporate another sub-clause to cover supply against an Advance Authorization which would simplify the process for the domestic manufacturer. Alternatively, supply against an Advance Authorization shall be allowed to avail of the benefit of Terminal Excise Duty under the erstwhile FTP, 2009-14.

3.0 FAQ's

3.1 Whether amendment to rule 3(5B) of the CCR, 2004 has a retrospective impact? - Rule 3(5B) of the CCR, 2004 as amended vide Notification No. 3/2011 C.E. (N.T.) with effect from 1 March, 2011 provides for reversal of the CENVAT credit even when inputs are partially written off or provision for partial write-off is made.

Since the amendment has come into effect only with effect from 1 March, 2011, partial write-off and provision for partial write-off of inputs prior to such date would not attract reversal of credit under rule 3(5B) of the CCR, 2004.

3.2 Whether semi-finished and finished goods are covered? - Inputs and capital goods have been defined under rule 2(k) and rule 2(a) respectively, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. With respect to applicability of rule 3(5B) to WIP/FG, clarification has been issued by the CBEC vide Circular No. 907/27/2009-CX. As per the circular, if the goods have been manufactured a manufacturer is liable to pay excise duty, unless duty is remitted under rule 21. Therefore, if the value of finished goods is written off, the manufacturer would be liable to pay excise duty or he would be required to reverse the credit on the inputs used, if duty has been remitted on finished goods.

As regards writing off work-in-progress (WIP), it is stated that if the WIP has reached the stage, when it can be considered as manufactured goods, in that case, the same treatment as is applicable to finished goods will be applicable. However, if the activity carried out on the WIP goods cannot be considered as amounting to manufacture, the said goods should be considered as inputs and the treatment for reversal of credit applicable to inputs would be applicable.

Rule 3(5) of the CCR, 2004 provides that if the inputs or capital goods on which CEVNAT credit is taken are removed as such, the CENVAT credit so taken has to be reversed.

Alternatively, where inputs are used in the manufacturing process and are removed as manufactured scrap, the company shall pay applicable excise duty and CENVAT shall not be reversed.

3.3 Whether write down of Inventory as per AS-2 attracts rule 3(5B)? - Write down in common business parlance represents restating the value with a lower amount, while write off generally results in permanent 'de-recognizing' or bringing down to Zero or negligible amount with no intention of writing back; unless situation otherwise warrants, write down is temporary reduction in value. On the other hand, in the case of provision, it is shown as a deduction from gross amount in the books of account. While rule 3(5B) covers write off provision, write down is not covered within the scope.

Backdrop

The economic slow-down, the rise in unemployment, fall in production and the general pessimism creeping in the country called for some substantial steps to be taken. The corporate tax rates in some of the neighboring and other relevant jurisdictions also necessitated a review of tax rates in India so that the arbitrages could be evened out and India emerges as a competitive regime for undertaking business activities, specially manufacturing.

In order to put more money in the hands of the private sector which would in turn translate into fresh investment and economic activity, as well as offer India as an attractive destination for making it a manufacturing hub thereby increasing employment and consumption, the Government has taken a bold step in substantially reducing the tax rates for companies.

Reduction in Tax Rates!

On September 20, 2019, the Union Finance Minister in a press conference announced that tax rates w.e.f. April 1, 2019, subject to certain conditions, for:

-

all existing and new companies, incorporated in India, shall be slashed to 22%^- Effective rate 25.168%; and

-

new manufacturing companies incorporated in India, on or after October 1, 2019 and commencing production on or before March 31, 2023, shall be 15%^.- Effective rate 17.16%

Companies opting to be governed in the above regime are not liable to pay Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT).

For existing corporates and other corporates not opting for the aforesaid regime, the MAT rate has been slashed from existing 18.5%^ to 15%^.- Effective MAT rate 16.692/ 17.472% depending on whether the quantum of book profits is upto INR 100 million or higher.

Conditions for applying the regime with reduced tax rates

I.

Following deductions cannot be claimed:

Deduction under section 10AA – available to a SEZ unit in respect of exports;

Additional Depreciation under clause (iia) of sub-section (1) of section 32 i.e. additional depreciation of 20%/35% on new plant and machinery;

Investment allowance of 15% of cost for undertakings/enterprises for manufacture or production of any article or thing, on or after the April 1, 2015 in any notified backward area under section 32AD;

Deduction under section 33AB in respect of deposits in special/ deposit account by entities growing and manufacturing tea, rubber, coffee;

Deduction for sums paid to approved research organizations/ companies, etc. (100%-150%) under section 35 – Incurring of research expenditure on its own (revenue or capital) can still be claimed as a deduction in accordance with the said section;

Deduction of capital expenditure for specified businesses under section 35AD;

II.

Any loss carried forward from earlier years which is attributable to deductions referred to in I above will not be allowed to be set-off and the same would be deemed to have been give full effect and no further deduction of such losses would be allowed in any subsequent year.

III.

Depreciation other than additional depreciation referred to in I above, would be allowed in the manner prescribed.

IV.

The reduced tax rate shall be applicable, only if opted in return filed for period ending on or after March 31, 2020 and shall be applicable from the year in which it is so opted. The companies opting for above option are not liable to pay minimum alternative tax (MAT).

Once the option is exercised, it cannot be withdrawn. Companies can evaluate and choose to opt for the new regime after they have exhausted the deductions, benefits under the existing regime.

Companies with high capex/expansion in past years and having huge carried forward losses on account of accelerated depreciation, which would lapse if they opt for the concessional tax regime, should also undertake a cost benefit analysis of which regime to follow and at what time.

Similarly, companies that have availed tax holidays/ incentives in the past and are having carried forward losses on this account should also undertake a cost benefit analysis of which regime to follow. While the industry is analysing the benefits of the beneficial tax regime, the new law also requires some clarifications and ambiguities, which require immediate attention and clarity:

1.

Method of computation of depreciation: Concessional tax regimes provide that depreciation (other than accelerated depreciation) should be computed in the manner as may be prescribed. The Government is yet to prescribe this method of computation of depreciation and it would be interesting to see if it prescribes anything new in this regard.

2.

Disallowance of past-accelerated depreciation: Indian tax law allows accelerated depreciation on plant and machinery. When this accelerated depreciation is allowed, the written down value of the relevant block of such plant and machinery is also correspondingly reduced. In the concessional tax regime, the unabsorbed accelerated depreciation of the past years is disallowed. However, there is no corresponding amendment to provide that the written down value of the relevant block of plant and machinery should be increased by the above disallowance. In the absence of the above, taxpayers will be denied from claiming full depreciation on the acquisition cost of the plant and machinery they purchase.

The option to avail concessional rate of tax as per the aforesaid sections is available from FY 2019-20 onwards and should be exercised before the due date of filing tax return of the year from which such option is exercised. A company not opting for the beneficial provisions due to its existing tax exemptions/deductions, can avail the option for beneficial provisions in the future; however, such option once exercised cannot be revoked in subsequent years. The take-it-or-leave-it nature of the above sections provide flexibility for any company to understand, analyse and then choose to exercise the option to adopt such beneficial provisions. The beneficial provisions provide a further tax rate reduction of approximately 4 percent for those companies having turnover below INR400 crores for specified years and currently paying tax at 29.12 percent.

Key considerations before opting for beneficial rate of taxation:

In view of the irrevocable nature of beneficial sections, it becomes important that a company before opting for such beneficial sections, undertakes a detailed cost-benefit analysis while considering various factors which include the following:

1.

Brought forward of losses attributable to exemption/deduction provisions: Such losses shall not be allowed to be set-off if the company opts for the beneficial sections. Hence, the company should factor in the impact of such brought forward losses.

2.

It is to be noted that brought forward losses not attributable to the specified deduction/exemption denied would be allowed to be set-off in the future.

3.

Unutilised MAT credit/s 115JAA: At present, in the absence of any corresponding amendment to section 115JAA regarding the MAT credit, it is not clear that a company which opts for the beneficial sections, would get the credit of unutilised MAT or not. This requires further clarifications and alternate views in this regard cannot be ruled out.

4.

Alternative incentives/exemptions currently available under other sections: A company fulfilling certain conditions can avail benefits under section 10AA, 80-IAC, 80-IBA, 80PA etc. The benefits devolved under these sections range as high as exempting entire profits from tax for a certain number of years. Such continuing/possible benefits should be factored in the decision-making.

5.

Also important to note that exemption available under section 10 for example 10(2A), 10(38), 10(34) can be claimed by the company availing the benefit of sections 115BAA/115BAB.

6.

Similarly restriction under chapter VI-A is applicable only to sections covered under "C –deduction in respect of certain income" (Section 80HH to section 80RRB (except section 80JJA with respect to employment of new employees)

7.

Exemptions associated with Research & Development (R&D) and/or sums paid to specified entities for research: Companies incurring or planning to incur such expenditure would want to weigh in the benefits under section 35(1)(ii) or (iia) or (iii) or section 35(2AA) or section 35(2AB), before considering to opt for beneficial sections.

8.

The above restriction is with respect to accelerated deduction under specific sections. In other words there is no bar in claiming such expenditure which is otherwise allowable, under any other section of the Act.

9.

Proposed expansion of the company: Many companies operate in an industry that require heavy investment in assets like plant and machinery. Here, it is important to analyse the beneficial provisions relating to additional depreciation and investment allowance embedded in the current tax regime before opting for beneficial sections. Further, a company having any plans of setting up a new manufacturing unit altogether, should consider the possibility of opting for section 115BAB.

10.

It is important to note that there is no bar in opting out for beneficial sections in subsequent years once the exemptions/deductions/loss is exhausted.

11.

Commencement of production before 31 March 2023 - A one-time window?: Generally manufacturing companies experience a time lag of 1-3 years from the date of incorporation to the date of commencement of manufacturing. Considering this, businesses looking forward to set up a new manufacturing company should take a timely call on whether to avail the beneficial section 115BAB for which manufacturing is required to commence by 31 March 2023. However, we have seen governments extending the duration of such sunset clauses in public interest.

Conclusion

The government has provided the option to companies to opt for newly inserted sections. However, one need to be very careful while making cost benefit analysis on the basis of factors discussed above It may happen that postponement of decision to opt for these newly inserted section for one year, may not cost as much as the wrong decision of opting for the same, since it is reversible in nature.

Such a bold step to slash the tax rates is likely to provide a boost in the cash flows and the eventual earning per share of many companies. It may also increase inbound investment into India, resulting in a favourable balance of payments situation or may also result in postponement/cancel of outbound investment.

However, while the amendments are aimed to provide a boost to the ambitious Make-in-India initiative, the government has estimated INR 1,45,000 crore as the total revenue foregone in tax and other reliefs.

1965, only sales made in nature of any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure or any sales in connection with or ancillary to such trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure were taxable. Thus, intention of doing the business measured by volume, frequency, continuity or regularity as well as profit motive was essential to tax a sale transaction. Any sale of goods done without intention of doing a business in those goods or without profit motive was not taxable. In this context Apex Court in the case of State of Gujarat v. Raipur Manufacturing Co. Ltd. [1967] 19 STC 1 had taken a view that to bring ancillary sales under tax net it must be shown by the revenue that they were made with an intention to do business and earn profit. It relied on its own decision in the case of State Of Andhra Pradesh v. Abdul Bakhi and Bros AIR 1965 SC 531. It was held that when a person in the course of carrying on a business is required to dispose of what may be called his fixed assets or his discarded goods acquired in the course of the business, an inference that he desired to carry on the business of selling his machinery or fixed assets or discarded goods would not ordinarily arise. Hence, the same will not be taxable.

Legislators amended the definition of 'business' by providing that any sale made in the nature of any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure; whether or not there was intention of makingany gain or profit; as well as sales in connection with or incidental orancillary to such trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure shall be covered.

First important decision on the issue post the amendment was rendered by the Hon. Supreme Court in the case of State of Tamil Nadu v. Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Co of India Ltd. [1973] AIR 1045. In this case the respondent under the Factories Act had to supply tea and edibles to its workmen for the Canteen established by it. It also supplied to its distributors calendars, purses and key chains. They also periodically sold items such as scraps, unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, rims, etc., Issue before the Court was whether these sales were 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' to the business ?

Before the above case, the Hon. Madras High Court in the case of Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. Sri Thirumagal Mills Limited [1967] 20 STC 287 had taken a view that even if by way of amendment to the definition of 'business' profit motive is deleted as an ingredient, still the ancillary activity has to be of commercial nature. It should still partake the nature of 'trade, commerce, manufacture, etc.' specified in the first limb and only then it can be taxed. Hence, it was held that turnover of fair price shop run for the employees will not be leviable to tax.

The Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court on the contrary in the case of Hyderabad Asbestos Cement Products Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh [1969] 24 STC 487 (SC) had taken a view that for an ancillary sale to be taxed it is not required that the same must be done with an intention of doing business. Any ancillary sale connected with the business shall be taxable.

The Hon. Supreme Court in the case of Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Co. of India Ltd. (supra) did not agree with the decision of the Hon. Madras High Court and affirmed the ratio decided by the Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court.

It held that the Hon. Madras High Court had not paid sufficient attention to word 'such' as appearing in clause 'any transaction in connection with, or incidental or ancillary to, such trade, commerce, manufacture,adventure or concern'. Hence, it held that after the omission of profitmotive, any sale which is ancillary to business whether or not made with an intention to do business of such ancillary goods shall be taxable. The Hon. Supreme Court thus held that once a transaction is covered within the ambit of terms 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' the same shall be taxable, whether or not there was any intention to do business in the commercial sense of 'business' in these ancillary goods.

In the given case the Apex Court held that whether sale of scrap such unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, etc, is ancillary to the business is a finding of fact. However, it observed that as the respondent was an oil company, all those items were parts of the business activity of trading in oil and, hence, the same were taxable. In respect of marketing items like calendars, wallets, etc. it was observed that such goods were given to dealers for increasing the sales. Hence, the same were also ancillary to business. With regard to canteen sales it was observed that Government Order specifically provided for exemption to sales made by canteen and, hence, the same must be considered by lower authorities.
