5.5-1 Scheme of section 80-IA - A recapitulation - To recapitulate, various provisions/conditions of section 80-IA are as follows: An industrial undertaking is entitled to certain deduction provided it fulfils the following conditions (including the conditions imposed by amendments):

■ It is not 'formed' by:

- splitting up, or reconstruction of a business already in existence [Section 8O-IA(2)(i)]; and

- transfer to a new business of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose [Section 80-IA(2)(ii)].

■ In case of a small scale industrial undertaking it manufactures or produces any article or thing [Proviso to section 80-IA(2)(iii)];

■ In case of units other than a small scale industrial undertaking, it manufactures or produces any article or thing not specified in Eleventh Schedule [Section 80-IA(2)(iii)].

■ It begins the relevant activity anytime during:

- 1-4-1993 to 31-1-1998 in case of a Power Undertaking/State Undertaking [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(b) - the amended clause]; and

- 1-4-1991 to 31-3-1995 in case of other undertaking (This period can be extended by the Central Government by a Notification) [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(a)].

■ It employs requisite number of workers [Section 80-IA (2)(v)].

The conditions and the amendments, may now be examined in the light of the Scheme of section 80-IA.

5.5-2 Analysis of the amendments The amendments lay down certain conditions or attributes of State undertaking or Power undertaking, which will entitle it to a higher deduction.

5.5-2a State undertaking - In respect of a State undertaking it lays down that:

■ It should be located in an industrially backward State specified in the Eighth Schedule; and

■ It begins to manufacture or produce article or thing, or begins to operate a cold storage plant at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

5.5-2b Power undertaking - In respect of a power undertaking, it lays down that:

■ It may be set up in any part of India for the generation or generation and distribution of power; and

■ It commences generation of power at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

The amendments only classify industrial undertakings for:

■ prescribing period during which the relevant activity has to commence; and

■ conferring higher amount of relief to certain undertakings.

The amendments do not lay down qualifying conditions for claiming a deduction under section 80-IA. Thus, any undertaking claiming a deduction under section 80-IA will, in any case, have to comply with the other condition laid down in section 80-IA(2) including clause (iii) thereof.

From the language of the amended clause, in relation to a State undertaking, it would be observed that it omits 'Union Territory', whereas the Eighth Schedule, Finance Minister's speech. Notes on clauses, and Memorandum explaining the Bill refers to 'Union Territories'. This seems to be a slip.

5.5-2c Initial assessment year - The higher deduction is available for initial five assessment years. 'Intitial assessment year' is defined by section 80-IA(12)(c) as follows:

‘initial assessment year’ means the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce articles or things, or to operate its cold storage plant or plants or the ship is first brought into use or the business of the hotel starts functioning".

From the definition it would be noticed that the previous year in which the prescribed activity commences is to be regarded as a starting point and the relevant assessment year relating thereto would be the initial assessment year.

Accordingly, the year in which the prescribed activity begins is relevant and not any other year including the year in which an industrial undertaking is located in a backward State and the year in which the power undertaking is being set up.

5.5-2C1 ISSUES CONNECTED WITH DATE OF COMMENCEMENT OF ACTIVITIES – The larger deduction is available, if the commencement of relevant activity is on or after 1-4-1993. Accordingly:

■ In a case where, the undertaking is set up or is being set up prior to 1-4-1993; but, commences manufacturing or generation or operation on or after 1-4-1993, the higher deduction would be available.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc. in backward areas [Computation of deduction] - Assessee-company had been carrying on two activities; one was business of manufacturing cement and second was mining operation of lime - Lime was used as raw material in manufacturing cement - Assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH from whole of business income - Same was disallowed on ground that assessee had been carrying on business of mining operation - Whether mining activity of assessee was distinct and independent from cement manufacturing activities and segregation of profit of two different business activities was permissible under law - Held, yes - Whether segregation of profit derived from cement manufacturing activity was permitted by law in order to find out profit derived from mining activities and, thus, deduction under section 80HH would be available only on profit derived from cement manufacturing activity - Held, yes [Paras 6 to 11] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee had two separate and distinct undertaking, one for manufacturing cement and another for mining of lime that was to be used in cement manufacturing, profit only from manufacturing of cement would be eligible for deduction under section 80HH

FACT: The assessee-company had been carrying on business of manufacturing cement and also carrying on mining operation of lime which was used as a raw material in manufacturing cement.

The assessee claimed deduction under section 80HH and the same was disallowed by Assessing Officer on the ground that assessee had been carrying on business of mining operation.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction by observing that the assessee carried business of manufacturing cement.

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee could be said to have been running two industrial undertakings. The assessee's main business of manufacturing of cement, was entitled to deduction under section 80HH in respect of items manufactured or produced, and it would not cease to be entitled to claim the deduction if the industrial undertaking is engaged in mining. The Tribunal, therefore, allowed deduction with respect to profit attributable to manufacturing cement.

On assessee's appeal to High Court :

HELD: From the records the Court find, as has been rightly contended by revenue that in the previous assessment years, namely 1984-85 and 1985-86, the Tribunal found on fact that the assessee has been running two industrial undertakings, one is mining of lime and another is manufacturing of cement. It is an admitted position further that against the aforesaid findings, no appeal has been preferred. Hence, the Court have to proceed on the premise that the mining activity of the assessee is distinct and independent from the cement manufacturing activity. Now the question remains is whether the use of the entire product of lime, extracted from mining operation for manufacturing of cement, looses its marketable value in order to ascertain the profit or not. [Para 6]

The argument of the assessee is that a manufacturer cannot trade with itself. Therefore, unless there is a factual sale in the market, no profit can be derived from this mining operation. In order to derive the entire profit, the cement manufacturing unit has to be taken into account and the product has to be sold in the market and then the profit will be ascertained. This submission, at the first blush, sounds logic, but while keeping in view the matter, this logic does not have any basis. It is the admitted position that lime is one of the raw materials in manufacturing cement and in order to manufacture the finished products, raw material is essential and the cost thereof is one of the factors for cost price of the finished goods. Therefore, in the manufacturing activity of cement unit, the cost of the finished product has to be ascertained and in that process, the cost of lime has also to be taken into consideration. In the case on hand, the lime, being a raw material, is not procured from open market and it has got its own indigenous supply. Therefore, the cost of the lime extracted from mining operation has to be ascertained from the cost price and it is found, while doing so, that the cost of lime of its own source (ordinarily it happens) is lesser than the market price. Therefore, the difference between the cost price of indigenous source and the market price is obviously the profit. Moreover, once lime is used from its indigenous source to manufacture the finished products and by virtue of sale of such finished products if there is any profit, then obviously that profit is also related to the mining operation. [Para 7]

Thus, it was clear from the reply that brass was not an ingredient used in the process of manufacture in industrial undertaking of the assessee. The brass scrap had no direct nexus with the appellant’s industrial undertaking. It could not be said that brass scrap was a profit or gain which directly flowed, neither it had close connection with undertaking of the assessee. By removal of brass scrap which was not useful for steel rerolling work no different and distinct article came into existence, it was only incidental as was apparent from the assessee’s reply. [Paras 13 and 14]

Further, composition of brass scrap was not at all changed, that was only removed as that was not useful to the assessee for the activity of manufacturing which he was carrying on. It was only a fortuitous circumstance that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee had purchased the guns without the knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in the process of manufacture. There was no nexus between brass and activity of steel rerolling. Brass was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25]

Thus, there was no nexus between the brass scrap obtained on dismantling of the guns and the main activity of the assessee of steel rerolling. Gun was not an essential raw material of appellants’ industrial unit, in any case, brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling. Thus, separation of brass could not be said to be in the process of manufacture or a product or a by-product of the activity of the assessee’s industrial undertaking. There was no direct nexus between the separation of the brass from the guns and the main activity. Thus, considering the provisions of sections 80HH and 80-I, it could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking. Thus, deductions on profits and gains under sections 80HH and 80-I were not admissible and had been rightly disallowed by the Tribunal. [Para 28]

Resultantly, the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 29]

On reference:

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with  section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profit and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1979-80 and 1980-81 - Whether business of tyre retreading does not amount to production of new article entitling assessee to relief under sections 80HH and 80J - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, which was retreader and established its plant in a backward area, claimed deductions under sections 80HH and 80J. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article and that, therefore, the assessee was entitled to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

On reference:

HELD: The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such, comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.

Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles, which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production new words are not being added to section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved, that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture, would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. In view of aforesaid, it could not be said that retreading of tyres resulted in the production of an article for the purpose of section 80HH.

Hence, the Tribunal was not right in holding that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article entitling the assessee to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment year 1977-78 - Whether assessee buying shrimps, peeling them and freezing them could be said to be engaged in manufacture or production, in absence of material on record to indicate what was done by assessee and how it was done, so as to eligible for allowance under section 80HH - Held, no

FACT: The assessee bought shrimps, peeled them and froze them. It claimed allowance under section 80HH on the ground that it was an industrial undertaking that manufactured/produced articles. There was no other material on the record which indicated what was done by the assessee and how it was done. The claim was rejected by the Assessing Officer but upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal. On reference, the High Court upheld the decision of the Tribunal on ground that buying and processing of shrimps involved production.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: There was, upon the record before the Court, no detailed description of what the assessee did to the shrimps it bought, other than the bald statement that it peeled and froze them. The Court could not accept the statement at the Bar that the process to which the assessee put the shrimps was the process that CIT v. Marwell Sea Foods [1987] 166 ITR 624/ 34 Taxman 52 (Ker.) used in regard to its prawns. That apart the Supreme Court in Sterling Foods v. State of Karnataka [1986] 68 STC 239, held that processed or frozen shrimps and prawns are commercially regarded as the same commodity as raw shrimps and prawns. When raw shrimps and prawns are subjected to the process of cutting of heads and tails, peeling, deveining, cleaning and freezing they do not cease to be shrimps and prawns and become other distinct commodities. There is no essential difference between raw shrimps and prawns and processed or frozen shrimps and prawns. In common parlance they remain known as shrimps and prawns. Therefore, the assessee who bought shrimps, peeled them and froze them was not entitled to the allowance under section 80HH as it did not involve in activity of manufacture or production.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - In respect of certain incomes of hotels or industries in backward areas - Assessee-company was engaged in business of centrifuging rubber latex and had employed more than ten persons - On 8-7-1983 Government of India issued a Notification No. 189/83 under rule 8 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, granting exemption to preserved latex and latex concentrate considering these to be items manufactured or produced - Whether decision of Government taken under the Central Excise Act had to be applied with equal force under the present Act - Held, yes - Whether assessee would be entitled to deduction under section 80HH - Held, yes

Section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from new industrial undertakings, ships or hotels - Whether on basis of facts under head ‘Deductions - In respect of certain incomes of hotels or industries in backward areas’, assessee would be entitled to deduction under section 80J - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of centrifug- ing rubber latex. It had employed more than then ten persons

in its concern. For the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under sections 80J and 80HH. The ITO rejected the assessee’s claim on the ground that it was not an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced any article or thing. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the ITO.

On second appeal:

HELD: By virtue of Notification No. 189/83-Central Excises, dated 8-7-1983, the Government of India granted exemption to preserved latex, latex concentrate, etc., because it considered the said goods as goods produced or manufactured in India. If preserved latex was not to be considered as goods produced or manufactured in India there would have been no necessity of exempting the same by issuing the aforesaid notification under rule 8 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. From this it had to be fairly inferred that the Government of India itself considered that preserved latex was an item manufactured or produced. The Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 and the Act in question are both Central enactments. The words used in the relevant sections are ‘produced or manufactured’. So, the decision of the Government taken under the Central Excise Act had to be applied with equal force under the Act also. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to deduction under sections 80J and 80HH.

Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas - Assessment year 1980-81 - Assessee, engaged in business of centrifuging rubber latex, claimed deduction under section 80HH - ITO rejected claim on the ground that assessee was not an industrial company manufacturing or producing any article or thing - Whether centrifuging process could be said to have resulted in manufacture or production of a marketable commodity and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH of the Act - Held, yes

Section 80HH is intended to encourage setting up new industrial enterprises and, hence, will have to be construed liberally in a broad commercial sense keeping its object in view. The Act does not define the expression 'industrial undertaking'. Therefore, reference to its definition in similar enactments or adoption of its ordinary meaning is inevitable.

In the instant case, 'CD', when taken over by the assessee, had neither any machinery nor was it making fuel injection pipes. It was carrying on only the business of selling diesel engines. The assessee made investment to the tune of Rs. 79,726 in purchasing new machinery for the purposes of making fuel injection pipes for diesel engines by making nipples and giving shape at both ends of the tubes. Tube was the raw material and the fuel injection pipe was the produce. Tube had undergone change as a result of operation performed on it by men and machine and a new identifiably different commercial and saleable commodity had emerged The Tribunal was satisfied after seeing the raw material and the demonstration of process of making the produce, that manufacturing activity was involved in the endeavour, and there was nothing on record to hold that this finding was in any way perverse.

Further, in the instant case, the revenue had not challenged the deduction under section 32A. The basic concepts of 'industrial undertaking', 'manufacture', 'produce' occur even in section 32A. If the unit having new machinery amounted to industrial undertaking and the process amounted to manufacture for the purposes of section 32A, it was difficult to see how any different legislative intent could be attributed to the identical expressions used in section 80HH.

Sub-section (2) of section 80HH refers to ‘industrial undertaking' and not to the assessee or his other business. There was no question in the instant case of formation of 'industrial undertaking', by splitting up of the business activity already in existence since there was no such activity before, or by transfer to a new business of machinery previously used for any purpose. Hence, condition Nos. (i) and (iii) in sub-section (2) were also fulfilled. The conclusion was inevitable that the assessee was entitled to deduction also under section 80HH.

Therefore, the Tribunal was correct in holding that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80HH.

Deduction in respect profits and gains from business of collecting and processing bio-degradable waste

6.3 A new section 80JJA has been inserted with effect from assessment year 1999-2000 to provide for deduction in respect profits and gains from business of collecting and processing bio-degradable waste.

The section provides that “Where the gross total income of an assessee includes any profits and gains derived from the business of collecting and processing or treating of bio-degradable waste for generating power, producing bio-gas, making pellets or briquettes for fuel or organic manure, there shall be allowed, in computing the total income of the assessee, a deduction from such profits and gains of an amount equal to the whole of such income, or five lakh rupees, whichever is less.”

6.3-1 Analysis of new provision : Note the following

◆ The deduction is available to all assessees.

◆ On a plain reading of the section, the deduction is available only if the assessee is engaged in the business of collecting as well as processing or treating bio-degradable waste. It is not available if the assessee is engaged in only collection or only processing/treating.

◆ The deduction is available only in respect of profit and gains of processing or treatment for generating power, producing bio-gas , making pellets or briquettes for fuel or organic manure. It is not available in respect of profits and gains of processing or treating for other purposes.

◆ The deduction is available to all entities, whether new or old. In other words unlike section 80-IA it is not restricted to new units.

Deduction in respect of employment of new workmen

6.4 In order to encourage the employers to further generate more employment opportunities, a new section 80JJAA has been inserted (with effect from 1-4-1999) to provide an incentive in the form of a special deduction against business profits of a company.

6.4-1 Conditions to be fulfilled - The following conditions have to be fulfilled in order to be eligible to the deduction provided in the section :

◆ the assessee should be an Indian company.

◆ its gross total income should include profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking.

◆ the industrial undertaking should be engaged in the manufacture or production of any article or thing.

◆ the industrial undertaking should not have been formed by splitting up of an existing undertaking.

◆ the industrial undertaking should not have been formed by reconstruction of an existing undertaking.

◆ the industrial undertaking should not have been formed by amalgamation with an existing undertaking.

◆ the assessee furnishes alongwith the return of income a report of an accountant.

◆ in case of a new industrial undertaking, in the first previous year, it employs more than 100 regular workmen.

◆ in the case of an existing industrial undertaking, the number of regular workers employed during the relevant previous year is equal to at least 110% of the regular workmen employed in such undertaking as on the last day of the preceding year.

The provisions relating to aforesaid conditions are elaborately explained in subsequent paragraphs.

6.4-2 Quantum of deduction - See para 6.4-11

6.4-3 Indian company - The section is applicable only if the assessee is an Indian company as defined in section 2(26) of the Act. Hence, it does not apply to other entities like foreign companies, firms, HUFs, etc.

6.4-4 Profits and gains derived - The term ‘derived’ has been explained in a number of judgments involving interpretation of section 80J/80-I/80-IA etc.,

It may be noted, however, that unlike other sections, section 80JJAA does not link the deduction to quantum of profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking. For the purpose of this section , it is sufficient that the gross total income includes profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking and once this condition is satisfied, the ultimate deduction is based on wages paid.

Again, it could also be argued that in the absence of a specific prohibition, the deduction under this section could exceed the profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking, as long as the deductions under Chapter VIA of the Act do not exceed the gross total income [section 80A(2)].

6.4-5 Industrial undertaking - The term industrial undertaking has not been defined in the section. In the context of section 15C, of the Income-tax Act, 1922 (corresponding to s. 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961), the Supreme Court in Textile Machinery Corporation Ltd. v. Deduction in respect profits and gains from business of collecting and processing bio-degradable waste

6.3 A new section 80JJA has been inserted with effect from assessment year 1999-2000 to provide for deduction in respect profits and gains from business of collecting and processing bio-degradable waste.

The section provides that “Where the gross total income of an assessee includes any profits and gains derived from the business of collecting and processing or treating of bio-degradable waste for generating power, producing bio-gas, making pellets or briquettes for fuel or organic manure, there shall be allowed, in computing the total income of the assessee, a deduction from such profits and gains of an amount equal to the whole of such income, or five lakh rupees, whichever is less.”

6.3-1 Analysis of new provision : Note the following

◆ The deduction is available to all assessees.

◆ On a plain reading of the section, the deduction is available only if the assessee is engaged in the business of collecting as well as processing or treating bio-degradable waste. It is not available if the assessee is engaged in only collection or only processing/treating.

◆ The deduction is available only in respect of profit and gains of processing or treatment for generating power, producing bio-gas , making pellets or briquettes for fuel or organic manure. It is not available in respect of profits and gains of processing or treating for other purposes.

◆ The deduction is available to all entities, whether new or old. In other words unlike section 80-IA it is not restricted to new units.

HELD: The phrase ‘profits and gains derived from industrial undertaking’ has not been defined in the Act. Hence, its meaning has to be understood in the general commercial sense. In order to arrive at the profit from an under-taking, only the actual expenses are deducted and not the notional expenses. Hence, the profits of an undertaking can mean the amount arrived at after deduction of actual expenses only and without deduction of the notional expenses like the relief under section 35B: This is really not an expense that goes out of the pocket of the assessee, and cannot, therefore, go to reduce the commercial profit, though it may reduce the taxable profit.

"(2) This section applies to any industrial undertaking which fulfils all the following conditions namely:—

The proviso to section 80HH(4) uses the words "provided that,—( i) in the case of an industrial undertaking which has begun to manufacture or produce articles". For the same reasons, we reject the assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: The important test, which distinguishes the word 'production' from 'manufacture', is that the word 'production' is wider than the word 'manufacture'. Further, the Legislature has used the words 'manufacture' or 'production'. Therefore, the word 'production' cannot derive its colour from the word 'manufacture'. Further, even according to the dictionary meaning of word 'production', the word 'produce' is defined as something which is brought forth or yielded either naturally or as a result of effort and work. It is important to note that the word 'new' is not used in the definition of the word 'produce'. [Para 8]

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in allowing the deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to the assessee holding that the ship breaking activity gave rise to the production of a distinct and different article. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Whether assessee engaged in business of rearing and development of chicks into broilers, could be said to be ‘manufacturing’ a product - Held, no

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the business of rearing of chicks to broilers, a saleable product, by applying scientific process and technology, established an industrial unit in the backward area and claimed deduction under section 80HH and section 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the claim. On the revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal, however, set aside the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) and affirmed that of the Assessing Officer.

On reference :

HELD: The process involved in the development of chicks into broilers is nothing but basically the chicks remains chicks only. There is no substantial change so as to acquire new commercial identity. Chicks are smaller ones and when they are reared for sometime, they develop suitably for table purposes. Therefore, there is no change of substance. Manufacture implies a change, but every change is not manufacture and yet every change in an article is the result of treatment, labour and manipulation and does not necessarily mean that on account of certain treatment and manipulation, new identity has come to be acquired.

In the instant case, chicks were only reared up for a few days and they were developed, thereafter they became broilers. Therefore, even after rearing, they remained chicks only. Hence, the view taken by the Tribunal that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I as an industrial undertaking was correct.

The assessee, a leading manufacturer of moulded luggage under the brand name of ‘VIP’, had set up a new industrial undertaking in addition to the existing undertaking for manufacturing some moulded luggage by installing new machines. The installed capacity for manufacturing moulded luggage, consequent to the installation of the new machines had substantially increased and its production had also increased as a result of increase on the investment and thus, the assessee claimed benefit under section 80-I. The claim was rejected by Assessing Officer on the ground that the action of installing a new capacity by purchasing new machines was merely an expansion of the existing unit and no expansion of the existing unit and no new industrial undertaking came into existence. It was further held that no new product was manufactured in the new industrial undertaking and the assessee was simply manufacturing old type of luggage. Therefore, the Assessing Officer came to the conclusion that the action of the assessee in installing new machinery in different years was only with a view to expansion of the existing industrial capacity and no new industrial undertaking came into existence for which deduction under section 80-I was admissible and this view was upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On second appeal :

The assessee furnished details of installation of the injection moulding machines indicating the capacity in metric tonnes and number of machines installed and the value in rupees and contended that the assessee had in fact installed a new industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 80-I, and it was entitled to the permissible deduction.

In order to earn rebate under the first proviso to para I of the Third Schedule of the Act (as it stood at the relevant time) income, including profits and gains from business, must be attributable to the business of manufacture and/or production of the articles specified in the list in para 2 thereof. In the instant case, the articles were those at item 2. The only question to be determined was whether extraction of aluminium, copper, lead and zinc (metals) out of scrap material amounted to manufacture or production of the same or not. It was obvious that the scrap purchased by the assessee was not pure and simple metal, but consisted of only parts of articles made of something which could not be pure or simple aluminium, copper, lead or zinc. When a metal was extracted from such scrap after subjecting the same to certain processes, it surely amounted to a business of production of the metal involved.

The composition of the new product was entirely different from the composition of the articles out of which it was extracted and the process of deriving this pure metal could be properly described as a manufacturing process. Consequently, the Tribunal had correctly held that the assessee was entitled to the relief claimed by it under the first proviso to para 1 of the Third Schedule, and deduction under section 80E of the Income-tax Act and the consequential deduction in computing its chargeable profits under the First Schedule to the Surtax Act.

Editor's note

Although the reference application was filed only by the revenue, the Tribunal referred two questions at the instance of the assessee also. In view of the Supreme Court's decision in the case of CIT v. V. Damodaran [1980] 121 ITR 572, the High Court held the reference of these questions to be void and declined to answer the same.

IT REFERENCE NO. 233 OF 1973.

The Legislature intended to extend the benefit of deduction under section 80HH only to the industrial undertakings which manufacture or produce articles. This section is not intended to be applied to industrial undertakings which are engaged in ‘processing of goods’ not amounting to manufacture or production of articles. The ship-breaking activity involves buying of damaged and unserviceable ships which are otherwise uneconomic to run, for the purpose of breaking and scrapping and sale of various goods and scrap obtained from such breaking and dismantling of old and used ships. Process is employed for breaking ship for dismantling and selling the scrap and substantial part of the items fitted in the ship and the oil contained in the tankers are sold in the same from without carrying out any further act, except removal of same from the ship and the remaining ship, made mainly of iron and steel, is then broken into different pieces of different sizes and shapes and sold by weight. Therefore, at the end of the process employed by the assessee, what is acquired are iron bars, plating rods, bronze, gunmetal copper and non-ferrous metal which, though marketable and commercial commodities, cannot be said to be manufactured or produced articles or things. For all practical purposes it is scrap. The scrap cannot be called a manufacture product or produced article because they are no new commodities but parts of the old and discarded ship as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of CST v. Delhi Iron & Steel Co. (P.) Ltd. [1995] 98 STC 202 the condemned and unserviceable ship purchased by the dealer is not a ship but re-rollable scrap in the form of an old ship for dismantling, in effect, the dealer acquires only the old materials and articles contained therein which are sold by it in the form in which they are acquired. No process whatsoever is applied to the goods, much less any process of manufacture. The issue stood squarely covered in favour of the revenue by the decision of the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asst. CIT v. Virendra & Co. [1995] 55 ITD 309 which held that ‘the meaning of manufacture and production of articles and things’ would have to be considered in their ordinary plain and natural meaning. Breaking or dismantling a ship would perhaps be just the opposite of manufacturing or production of an article or an thing. When a ship is dismantled or broken, what is obtained by the persons who are engaged in that process are the components by which the ship is constructed or manufactured and if it is possible to reassemble those pieces or parts, the ship may be manufactured or constructed. Hence, it would be doing violence to the language of the section if it is said that while a ship is being dismantled or broken or destroyed, in effect an article or thing is being manufactured or produced. Hence, the activity of breaking or dismantling of a ship cannot be considered to be an industrial undertaking which manufactured or produced articles or things and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

Regarding the contention of the assessee that the Government of India had recognised ship breaking as industry and, hence, the assessee was entitled to deduction claimed, there was no presumption that every industry is engaged in ‘manufacture’ or ‘production of articles or things’. Even if ship breaking is considered as an industry in the light of the definition of section 2(f) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, it will not mean that it would amount to manufacture or production so as to entitle the assessee to claim deductions under the respective sections. The assessee being governed by the Factories Act also would not change the matter in any way because that is broadly meant for welfare of labourers employed. The argument that a ship-breaking industry is labour intensive and that in the process heavy machinery like cranes and winches are employed is not relevant in absence of any manufacturing process involved. Mere application of systematic and sophisticated machines in the process would not treat an activity into manufacture. Thus, ship breaking activity amounts to carrying out the manufacturing process in a reverse order, as originally the ship is built from iron sheets and iron bars and other materials and by process of breaking the same, ship was reconverted into iron scrap and other materials. In view of the above, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) were to be reversed.

5.5-1 Scheme of section 80-IA - A recapitulation - To recapitulate, various provisions/conditions of section 80-IA are as follows: An industrial undertaking is entitled to certain deduction provided it fulfils the following conditions (including the conditions imposed by amendments):

It is not 'formed' by:

-

splitting up, or reconstruction of a business already in existence [Section 8O-IA(2)(i)]; and

-

transfer to a new business of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose [Section 80-IA(2)(ii)].

In case of a small scale industrial undertaking it manufactures or produces any article or thing [Proviso to section 80-IA(2)(iii)];

In case of units other than a small scale industrial undertaking, it manufactures or produces any article or thing not specified in Eleventh Schedule [Section 80-IA(2)(iii)].

It begins the relevant activity anytime during:

-

1-4-1993 to 31-1-1998 in case of a Power Undertaking/State Undertaking [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(b) - the amended clause]; and

-

1-4-1991 to 31-3-1995 in case of other undertaking (This period can be extended by the Central Government by a Notification) [Section 80-IA(2)(iv)(a)].

It employs requisite number of workers [Section 80-IA (2)(v)].

The conditions and the amendments, may now be examined in the light of the Scheme of section 80-IA.

5.5-2 Analysis of the amendments The amendments lay down certain conditions or attributes of State undertaking or Power undertaking, which will entitle it to a higher deduction.

5.5-2a State undertaking - In respect of a State undertaking it lays down that:

It should be located in an industrially backward State specified in the Eighth Schedule; and

It begins to manufacture or produce article or thing, or begins to operate a cold storage plant at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

5.5-2b Power undertaking - In respect of a power undertaking, it lays down that:

It may be set up in any part of India for the generation or generation and distribution of power; and

It commences generation of power at any time during the period 1st April, 1993 to 31st March, 1998.

The amendments only classify industrial undertakings for:

prescribing period during which the relevant activity has to commence; and

conferring higher amount of relief to certain undertakings.

The amendments do not lay down qualifying conditions for claiming a deduction under section 80-IA. Thus, any undertaking claiming a deduction under section 80-IA will, in any case, have to comply with the other condition laid down in section 80-IA(2) including clause (iii)thereof.

From the language of the amended clause, in relation to a State undertaking, it would be observed that it omits 'Union Territory', whereas the Eighth Schedule, Finance Minister's speech. Notes on clauses, and Memorandum explaining the Bill refers to 'Union Territories'. This seems to be a slip.

5.5-2c Initial assessment year - The higher deduction is available for initial five assessment years. 'Intitial assessment year' is defined by section 80-IA(12)(c) as follows:

'initial assessment year' means the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce articles or things, or to operate its cold storage plant or plants or the ship is first brought into use or the business of the hotel starts functioning".

From the definition it would be noticed that the previous year in which the prescribed activity commences is to be regarded as a starting point and the relevant assessment year relating thereto would be the initial assessment year.

BACKWARD AREAS-WHETHER INTEREST ON FIXED DEPOSITS MADE OUT OF ACCUMULATED PROFITS AND RESERVES IS INCOME DERIVED FROM INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKING-HELD, YES-WHETHER DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH IS ALLOWABLE ON SUCH INTEREST INCOME-HELD, YES

FACT: The assessee-company had not paid any dividend since its inception, but had invested its accumulated profits and reserves in fixed deposits, the interest income from which was assessed under the head ‘Income from other sources’. The assessee’s claim that deduction under section 80HH should be allowed on this interest income also, was rejected by the ITO, whose order was upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In second appeal, the assessee contended that the fixed deposits represented accumulated funds not required immediately, but intended to be spent on various projects the company planned to undertake, some of which had in fact been undertaken and as such constituted funds invested in its business undertaking and, therefore, the interest earned thereon should be regarded as income derived from the assessee’s business undertaking. The revenue contended that the nexus of the interest income was the invest- ment in fixed deposits and not the manufacture or production of goods dealt in by the assessee and, therefore, it could not be equated to income derived from profits and gains of industrial undertaking.

HELD: Section 80HH speaks of deduction in respect of any profits and gains derived from newly established industrial undertaking. The term ‘undertaking’ has not been defined in the Act and has to be given the normal meaning. It envisages not only the activity of manufacture or production of goods or arti-cles but the entire set up including all the paraphernalia, the various assets and liabilities, i.e., the entire set up with which the business of manufacture or production of goods is carried on. Therefore, cash resources not imme-diately ploughed back in the day to day operations but nonetheless forming part of the undertaking, are also a constituent part of the undertaking. It is, therefore, obvious that income generated by way of interest on deposits of money held as part of the industrial undertaking is nothing but an ingredient of the profits and gains derived from such undertaking. It makes no diffe-rence whether any such income is assessed under the head ‘Profits and gains of business or profession’ or under the head ‘Income from other sources’. Even if the interest income cannot be strictly referable to the business activity of manufacture of goods dealt in by the assessee and has no direct nexus thereto, it can still be regarded as profit or gain derived from the undertaking as a whole.

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified.

An industrial undertaking which is engaged in manufacture and production of an article or thing would be eligible for the deduction under section 32AB; it would be eligible for the deduction under section 80HH if situated in backward area; it would, if established after 31-3-1976, be eligible for the deduction allowed under section 80J. In the instant case, all the ingredients were undisputedly satisfied. [Para 6.4]

PRODUCTION : MEANING OF : In the instant case, the relief was claimed on the ground that the establish-ment of the assessee was engaged in the production of logs. Trees cannot be sold in the open market with all their branches and leaves even if felled, as a whole. The branches are slopped, the trunk is cut into pieces and then converted into logs which primarily involves effort or exercise or enterprising or undertaking of some process. The conversion of trunk into logs is the first step towards extraction of timber for which human efforts are necessary. In order to make it a saleable commercial article, the logs are seasoned. The commercial activity that the assessee undertook was the sale of logs, the main purpose of the assessee’s business. The enterprise undertaken in the industrial undertaking of the assessee was to produce commercially saleable logs out of the felled trees. Thus, the production of logs, though may not involve manufacture, is yet a production within the meaning of sections 32AB, 80HH and 80J respectively. [Para 6.5]

The conversion of logs would not amount to manufacture since no article other than wood is brought out and no change in the characteristics is effected. Conversion of tree into logs would not change the character, which remains wood as before. Admittedly, in the instant case, the assessee did not claim conversion of felled tree to log as manufacture. An establishment, which is engaged in production of something is an industrial undertaking eligible under the provisions of sections 32A, 80HH and 80J. [Para 6.8]

The de-embarking of the trunk of the tree and cutting the same into pieces and seasoning the same in order to convert the tree trunk into logs as commercially saleable commodity requires a human effort to undertake such process and the end-product is something different from the tree though its characteristics remains the same, viz., wood yet definitely it is an article or thing which is commercially saleable and as such the process undertaken for conversion of trees into logs as commercially saleable commodity would amount to production within the meaning of the provisions of the said section . [Para 6.9]

The word ‘production’ has been used in a very wide sense within the scope of section 32A to mean to bring out a commercially new product. [Para 6.13]

CONCLUSION :

Thus, the de-embarking and seasoning the tree trunks and converting the same into logs would amount to production of a new commercial article or thing within the meaning of sections 32AB, 80HH and 80J. The assessee was entitled to the benefit of deductions thereunder for the relevant assessment years. [Para 7]

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with  section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains of newly established industrial undertaking in backward areas - Whether assessee engaged in business of rearing and development of chicks into broilers, could be said to be 'manufacturing' a product - Held, no

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the business of rearing of chicks to broilers, a saleable product, by applying scientific process and technology, established an industrial unit in the backward area and claimed deduction under section 80HH and section 80-I. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the claim. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal, however, set aside the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) and affirmed that of the Assessing Officer.

HELD: AS HELD BY HIGH COURT

The process involved in the development of chicks into broilers is nothing but that the chicks basically remains chicks only. There is no substantial change so as to acquire new commercial identity. Chicks are smaller ones and when they are reared for sometime, they develop suitably for table purposes. Therefore, there is no change of substance. Manufacture implies a change, but every change is not manufacture and yet every change in an article is the result of treatment, labour and manipulation which does not necessarily mean that on account of certain treatment and manipulation, new identity has come to be acquired.

In the instant case, chicks were only reared up for a few days and they were developed, thereafter they became broilers. Therefore, even after rearing, they remained chicks only. Hence, the view taken by the Tribunal that the assessee was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I as an industrial undertaking was correct.

AS HELD BY SUPREME COURT

It was not in dispute that the case was covered against the assessee by the judgment of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Venkateswara Hatcheries (P.) Ltd. [1999] 237 ITR 174/103 Taxman 503. The further point that was made by the assessee was that it not only reared the chicken but also dressed them for sale in the market and, therefore, a process of manufacture was carried out. But, it appeared that there was no material laid before the Tribunal in this behalf. It was, therefore, not possible to conclude in the present matter that the dressing of poultry tantamounted to manufacture.

The appeal was dismissed.

4.6 The Finance Act, 1994 has amended section 80-IA and has widened its scope in the following manner:

■ Extension of five year holiday to new industrial undertaking in backward district of other States, ie., backward district of States other than those specified in the Eighth Schedule (see para 4.6-1).

4.6-1 New Industrial undertakings set up in backward districts of States other than those specified in Eighth Schedule - The Finance Act, 1993 introduced a five year tax holiday under section 80-IA, for new industrial undertakings which start production after 1-4-1993 but before 31-3-1998 in any of the backward States specified in the Eighth Schedule to the Income-tax Act. Pursuant to representations and demand, the five year tax holiday has been also extended to industrially backward districts of other States.

4.6-1a Eligible undertakings, amount of deduction and conditions - Following points need be noted:

■ The undertaking should be located in a backward district of States other than those specified in Eighth Schedule as may be notified by the Central Government.

■ The five-year tax holiday will be available to undertakings which begin production on or after 1-10-1994, but before 31-3-1999.

■ The deduction under section 80-IA will be available at the rate of 100 per cent of profits in respect of the first five assessment years starting from the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the industrial undertaking starts manufacture or production. For the subsequent assessment years, deduction from the profits from such undertakings will be allowed at the normal rate and for the residual period as may be applicable (see para 4.6-3).

■ The undertaking will have to comply with the other conditions of section 80-IA, like:

- not formed by reconstruction, etc.;

- employment of requisite number of workers;

- not engaged in manufacture of any article listed in Eleventh Schedule, where the undertaking is other than a small scale undertaking, etc

■ The amendment is effective from assessment year 1995-96.

An undertaking located in a backward district should commence manufacture on or after 1-10-1994. The date selection is rather curious and not consistent with such date(s) prescribed in past. Further, as a result the aggregate period works out to four and a half years as against the period of five years normally prescribed in the past.

The deduction is available, in case of an undertaking located in a backward district, if the commencement of relevant activity is on or after 1-10-1994. Accordingly:

■ In a case where the undertaking is set up or is being set up prior to 1-10-1994; but, commences manufacturing operation on or after 1-10-1994, the deduction would be available.

■ In a case where, the undertaking has commenced commercial production of intermediates) and not the final product (for which the undertaking is established) prior to 1-10-1994, whether the deduction could be availed of or not will have to be decided having regard to the ratio of the Supreme Court's decision in CIT v. Cellulose Products of India Ltd [1991] 192 ITR 155. If the ratio applies, one may have to examine whether the undertaking manufacturing intermediate and final product could be regarded as two separate and distinct undertakings and whether in respect of undertaking manufacturing final product (which commences manufacture on or after 1-10-1994), a deduction could be claimed. These questions will have to be resolved having regard to the facts and the law laid down by Supreme Court in Cellulose Products (supra) and Textile Machinery Corpn. Ltd v. CIT [1977] 107 ITR 195 (SC) and the cases following the said decision.

11.2 We have heard the rival submission. While deciding the earlier two grounds we have held that appellate authorities are not prohibited from entertaining the new claims, though the AO cannot accept such a claim if same is not raised by way of filing of revised return. Following the judgment of Prithvi Brokers (supra) we are restoring back the matter to the file of the FAA for fresh adjudication. Ground no. 5 is decided in favour of the assessee, in part. 12. Sixth ground pertains to computation of deduction u/s. 80IB/80IC of the Act. During the assessment proceedings, the AO found that the assessee had claimed deduction of Rs. 74.33 crores under section 80 IB/80IC of the Act, in the revised return of income. He computed the deduction by making adjustment under the heads rent and store charges, miscellaneous sales and other income. He observed that the assessee had allocated expenses to undertaking of Goa, Pondicherry and Dehradun on the basis of rent and storage cost directly identifying product wise and undertaking wise, that rent and storage charges in respect sales division in ratio of turnover of the undertaking to the total turnover of the company were computed. The AO held that such expenses could not be allocated on the basis of ratio of turnover of the undertaking. He further found that the assessee had considered income from by products, sale of scrap and other items, sale of assets, insurance claim and lease rent, while claiming deduction under section 80 IB/80 IC. But, the AO did not agree with the assessee and excluded such income from the profit of the respective undertaking while computing the deduction on the ground that above income could not be said to be arising out of business of the assessee, that though the income was attributable to the business of the assessee it was not derived from the business carried out by it.

12.1 Aggrieved by the order of the AO, the assessee preferred an appeal before the FAA. Before him, it was argued that the assessee had allocated rent and storage expenses on the basis of cost directly identifiable, that common rent and storage expenses were allocated in the ratio of turnover of each unit, that the AO had not assigned any reason for deviating from the basis of allocation made by the assessee, that it was consistently following the above method of a location in the earlier years. The AR pointed out the mistakes committed by the AO in working out the deduction.

With regard to miscellaneous sales (Rs. 3.59 crores +Rs. 12.5 lakhs +Rs. 7.07 crores) the AR contended that the assessee was in the business of manufacturing and dealing in FMCG, that sale of miscellaneous items included sale of by products, scrap that would arise during the course of manufacturing, that at Pondicherry unit crushing of Copra to extract oil, after filtration, would generate by product called cake, that sale of scrap comprised of sale of gunny bags, chemical empty drums and unusable oil, that generation of by products/scrap was directly linked to the manufacture of products by the eligible undertaking, that the by products/scrap could not be generated independent of the Manufacturing process, that the miscellaneous sales had direct nexus with the industrial undertaking and ought to be considered as forming part of the profits eligible for deduction under section 80 IB/80IC. The AR relied upon certain case laws.

With regard to other miscellaneous income, it was argued that the income included insurance claim received, lease rent, exchange gain and money received for the material return to the vendor. It was further argued that insurance claims (Rs. 2.85 lakhs +Rs. 2.64 lakhs) were received for loss of products on transport from eligible undertaking to the depot, that the insurance claim received was in relation to products manufactured and sold, that costs with respect to loss was debited to P&L account, that the insurance claim received was nothing but reimbursement of such loss and was directly related to respective undertaking, that such loss was considered as expenditure while computing the profit under section 80 IB/80IC, that the corresponding insurance claim received on the same had to be considered as business income.

The judgment relied by the revenue is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case as the issue involved in the said judgment was pertaining to section 80HHC.

However, in the present case, the issue is of section 80-IC and not of section 80HHC. Both the provisions apply and operate in different fields. Whereas section 80HHC revolves around the issue of export benefit on the turnover whereas in the case of section 80-IC the benefit is to be calculated on the profit and loss of an undertaking qualifying as per Section 80-IC(2). The treatment of the scrap for the purposes of manufacturing activity is required to be appreciated in the context that the sale of scrap which will go to reduce the input cost of the undertaking and thereby decline the profit margin of the undertaking whereas in the case of section 80HHC if the sale of scrap is made a part of the turnover the export benefit of the undertaking will increase.

Therefore two different effects are there for treating the sale being part of the turnover and also treating the receipt of sale of scrap being part and parcel of the activity being proximate to the activities of the industrial undertaking while computing the deduction under section 80-IC of the Act. For the reasons stated above, the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) is upheld. The sale of scrap being part and parcel of the activities of the assessee-undertaking gains derived from the said activity was arising out of core activity of the assessee and therefore, was required to be taken into consideration for the purposes of computation of the deduction under section 80-IC provisions. Dy. CIT [2006] 155 Taxman 330 (Guj.).

Receipts from sale of import entitlements - The source of the import entitlements cannot be said to be the industrial undertaking of the assessee. The source of the import entitlements can, in the circumstances, only be said to be the Export Promotion Scheme of the Central Government whereunder the export entitlements become available. In the instant case, the nexus is not direct but only incidental. The industrial undertaking exports processed sea food. By reason of such export, the Export Promotion Scheme applies. Thereunder, the assessee is entitled to import entitlements, which it can sell. The sale consideration therefrom cannot be held to constitute a profit and gain derived from the assessee's industrial undertaking, so as to be eligible for deduction - CIT v. Words & phrases - 'industrial undertaking' occurring in section 80HH(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on business of manufacturing different brands of IMFL products. The business of the assessee was to process raw alcohol and sell the same with a new brand name. According to it, production of potable liquor involved dilution of the alcohol which was the raw material with de-mineralised water to prepare an admixture of alcohol and the same had to be properly blended with the right amount of essence and colouring substance by which an entirely new product emerged which had got a different name like brandy, whisky and rum etc. in the market and, therefore, it was entitled to the benefit of deduction under section 80HH. On the other hand, the revenue submitted that by mere blending of spirit and bottling the same, there, was no change in the commodity and, hence, the process of blending did not amount to manufacture; further, the quality of the original remained in the end products also.

HELD: The undisputed facts of the instant case were that the assessee purchased potable spirit from the distilleries as per agreement. This potable spirit was already manufactured and did not require any further manufacturing. Only some processing was required to produce IMFLs like brandy, whisky and rum etc. by adding certain percentage of water, colour, essence and, for safe marketing, required bottling. Generally manufacturing means consumption of one article for production of another. But, in the instant case, no article or thing was consumed for production of another. Alcohol remained alcohol. There was only reduction of degree of alcohol content because of addition of water to potable alcohol and stirring it. This action at best could be said to be processing and not manufacturing. There should also be transformation of article or thing if manufacturing is involved for the same. But, in the instant case no such transformation had taken place as alcohol remained alcohol both in the beginning and after processing also. In case of manufacturing also, article or thing should be distinct and separate. In the instant case, no new product had come as a by-product which could be said to be distinct and separate from the original one and alcohol remained alcohol with reduced content of alcohol because of the addition of water. There was also no change in its basic identity. Generally in case of manufacturing there will be change which is considerable and substantial but in the instant case it was not so. In order to encourage industrial activity in backward areas, section 80HH grants deduction to an assessee, whose total income includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking (other than a mining undertaking) or the business of a hotel in a notified backward area. Section 80GG(1) defines the word 'derived' from an industrial undertaking. The meaning of the term 'derived' has been construed to have a definite narrow and restrictive meaning compared to the word 'attributable' or 'referable to'. The industrial undertaking must itself be the source of the profits and gains and it would not be sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits and gains earned and the industrial undertaking. From section 80HH(2) it is clear that the Act has not given any definition of the expression 'industrial undertaking'. The requirement of section 80HH(2) is that to be eligible, the industrial undertaking should be one which is engaged in the manufacture or production of an article or thing. Therefore, the expression can be understood by looking upto the meaning as understood in common parlance or by making a reference to its definition in cognate legislation.

The assessee claimed deduction under section 80-IB(1) read with section 80-IB(4) at hundred per cent of its profit stating that it was engaged in the manufacture of electrical power distribution and control equipments [electrical control panels] at its undertaking located at Daman (UT), a backward area.

The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of deduction on the grounds that (i) the assessee's workers were mounting bought out components on the panel and wiring them and, therefore, the processes involved, though loosely termed as 'manufacture', was essentially only an assembly job, (ii) the assessee was procuring goods on a contract basis from the contractors, who supplied electric control panels as assembled by them at their own premises located at Kalyan, Thane and Mumbai, as the case may be, (iii) there was low power consumption, and (iv) there was low quantum of plant and machinery.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim of deduction.

On second appeal:

Sub-section (2) of section 80HH lays down certain conditions, one of which is that the industrial undertaking should manufacture or produce articles in any backward area and another condition is that it should employ 10 or more workers in the manufacturing process carried on with the aid of power. It was not the case of the revenue that any of these conditions were not fulfilled. Their only case was that the entire manufacturing activity from beginning to end was not carried on in the backward area and an initial part of it had been entrusted to the contractors who carried on that part of the activity outside the backward area. The contention, therefore, was that the profit shown as the profit of the industrial undertaking in the backward area might actually include a small part of the profit derived from activity outside the backward area and, therefore, there was inflation of the profit and consequentially inflation of the deduction claimed by the assessee, that could be withdrawn by reopening the assessment. [Para 5]

Sub-section (7) of section 80HH provides for this contingency by stating that where it appears to the Assessing Officer that owing to the close connection between the assessee carrying on the business to which this section applies and any other person, the business between them is so arranged that it produces to the assessee more than the ordinary profit, the profits and gains of this industrial undertaking may be reasonably estimated. In the instant case also, if the Assessing Officer had carefully scrutinised the accounts of the assessee and drawn the inference that because of the entrustment of the initial part of the contract process to contractors, the income from the industrial undertaking was likely to be inflated, with reference to the profit derived from the backward area, he could have reasonably estimated the profit instead of accepting the profit as shown by the assessee. That estimate, he failed to do at the time of the assessment and he sought to do the same by reopening the assessment. The question was whether he could do it by stating that there was an omission on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts. In the case of Parashuram Pottery Works Co. Ltd. v. ITO [1977] 106 ITR 1, the Supreme Court stated that the duty of an assessee in any case does not extend beyond making a true and full disclosure of primary facts. Once he has done that, his duty ends. It is for the ITO to draw the correct inference from the primary facts. It is no responsibility of the assessee to advise the ITO with regard to the inference, which he should draw from the primary facts. If an ITO draws an inference which appears subsequently to be erroneous, mere change of opinion with regard to that inference would not justify initiation of action for reopening assessments. In the instant case, the ITO failed to draw an inference that because of the entrustment of the initial manufacturing activity to contractors, the income derived from the industrial undertaking with reference to the backward area could be inflated and to that extent the income had to be estimated for confining the deduction to that profit which could be said to have been derived only from the backward area. Failing to draw that inference, blame could not be put on the assessee, when at the time of assessment the list of contractors, the quantity of beedies manufactured and the amount paid had been disclosed by the assessee. That disclosure was admitted in the counter affidavit. The ITO was not able to specify what extra information was required by him to have applied his mind to draw that inference for reducing the deduction to which the assessee was entitled. As long as it was not possible for the ITO to specify the exact information which was required and which was not disclosed, it was not possible to accept the claim that there was no true and full disclosure in the case. When that jurisdictional fact was not established, the ITO could not issue a notice under section 147(a). In the circumstances, the impugned notices were quashed. [Paras 6 & 7]

The writ petition was allowed. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH, read with section 80-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertakings, etc., in backward areas - Assessment years 1988-89 and 1989-90 - Whether, where assessee was engaged in business of fire works on job work basis and was supplied with raw materials by its customers and had engaged 200 labourers for producing end- product of crackers, it could be said that assessee had satisfied test of manufacturer as well as an industrial undertaking - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of fire works on job work basis. It was supplied with the raw materials by its customers, and had engaged coolies, viz., 200 labourers, to produce crackers. The assessee claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of the assessee on the ground that the assessee was only a labour contractor and not an industrial undertaking eligible for the benefits of sections 80HH and 80-I. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal held that the assessee was an industrial under-taking eligible for the benefits of sections 80HH and 80-I.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the assessee had only been supplied with the raw materials by its customers and of course, the assessee had engaged coolies, viz., 200 labourers, to produce the end-product of crackers. Thus, the assessee satisfied the test of manufacturer by producing the new material, namely, crackers, and also satisfied the test of industrial undertaking, as the assessee had involved in a systematic activity, organized by cooperation between employer and employees, viz., 200 labourers, and for the production and distribution of goods, viz., new product, crackers. [Para 10.3]

In that view of the matter, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal rightly held that the assessee was an industrial undertaking eligible for the benefits of sections 80HH and section 80-I . [Para 11]

15. Relevant provisions of section 80HH are reproduced below:—

"Deduction in respect of profits & gains from newly established industrial undertakings or hotel business in backward areas.—(1) Where the gross total income an assessee includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking, or the business of a hotel, to which this section applies, there shall, in accordance with and subject to the provisions of this section, be allowed, in computing the total income of the assessee, a deduction from such profits and gains of an amount equal to twenty per cent thereof.

(2) This section applies to any industrial undertaking which fulfils all the following conditions, namely:—

Ex planation.—Where any machinery or plant or any part thereof previously used for any purpose in any backward area is transferred to a new business in that area or in any other backward area and the total value of the machinery or plant or part so transferred does not exceed twenty per cent of the total value of the machinery or plant used in the business, then, for the purposes of clause (iii) of this sub section, the condition specified therein shall be deemed to have been fulfilled."

Lastly the learned Standing Counsel while summerising the arguments submitted that the production of whisky, brandy and rum amounts to only processing and not manufacturing and, therefore, the benefits of Section 80HH are not available to the assessee. 7. We have considered the submissions of the parties, gone through the appellate order in the assessee's own case for the assessment year 1983-84 and the decision A. Joseph Louis's case (supra). We have also perused the case laws relied on by both the parties which have already been mentioned in the foregoing paragraphs. We may state here the fact which is not in dispute is that the assessee purchases potable spirit from Rampur Distilleries as per the agreement. This potable spirit is already manufactured and does not require any further manufacturing. Only some processing is required to produce IMFLs like brandy, whisky and rum etc. by adding certain percentage of water, colour, essence and for safe marketing requires bottling. Generally manufacturing means consumption of one article for production of another. But in the instant case no article or thing is consumed for production of another. Alcohol remains alcohol. There is only reduction of degree of alcohol content because of addition of water to potable alcohol and stirring it. This action at best can be said to be processing and not manufacturing. There should also be transformation of article or thing if manufacturing is involved for the same. But in the instant case no such transformation has taken place as alcohol remains alcohol both in the beginning and after processing also. In case of manufacturing also article or thing should be distinct and separate. In the instant case no new product has come as a bye-product which can be said as distinct and separate from original one and alcohol remained alcohol with reduced content of alcohol because of addition of water. There is also no change in its basic identity. Generally in case of manufacturing there will be change which is considerable and substantial but in the instant case it is not so. Here we consider necessary to refer Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961. In order to encourage industrial activity in backward areas, this section grants deduction to an assessee, whose total income includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking (other than a mining undertaking) or the business of a hotel in a notified backward area. Section 80GG(1) defines the word "derived" from an industrial undertaking. The meaning of the term "derived" has been construed to have a definite narrow and restrictive meaning compared to the word "attributable" or "referable to". The industrial undertaking must itself be the source of the profits and gains and it would not be sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits and gains earned and the industrial undertaking. From Section 80HH(2) of the Act it is clear that the Act
has not given any definition of the expression "industrial undertaking". The requirement of Section 80HH(2) is that to be eligible, the industrial undertaking, should be one which is engaged in the manufacture or production of an article or thing. Therefore, the expression can be understood by looking upto the meaning as understood in common parlance or by making a reference to its definition in cognate legislation. In this connection we may mention the Supreme Court's decision in the case of N.C. Bhudharaj & Co. (supra) wherein their Lordships have held that construction of a 'dam' did not amount to production or manufacture of an article or thing. That the words used in the Act, take their colour from the context in which these are used. That the expression "manufacture" or "produce" are normally associated with movable articles or goods. That the words "article" and "things" are used interchargeably. That these words never denote construction of a dam or building. That the word "article" in Section 80HH(2) cannot include, a dam, a bridge, a building, a road, a canal or so on.

In the accounting year relevant to assessment year 1997-98, the assessee-company set up an industrial undertaking for the manufacture of applique/indexes for watch dials in a backward area. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the stand of the Assessing Officer.

In appeal, the assessee contended that it started its commercial production on 1-1-1996, and that the production carried out for the period 4-10-1995 to 1-1-1996 was only a trial production and that too did not involve the complete manufacturing process, and thus, the condition stipulated in Explanation 2 to section 80-IA(3) had to be examined on the basis of value of plant & machinery on 1-1-1996.
