The Assessing Officer had required the assessee to give specific information regarding establishment of the factory No. III as new industrial undertaking and also required the assessee to prove that it fulfilled the conditions laid down in sections 80HH and 80-I. The assessee furnished its explanations and documentary evidences to prove that the said factory No. III was set up as a new industrial undertaking and commenced production in March 1984 relevant to the assessment year 1985-86. The said factory No. III was given a new factory licence and central excise licence. The Central Excise authorities also certified that the first dispatch from the said factory took place only on 29-3-1984. Therefore, before the Assessing Officer in the assessment proceedings, the assessee had brought on record sufficient material and evidence to prove that a new industrial undertaking was set up during the calendar year 1984 relevant to the assessment year 1985-86. In the assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95, the deductions under sections 80-I and 80HH were allowed in respect of profits of factory No. III. Those orders were not made subject-matter of appeals or revision and the deductions allowed by the Assessing Officer had become final. In the above factual circumstances, therefore, in the succeeding assessment years on the same set of facts, the revenue authorities accepted factory No. III as new industrial undertaking eligible to deductions under sections 80-I and 80HH. On those facts, therefore, there was no justification for the Commissioner to doubt the establishment of factory No. III as new industrial undertaking only in the assessment year 1991-92. Though the principle of res judicata was not strictly applicable to revenue proceedings, yet the said principle was no stranger to the tax proceedings. If on the same set of facts the revenue authorities in the later years allowed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I to factory No. III treating it as an industrial undertaking set up in the assessment year 1985-86, then there was no reason for the Commissioner to disturb the finding of the Assessing Officer in the assessment year 1991-92 as the Commissioner did not bring on record any specific evidence to prove contrary. Therefore, the Commissioner was not justified in doubting the establishment of factory No. III as new industrial undertaking during 1985-86. [Para 23]

During the assessment year 1985-86, the deduction under section 80HH was permissible to a newly established undertaking if it was situated in any of the districts specified in the eighth schedule. By Notification dated 19-12-1986, the Central Government notified list of backward districts and District Udaipur was included therein. The Raj Samund Block of Udaipur District, where factory No. III was situated, was in excluded category of the said notification. However, the CBDT in its circular No. 484 dated 1-5-1987 had clarified that all areas specified in the Eighth Schedule continued to enjoy the benefit of section 80HH if the industrial undertaking had begun manufacture before 10-9-1986. Therefore, factory No. III situated in Raj Samund Block of Udaipur District was eligible for deduction under section 80HH since it began production in March 1984 as certified by the Central Excise authorities. [Para 24]

According to the Commissioner, factory No. III merely represented expansion of the assessee’s existing business and, therefore, not eligible for beneficial deductions as no new business was set up. However, this proposition has not been accepted by the Supreme Court as well as by the various High Courts. In the assessee’s own case for the assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95, the department had allowed deduction under sections 80-I and 80HH in respect of profits derived by factory No. III. Therefore, the order of the Assessing Officer, allowing deductions under sections 80HH and 80-I considering factory No. III as new industrial undertaking was supported by various judicial decisions wherein it was held that for claming the deductions it was not necessary to manufacture a new or different product. Therefore, the order of the Assessing Officer on this issue could not be considered as erroneous. [Para 25]

[1984] 145 ITR 416 that the relief provided under section 80J is an incentive to the assessee which has established a new industrial undertaking, which is available for the full five years inclusive of the year in which the manufacturing operations started and the relief depends not only upon the commencement of production but also on the capital employed. As regards the assessee's claim for higher development rebate, item (2) of the Fifth Schedule includes aluminium, copper, lead and zinc (metals). The question is whether 'aluminium caps' cannot be considered as 'aluminium metal' within the meaning of the said item (2). It is clear from the observations of the Supreme Court in State of Madhya Bharat v. Hiralal [1966] 17 STC 313 that if a metal has been used as a raw material for making an article which is known and accepted in common or commercial parlance as a specific article, then that article can no more be understood basically as a metal. In the instant case, the assessee was manufacturing aluminium caps from the aluminium metal which was a raw material in the form of sheets. The said finished product could hardly be said to be aluminium metal. To call it aluminium metal would perhaps be an abuse of the word 'metal' used in item (2). If that is the interpretation given, then no article made of aluminium could escape item (2).

Thus, the assessee was not a manufacturer of aluminium metal within the meaning of item (2) of the Fifth Schedule and was not entitled to higher development rebate.

The matter required to be re-examined so as to give a finding by the Assessing Officer whether those amounts written back by the assessee were claimed as deduction in any earlier year. If such deduction was claimed and allowed in any earlier year then clearly there was reduction of profit in those earlier years and once the creditors remitted the liability or liability ceased to exist and assessee declared it as part of the profit then nexus of such profit written back with the industrial undertaking was not severed. It was because while allowing deduction the eligible profits of the business derived from the industrial undertaking were reduced as they were allowable expenditure. Once the liability ceased to exist in favour of the assessee then they become profits of the assessee in the current year as per provisions of section 41(1). When one examines the nexus of the profit with the industrial undertaking it is not to be seen as to from whom the profit is derived but it is to be seen whether it is derived from the business. So long money is recoverable from the parties or payable to the parties during the course of business the transactions have a direct nexus with the business and one cannot view these transactions away from the business. Such transactions include receipts and payment of money in cash or in kind immediately or on credit and are part of business activities. If the assessee had to make the payment to the above four parties, which were standing in the balance sheet as creditors and which had been claimed as business deduction in an earlier year then only course left to the assessee was either to make the payment or if no payment was legally required, to show as profit under section 41(1) which had been so done by the assessee. There was a clear and direct business connection of such cessation or remission and such profits taxable under section 41(1) could be held as derived from industrial undertaking. The arguments of the revenue that they were not current year's profit from manufacturing activity was devoid of any merit because deduction under section 80-IA is available only on profits derived from industrial undertaking which is carrying on manufacturing activities and it is not confined to only current year's profit as per profit and loss account. The deduction under section 80-IA or 80-IB is available on profits and gains computed in accordance with section 20A-43D which includes section 41(1) also. [Para 11]

Thus, where Assessing Officer finds that claim has already been allowed in the earlier year then such benefit under section 80-IA should be given to the profit taxed under section 41(1). The argument of assessee was that once it had declared profits under section 41(1) it would mean that the assessee has already claimed and allowed deduction thereof in earlier years but it required verification and for that matter the matter was to be restored to the file of Assessing Officer. HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from newly established industrial undertakings in backward areas - Assessment years 1983-84 to 1987-88 - Whether process of processed (including frozen) fish and fish products should be regarded as an activity of manufacture or production of an article, or thing entitled to benefit of section 80HH - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacture or production of frozen sea foods from shrimps obtained from the sea. The catch obtained from the sea was cleaned, beheaded, deskinned, sorted, frozen and was converted or produced into frozen sea foods which were exported in packs to foreign countries. The assessee claimed that it was an industrial undertaking engaged in the business of manufacture or production of frozen sea food and, thus, claimed deduction under section 80HH. The ITO allowed the said claim of the assessee. The Commissioner, however, exercising his powers under section 263, disallowed the said deduction.

On appeal :

HELD: In section 80HH the words ‘manufacture’ or ‘produce’ appear. The same words appear in section 33 of the Act which relates to grant of relief of development rebate to the assessee. It is implicit in section 33(1)(b )(B)(i ) that processed (frozen).fish and fish products produced by the assessee constituted new commercial article compared to raw fish as far as provisions in section 33 were concerned. Thus, the legislative intent under the provisions of the Act is that process of the processed (including frozen) fish and fish products should be regarded as an activity of manufacture or production of an article or thing eligible for grant of development rebate. There is no reason why the same intent should not be presumed to be present in enacting section 80HH where same words ‘manufacture’ or ‘production’ of articles have been used. Consequently, as far as the Act was concerned, processing which resulted in processed (including frozen) fish and fish products amounts to an activity of manufacture or production of an article or thing within the ambit of sections 33 and 80HH. Consequently, in the present case, the activity of the assessee would be regarded as an activity of manufacture or production of an article or thing. Accordingly, the order of Commissioner was to be set aside and that of the ITO was to be restored.

As per the provision of section 80-IA, the same would be applicable to a company, which manufacture or produce any article or things. In the present case, the assessee company perform work in the nature of business for repairing and manufacturing of transformer. It has also been contended by the assessee that the company has been manufacturing aluminium HT/LT Leg Coils, which were used in old burnt transformers and in this regard, it had also submitted in detail before the assessing authority. The company did not manufacture or produce transformer oil and scrap, rather it has purchased the T/Oil from the market and only centrifuging has been done and no new article or things has been produced/manufactured, only processing has been done. In the processing scrap, it had obtained from old/burnt Transformers Coils, which were made of aluminium wires of different amperes. It also appeared from the record that the scrap has not been manufactured/produced. Certain more small parts have been purchased and have been used in manufacture of new HT/LT Leg Coils. It also appears that the assessee has purchased the transformer oil from the market and after centrifuging the transformer oil by centrifugal machine, the centrifuged transformer oil has been made useful in old/burnt transformer. It is a sort of processing only and cannot be termed as manufacture of centrifuged transformer oil. [Para 19]

It is apparent that the assessee did indulge in processing activities, but no manufacture or production of new articles or things is involved in this processing. [Para 20]

Here we consider necessary to refer section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961. In order to encourage industrial activity in backward areas, this section grants deduction to an assessee, whose total income includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking (other than a mining undertaking) or the business of a hotel in a notified backward area. The meaning of the term "derived" has been construed to have a definite narrow and restrictive meaning compared to the word "attributable" or "referable to". The requirement of section 80HH(2) is that to be eligible, the industrial undertaking, should be one which is engaged in the manufacture or production of an article or thing. That the words used in the Act, take their colour from the context in which these are used. That the expression "manufacture" or "produce" are normally associated with movable articles or goods. FACT: The assessee-company, a small-scale industrial undertaking, was carrying on the business of manufacturing ‘Jarda’ from raw tobacco in a backward area. The processing operations employed by the assessee were that raw tobacco (angad) was stripped off the midrib by manual labour. It was then sand-screened to control the moisture content. The raw tobacco was fed into a vibratory feeder and it was conveyed into a pneumatic pick up duct where heavy stems and stones would drop down. In the pick up duct, the tobacco was lifted up by suction and discharged into first tower classifier. In this tower classifier, the heavier tobacco flakes were separated from lighter ones and left behind. The lighter flakes were carried by air into second tower classifier. Here, the tobacco dust and flakes were differentiated. Finally, the lamina was sent to a sleeve chamber where it was cut and graded to suit the requirement of beedi manufacturer. The pure tobacco flakes came out after the dust was sucked out in the dust collecting unit. The end-product was called ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’. The assessee claimed reliefs under sections 32A, 80HH and 80-I for the assessment years 1984-85 and 1985-86. The assessee also claimed that it should be charged at a concessional rate treating it as an industrial company as defined under section 2(8)(c) of the Finance Act, 1985. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claims on the ground that the assessee was not manufacturing or producing any article or any thing. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance.

On second appeal:

HELD: The instant case was not a border line case and a firm conclusion was easily approachable. By subjecting tobacco to treatment beedi patti was produced. By ginning cotton, pure cotton is obtained or pressed cotton is produced. Raw wool subjected to processing to eliminate dirt, grease and other vegetable matter results in production of pure wool. Leather is said to be manufactured when raw hide is treated. In all these cases a different product in commercial realm is said to be produced. In the same strain, it was equally possible to say that ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’ was produced or manufactured from raw tobacco as a result of some manual or mechanical treatment, or both. Anybody could go to the market and purchase the article known as raw tobacco and it is equally possible to go and purchase in the market an article called Jarda or Jardi. The physical property in raw tobacco and Jarda or Jardi might be same. While raw tobacco is unfit for beedi manufacture in the same condition, Jarda or Jardi can ready be used in the beedi manufacture. In commercial parlance Jarda or Jardi is distinctively different from raw tobacco. For the aforesaid reasons, in the instant case, the assessee’s business was one of manufacture or production of an article or thing. The assessee’s business undertaking was in a backward area and there was no dispute about it. Then, if the assessee was manufacturing or producing an article, it must be taken that all the conditions in sub-section(2) of section 80HH were fulfilled. The assessee was having a mechanised tobacco processing plant which was even patented. It was registered as a small scale industrial unit by the Government. The most vital was the schedule of assets which formed part of the balance sheet, which showed that the cost of machinery employed was below the limit placed in Explanation to section 32A(2) or Explanation 3 to section 80-I(2), read with section 80HHA(8). The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the reliefs under sections 32A, 80HHA and 80-I. Since the assessee was found manufacturing an article it should be treated as an industrial company as defined in the Finance Act, though even processing, which the assessee was certainly doing, may be sufficient to justify a claim for concessional rate of tax. Thus, the assessee was also entitled to concessional rate of tax for both the years being an industrial company within the meaning of section 2(8)(c).

1.2-6 Manufacture of any item is permitted - Additional depreciation would be available to any undertaking including those manufacturing items listed in Eleventh Schedule. This is unlike section 80-IB which provides that the deduction under that section is not available to any undertaking other than a small scale undertaking if it manufactures or produces any article or thing specified in the Eleventh Schedule.

1.2-7 ‘Not formed by transfer to a new business of old machinery’ - The section defines a new industrial undertaking as an undertaking which is not formed by the transfer to a new business of machinery or plant previously used for any purpose. Similar expression is found in section 10A/10B/80-IA/80-IB. However, in those sections it is provided that if the value of machinery or plant transferred does not exceed 20% of the total value of the machinery or plant used in the business then the condition prohibiting transfer of old machinery should be deemed to be complied with. Now, a similar exception is not provided in the provision relating to additional depreciation. Does this mean that transfer of machinery of any insignificant value will disentitle the assessee from the grant of additional depreciation? In this context the meaning of the word ‘formed’ as given by the Supreme Court in Bajaj Tempo Limited v. CIT [1992] 196 ITR 188 becomes relevant.

In that case, the new industrial undertaking for which deduction under section 15C of the Income-tax Act, 1922 was claimed had taken a building on lease and some tools and implements valued at Rs. 3,500. The Assessing Officer argued that the undertaking was formed by transfer of the building and machinery previously used in another business.

The Supreme Court held as follows :

“The word ‘form’ according to the dictionary has different meanings. In the context in which it has been used it was intended to connote that the body of the company or its shape did not come up in consequence of transfer of machinery and plant used previously for business purpose. Use of the negative before the word ‘formed’ further strengthens it. In other words, machinery and plant used previously in other business should not result in the undertaking being formed by it. The transfer to take out the new undertaking out of the purview of the provision must be such that but for transfer the new undertaking could not have come into being.”

It observed that since on the facts, the part played by taking the building on lease was not dominant, the undertaking was not formed by such transfer.

Applying the ratio of the aforesaid judgment, it is submitted that transfer of machinery (of any insignificant value or otherwise) which does not result in formation of the industrial undertaking or without which the undertaking could have come into being should not disentitle the assessee from the grant of additional depreciation.

1.2-8 Eligible assessee - The benefit is available only if the machinery or plant is acquired and installed by an assessee engaged in the business of manufacture or production of an article or thing. Hence, the deduction will not be available to any assessee who is not engaged in a business of manufacture or production.

Further, even in the case of such assessee who is engaged in manufacture/production, the first proviso to section 32(1)(iia) provides that the deduction shall be allowed to an industrial undertaking. Now, any deduction including depreciation (especially with the block of assets concept) is available to an assessee and not to an undertaking. Hence, the purpose/effect of this proviso is not clear; perhaps, the intention is to allow deduction only in respect of machinery or plant installed in the industrial undertaking manufacturing or producing such article or thing and not to machinery or plant which is not installed in such industrial undertaking. It may be noted that section 32A which dealt with grant of investment allowance clearly provided that the said allowance was available only in respect of machinery or plant installed in an industrial undertaking [section 32A(2)(b)].

1.2-9 Plant and machinery used outside India - Unlike other sections where use of a machinery or plant outside India does not disentitle an assessee from claiming a deduction [see Explanation 1 to section 80-IB(2), sections 10A, 10B, etc.], under this section, deduction is not allowed even if the machinery or plant is used outside India.

1965, only sales made in nature of any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure or any sales in connection with or ancillary to such trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure were taxable. Thus, intention of doing the business measured by volume, frequency, continuity or regularity as well as profit motive was essential to tax a sale transaction. Any sale of goods done without intention of doing a business in those goods or without profit motive was not taxable. In this context Apex Court in the case of State of Gujarat v. Raipur Manufacturing Co. Ltd. [1967] 19 STC 1 had taken a view that to bring ancillary sales under tax net it must be shown by the revenue that they were made with an intention to do business and earn profit. It relied on its own decision in the case of State Of Andhra Pradesh v. Abdul Bakhi and Bros AIR 1965 SC 531. It was held that when a person in the course of carrying on a business is required to dispose of what may be called his fixed assets or his discarded goods acquired in the course of the business, an inference that he desired to carry on the business of selling his machinery or fixed assets or discarded goods would not ordinarily arise. Hence, the same will not be taxable.

Legislators amended the definition of 'business' by providing that any sale made in the nature of any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure; whether or not there was intention of makingany gain or profit; as well as sales in connection with or incidental orancillary to such trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure shall be covered.

First important decision on the issue post the amendment was rendered by the Hon. Supreme Court in the case of State of Tamil Nadu v. Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Co of India Ltd. [1973] AIR 1045. In this case the respondent under the Factories Act had to supply tea and edibles to its workmen for the Canteen established by it. It also supplied to its distributors calendars, purses and key chains. They also periodically sold items such as scraps, unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, rims, etc., Issue before the Court was whether these sales were 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' to the business ?

Before the above case, the Hon. Madras High Court in the case of Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. Sri Thirumagal Mills Limited [1967] 20 STC 287 had taken a view that even if by way of amendment to the definition of 'business' profit motive is deleted as an ingredient, still the ancillary activity has to be of commercial nature. It should still partake the nature of 'trade, commerce, manufacture, etc.' specified in the first limb and only then it can be taxed. Hence, it was held that turnover of fair price shop run for the employees will not be leviable to tax.

The Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court on the contrary in the case of Hyderabad Asbestos Cement Products Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh [1969] 24 STC 487 (SC) had taken a view that for an ancillary sale to be taxed it is not required that the same must be done with an intention of doing business. Any ancillary sale connected with the business shall be taxable.

The Hon. Supreme Court in the case of Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Co. of India Ltd. (supra) did not agree with the decision of the Hon. Madras High Court and affirmed the ratio decided by the Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court.

It held that the Hon. Madras High Court had not paid sufficient attention to word 'such' as appearing in clause 'any transaction in connection with, or incidental or ancillary to, such trade, commerce, manufacture,adventure or concern'. Hence, it held that after the omission of profitmotive, any sale which is ancillary to business whether or not made with an intention to do business of such ancillary goods shall be taxable. The Hon. Supreme Court thus held that once a transaction is covered within the ambit of terms 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' the same shall be taxable, whether or not there was any intention to do business in the commercial sense of 'business' in these ancillary goods.

In the given case the Apex Court held that whether sale of scrap such unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, etc, is ancillary to the business is a finding of fact. However, it observed that as the respondent was an oil company, all those items were parts of the business activity of trading in oil and, hence, the same were taxable. 3. Hurdle in expansion

Where a company buys land with an intention to earn rental income from it or to earn profit by dividing it into smaller plots, the company can be said to have been engaged in the rental business or sale of land. Where a co., after commencing the manufacturing operations, begins such activities, the option of Section 115BAB shall be withdrawn for that assessment year and for all subsequent assessment years. Thus, if a domestic manufacturing company intends to expand its operations which are not directly related to its manufacturing activities, income arising from such activities should be classified either as income from incidental activity or income from non-manufacturing business. Where company earns huge profit from incidental activities (like, sale of scrap, interest income, etc.) it can continue to remain in new tax regime, but earning minimal profits from non-manufacturing business will render it ineligible for the new regime. The incidental income will be taxable on gross basis at the rate of 22% without claiming any deduction for any allowance or expense. In case some income arises from non-manufacturing activity, the company will have to switch its taxability from Section 115BAB to Section 115BAA or Section 115BA or provisions of the Finance Act.

The companies, with plans to expand their operation to non-manufacturing areas, should ensure that they undergo such activities in a new company. The manufacturing co. should remain a manufacturing co. if it does not wish to lose the benefit of 15% corporate tax rate.

Issues

The sections 115BAA and 115BAB start with a non-obstante clause and overrides the other provisions of the Act. However, the sections are subject to the provisions of Chapter XII.

Owing to manner in which the sections have been introduced in the Act, certain issues have emerged which would need clarification, which are briefly discussed here-in-below:

1. Applicable tax rate on Long-term capital gains, short-term capital gains on listed securities and income under other heads

The sections do not override the provisions of Chapter XII of the Act i.e. provisions contained in the said chapter would hold forte. Hence special rates mentioned in sections 111A, 112, 112A, etc. would continue to apply.

Having regard to the language used in the sections, in our view, companies having income from House Property, Short-term capitals gains (other than on listed securities) and Income from Other Sources viz. bank interest, etc. should be taxed at 17.16%/ 25.168% if the reduced tax rate regime is opted for. A new manufacturing company holding sizeable rent yielding real estate and fixed deposits would stand to benefit (on account of lower tax rate of 17.16%) as compared to any other company having similar sources of income. The tax authorities may however, seek to dispute the adoption of section 115BAB by such companies by contending that the intention is not to extend benefit of lower taxes to non-business income.

2. Whether past MAT credit would be allowed

Sub-section 5A of section 115JB has been amended stating that provisions of section 115JB would not apply to companies which have exercised option to be governed by the aforesaid regime. It may be noted that no amendment has been made in section 115JAA of the Act which deals with utilization of MAT credit on account of MAT paid in earlier years. A plain reading of the provisions, in our view, suggest that past MAT credit available to an existing company should be allowed as a set-off against the tax liability under section 115BAA. There is no express prohibition in section 115BAA to deny MAT credit unlike several other deductions and losses specifically mentioned.

In our view, the MAT credit to be allowed in a year should be limited to the difference between the tax liability under section 115BAA and that under section 115JB which would have been payable. The fact that provisions of section 115JB are not applicable should not impact the computation of the credit which is separately provided in section 115JAA(5) and is an independent exercise for the purpose of determining and granting MAT credit only.

However, considering that the section seeks to override all the provisions of the Act, there may be litigation on the issue.

3. Applicability of interest under section 234B, 234C, etc.

The new sections start as under:

"(1) notwithstanding anything contained in this Act……"

On account of the non-obstante clause in the sections which overrides the other provisions of the Act, there could be an argument that interest under section 234B and 234C cannot be levied.

Section 115JB of the Act has similar non-obstante clause but also has a sub-section (5) which states as under:

Special provision for payment of tax by certain companies.

The undisputed facts of the instant case were that the assessee purchased potable spirit from the distilleries as per agreement. This potable spirit was already manufactured and did not require any further manufacturing. Only some processing was required to produce IMFLs like brandy, whisky and rum etc. by adding certain percentage of water, colour, essence and, for safe marketing, required bottling. Generally manufacturing means consumption of one article for production of another. But, in the instant case, no article or thing was consumed for production of another. Alcohol remained alcohol. There was only reduction of degree of alcohol content because of addition of water to potable alcohol and stirring it. This action at best could be said to be processing and not manufacturing. There should also be transformation of article or thing if manufacturing is involved for the same. But, in the instant case no such transformation had taken place as alcohol remained alcohol both in the beginning and after processing also. In case of manufacturing also, article or thing should be distinct and separate. In the instant case, no new product had come as a by-product which could be said to be distinct and separate from the original one and alcohol remained alcohol with reduced content of alcohol because of the addition of water. There was also no change in its basic identity. Generally in case of manufacturing there will be change which is considerable and substantial but in the instant case it was not so. In order to encourage industrial activity in backward areas, section 80HH grants deduction to an assessee, whose total income includes any profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking (other than a mining undertaking) or the business of a hotel in a notified backward area. Section 80GG(1) defines the word 'derived' from an industrial undertaking. The meaning of the term 'derived' has been construed to have a definite narrow and restrictive meaning compared to the word 'attributable' or 'referable to'. The industrial undertaking must itself be the source of the profits and gains and it would not be sufficient if a commercial connection is established between the profits and gains earned and the industrial undertaking. From section 80HH(2) it is clear that the Act has not given any definition of the expression 'industrial undertaking'. The requirement of section 80HH(2) is that to be eligible, the industrial undertaking should be one which is engaged in the manufacture or production of an article or thing. Therefore, the expression can be understood by looking upto the meaning as understood in common parlance or by making a reference to its definition in cognate legislation.

In the instant case, the alcohol in the beginning and after processing also remained alcohol. No distinct article or thing had been produced. Alcohol remained alcohol throughout the processing stage till it was marketed. There is no difference between potable spirit and whisky or brandy except in the process of production, water and certain essences have been added to them. Therefore, although it had undergone a degree of processing, it
must be regarded as still retaining its original identity. The original commodity was alcohol and the commodity produced had also remained alcohol. Therefore, it would be said that no commodity was consumed in the manufacture of another in the instant case. Therefore, there was no essential difference between the potable spirit and the bottled IMFLs. The dealer and the consumer both regard it as alcohol. The only difference was that in potable spirit some water and essences were added and bottled up nicely to make it presentable for marketing. Therefore the above discussion clearly showed that the bottled IMFLs and potable spirit must be held to possess the same character, identity as the original before its bottling. Hence, the activities of the assessee did not involved any manufacturing but only processing and, therefore, it was not entitled to the benefit of section 80HH.

Further, the legislature has used the words "manufacture" or "production". Therefore, the word "production" cannot derive its colour from the word "manufacture". Further, even according to the dictionary meaning of word "production", the word "produce" is defined as something which is brought forth or yielded either naturally or as a result of effort and work. The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to Section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions, and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production, new words are not being added to Section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. In view of the aforesaid, it could not be said that retreading of tyres resulted in the production of an article[CIT v. Madurai Pandian Engineering Corpn. Ltd. 9.4-4c Article or thing - The word "article" is not defined in the Act or the Rules. It must, therefore, be understood in its normal connotation, the sense in which it is understood in the commercial world. The word "articles" in Section 80HH is preceded by the words "it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce". The word "articles" occurring in Section 80HH(2)(i) does not comprehend and take within its ambit a dam, a bridge and so on. If a dam is an article, so would be a bridge, a road, an underground canal and a multi-storeyed building. To say that all of them fall within the meaning of the word "articles" is to overstrain the language beyond its normal and ordinary meaning. It is equally difficult to say that the process of constructing a dam is a process of manufacture or a process of production. It is true that a dam is composed of several articles, viz., stones, concrete, cement, etc. But to say that the end product, the dam, is an article is to be unfaithful to the normal connotation of the word. A dam is constructed; it is not manufactured or produced. The expressions "manufacture" and "produce" are normally associated with movables - articles and goods, big and small - but they are never employed to denote the construction activity of the nature involved in the construction of a dam or for that matter a bridge, a road or a building [CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 70 Taxman 312 (SC)]

Therefore, the tribunal was right in allowing the deduction under Section 80HH and Section 80-I to the assessee, holding that the ship breaking activity gave rise to the production of a distinct and different article [Vijay Ship Breaking Corpn. v. CIT [2008] 175 Taxman 77 (SC)]

The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to Section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions, and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production, new words are not being added to Section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. In view of the aforesaid, it could not be said that retreading of tyres resulted in the production of an article[CIT v. Madurai Pandian Engineering Corpn. Ltd. [1999] 239 ITR 375 (Mad.) affirmed in Tamil Nadu State Transport Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [2001] 252 ITR 883 (SC)].

9.4-4c Article or thing - The word "article" is not defined in the Act or the Rules. It must, therefore, be understood in its normal connotation, the sense in which it is understood in the commercial world. The word "articles" in Section 80HH is preceded by the words "it has begun or begins to manufacture or produce". The word "articles" occurring in Section 80HH(2)(i) does not comprehend and take within its ambit a dam, a bridge and so on. If a dam is an article, so would be a bridge, a road, an underground canal and a multi-storeyed building. To say that all of them fall within the meaning of the word "articles" is to overstrain the language beyond its normal and ordinary meaning. It is equally difficult to say that the process of constructing a dam is a process of manufacture or a process of production. It is true that a dam is composed of several articles, viz., stones, concrete, cement, etc. But to say that the end product, the dam, is an article is to be unfaithful to the normal connotation of the word. A dam is constructed; it is not manufactured or produced. The expressions "manufacture" and "produce" are normally associated with movables - articles and goods, big and small - but they are never employed to denote the construction activity of the nature involved in the construction of a dam or for that matter a bridge, a road or a building [CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 70 Taxman 312 (SC)]

the development rebate has not been fully set off against the total income of the assessee in the past assessment years and a part of it has remained unabsorbed and is carried forward that it can be set off against the profits or gains of the business for the particular assessment year. But if the whole of the development rebate has been absorbed and no part of it is carried forward, there can be no question of allowing it against the profits or gains of the business for the assessment year in question. Now, sub-section (3) of section 15C of the 1922 Act provides that the profits or gains of a new industrial undertaking shall be computed under section 10 of 1922 Act and, therefore, according to clause (vi) read under proviso (b) to section 10 of 1922 Act, no part of the depreciation allowance and according to clause (vib), Explanation 1 of section 10 of 1922 Act, no part of the development rebate in respect of the new industrial undertaking for the past assessment years can be allowed as a deduction in computing the profits and gains, unless it has remained unabsorbed by reason of inadequacy of the total income chargeable to tax in the past assessment years—and, by total income we mean not only profits or gains derived from the new industrial undertaking but the totality of profits or gains computed under various heads—and is carried forward to the assessment year in question. There is nothing in sub-section (3) of section 15C of the 1922 Act or in any other provision of the Act which requires that in computing the profits or gains of a new industrial undertaking under section 10 of the 1922 Act, depreciation allowance or development rebate in respect of the new industrial undertaking for the past assessment years should be taken into account, even if it has been set off fully against the profits or gains of any other business carried on by the assessee or against income under any other head and there is no unabsorbed depreciation allowance or development rebate to be carried forward. It is indeed difficult to see how effect can be given to depreciation allowance and development rebate twice over, once in the past assessment years and again in the assessment year in question. To give effect to depreciation allowance or development rebate for the past assessment years, even though it has been set off and absorbed completely against the total income of the assessee for those assessment years would be to allow a deduction not warranted by any provision of the Act and indeed it would be going contrary to the express provision of proviso (b) to clause (vi ) and Explanation 1 to clause (vib) of section 10 of 1922 Act. Sub- section (3) of section 15C of 1922 Act clearly does not have any such effect. What it does is no more than provide as to how "the profits or gains derived from new industrial undertaking" referred to in sub- section (1) of section 15C shall be computed. If sub- section (3) of section 15C of 1922 Act had not been enacted, it might have been a matter of some controversy as to what is meant by the expression "the profits or gains derived from new industrial undertaking". Does it mean commercial profits or gains or profits or gains chargeable to tax or does it have any other connotation ? It was to set this controversy at rest that sub- section (3) of section 15C of 1922 Act enacted that the profits or gains of the new industrial undertaking shall be computed in accordance with the provisions of section 10 of the 1922 Act. Sub- section (3) of section 15C of 1922 Act does not enact any legal fiction providing that the profits or gains of the new industrial undertaking shall be computed as if the new industrial undertaking were the only business of the assessee from the date of its establishment or the past years, depreciation or development rebate had not been set off against other income of the assessee. The new industrial undertaking is not retrospectively quarantined or isolated from the other income producing activities of the assessee for determining its profits or gains for the purpose of applicability of sub- section (1) of section 15C of 1922 Act. What sub- section (3) of section 15C of 1922 Act does is merely to lay down the same rule of computation for the profits or gains of a new industrial undertaking as in respect of any other business and, therefore, neither depreciation allowance nor development rebate in respect of the new industrial undertaking for the past assessment years can be allowed as a deduction in computing the profits or gains for the assessment year in question, except where and to the extent to which, it has not been set off against the total income of the assessee for those assessment years and has remained unabsorbed. This is the plain and undoubted effect of the language used in sub- section (3) of section 15C of the 1922 Act. Indeed, the language is so clear and unambiguous that it is impossible to place any other construction upon it

MANUFACTURE/PRODUCTION* General tests - Manufacture and processing are not clearly demarcated fields. The test of manufacture lies in the answer to the question whether what is processed or produced as the end-product is commercially known as a different product from the materials out of which it is so produced. Therefore, if the product has a different name and is identified by the buyers and sellers as a different product and is bought and sold as a distinct product from its raw materials, one can say that it is a manufactured product. There may be some room for debate as to whether this test is fully satisfied by edibles that come as end-products from the raw materials out of which they are made. But the expression 'produce' has to be taken in a more liberal sense than manufacture. If the end-product is different, that by itself would suffice to meet the requirement of 'producing'. Hence, an exclusive catering unit of a hotel supplying eatables in bulk for consumption by air passengers will be eligible for relief - CIT v. East India Hotels Ltd. [1994] 209 ITR 854 (Cal.).

Department should study actual process undertaken by assessee - Section 80-IA comes in Chapter VI-A. That Chapter, in any way, is a code by itself. It provides for special deductions. Broadly, these special deductions are incentives provided for setting up industrial undertakings in backward areas, for earning profits in foreign exchange, for setting up hotels, etc. It is in this background that one has to interpret the meaning of the expression 'manufacture or processing of goods'. One more aspect needs to be highlighted. Technological advancement in computer science makes knowledge as of today obsolete tomorrow. One needs to move with the times. At the same time, one needs to take note of the fact that unlimited deductions are not permissible under Chapter VI-A. Therefore, in each case, where an issue of this nature arises for determination, the department should study the actual process undertaken by the assessee - CIT v. Oracle Software India Ltd. [2010] 187 Taxman 275 (SC).

Tyre retreading is not 'manufacture' - Tyre retreading does not amount to manufacture. - Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [2001] 252 ITR 883 (SC).

Ginning of cotton is a process - Ginning of cotton is also a process of manufacture, and hence, a ginning factory is an 'industrial undertaking' entitled to deduction - Poonam Chand Prem Raj v. CIT [1994] 207 ITR 895 (Raj.).

Packing of tea is not covered - The words 'manufacture' and 'production' apply to a case which brings into existence something different from its components. [Para 29] The deduction under section 80-IA is available to an assessee whose gross total income includes profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking as per stipulations in section 80-IA(2), which, inter alia, requires the manufacturing or production of an article or thing not being any article or thing specified in the Eleventh Schedule. In the instant case, the assessee was manufacturing components of cooling towers in its factory unit at ‘C’, which in turn were exigible to excise duty. The profits on sale of said components were entitled to deduction under section 80-IA and as allowed by the Assessing Officer. The assessee was not in the business of sale of components of cooling towers, but the cooling tower as a whole. The assessee purchased various bought out components, which along with manufactured components were assembled at the client’s site and the cooling tower was erected. The ultimate product erected by the assessee was a cooling tower, which was a distinct product from the various components, bought from outside or manufactured by it.

The said activities of the assessee were covered within the definition of manufacture of an ‘article’ or ‘thing’. The assessee had undertaken the job of erection of cooling tower as per the individual specification of the client, and after erection, the assessee gave guarantee for the performance of the cooling tower as a whole and not that of manufactured items only. All the activities carried on by the assessee fell within the ambit of ‘manufacture’ or ‘production’ of an article or thing. The end-product being the cooling tower, the assessee was entitled to claim of deduction under section 80-IA on the whole including profits on manufactured items and bought out components. [Para 31]

Therefore, the assessee was also entitled to the benefit of deduction under section 80-IA - both on the manufactured items and the bought out components used for the erection of cross flow (XE series) and counter flow (CM series) cooling towers. In view of the decision that the assessee was not entitled to any deduction under section 80-IA on round bottle (RB) cooling towers, no deduction/benefit under section 80-IA would be allowed on bought out components used for erection of round bottle cooling towers. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was directed to allow the deduction under section 80-IA only on profits on sale of cross flow (XE series) and counter flow (CM series) cooling towers. [Para 32]

The next question for consideration was as to whether the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA on the installation charges, forwarding charges and service charges received from the clients. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of the assessee observing that all these charges had no connection with the manufacturing activities of the assessee. The assessee was engaged in the manufacturing of cooling towers, which were manufactured as per the specific requirements of the clients, who in-turn attached it to their industrial units. The cooling tower being voluminous, the erection of the same was carried out at the sites of the clients. The forwarding charges and installation charges were billed to the clients. The service charges were received from clients against services provided to them. The said charges were linked to the manufacturing activity carried on by the assessee. The said receipts were to be included in profits derived from manufacturing operations. [Para 33]

The assessee had also incurred certain expenditure on transportation and also on installation by way of payment to contractor and any expenditure linked to providing the services shall be debited to the gross receipts received from clients. The assessee would also be entitled to the benefit of deduction under section 80-IA only on net receipts from installation, forwarding and service charges. It must be held to be implicit in the word "manufacture". Having regard to the fact that the word "production" or the word "produce" is used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" these terms also must be regarded as referring to production, which brings into existence a new article. As to what is a new article has been explained by Pathak J., as he then was, in the test proposed by him, in the case of Pio Food Packers [1980] 46 STC 63, adopted by the apex court in the case of N.C. Budharaja and Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412, to section 80HH of the Income-tax Act. An article is new when the substance out of which it is made is different and distinct from the new article. The new article being commercially different from the one from out of which the new article was made. The identity of the old article must cease and the distinct identity of the new article must have been established commercially. On this aspect, we may usefully refer to the recent decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. J.G. Glass Industries Ltd, [1998] AIR 1998 SC 839; [1999] 114 STC 387, wherein the court held after a review of the earlier decisions of the Supreme Court interpreting the word "manufacture" used in the Sales Tax Act and in the Central Excises Act, that (page 844) "On an analysis of the aforesaid rulings, a two fold test emerges for deciding whether the process is that of 'manufacture'. First, whether by the said process a different commercial commodity comes into existence or whether the identity of the original commodity ceases to exist; secondly, whether the commodity which was already in existence will serve no purpose but for the said process." In that case, the court was dealing with a claim that printing of names or logos on the bottles brings into existence a new commercial commodity. The court rejected the claim by observing that the plain bottles are themselves commercial commodities and the basic character of the commodity, viz., being bottles does not change as a result of the printing of names or logos on the bottles.

Counsel submitted that even by applying the test stated in the case of J.G. Glass Industries Ltd. [1998] AIR 1998 SC 839, production of retreaded tyres must be held to be an instance of manufacture, as the worn out tyres, which are retreaded, have no commercial value and it is only after retreading, they acquire a value, although at all stages they are regarded as tyres intended for the same use. This argument overlooks the fact that the new tyre is manufactured, and that a new tyre is intended to serve the user for a fairly long period of time. The tyre continues to be a tyre throughout and when it is worn out, it may be either discarded or its life renewed by retreading, so that it is made serviceable for some more time. The commodity at all stages is the tyre. There is no change in the character of that commodity. A different and distinct commodity cannot be said to have come into existence as a result of the retreading.

Fish processing - Fish processing is not manufacture or production of an article and, therefore, assessee engaged in fish processing is not entitled to deduction under section 80-IA - Bhatsons Acquatic Products v. CIT [2011] 198 Taxman 51 (Ker.) (Mag.).

Activities undertaken by assessee in converting raw fish into tinned fish amounted to processing and not manufacturing and, therefore, assessee was not entitled to deduction under section 80-IB - CIT v. Gitwako Farma (I) (P.) Ltd. [2011] 10 taxmann.com 261 (Delhi).

Preparation of foodstuffs/food packages by hotels does not amount to manufacture - In a case of preparing food packages or selling the same or preparing food-stuffs for serving in the hotel there is no question of manufacture or production - Indian Hotels Co. Ltd. v. ITO [2000] 245 ITR 538 (SC).

Canteen - Canteen cannot be said to be an 'industrial undertaking' as it does not manufacture or produce any article or thing - Escorts Tractors Ltd. v. CIT [2012] 211 Taxman 38/27 taxmann.com 95 (SC).

Conversion of chicory roots into chicory powder is not manufacture - Where the assessee was engaged in the activity of purchasing chicory roots from farmers and converting them into chicory powder, the assessee cannot be treated as an 'industrial undertaking', even though it had been registered as a small-scale industry and its claim for being treated as an industry had been accepted under the Wealth-tax Act. There is no element of 'manufacture' in this case, since chicory powder is chicory in powder form and nothing else, and mere change in the form of the same commodity does not necessarily involve change of identity - Sacs Eagles Chicory v. CIT [2002] 123 Taxman 24 (SC).

Conversion of plain glassware into decorative glassware - The transformation of plain glassware into decorative glassware with a process which is irreversible, and marketing the end-product as a commodity different from plain glass, is a process of 'manufacture'. The assessee engaged in such business is eligible for deduction under section 80-I - CIT v. Darshak Ltd. [2001] 247 ITR 489 (Kar.).

Ship-breaking activity - Ship-breaking activity results in production of a distinct and different article and, therefore, assessee doing said activity would be entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I - Vijay Ship Breaking Corpn. v. CIT [2008] 175 Taxman 77 (SC).

Applying the yardsticks adopted by the Supreme Court in CIT v. N.C. Budharaja & Co. [1993] 204 ITR 412, ship-breaking activity gives rise to manufacture and production of altogether new commercial article or thing which is commercially identifiable in the commercial world as other than the ship. An assessee engaged in such activity is entitled to claim deduction under section 80-I - Ship Scrap Traders v. CIT [2001] 251 ITR 806 (Bom.).

In order to be eligible for deduction under section 80-IA, the gross total income of an assessee must include profits derived from any business (eligible) of an industrial undertaking which in terms of section 80- IA(12)( b) is given the same meaning as is assigned to that expression vide the Explanation to section 33B. As can be seen from the Explanation to section 33B, an industrial undertaking, inter alia, has been defined to mean any undertaking which is engaged, inter alia, in the manufacture or processing of goods. [Para 6]

Section 80-IA comes in Chapter VI-A. That Chapter, in any way, is a code by itself. It provides for special deductions. Broadly, these special deductions are incentives provided for setting up industrial undertakings in backward areas, for earning profits in foreign exchange, for setting up hotels, etc. It is in this background that one has to interpret the meaning of the expression 'manufacture or processing of goods'. One more aspect needs to be highlighted. Technological advancement in computer science makes knowledge as of today obsolete tomorrow. One needs to move with the times. At the same time, one needs to take note of the fact that unlimited deductions are not permissible under Chapter VI-A. Therefore, in each case, where an issue of this nature arises for determination, the department should study the actual process undertaken by the assessee. Duplication can certainly take place at home; however, one needs to draw a line between duplication done at home and commercial duplication. Even a pirated copy of a CD is a duplication, but that does not mean that commercial duplication as undertaken in the instant case should be compared with home duplication which may result in pirated copy of a CD. The point to be noted by the department in each of such cases is to study the actual process undertaken by the licensee who claims deduction under section 80-IA. [Para 7]

In the instant case, it was found that the software on the master media was an application software. It was not an operating software or a system software. It could be categorized into 'Product Line Applications', 'Application Solutions' and 'Industry Applications' . A commercial duplication process involves four steps. For the said process of commercial duplication, one requires master media, fully operational computer, CD blaster machine (a commercial device used for replication from Master Media), blank/unrecorded compact disc, also known as recordable media and printing software/labels. The master media is subjected to a validation and checking process by software engineers by installing and rechecking the integrity of the master media with the help of the software installed in the fully operational computer. After such validation and checking of the master media, the same is inserted in a machine which is called as the CD Blaster and a virtual image of the software in the master media is thereafter created in its internal storage device. This virtual image is utilized to replicate the software on the recordable media. Virtual image is an image that is stored in computer memory but it is too large to be shown on the screen. Therefore, scrolling and panning are used to bring the unseen portions of the image into view. [ Paras 8 and 9]

If one examines the above process in the light of the details given hereinabove, commercial duplication cannot be compared to home duplication. Complex technical nuances are required to be kept in mind while deciding issues of the instant nature. The term 'manufacture' implies a change, but every change is not a manufacture, despite the fact that every change in an article is the result of a treatment of labour and manipulation. However, this test of manufacture needs to be seen in the context of the above process. If an operation/process renders a commodity or article fit for use for which it is otherwise not fit, the operation/process falls within the meaning of the word 'manufacture'. Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, it was clear that the assessee had undertaken an operation which rendered a blank CD fit for use for which it was otherwise not fit. The blank CD was an input. By the duplicating process undertaken by the assessee, the recordable media, which was unfit for any specific use, got converted into the programme which was embedded in the Master Media and, thus, blank CD got converted into recorded CD by the aforestated intricate process. The duplicating process changed the basic character of a blank CD, dedicating it to a specific use. Without such processing, blank CDs would be unfit for their intended purpose. Therefore, processing of blank CDs dedicating them to a specific use, constitutes a manufacture in terms of section 80-IA(12)( b) , read with section 33B. [Para 10]

Compound rubber produced by the assessee on the job work basis for the tyre manufacturing companies was an intermediary product, from which tyre was manufactured. If the processing of iron ore, which is only raw material for producing iron therefrom, amounts to manufacture or production of any article or thing, then there was no reason why compound rubber could not be treated as an article produced by the assessee, though for the tyre manufacturing company under contract. In other words, there is nothing in the section to indicate that article or thing produced or manufactured should be final product in itself. So much so, the activity of the assessee in its new industrial unit, which was mixing rubber with chemicals, process oil, etc., for making compound of rubber, was covered by section 80-IB. The word "manufacture" or "produce articles" used in the provision to section 80HH have not been defined in the Act. The word "manufacture" has been considered by the Supreme Court and the High Courts on numerous occasions and the common thread which runs in all the decisions is that it is only when a new and distinct commodity commercially accepted as such, comes into existence as a result of the processing, that a commodity can be said to have been manufactured.

Having regard to the fact that the word "article" used in the section is an article which is manufactured or produced and the word "produce" having been used in juxtaposition with the word "manufacture" it connotes the bringing into existence of new goods. The result of production should be the coming into existence of a new article. The terms "production" and "produce" would also take in by-products, intermediate products and residual products. All of them should be products or articles, which are capable of being regarded as new articles. By holding that a "new" article should emerge from manufacture or production new words are not being added to section 80HH. The term new has been employed in the decisions of the courts only to indicate the end result of the process of production or manufacture. It is only when that result can be said to have been achieved, that the industrial undertaking which brings about such a result by its process of production or manufacture, would qualify for the benefits conferred under the section. In view of aforesaid, it could not be said that retreading of tyres resulted in the production of an article for the purpose of section 80HH.

Hence, the Tribunal was not right in holding that the business of tyre retreading amounted to the production of a new article entitling the assessee to the relief under sections 80J and 80HH.

Therefore, even if the undertaking is established by transfer of building, plant or machinery, but it is not formed a result of such transfer, the assessee could not be denied the benefit.".

(i) The assessee may continue to produce the same kind of article as hitherto but that is not a relevant factor at all to consider whether the section is attracted. What is relevant is that the industrial unit set up must be new. In that sense, though new plant and machinery are erected for producing either the same commodities or some distinct commodities, it should not be a case of reconstruction of the old business. The assessee will have to plead and establish that a new unit has come into existence which independently produces articles of whatsoever nature and that this new unit is not dependent upon the old existing unit, in the sense that the new unit cannot be equated as an expansion of the old unit [Canara Wire & Wire Products Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 196 ITR 426 (Kar.)].

(j)

The true test is not whether the new industrial undertaking connotes expansion of the existing business of the assessee, but whether it is all the same a new and identifiable undertaking, separate and distinct from the existing business. The reconstruction of a business or an industrial undertaking must necessarily involve the concept that the original business or undertaking is not to cease functioning, and its identity is not to be lost or abandoned. The concept essentially rests on changes, but the changes must be constructive and not destructive. There must be something positive about the whole matter as opposed to negative. The underlying idea of a reconstruction evidently must be - as is brought out by the section itself - of a 'business already in existence'. There must be a continuation of the activities and business of the same industrial undertaking, which must continue to carry on the same business, though in some altered or varied form. If the alteration and changes are substantial, there would be little scope for describing what emerges as a reconstruction of the business. From the perusal of the section, it is clear that the statute itself has envisaged and approved of a situation in which an old existing, smaller industrial undertaking is absorbed by a new and much bigger industrial undertaking. In the instant case, only capacity had been increased, and there was an expansion of the old business with some modifications. As for the reconstruction of the business, it was nowhere evident that the old industrial unit was split up or damaged or destroyed and was supposedly reconstructed as a new unit by the assessee. What the assessee had done was to set up an industrial undertaking with the latest technology and increased capacity and, of course, with a fairly good amount of fresh investment. The formation of the new undertaking was not as a consequence of the transfer of the plant or machinery of the old business. The value of the plant and machinery utilised in the new undertaking had been less than 20 per cent of the total investment. Thus, the assessee's case also did not get disqualified under this provision. Investment in new plant and machinery was Rs. 104.88 lakhs. Investment in old plant and machinery was Rs. 20.86 lakhs. In that view of the matter, the conclusion was inevitable that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA in respect of the profits of the new industrial undertaking having satisfied the requisite conditions [CIT v. 62 Taxman 480 (SC), it was held that "even though this decision was concerned with the clause dealing with reconstruction of an existing business, the expression "not formed" was construed to mean that the undertaking should not be a continuation of the old but emergence of a new unit. Therefore, even if the undertaking is established by transfer of building, plant or machinery, but it is not formed a result of such transfer, the assessee could not be denied the benefit.".

(i) The assessee may continue to produce the same kind of article as hitherto but that is not a relevant factor at all to consider whether the section is attracted. What is relevant is that the industrial unit set up must be new. In that sense, though new plant and machinery are erected for producing either the same commodities or some distinct commodities, it should not be a case of reconstruction of the old business. The assessee will have to plead and establish that a new unit has come into existence which independently produces articles of whatsoever nature and that this new unit is not dependent upon the old existing unit, in the sense that the new unit cannot be equated as an expansion of the old unit [Canara Wire & Wire Products Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 196 ITR 426 (Kar.)].

(j)

The true test is not whether the new industrial undertaking connotes expansion of the existing business of the assessee, but whether it is all the same a new and identifiable undertaking, separate and distinct from the existing business. The reconstruction of a business or an industrial undertaking must necessarily involve the concept that the original business or undertaking is not to cease functioning, and its identity is not to be lost or abandoned. The concept essentially rests on changes, but the changes must be constructive and not destructive. There must be something positive about the whole matter as opposed to negative. The underlying idea of a reconstruction evidently must be - as is brought out by the section itself - of a 'business already in existence'. There must be a continuation of the activities and business of the same industrial undertaking, which must continue to carry on the same business, though in some altered or varied form. If the alteration and changes are substantial, there would be little scope for describing what emerges as a reconstruction of the business. From the perusal of the section, it is clear that the statute itself has envisaged and approved of a situation in which an old existing, smaller industrial undertaking is absorbed by a new and much bigger industrial undertaking. In the instant case, only capacity had been increased, and there was an expansion of the old business with some modifications. As for the reconstruction of the business, it was nowhere evident that the old industrial unit was split up or damaged or destroyed and was supposedly reconstructed as a new unit by the assessee. What the assessee had done was to set up an industrial undertaking with the latest technology and increased capacity and, of course, with a fairly good amount of fresh investment. The formation of the new undertaking was not as a consequence of the transfer of the plant or machinery of the old business. The value of the plant and machinery utilised in the new undertaking had been less than 20 per cent of the total investment. Thus, the assessee's case also did not get disqualified under this provision. Investment in new plant and machinery was Rs. 104.88 lakhs. Investment in old plant and machinery was Rs. 20.86 lakhs. In that view of the matter, the conclusion was inevitable that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA in respect of the profits of the new industrial undertaking having satisfied the requisite conditions [CIT v. Mahaan Foods Ltd. [2009] 177 Taxman 274 (Delhi)].

There must be direct nexus between the income and the industrial undertaking meaning thereby, the source of income must be the industrial undertaking. If the source of the income is other than the industrial undertaking than it cannot be said that such income is derived from the industrial undertaking.

With regard to the issue of duty drawback, perusal of section 75(1) of Customs Act, 1962 clearly shows that the duty drawback is given by way of incentive to boost the export of goods manufactured in India. If any imported goods on which custom duty has been levied, has been used in the manufacture of any goods of any class or description and such manufactured goods have been exported out of India, then custom duty paid on imported goods is given back to the manufacturer by way of rebate. This duty drawback is given only to manufacturers making export as is apparent from sub-section (2) of section 75. In other words, it is nothing but reimbursement of duty already paid. Whenever such duty is paid, it directly affects the profits of industrial undertaking inasmuch as it is debited to Manufacture & Profit and Loss account. Such payment of custom duty increases the cost of manufacturing but when the same is received back as drawback, it nullifies the effect of aforesaid increase in the cost of manufacturing. Therefore, the duty drawback is inextricably linked with the production cost of the goods manufactured by the assessee. Accordingly, duty drawback is the trading receipt of the industrial undertaking having direct nexus with the activity of such industrial undertaking and accordingly, the same forms part of the income derived from such industrial undertaking. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was, therefore, upheld with reference to this item.

For the similar reasons, the assessee was entitled to succeed in respect of claims received from insurance company and transporters. The payment of freight charges to the transporter as well as the premium to the insurance company is directly connected with the activity of the industrial undertaking affecting the profits of the business and consequently, refund thereof has a direct nexus with such business activity. The details furnished before the Tribunal clearly showed that amount received from transporters was on account of shortage of rubber and tyres transported. Further the claim from insurance company was on account of the damage of stock due to flood. So, there was direct nexus between the amount received from the transporter/insurance companies and the activity of the industrial undertaking. Accordingly it was to be held that such receipts formed part of the profits derived from industrial undertaking.

As far as income from sale of import entitlement was concerned, the same did not form part of profits derived from industrial undertaking in view of the decision in the case of CIT v. Sterling Foods [1999] 237 ITR 579/ 104 Taxman 204 (SC).

As far as difference in foreign exchange was concerned, it was not clear from the facts of the case whether such foreign exchange was utilised in the field of capital or revenue. Therefore, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was set aside on this issue and the matter was restored to the file of the Assessing Officer who was directed to allow the claim of the assessee if it was found that foreign exchange was utilised in the revenue field. However, if it was found that it was utilised in the capital field then the Assessing Officer might not include the same in the business profits derived from industrial undertaking.
