During the financial year 1991-92, the assessee had set-up a new unit at ‘C’ in order to revamp its business activities and ente- red into collaboration agreement with a foreign company ‘G’ and obtained technical know-how for making ‘cross flow’ (XE series) and ‘counter flow’ (CM series) cooling towers. The assessee had also closed down its original unit situated at ‘O’ during the year 1992 and plant and machinery and moulds from the ‘O’ unit were transferred to the new unit at ‘C’. As per the assessee the total extent of such items transferred was 11.60 per cent of the total investment in new plant in terms of cost and 0.63 per cent in terms of WDV. Most of the employees of the old unit were also transferred to the new unit and certain new employees were also recruited. The assessee thereafter started manufacturing in the new unit, certain components required for cooling towers, i.e., RB series, XE series and CM series. The modus operandi of the assessee in carrying out business was that on receipt of enquiries from the clients, it designed the cooling tower as per requirement of the clients and the quotations were forwarded to the clients along with detailed analysis of the said towers. The assessee on receipt of the orders from the clients manufactured the basic compo-nents required for the said cooling towers in its unit and certain items/components like electric motors, fans, etc., were purchased from the market. As per the assessee, these items were tested and checked in the factory of the assessee. The said components, i.e., manufactured and bought out items were transferred to the site of the customers and two separate invoices were prepared, one for in-house manufactured components on which excise duty was paid and another for the bought out components and, accordingly, the sales were shown under the head ‘Manufactured items and bought out components’. The assembly of the unit and erection of the same was carried out at the customer’s site and the assessee in addition raised the bill for installation charges, forwarding charges and service charges, which were booked under the respective heads in the books of account. For the relevant assessment years, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80-IA on the total turnover of the manufactured items during the year, including sale of bought out components, installation charges, forwarding charges and service charges. The Assessing Officer held that the new unit set-up by the assessee manufactured the items required for XE and CM type cooling towers only and the machinery, which had been shifted from the old unit, manufactured the parts required for round bottle cooling towers; and that since the moulds required for manufacturing the round bottle and CM/XE type cooling towers were independent and totally different and the assessee started manufacturing both under one roof for the sake of convenience and the old equipment was acquired in the year 1985 while the new equipment was purchased in 1992, the profits arising from the sale of items manufactured by the assessee for round bottle cooling towers were not eligible for deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer further held that bought out components purchased by the assessee from the market were never integrated at the assessee’s factory into the cooling tower and tested and, therefore, the assessee was not manufacturing the cooling tower but manufacturing only certain parts required for cooling towers and assembling the cooling tower at the clients’ place as per the requirement of the clients. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the profit earned by the assessee on the bought out components did not have any nexus with the manufacturing activity carried out by the assessee in its factory and the said profit could not be treated as profits of industrial undertaking for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer in respect of the forwarding charges, installation charges and service charges held that the assessee had incurred expenditure on account of transport, labour charges both for loading/unloading and assembling, which were not adjusted against the receipts and, therefore, all these charges did not have any connection with the manufacturing activity of the assessee and, accordingly, the profit earned by the assessee on the said charges was not eligible for deduction under section 80-IA. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 80-IA only in respect of profits arising from sale of components manufactured by the assessee required for XE and CM cooling towers. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the impugned order.

Section 10B is a special provision in respect of newly established 100 per cent Export Oriented undertakings: Subject to the provisions of section 10B, a deduction of such profits and gains as are derived by a hundred per cent Export Oriented Undertaking from the export of articles or things or computer software for a period of ten consecutive assessment years shall be allowed from the total income of the assessee. To attract this provision, the assessee has to comply with the requirement mentioned in sub-section (2). One of the requirements is that the products so exported should have been manufactured by the assessee or it should be an article or thing produced by the assessee. It is only then, the benefit of section 10B is available.

In the instant case, the assessee is importing spare parts. The said spare parts are used in the production of articles for export. Those spare parts which are used for producing articles are extended the benefit of section 10B, there is no dispute on that count. The dispute is that, when the spare parts are imported and without any change or they being used in any production/manufacturing activity, if they are exported, the profits and gains derived from such export is eligible for the benefit under section 10B of the Act having regard to the condition prescribed under sub-section (2) which is a conditions precedent for availing the benefit under section 10B.

Until those conditions are fulfilled, the assessee is not entitled to the benefit of section 10B. When the assessee imports spare parts and exports them in the same condition, may be along with the articles produced and the spare parts exported are not involved in any manufacturing activity or in production activity. Section 10B is not attracted. Therefore, all the three authorities have rightly held that the assessee is not entitled to the benefit of section 10B. In the facts and circumstances, there is no infirmity in the said orders.

However, when the income derived from the sale of spare parts is held to be ineligible for the benefit under section 10B, the entire amount representing the value of spare parts is to be excluded and the profits and gains derived from sale of such spare parts alone is liable for tax. That is the exercise to be undertaken by the assessing authority and the said amount is to be excluded. [Para 8]

Coming to the question of sale of scrap, no doubt the assessee is not in the business of export of scraps but is in the business of export of X-ray equipments, high voltage tanks and detectors used in CT scanners and after manufacturing these products, they are exported. In the process of manufacturing, the untilised raw materials forms part of scraps and that scraps also has value. But it is not exported and hence, they are eligible for the benefit under section 10B of the Act. The assessee should have earned profits and gains from such export of articles or things. The said articles or things should have been manufactured or produced by the assessee. The section does not require that the profits and gains derived should be from the articles or things which are exported only.

It is the profits and gains derived by an 100 per cent Export Oriented Undertaking from the export of articles. Therefore, when the assessee undertakes manufacturing activity or production activity and in process it results in any scraps, the scraps attract the nexus between the profits and gains derived from the assessee from export business and, therefore, it satisfies the requirements of section 10B and the Tribunal has rightly held that the assessee is entitled to the benefit of section 10B even in respect of the profits earned out of sale of scraps materials within country. In that view of the matter, there is no infirmity in the order passed by the Tribunal. [Para 11]

The instant case was not a border line case and a firm conclusion was easily approachable. By subjecting tobacco to treatment beedi patti was produced. By ginning cotton, pure cotton is obtained or pressed cotton is produced. Raw wool subjected to processing to eliminate dirt, grease and other vegetable matter results in production of pure wool. Leather is said to be manufactured when raw hide is treated. In all these cases a different product in commercial realm is said to be produced. In the same strain, it was equally possible to say that ‘Jarda’ or ‘Jardi’ was produced or manufactured from raw tobacco as a result of some manual or mechanical treatment, or both. Anybody could go to the market and purchase the article known as raw tobacco and it is equally possible to go and purchase in the market an article called Jarda or Jardi. The physical property in raw tobacco and Jarda or Jardi might be same. While raw tobacco is unfit for beedi manufacture in the same condition, Jarda or Jardi can ready be used in the beedi manufacture. In commercial parlance Jarda or Jardi is distinctively different from raw tobacco. For the aforesaid reasons, in the instant case, the assessee’s business was one of manufacture or production of an article or thing. The assessee’s business undertaking was in a backward area and there was no dispute about it. Then, if the assessee was manufacturing or producing an article, it must be taken that all the conditions in sub-section(2) of section 80HH were fulfilled. The assessee was having a mechanised tobacco processing plant which was even patented. It was registered as a small scale industrial unit by the Government. The most vital was the schedule of assets which formed part of the balance sheet, which showed that the cost of machinery employed was below the limit placed in Explanation to section 32A(2) or Explanation 3 to section 80-I(2), read with section 80HHA(8). The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the reliefs under sections 32A, 80HHA and 80-I. Since the assessee was found manufacturing an article it should be treated as an industrial company as defined in the Finance Act, though even processing, which the assessee was certainly doing, may be sufficient to justify a claim for concessional rate of tax. Thus, the assessee was also entitled to concessional rate of tax for both the years being an industrial company within the meaning of section 2(8)(c).

4.3.1.7 ISSUE NO. 7- Whether tax benefits under section 10AA can be enjoyed by an eligible SEZ unit consequent to its transfer to another SEZ?

4.3.1.7.1 THE CONTROVERSY- The revenue authorities are construing the newly shifted unit as having been formed by way of splitting-up or reconstruction of the existing SEZ unit and, hence, questioning the allowability of tax holiday claim in such cases. On the other hand, the industry players assert that mere shifting of a unit from one SEZ to another should not be a ground for denial of income-tax benefit, since the formation of undertaking criteria should be tested in the initial year of setting-up of a unit. It is also pleaded that the operational difficulties like accommodation of additional staff, space and desired location are overlooked by the revenue.

4.3.1.7.2 RECOMMENDATION OF RANGACHARY COMMITTEE- The tax benefit is attached to the undertaking and, therefore, the movement of an eligible SEZ unit from one SEZ to another should not be to the detriment of the unit. 4.3.1.7.3 CLARIFICATIONS IN CIRCULAR NO. 1- The Circular conforms to the views of the Rangachary Committee and clarifies that the relocated unit will be eligible to avail of the tax benefit for the unexpired period.

4.3.1.8.1 THE CONTROVERSY - If a new undertaking is set-up at the same location where there is an existing undertaking, the revenue regards it as an expansion of an existing undertaking and grants tax holiday only for the residual period commencing from the setting-up of the existing undertaking.

4.3.1.8.2 RECOMMENDATION OF RANGACHARY COMMITTEE- The Committee is of the view that there is no presumption, in law, that only one undertaking can be set-up under one license and can claim the benefits of sections 10A and 10AA. The facts of a particular case need to be examined in detail for determining the eligibility for deduction of the new undertaking.

On 20 September 2019, the government amended the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) vide The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019 (the Ordinance). The primary purpose of the Ordinance was to bring India's corporate tax rate at par with key competing economies. In addition to reducing the cost of capital, the reduced tax rate was also intended to act as a catalyst for companies to make fresh investments and consequently generate new avenues for employment.

Amongst other things, the Ordinance provided for reduced corporate tax rate of 15% under section 115BAB of the Act to new manufacturing companies which are not availing specified tax exemptions/incentives. The move was seen as a push towards the government's "Make in India" initiative and making India a US $5 trillion economy by 2024-25.

New manufacturing companies have been defined to mean companies which are formed after 1 October 2019 and begin to manufacture article or thing by 31 March 2023. While there are various conditions that a company needs to satisfy for claiming the lower tax rate, the main condition which is the subject matter of discussion in this article is as under:

"the company is not engaged in any business other than the business of manufacture or production of any article or thing and research in relation to, or distribution of, such article or thing manufactured or produced by it"

However, the term 'manufacture' or 'production' has not been defined under section 115BAB for the purpose of availing the reduced tax rate. Hence, it is generally understood that the definition of the term 'manufacture' as prescribed under section 2(29BA) of the Act may be relied upon while interpreting section 115BAB.

Section 2(29BA) of the Act defines the term 'manufacture' as follows:

"manufacture", with its grammatical variations, means a change in a non-living physical object or article or thing,—

(a)

resulting in transformation of the object or article or thing into a new and distinct object or article or thing having a different name, character and use; or

(b)

bringing into existence of a new and distinct object or article or thing with a different chemical composition or integral structure;

The government has on 25 November 2019 tabled the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2019 in the Lok Sabha. Amongst other things, the Amendment Bill seeks to clarify that business of 'development of computer software in any form or in any media' would not be regarded as a manufacturing activity for the purpose of section 115BAB.

It seems that the intention of the government is to only allow the reduced corporate tax rate to traditional manufacturing of physical goods generating large scale employment of unskilled and semi-skilled work-force, aka blue-collar jobs. Nevertheless, specifically excluding software development from the ambit of the section 115BAB could have more adverse consequences than originally anticipated.

Key arguments in favour of retaining software development within the ambit of 'manufacture' are discussed in the ensuing paragraphs.

Employment generation

As of 2018, the Information Technology (IT) industry employed nearly 39 lakh people in India. The industry is expected to add over 250,000 new jobs in 2019. [Source: Ibef.org]

It should be noted here that employment generation has been one of the major goal of the government to arrest the sliding economy. While traditional heavy manufacturing has a potential for employment generation, software development industry has also played a significant role in employment generation, albeit in white-collar jobs.

Impetus to Investments in IT industry

Because fresh investments have a cascading effect on various facets like employment generation and increase in disposable income etc, the government has taken various steps to attract investment, especially foreign investments. The liberalization of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) norms in manufacturing and more specifically related to contract manufacturing is a testament to this.

In this regard, it should be noted here that the computer software and hardware sector in India attracted cumulative FDI inflows worth US $37.23 billion between April 2000 and March 2019 and ranks second in inflow of FDI, as per data released by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)

This is despite the fact that India's share in the global software product market, which is valued at US $438 billion, is miniscule and the country continues to be a net importer of software products. The total software business in India stands at US $8.2 billion, out of which exports amount to a mere US $2 billion.

Keeping software development out of the ambit of manufacturing is also disconcerting since over the years, various Courts/Tribunals have held software development activity to be manufacturing under various provisions of the Act.

3.2 Bagasse held non-manufactured by Supreme Court : The Circular aforesaid was challenged successfully in Balrampur Chini Mills Ltd. v. UOI [2013] 30 taxmann.com 175 (Allahabad) and CCE v. Facts : Assessee was manufacturing sugarcane and molasses. In the process of manufacture of sugar, sugarcane is crushed, its juice is extracted and Bagasse emerges as residue/waste of sugarcane. Held :

No manufacture/deemed manufacture : Bagasse is only an agriculture waste and residue and not result of any process; hence, it is not covered in definition of 'manufacture' under section 2(f) of Central Excise Act, 1944. Further, there is no Chapter note or Section note in Central Excise Tariff declaring process in respect of bagasse as amounting to manufacture.

Not excisable, even if deemed to be marketable : Hence, notwithstanding amendment in 2008 in section 2(d) ibid, creating a fiction of deemed marketability, bagasse is not excisable as it is not passing test of 'manufacture'.

Cenvat Rule 6 inapplicable [for period prior to 1-3-2015] : Since bagasse is not excisable, hence, even if NIL-rated, cenvat rule 6 is inapplicable thereto. Therefore, denial of credit on electricity on ground that bagasse is excisable exempted goods, was incorrect.

Merely because goods satisfy test of being marketed and saleable and merely because goods are listed in tariff, it does not mean that they are 'manufactured goods'. In various judgments, Supreme Court held that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' are not manufactured goods and said view was followed in context of 'zinc dross and flux skimming'. 1. Our company took wrong cenvat credit of Rs. 100 in the month of Oct. 13 which was reversed in the month of Dec. 13. Actual Cenvat credit for the month of Dec. 13 was Rs. 150. Is Department's view correct or there are any case laws against this ?

It appears that the procedure stated by the department is correct; any reversal of ineligible credit taken in Oct., 2013 should be shown separately and cannot be netted off against eligible credit of Dec., 2013.

Having said that, it is also trite law that when reversal of credit of October 2013 has been made in December, 2013 (though using unrecognized procedure), no demand can be raised again. You may still claim that credit was taken in Oct. 13 and reversed in Dec. 13 but wrongly shown as net credit. Moreover, entire exercise is revenue neutral.

Nevertheless, the credit of Dec. 2013 can be taken even now because there was no time-limit to take credit at that time and time-limit of 6 months/1 year was introduced only from September 2014 and cannot apply to credits found to be eligible before September 2014.

In order to set over this controversy in the above definition of ‘input’, the Legislature has clarified that even if an item is not contained in the final product still it would be classifiable as an ‘input’ under the above definition. In other words, it has been clarified by the definition of ‘input’ that the following considerations will not be relevant :

(a)Use of input in the manufacturing process be it direct or indirect; and (b)even if the input is not contained in the ‘final product’ it would still be covered by the definition.

These considerations have been made irrelevant by the use of expression ‘goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ which, as stated above, is the crucial requirement of the definition of ‘input’. In this regard, some case laws are cited hereunder :

In J.K. Cement Works v. CCE 2010 (252) ELT 249 (Trib. - Delhi), it was held that only those goods which form part of the process carried out by a manufacturer for converting raw material into finished goods can be considered as inputs and the goods which are not integrally connected with the process of manufacture resulting in utilization of such product directly or indirectly in the manufacture of finished product cannot be said to be input. Therefore, oxygen, helium and acetylene gases used for repair and maintenance of plant and machinery are not covered by the definition of ‘input’.

In Reva Electric Car Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (250) ELT 149 (Trib. - Bang.), the Tribunal held that it is unambiguously clear that the rejection was at the pre-manufacturing stage and for no reasons attributable to the appellant. Rejection at the pre-manufacturing stage is also indispensable for quality control. It can be said that any rejection of input without ulterior motive or oblique purpose may not disentitle an assessee from the benefit of law relating to CENVAT credit.

It did not appear that the car manufacturer had escaped duty. The revenue should, therefore, allow entitlement of CENVAT credit in the absence of any violation of law. Accordingly, the demand of Rs. 6,90,150 on the count of using of inputs for R&D was unsustainable in the absence of any finding to show that the R&D had not resulted in finished goods and that finished goods had escaped duty. Exercise of Research having resulted in the finished goods and that had suffered duty, CENVAT credit was admissible for which demand of Rs. 6,90,150 was set aside.

In HIM Technoforge Ltd.’s case (supra), the respondent was a manufacturer of rough forgings and forging articles of steel falling under Chapter 7326 of the CETA, 1985. They also availed CENVAT credit of inputs and capital goods. The dispute related to ‘metal band saw blades’ and ‘steel shots’ as to whether they could be considered as capital goods as contended by the department or could be treated as inputs as claimed by the respondent. The original authority after taking note of the duration of use of these items and the purpose for which they were used held that they were capital goods.

The Commissioner (Appeals) treated the above products as ‘inputs’. He held that under the CENVAT Credit Rules, the term ‘input’ has been defined to mean all goods, except HSD oil, LSD and motor spirit used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. In view of this above definition of the ‘input’ under the CENVAT Credit Rules, both the items, namely, ‘metal saw blade’ and ‘steel shots’ used by the appellants in connection with the production of goods on consumable would merit classification under inputs only and, therefore, the credit taken by them was in order.

CCE 2010 (258) ELT 111 (Trib. - Ahd.), a small amount of Rs. 9,456 stood denied to the appellant on the ground that the credit had been availed on the waste and scrap, which could not be considered as an input for the appellant’s final product. The lower authorities had nowhere discussed as to how the waste and scrap could not be considered as an input. The cable waste of cut length was being utilized and consumed by the appellant in its own factory in the manufacture of finished goods. The duty paid cable waste received in the factory had been accounted for in the input register and its consumption had been shown in the manufacture of the final product. The final product manufactured out of the same was accounted for in the RG-1 Part I Register, which stood cleared on payment of duty. As such to deny the benefit of waste and scrap on the ground that the same was not an input was not justified.

1. We have two factories registered under central excise with the following details —

1st Factory - Manufacturer of fine chemicals falling under Chapter 34

2nd Factory - Declared as job worker (a bottling plant) of first factory.

We sent 100 Kgs. of chemicals to be packed in 100 gms. bottles to bottling plant. After completion of packing in small packs we received only 90 Kgs. chemicals packed in small container. What would be the treatment of non-collectible waste of 10% (10 Kgs. out of every lot of 100 kgs.) ?

It is clearly stated by you that both the factories are registered separately. In this case the manufacturing factory is clearing 100 Kgs. to job-worker and receiving back the same in entirety (subject to processing loss). The process loss of 10% will not be chargeable to duty, only if the same is normal process loss.

The benefit may be claimed under rule 21 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, as —

the same is due to natural causes or unavoidable reasons, and

is incurred prior to removal of finished goods from the factory.

An alternative view may be that only 90 Kg. is the manufactured product, because manufacture under section 2(f) is complete only after the completion of all incidental or ancillary processes, which include packing/bottling.

In any case, the duty can be levied only on 90 Kgs.

As per rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, credit is allowed of duty or tax paid on inputs or input services or capital goods used in factory/manufacture purposes.

The said credit may be used to pay duty on final product. Goods exported under claim of rebate are cleared on payment of duty and said duty can very well be paid by using Cenvat credit as per rule 3(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Taking classification put forth by you to be correct, since the goods are classifiable under Chapter 44, they are not listed in any of the categories of capital goods as provided in rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. However, if —

they are purchased as 'components or spares or accessories' of some other machinery ; and

such other machinery is a capital goods under rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004,

The classification and treatment under financial accounts is not relevant for the purpose of deciding eligibility to Cenvat credit.

MAITREE MUZUMDAR

According to the Export and Import Policy/Foreign Trade Policy, a Special Economic Zone is considered principally as a foreign territory when it comes to trade, duties & tariffs. The goods supplied thereto from a Domestic Tariff Area are treated as deemed exports and goods brought to a Domestic Tariff Area from there are treated as deemed imports in such a context. When materials are imported and used for the manufacture of goods that are manufactured in India and exported, a rebate called as drawback can be claimed on them. However, the difference between the 'import' and a 'deemed import' when it comes to claiming duty drawback on goods being sold by an SEZ unit to a DTA for input in export manufacture remains a question that has not been pondered upon. This article tries to understand if such a sale by SEZ is, in fact, a 'deemed import' and if duty drawback can be claimed on it by looking at the law and case citations.

Introduction

1. The Export and Import (EXIM) Policy introduced a new export promotion scheme called Special Economic Zone (SEZ) that came into force from April 1, 2000. It aimed at boosting foreign investments and expedited an internationally competitive and a hassle free atmosphere for exports. SEZ units in India operated from November 1, 2000 to February 9, 2006 under the provisions of the EXIM policy/Foreign Trade Policy and fiscal incentives were provided through the provisions of significant statutes. Five years later, the Special Economic Zone Act, 2005 was also introduced and in 2006 the Special Economic Zone Rules, 2006 were formulated through which various direct and indirect tax concessions had been granted for authorized operations to the SEZ units. The most significant feature of this scheme is that the SEZ area is considered essentially as a deemed foreign territory (within India) for the purposes of trade operations, duties & tariffs. Therefore, goods supplied to SEZ from the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) are treated as deemed exports and goods brought from SEZ to DTA are treated as deemed imports in this context. The SEZ areas have fiscal and economic laws that are additionally generous as compared to the business undertakings in the DTAs. Confusion often arises as to the scope of the exemptions. One of them is regarding applicability of drawback on goods sold by SEZ to DTA for the purpose of inputs for manufacture of export goods.

Why the confusion?

2. A drawback is a rebate of duty chargeable on any imported materials or excisable materials used in manufacture or processing of goods that are manufactured in India and exported. This scheme of drawback had been introduced by the Ministry of Finance to ensure that the exported products are revenue neutral. The Central Government is empowered to grant duty drawback under sections 74 and 75 of the Customs Act, 1962. Under section 74 of the Customs Act, duty drawback to the extent of 98 per cent of the duty paid on imported goods can be claimed for re-export, provided the goods are re-exported within 2 years of payment of import duty. Under Section 75 of the Customs Act, duty drawback is provided on imported raw materials and inputs that have gone in production of goods for exports. Section 75 presents a heavy relief to such manufacturers-exporters. In State of U.P. v. Delhi Cloth Mills1 the Supreme Court defined a drawback as: "Drawback means the repayment of duties or taxes previously charged on commodities from which they are relieved on exportation. For example, in the customs laws of some countries an allowance is made by the Government upon the duties due on imported merchandise when the importer, instead of selling it within the country, re-exports it, and then the difference of duty is refunded, if already paid."

Intellectual property or information technology being an intangible asset if once put on a paper, cassette, diskettes or any other thing to supply the same, fall under the category of ‘excisable goods’ just like drawings, designs, manuals and technical materials - Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. CCE 2001 (128) ELT 21 (SC). Removal of unfinished unrefined goods because of marketable goods is liable to duty at the time of removal from the factory - Union of India v. J.G. Glass Industries Ltd. 1998 (97) ELT 5 (SC). Subsequent processing of refining/finishing has no relevance merely because of adding the value, but ultimately subject to the concerned Chapter Notes/Section Notes of the Tariff Heading.

Since a plant and machinery (being an immovable property) cannot be treated as marketable, it is not treated as an excisable goods because it is attached to the earth - Triveni Engg. & Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2000 (120) ELT 273 (SC) [in the same case, the Supreme Court has admitted the assembly operation as amounting to manufacture] but in light of the marketability concept, it was held that the plant and machinery assembled at site is not excisable good - CCE v. Virdi Bros. 2007 (207) ELT 321 (SC).

Since the definition of the term ‘manufacture’ given in section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 has been replaced by section 4 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, the existing Chapters of Central Excise Tariff Act have been governed by relevant Chapter Notes and Section Notes. The term ‘removal’ in terms of rules 4 and 5 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 is a legal fiction. Section Note of section XVI read with section notes 3 and 4 and heading No. 84.19 assumes ‘plant’ as an excisable commodity in terms of section 2(d ) and 2(f) of the 1944 Act. But because of the test of marketability, the CBEC Circular No. 53/2/98-CX, dated April 2, 1998 - 100 ELT T10 issued under section 27B, provides a great degree of relief to the assessee. While applying the order No. 58/1/2002-CX, dated January 15, 2002 (139) ELT - T34 of Triveni Engg. & Industries Ltd. (supra), it could be concluded that :—

u In case of piece-by-piece assembly/installation, involving equipments, pipes, tubes, insulation, ducting, etc. if the goods have been converted into an immovable property which could not be moved to the market as such, then assembly shall not amount to manufacture (for Chapters 84 and 85).

u Several goods like storage tanks, etc., having the height, could not be removed as such to the market and their dismantling creates waste and scrap, such storage tanks and other goods shall not be subject to levy.

u Assembly/fabrication of complete system creating a new commodity which is specified in the tariff and which is capable of being bought to the market for sale or purchase but temporarily installed for effective use shall be dutiable as per respective tariff headings as prescribed.

Duty on waste and scrap

3. For the same, there are 3 points :

u Whether it is an excisable good in terms of the relevant Chapter Notes or Section Notes;

u Whether it arises during the course of manufacturing process;

u Whether it is marketable, if not, then it is not called as an excisable commodity. Mere fetching a nominal value has no relevance.

Any waste and scrap arising from manufacture or mechanical working of input/raw materials (i.e., due to manufacturing process) is only liable to duty - Hindalco Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (144) ELT 339 (Trib. - Delhi) provided that the same shall be marketable. Scrap arising through dismantling of buildings, repair of machinery, etc., is not liable to duty - Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (144) ELT 555 (Trib. - Bang.), National Winder v. CCE 2002 (147) ELT 463 (Trib. - Delhi). However, scrap generated in workshop used for maintenance of plant other than old part or scrap generated by dismantling of used machinery shall be liable to pay duty - Budhewal Co-op. Sugar Mills Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (141) ELT 490 (Trib. - Delhi) but subject to fulfilment of other conditions. However, packing materials of inputs/raw materials could not be treated to be waste arising out of processing of the input for which credit has been taken - CCE v. West Coast Industrial Gases Ltd. 2003 (155) ELT 11 (SC).

4.4 Certain additional issues on which the Rangachary Committee has opined but which have not been covered in Circular No.1 4.4.1 Issue No.1- Whether hiring of new employees is a condition for eligibility to claim deduction under section 10AA?

4.4.1.1 BACKGROUND AND RANGACHARY COMMITTEE'S VIEWS - Post the introduction of the sunset clause of the erstwhile section 10A provisions in the Finance Act, 2010, STPI units are no longer eligible to claim any tax benefit. On the other hand, SEZ units in software development segment enjoy a 15 year tax holiday under the provisions of section 10AA. The revenue denies benefits of section 10AA in certain cases where old employees are transferred from STPI unit to SEZ unit, stating that there should be a certain percentage of new employees in the new SEZ units to enable the units the tax holiday benefit.This contention of revenue is widely opposed by the industry experts in the absence of specific provisions in the income-tax statute on this issue. The Rangachary Committee endorses the industry's view in this matter and advocates that in the absence of specific conditions on employing new employees, denial of deduction under this section by insisting upon the employment of new employees is unwarranted. The Committee also recommends the insertion of prospective amendment to the income-tax provisions to set the qualification criteria in this regard.

4.4.2 Issue No.2 - Reduction in tax holiday owing to absence of parity in treatment of the terms 'export turnover' and 'total turnover'.

4.4.2.1 BACKGROUND AND RANGACHARY COMMITTEE'S VIEWS - In the absence of a definition of the term 'total turnover', the revenue while computing export turnover, excludes freight and insurance charges, in view of the fact that a specific exclusion of such charges is mandated in the Income-tax Act but does not exclude the above expenses while computing the value of 'total turnover'. This results in the reduction of the tax holiday available to the IT companies. The Committee recommends that whenever certain items of expenses or receipts are removed from export turnover, the same items of expenses or receipts should also be removed from the total turnover to ensure parity between the numerator and denominator.

In case of the above two issues, the recommendations of the Rangachary Committee are supporting the industry's views and an absence of any clarification being offered in Circular No. 1 issued by the tax department on the above two matters shows that the department holds its stand iterated in the legal precedents on the above two issues.

Conclusion

5. On an overall basis, as far as the tax issues around the profit linked incentives are concerned, the department has subscribed to the recommendations of the Rangachary Committee in most of the cases. Issuance of relevant Circular No.1 evidences such reliance on the approach adopted by the Committee. Subsequently, Circular Nos. 2 and 3 were issued in the month of March this year. The ratios derived from the aforesaid Circulars were different from the recommendations of the Rangachary Committee and received a lot of adverse representations from the legal corners of the country. Therefore, last month, Circular No. 2 was withdrawn and Circular No. 3 stands modified. This has come up as a sigh of relief for the Indian IT industry, since most of the recommendations of the industry have been duly considered. Inclusive Part

5. The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

In Indo Rama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (219) ELT 122 (Bom.), the High Court held that the credit of duty paid on the goods or fuel used in the generation of electricity is available, provided the electricity is used for the manufacture of final product. The use of electricity must have nexus with goods manufactured in the factory.

5.1 Primary packing material - In Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 201 (Punj. & Har.), it was held that it is not a matter of dispute that chewing gum/bubble gums manufactured by the assessees are directly or primarily packed with the printed aluminium foils without tattoos. It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

Withdraw amendment denying depreciation on goodwill; or the amendment may be made prospective, and grandfathering be allowed for pre-existing goodwill The Government in the Finance Act 2021 made a far-reaching amendment of denying depreciation on goodwill. Though the amendment is slated to be effective prospectively, in substance it has the effect of denying depreciation on past transactions. Such retrospective amendments create hardship for taxpayers, and also impact the investment climate.

Also, denial of depreciation on purchased goodwill arising in non-tax neutral transactions (such as where the seller has paid appropriate tax on a slump sale or simpliciter sale of goodwill) is against the principle of tax neutrality.

Therefore, it is recommended that the amendment be withdrawn, or that specific kinds of goodwill (arising on a slump sale/simpliciter purchase) be allowed to be amortized over 4-5 years. Alternatively, the amendment may be made prospective, and pre-existing goodwill in the block of assets as on 1 April 2020 can be grandfathered.

4. Limitation of Interest Benefit – Section 94B

Section 94B provides a capping of 30% of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization ("EBITDA") on the interest deduction that can be claimed by an entity in respect of funds borrowed from non-resident associated enterprises ("AE").

(a)

In terms of sub-section (2) of section 94B, 'excess interest' is defined to mean an amount of total interest paid or payable in excess of 30% of EBITDA of the borrower, or interest paid or payable to AE for that previous year, whichever is less. Since the expression used in sub-section (2) is 'total interest', a question arises as to whether it would include only foreign interest, or both foreign and domestic interest, paid by the entity. If domestic interest is also to be included, then, it would result in a higher disallowance of foreign interest compared to the normal scenario where there is no domestic borrowing. Hence, it is recommended to clarify that interest may be restricted only to foreign AE interest and not total interest.

(b)

In the event of borrowing by an infrastructure company from outside India, it often happens that foreign lenders insist on a joint guarantee by a parent company and SPV for the project. In this regard, the current reading of section 94B provides that debt issued by a non-resident lender (being non-AE) to a resident subsidiary under the guarantee of a resident parent (being an AE) would be covered under the provision. Hence, limit on interest deduction leads to additional disallowance in the hands of subsidiary, even when the transaction is entered into with non-AE, thereby discouraging funding to such sectors from outside India, which does not appear to be in line with government's policy of attracting foreign funds for key debt-intensive sectors. Hence, it is recommended that the restriction be applicable only in the case of borrowing from AEs.

(c)

Furthermore, the infrastructure sector generally warrants high capital requirement, especially in the initial years. Hence, it is recommended that considering the sector-specific requirement, a higher limit (i.e. a higher percentage of EBITDA) ought to apply in case of infrastructure companies, at least in the first 8-10 years.

ABHAY DESAI

CA

Background

1. In industries like pharmaceuticals and agro-chemicals many times near-about expired goods, defective goods or damaged goods (for the sake of convenience let us say "defective goods") are sent again by various marketing depots (not registered under excise) for reprocessing. Usually it happens that the original goods have been manufactured by let us say factory A, B and C but the defective goods are returned to only one factory, let us say factory D for reprocessing. This is so because it will be impractical to send the defective goods for reprocessing to the very same factory which had manufactured the original goods due to logistical costs as well as difficulties in identifying them on one-to-one basis.

In such scenario, only document available will be copy of excise invoice issued by the original factory. Had the defective goods been returned to the same factory, manufacturer could have easily claimed CENVAT credit on the basis of originally issued invoice (as the excise invoice was issued by the same factory). However, here the case is different. Factory D wants to claim CENVAT credit of returned defective goods on the basis of excise invoice issued by other factories.

Critical Issues

2. Following critical issues arise in this set-up:

2.1 Whether CENVAT credit can be claimed by factory D when the invoices on the basis of which credit will be claimed has been issued by factory A, B and C ?

2.2 W.e.f. 11-07-2014, third proviso has been added to rule 4(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which provides that credit cannot be claimed after a period of six months from the date of issuance of any document (in our case excise invoice) on the basis of which credit is claimed. In our case, as we are dealing with near-expired or defective goods, in all likelihood excise invoice issued by original manufacturer would have been dated beyond statutory period of six months. Issue is whether the third proviso will apply to the present case ?

2.3 What are the procedures one needs to follow to claim the said credit ?

3. Legal Analysis

3.1 To answer the first question, i.e., whether factory D can avail CENVAT credit on the basis of invoices issued by factory A, B and C for defective goods which are received back, one has to refer to rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. Relevant extract is reproduced below for ready reference:

"Rule 16. Credit of duty on goods brought to the factory.—(1) Where any goods on which duty had been paid at the time of removal thereof are brought to any factory for being re-made, refined, re-conditioned or for any other reason, the assessee shall state the particulars of such receipt in his records and shall be entitled to take CENVAT credit of the duty paid as if such goods are received as inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and utilize this credit according to the said rules.

(2) If the process to which the goods are subjected before being removed does not amount to manufacture, the manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the CENVAT credit taken under sub-rule (1) and in any other case the manufacturer shall pay duty on goods received under sub-rule (1) at the rate applicable on the date of removal and on the value determined under sub-section (2) of section 3 or section 4 or section 4A of the Act, as the case may be.

[Explanation.—The amount paid under this sub-rule shall be allowed as CENVAT credit as if it was a duty paid by the manufacturer who removes the goods.]

3.2 Careful reading of above rule provides that CENVAT credit will be available of any goods on which duty has been paid and are brought to any factory for re-making, refining, re-conditioning or for any other reason as inputs. Thus, only condition to be fulfilled for claiming credit is that duty should have been paid on said goods. It is not necessary that goods should be received back in the same factory. It can be received in any factory. Further, goods can be brought back for reprocessing under rule 16 even if shelf life has expired (CCE v. Rako Agrochem (P.) Ltd. 2010 (260) ELT 479 (Trib. - Delhi)). Thus, credit can be claimed of goods received by factory D on the basis of invoices issued by original manufacturers. One may also refer to Board's Circular 607/44/2001-CX, dated 13-12-2001 which confirms the above view. Thus, CENVAT credit can be claimed on basis of manufacturers invoice available with depot to the extent of quantity received by factory D.

3.1 Whether amendment to rule 3(5B) of the CCR, 2004 has a retrospective impact? - Rule 3(5B) of the CCR, 2004 as amended vide Notification No. 3/2011 C.E. (N.T.) with effect from 1 March, 2011 provides for reversal of the CENVAT credit even when inputs are partially written off or provision for partial write-off is made.

3.2 Whether semi-finished and finished goods are covered? - Inputs and capital goods have been defined under rule 2(k) and rule 2(a) respectively, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. With respect to applicability of rule 3(5B) to WIP/FG, clarification has been issued by the CBEC vide Circular No. 907/27/2009-CX. As per the circular, if the goods have been manufactured a manufacturer is liable to pay excise duty, unless duty is remitted under rule 21. Therefore, if the value of finished goods is written off, the manufacturer would be liable to pay excise duty or he would be required to reverse the credit on the inputs used, if duty has been remitted on finished goods.

As regards writing off work-in-progress (WIP), it is stated that if the WIP has reached the stage, when it can be considered as manufactured goods, in that case, the same treatment as is applicable to finished goods will be applicable. However, if the activity carried out on the WIP goods cannot be considered as amounting to manufacture, the said goods should be considered as inputs and the treatment for reversal of credit applicable to inputs would be applicable.

Rule 3(5) of the CCR, 2004 provides that if the inputs or capital goods on which CEVNAT credit is taken are removed as such, the CENVAT credit so taken has to be reversed.

Alternatively, where inputs are used in the manufacturing process and are removed as manufactured scrap, the company shall pay applicable excise duty and CENVAT shall not be reversed.

3.3 Whether write down of Inventory as per AS-2 attracts rule 3(5B)? - Write down in common business parlance represents restating the value with a lower amount, while write off generally results in permanent 'de-recognizing' or bringing down to Zero or negligible amount with no intention of writing back; unless situation otherwise warrants, write down is temporary reduction in value. On the other hand, in the case of provision, it is shown as a deduction from gross amount in the books of account. While rule 3(5B) covers write off provision, write down is not covered within the scope.

The option to avail concessional rate of tax as per the aforesaid sections is available from FY 2019-20 onwards and should be exercised before the due date of filing tax return of the year from which such option is exercised. A company not opting for the beneficial provisions due to its existing tax exemptions/deductions, can avail the option for beneficial provisions in the future; however, such option once exercised cannot be revoked in subsequent years. The take-it-or-leave-it nature of the above sections provide flexibility for any company to understand, analyse and then choose to exercise the option to adopt such beneficial provisions. The beneficial provisions provide a further tax rate reduction of approximately 4 percent for those companies having turnover below INR400 crores for specified years and currently paying tax at 29.12 percent.

Key considerations before opting for beneficial rate of taxation:

In view of the irrevocable nature of beneficial sections, it becomes important that a company before opting for such beneficial sections, undertakes a detailed cost-benefit analysis while considering various factors which include the following:

1.

Brought forward of losses attributable to exemption/deduction provisions: Such losses shall not be allowed to be set-off if the company opts for the beneficial sections. Hence, the company should factor in the impact of such brought forward losses.

2.

It is to be noted that brought forward losses not attributable to the specified deduction/exemption denied would be allowed to be set-off in the future.

3.

Unutilised MAT credit/s 115JAA: At present, in the absence of any corresponding amendment to section 115JAA regarding the MAT credit, it is not clear that a company which opts for the beneficial sections, would get the credit of unutilised MAT or not. This requires further clarifications and alternate views in this regard cannot be ruled out.

4.

Alternative incentives/exemptions currently available under other sections: A company fulfilling certain conditions can avail benefits under section 10AA, 80-IAC, 80-IBA, 80PA etc. The benefits devolved under these sections range as high as exempting entire profits from tax for a certain number of years. Such continuing/possible benefits should be factored in the decision-making.

5.

Also important to note that exemption available under section 10 for example 10(2A), 10(38), 10(34) can be claimed by the company availing the benefit of sections 115BAA/115BAB.

6.

Similarly restriction under chapter VI-A is applicable only to sections covered under "C –deduction in respect of certain income" (Section 80HH to section 80RRB (except section 80JJA with respect to employment of new employees)

7.

Exemptions associated with Research & Development (R&D) and/or sums paid to specified entities for research: Companies incurring or planning to incur such expenditure would want to weigh in the benefits under section 35(1)(ii) or (iia) or (iii) or section 35(2AA) or section 35(2AB), before considering to opt for beneficial sections.

8.

The above restriction is with respect to accelerated deduction under specific sections. In other words there is no bar in claiming such expenditure which is otherwise allowable, under any other section of the Act.

9.

Proposed expansion of the company: Many companies operate in an industry that require heavy investment in assets like plant and machinery. Here, it is important to analyse the beneficial provisions relating to additional depreciation and investment allowance embedded in the current tax regime before opting for beneficial sections. Further, a company having any plans of setting up a new manufacturing unit altogether, should consider the possibility of opting for section 115BAB.

10.

It is important to note that there is no bar in opting out for beneficial sections in subsequent years once the exemptions/deductions/loss is exhausted.

11.

Commencement of production before 31 March 2023 - A one-time window?: Generally manufacturing companies experience a time lag of 1-3 years from the date of incorporation to the date of commencement of manufacturing. Considering this, businesses looking forward to set up a new manufacturing company should take a timely call on whether to avail the beneficial section 115BAB for which manufacturing is required to commence by 31 March 2023. However, we have seen governments extending the duration of such sunset clauses in public interest.

Conclusion

The government has provided the option to companies to opt for newly inserted sections. However, one need to be very careful while making cost benefit analysis on the basis of factors discussed above It may happen that postponement of decision to opt for these newly inserted section for one year, may not cost as much as the wrong decision of opting for the same, since it is reversible in nature.

Such a bold step to slash the tax rates is likely to provide a boost in the cash flows and the eventual earning per share of many companies. It may also increase inbound investment into India, resulting in a favourable balance of payments situation or may also result in postponement/cancel of outbound investment.

However, while the amendments are aimed to provide a boost to the ambitious Make-in-India initiative, the government has estimated INR 1,45,000 crore as the total revenue foregone in tax and other reliefs.

Introduction

1. In September 2014 as part of a wider set of nation-building initiatives, the Central Government had launched a programme called as 'Make in India', to market India's image as a global manufacturing and export hub. For the said goal to be achieved, the first and foremost important thing would be to have Economic, Tax, etc., policies guiding and motivating the interests of business organizations. It is further an endeavour of all the Ministries of the Central Government that their policy framework shall be in complete synchronization with one another towards achieving the common goal and to ensure "Ease of Doing Business" in India. In present article, we will address one such issue wherein there appears to be conflict of policy and a tussle between two Ministries of the Central Government.

Chapter 7 of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015-20 ('FTP') issued by the Ministry of Commerce enlists various supplies which are considered as deemed exports and prescribes incentives for the domestic manufacturers carrying out such deemed exports. One of such supplier is supplying intermediate goods against an Advance Authorization. The benefits available for effecting such deemed export as enlisted in Para 7.03 of FTP are as under:

(a)

Refund of Terminal Excise Duty, if exemption is not available

(b)

Refund of duty by way of Deemed Export Drawback

(c)

Availing of the benefit of Advance Intermediate Authorization.

Similar provisions also existed in the erstwhile Foreign Trade Policy, 2009-14. However, vide Policy Circular No. 16, dated 15-3-2013, the DGFT had clarified that the benefit of deemed export in the form of "Terminal Excise Duty" shall not be available in respect of supplies which are entitled to an ab-initio exemption. It is to be noted that the above referred to Public Notice was challenged before various High Courts on ground of being unconstitutional and was later on was quashed for being unconstitutional and in contradiction to the Foreign Trade Policy, 2009-14.

The intent behind the Policy Circular dated 15-3-2013, was to ensure that the refund of excise duty collected by the Ministry of Finance, shall not be granted by DGFT. Hence, the aforesaid policy circular was specifically incorporated in the FTP by introducing Para 7.05 which had specifically denied the benefit of "Terminal Excise Duty" in respect of supplies entitled to an ab initio exemption.

An example

2. Now let us assume a situation where the supplies against an Advance Authorization are entitled to ab inito exemption under Notification No. 44/01-C.E-(N.T). As per Para 7.05 of FTP, a domestic supplier carrying out deemed exports cannot opt for availing of the benefit of Terminal Excise Duty for supplying of goods against an Advance Authorization and has to compulsorily clear the goods without payment of duty by availing of the benefit of exemption notification in force.

However, considering the fact that the domestic supplier is availing of the benefit of Notification No. 44/2001-C.E-(N.T) for effecting the exempted clearances, it is also required to reverse the proportionate CENVAT credit as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 inasmuch as the inputs/input services commonly received are also used in the manufacture of exempted goods which are cleared by availing of the benefit of Notification No. 44/01-C.E-(N.T). Moreover, the domestic supplier would also not be entitled for availing of the CENVAT credit of duty suffered on the inputs exclusively used in the manufacture of exempted goods which are supplied against an Advance Authorization as per provisions of rule 6(1).

Rule 6 issues under the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004

Rule 6(6) has prescribed certain supplies, wherein reversal of the CENVAT credit will not apply even if the goods are cleared without payment of duty. Rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 covers all such supplies which are qualifying as deemed exports and also entitled to avail of the benefit of ab initio exemption, viz., supply to an EOU, supply to an ICB, etc., which are also covered by Para 7.05 of FTP, except supplies against an Advance Authorization.

SPECIAL SCENARIOS TO WATCH

Inter-Unit Transfers Allowed- Goods can be transferred from one MOOWR unit to another.

Scrap/waste disposal in the domestic market attracts duty; it's waived if exported.

Goods received from SEZs or FTWZs are treated as imports and must follow bonding formalities. Inputs received free of cost must be declared at nominal value and properly recorded.

Goods returning from testing or repairs should be handled as fresh imports or DTA inputs.

CHALLENGES AND FUTURE UNCERTAINTY

While MOOWR is a beneficial scheme, these challenges are hindering its performance.

Complex compliance: Filing multiple BOEs for each DTA sale is time-consuming and complex.

No depreciation is allowed when capital goods are sold in the domestic market—duty is on full import value.

No RODTEP or Drawback: MOOWR-based exports are less competitive given they are not eligible for RODTEP scrips or Drawback. Typically benefits RODTEP and Drawback would be in the range of 4-5% of the value of exported good, which is significant for a lot of exporters.

New concern: The Finance Act 2024 empowered the Government of India to exclude certain goods or operations from the applicability of MOOWR scheme. This adds unpredictability, making long-term planning difficult for businesses relying on this scheme and creating an unease in doing business.

Takeaways

If you are importing raw materials or machinery regularly, consider obtaining a MOOWR license.

Be prepared for higher compliance costs.

Evaluate if loss of RODTEP/Drawback is offset by duty deferment benefits.

MOOWR is one of the most flexible and cash-flow-friendly customs schemes available in India. It's ideal for businesses that import raw material or machinery and sell their finished goods either in domestic market or export market.

Small and Mid-sized manufacturers initially hesitate to register under MOOWR because of compliance worries. But once they set up the systems, the cash flow benefits are too significant to ignore.

CCE 2012 (285) ELT 274 (Tri. - Ahd.) - The Tribunal found that it was not in dispute that the H.R. coils received by the appellant were exclusively used for manufacturing of MS pipes by availing of exemption Notification No. 6/2002-CE, as amended. It was also undisputed that the appellant had maintained the separate records and also had availed the CENVAT credit of the duty paid on said inputs. Rule 6(1) provides that CENVAT credit shall not be allowed on the quantity of input which is used for the manufacture of exempted goods. The appellants contended that they had not maintained separate accounts asmuchas they had reversed an amount of the 8% of the value of the exempted goods which contention would not hold any water inasmuch as there was nothing on record to show that there was use of the H.R. Coils for dutiable products. An attempt was made by the appellants that they had cleared that MS scrap arising out of utilization of such HR Coils was on payment of duty. By any stretch of imagination, scrap could not be considered as a manufactured product, at least in the case in hand before us. The Tribunal also found that General Manager of the appellant had clearly and categorically stated that the HR Coils which were received by them were used only for the purpose of manufacturing of pipes which were cleared without payment of duty. This being the factual matrix the Tribunal found that the appellant could not claim the benefit of Rule 6(3) by debiting the amount equivalent to 8% of the value of the exempted goods and avail CENVAT credit on the H.R. Coils received by them. On merits the Tribunal did not find any case in favour of the assessee.

6.4-3 In Unn Sugar Complex v. CCE 2013 (293) ELT 236 (Tri. - Delhi) - The appellant manufactured sugar and molasses chargeable to Central Excise duty. They availed CENVAT credit of excise duty paid on inputs. In course of manufacture of sugar during crushing of sugar cane by produce/waste - bagasse emerged. The Department was of the view that since the appellant had not maintained separate accounts and inventory of the inputs used in or in relation to manufacture of dutiable final products - sugar and molasses and exempted final product - bagasse, in accordance with the provisions of Rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, they would be required to pay an amount equal to 8% of the sale value of the bagasse. The Additional Commissioner confirmed the demand with interest and also imposed penalty. The first Adjudicating Authority confirmed the same. The Tribunal held that by no stretch of imagination it could be said that the assessee possibly could have maintained separate accounts for the inputs for the production of sugar and molasses (excisable items) and bagasse. The assessee was liable to pay amount equal to 8% of the sale value of bagasse and confirmed the order.

6.5 Statutory requirement

6.5-1 In Hero Motocorp Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (285) ELT 218 (Tri. - Delhi) - The Tribunal held that on bare reading of Rule 2(k) it was clear that 'input' meant and included accessories of final product cleared along with final product. Rule 138(4)(b) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1989 made it incumbent on driver of every vehicle to carry the tool kit prescribed by the manufacturer. Since carrying of the tool kit in the vehicle was obligatory for the driver, it could be safely inferred that tool kit was necessary accessory of the motor vehicle because driving of the vehicle without those accessories would be violative of Rule 138(4)(b) of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989. Thus, the Tribunal was of the view that the appellants had supplied the tool kit as per the statutory requirements under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 as accessories to be used in relation to the manufacture of vehicle. Thus 'tool kit' was squarely covered by the definition of 'input' under Rule 2(k)(i) of the CENVAT credit Rules and that the appellants had rightly availed of the CENVAT credit in relation to tool kit.

Keeping software development out of the ambit of manufacturing is also disconcerting since over the years, various Courts/Tribunals have held software development activity to be manufacturing under various provisions of the Act. Cenvat credit relating to service provided at the residential colony outside the assessee’s factory 5.4 In the case of CCE v. Manikgarh Cement Works [2010] 24 STT 1 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee availed the Cenvat credit of service tax paid on (a) construction service, (b) repair and maintenance service, (c) manpower recruitment service, and (d) cleaning service, all of which were provided by the respective service providers at the residential colony outside the assessee’s factory. The employees of the assessee reside in the said colony. The residential buildings were constructed, old residential buildings were repaired and maintained, security guards for the colony were recruited by a manpower recruiting agency and the residential premises was cleaned by another agency. The adjudicating authority held the said services to be outside the purview of the definition of ‘input service’ given under rule 2(l) and, accordingly, disallowed the Cenvat credit to the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the Cenvat credit.

On appeal, the Tribunal held as under :

u The Supreme Court in the case of Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54 has considered the definition of ‘input’ given under rule 2(k) to be divisible into three parts; (1) specific part (main or substantive part); (2) inclusive part; (3) place of use and laid down an important ruling to the effect that, where the inclusive part of a definition provides a list of items, any such item should also satisfy the quintessential ingredients of the main part of the definition. In other words, the definition has to be considered in its entirety. The inclusive part is not independent of the main part. It is not a ‘stand-alone’ provision. This ruling is applicable to the definition of ‘input service’, given under rule 2(l). There is nothing in the said definition to indicate that the legislative intent behind it is different from the one underlying the definition of ‘input’. Accordingly, any service which is apparently covered by the parameters of the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ should also satisfy the quintessential requirements of the main part of the definition and, accordingly, any person claiming the benefit of Cenvat credit on input service in terms of the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ should establish that such service was used, directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of his final products or the clearance of such products from his factory.

u The assessee had sought to distinguish the decision of the Supreme Court rendered in the case of Maruti Suzuki Ltd. (supra) from the decision of the Bombay High Court rendered in the case of Coca Cola India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 130, wherein the Court examined the scope of the definition of ‘input service’ given in section 2(1) and argued that the Supreme Court’s decision relating to ‘input’ could not be applied to ‘input service’. The argument was not acceptable whether it be input or input service. The main part of the definition contains the quintessential ingredients and the inclusive part provides a non-exhaustive list of items each of which should satisfy the requirements of the main part. The assessee had pointed out that, in the case of definition of ‘input’, ‘place of use’ was the third part of the definition, which was conspicuously absent in the definition of ‘input service’. It had been argued that an input service need not necessarily be rendered within the factory premises whereas an input should normally be used within the factory. Broadly, this distinction sounds valid. But, again, it does not offer an answer to the question whether the service (which is rendered within the factory or outside) satisfies other essential requirements laid down in the main part of the definition. Even if it be held that there is no ‘place of use’ in relation to input service, the basic requirement remains to be that anything mentioned as an input service in the inclusive part of the definition should be shown to have been used in or in relation to the manufacture or clearance of final products, whether directly or indirectly.

u Accordingly, as the assessee had not established nexus between any of the four services and the manufacture or clearance of excisable goods, the benefit of Cenvat credit in respect of such services could not be allowed. However, in a case of this nature, the assessee should not be penalized. The instant case involves rival interpretations of a provision of law. In typical cases of interpretative nature, penalties have been waived by the Tribunal. In this view of the matter, the order-in-original was sustained except in respect of penalty imposed by the original authority.

Rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 covers all such supplies which are qualifying as deemed exports and also entitled to avail of the benefit of ab initio exemption, viz., supply to an EOU, supply to an ICB, etc., which are also covered by Para 7.05 of FTP, except supplies against an Advance Authorization. Therefore, effectively a domestic supplier supplying goods against an Advance Authorization would be liable to reverse the CENVAT credit in accordance with the rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, with respect to inputs and input services consumed commonly in the manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods which was/is never the intention of the Legislature. Further, said intention can also be evidenced from the provisions of rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and, hence, the corresponding rule has not been taken to logical conclusion by the Legislature.

Having said above, now the supplier is left with no economically viable option but to avail of the benefit of "Deemed Export Drawback" and avail of the refund of duties suffered on the input and input services used in relation to manufacture of goods supplied against Advance Authorization. Further, the process of deemed export drawback is complicated inasmuch as the supplier has to produce all the duty paying documents to the satisfaction of DGFT for fixation of Brand Rate of duty drawback.

Alternatively, an assessee may prefer to avail of the benefit of "Advance Intermediate Authorization" for procuring inputs without payment of duty. However, in such situation, it will have to carry out double compliance in the form of "Deemed Export Drawback" in respect of the service tax paid on the input services which are used in manufacture of goods supplied against Advance Authorization and also the compliance for obtaining and closure of "Advance Intermediate Authorization".

Therefore, effectively on account of lack of clarity in policies between the two Ministries of the Central Government, a manufacturer in India would have to unnecessarily carry out either double compliances or incur excessive cost to avail of the refund of duties, which could have been easily granted exemption from reversal under rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Further, such escalated cost and tiresome compliance would also effect the interest and efficiency of the business and pose a direct contradiction to the very intention of the Central Governments programme of 'Make in India' or 'Ease of Doing Business'.

Conclusion

4. In order to promote the "Make in India" initiative a uniform, unambiguous, stable and effective policy framework has to be established which will reduce the unwarranted cost of business in relation to compliances and ensure seamless benefit to the assessee as outlined in the respective policy. Eventually, making the manufacturing in India a profitable venture.

In the present case, considering the issue faced by the industry at large in respect of supplies against an Advance Authorization discussed hereinabove, it is expected that an appropriate amendment to rule 6(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 should be carried out to incorporate another sub-clause to cover supply against an Advance Authorization which would simplify the process for the domestic manufacturer. Alternatively, supply against an Advance Authorization shall be allowed to avail of the benefit of Terminal Excise Duty under the erstwhile FTP, 2009-14.
